The county’s resolution is set to expire Dec. 31, but at Monday’s legislature meeting, lawmakers introduced a resolution to extend the policy through noon on Jan. 20, 2029, which would mark the inauguration of the next president.

“Albany County was in the lead on this issue,” Kuhn said. “We took the initiative with a resolution that was designed to protect public safety, preserve county taxpayer resources and discourage mass ICE operations in our community.”

But the county resolution does not apply to city or state property within Albany County. Immigrant rights advocates have claimed that ICE has used public lots in the city of Albany as staging grounds for its operations, but the Times Union has not been able to verify those accounts.

A spokesperson for Albany Mayor Dorcey Applyrs said in a statement that the mayor is “committed to protecting the safety and dignity of all residents as it relates to ICE activity,” adding that the city continues to work with local partners to “strengthen city policies that expand protections for all residents.”

Albany Common Councilmember Tom Hoey, who represents District 15 and chairs the Public Safety Committee, said he would need to discuss the matter with Albany Police Chief Brendan Cox and the greater Common Council.

Common Councilmember Alfredo Balarin, who represents District 11, said he would support a move to adopt legislation similar to that of the county, placing additional guardrails to prevent ICE from using city property as a staging ground for operations. He said he has heard from concerned constituents about the federal agency conducting arrests in his district, particularly on the boundary of Central Avenue. He believes legislation would receive strong support from the body.

“Unfortunately, this is an issue residents are concerned with,” Balarin said. “We are limited in what we can do at the local level, but that doesn’t mean we can’t do anything. Making clear that our city property shouldn’t be used for these initiatives is something we should definitely push forward with.”

WASHINGTON (OSV News) — In the aftermath of Republicans losing control of both chambers of Congress in a Democratic landslide, President Donald Trump suggested he was open to working with Democrats on immigration policy, before his administration indicated its deportation policy would continue.

Initial exit polls of 2026 midterm voters conducted by NBC News in coordination with a group of other news organizations found 57% of voters said Trump’s immigration enforcement actions have gone too far.

In an interview on the CBS News program “60 Minutes” that aired Nov. 8, Trump appeared to acknowledge that data, saying the results suggested his administration’s immigration crackdown was “too tough” and that he could “work something out” with Democrats when they take control of Congress.

“I think ultimately that hurt me,” Trump said on immigration, adding, “I think it both helped and hurt. I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out. But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that — that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.”

Trump leans into hardline deportation policy and elevates its architects

The interview was taped on the morning of Nov. 6. Hours later, Trump named Stephen Miller, previously his deputy chief of staff and senior policy adviser, as his new White House chief of staff after the departure of Susie Wiles. Miller is seen as a key architect of many of the Trump administration’s immigration policies.

On Nov. 9, Trump told reporters at the White House, “There won’t be amnesty.”

“Somebody suggested, ‘Will there be amnesty?’ No, but — they came in. They knew the law,” he said.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a Nov. 10 post on X, “Amnesty will NEVER be on the table.”

Kevin Appleby, senior fellow for policy and communications at the Center for Migration Studies of New York and the former director of migration policy for the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, told OSV News, “It’s important to note what policies the administration are implementing, not what the president says, to measure where they are on immigration.”

According to the Migration Policy Institute’s “Fact Sheet” report from October, domestic immigration-related arrests rose from 8,000 per month in the first three months of Trump’s term to 19,000 per month from May through July 2026. Of those deported by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, 61% had been in the U.S. at least two years and 15% had lived in the U.S. 10 years or more. Of these immigrants, 71% had never been convicted of a crime, and 61% of those in the U.S. 10 years or more had no criminal convictions.

Catholics impacted directly by mass deportation

A joint report issued last year by the USCCB’s Migration and Refugee Services, the Center for the Study of Global Christianity at Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary, and World Relief, found that more than 10 million Christians living in the U.S. would be vulnerable to deportation under Trump administration policies implemented in 2025. A majority of them — 61% — were Catholic followed by a sizable number of evangelicals.

It also found more than 1 in 6 Catholics are either vulnerable to deportation themselves or could see a family member deported, barring law or policy changes.

“I don’t think there can be a real bipartisan conversation on immigration reform until the administration shows it has changed its approach and moderated its enforcement tactics, consistent with the protection of human dignity,” Appleby said.

Catholic social teaching on immigration balances three interrelated principles: the right of persons to migrate in order to sustain their lives and those of their families, the right of a country to regulate its borders and control immigration, and a nation’s duty to regulate its borders with justice and mercy.

Church’s voice needed in the immigration discourse

Dylan Corbett, executive director of the Hope Border Institute, a group that works to apply the perspective of Catholic social teaching in policy and practice to the U.S.-Mexico border region, told OSV News, “Even President Trump recognizes that an exclusively enforcement-driven approach to immigration remains fundamentally counterproductive and unsustainable.”

“He now possesses a pivotal opportunity to foster broad consensus by pairing meaningful legalization with addressing our nation’s critical labor needs — expanding lawful pathways for Dreamers, caregivers, and long-standing community members who have contributed to the fabric of our society for years, if not decades,” Corbett said. “A policy centered on mass deportation is not only morally indefensible and economically harmful, but also a demonstrable political liability. Now is the defining moment to champion substantive reform and for the Church to uphold the moral imperative at the heart of this discourse.”

Catholics, Appleby said, “should certainly engage the debate, but not be caught up in a race to the bottom, where we wind up with legislation which is more damaging than beneficial.”

“In other words, we must enter the dialogue with eyes wide open and not compromise our principles,” he said. “I expect that the next two years will set the parameters for the reform debate, which will happen under a new administration.”

US bishops call for Haitians to be shielded from mass deportation

Among the Trump administration immigration policies the U.S. bishops have criticized is its termination of Temporary Protected Status for Haiti earlier this year and subsequent mass deportations of Haitian nationals.

Temporary Protected Status grants the U.S. government the power to shield eligible migrants from deportation if they are from countries experiencing dangerous conditions such as war, disaster, or other unrest. The Trump administration has sought to end TPS for several countries, notably Haiti, which is racked by extreme levels of gang violence, but it also recently granted an extension to migrants from El Salvador.

In a Nov. 10 letter to members of the U.S. Senate, Bishop Brendan J. Cahill of Joliet, Illinois, chair of the USCCB’s Committee on Migration, and Bishop A. Elias Zaidan of the Maronite Eparchy of Our Lady of Lebanon, chair of its Committee on International Justice and Peace, reiterated the conference’s previous call for the extension of Haiti’s TPS status, writing, “We pray that, in its remaining weeks, the current Congress, along with the incoming 120th Congress, will devote more attention to the situation facing both Haitian families in the United States, especially those who have recently been stripped of their legal protections, and the human tragedies unfolding in Haiti itself.”

BIDDEFORD, Maine (WGME) -- The ICE agent accused of shooting and killing a young father in Biddeford had a record of workplace problems, alleged domestic abuse and mental health issues, according to the New York Times.

At least four gunshots went through the windshield of a car, and Guerrero died at the scene.

The Department of Homeland Security said the vehicle tried to flee and that Brouillette fired because he feared for public safety.

In July, Ashley Brouillette, an ex-wife of Brouillette, spoke with CNN, and claimed her ex called her after the shooting and admitted to being the agent who shot Guerrero. She said he told her it was "justified" and done in self-defense.

Guerrero’s family said they shot and killed an innocent man who was in the country legally and had been issued a work permit and a Social Security number. Guerrero was a father to a young daughter, and his wife, Karolina Rojas Alvarez, said she and her husband dreamed of a long life together. He used to say until they were ‘little old people.’

According to the New York Times, Brouillette had a record of workplace problems, alleged domestic abuse and mental health issues. The article also detailed anti-immigrant and anti-Colombian comments Brouillette made in emails to relatives in 2021.

Brouillette’s sister shared emails with the New York Times in which he reportedly disparaged her Colombian partner, who was living legally in the United States, telling her that her partner could take "his non-citizen a** back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries."

Brouillette also told his sister that she was, “Dead to me. DEAD,” and her partner’s “bloodline” did not understand the value of American freedom.

His mother told the Times that he was dangerous and urged people to believe his alleged victims. His former wives accused him of physical abuse in court filings; he disputed those claims. His mother also said he had been diagnosed with bipolar disorder and hospitalized multiple times.

The article said Brouillette joined ICE in December 2025 during a major hiring surge, when the agency had reportedly relaxed parts of its vetting process.

According to the Times, he was cleared to start before the agency had reviewed his full background report, which remained in a backlog at the time of the shooting. He also skipped ICE’s full training course, completing a shorter online program because of prior law enforcement experience, according to the Times.

A DHS spokesperson responded to the report, saying in part:

"Incoming ICE officers, many already with years of law enforcement experience, are onboarded in accordance with applicable policies and standards. Any claims of substandard training or vetting are FALSE. This administration is preserving ICE’s reputation as one of the most elite law enforcement agencies not only in the U.S., but the entire world.

ICE maintains rigorous standards for all personnel. We ensure that every applicant is thoroughly assessed through mandatory pre-employment vetting protocols. All federal personnel must be found suitable for employment in accordance with 5 CFR Part 731 and, for those occupying national security positions, must be eligible based on Security Executive Agent Directive (SEAD) 4 guidelines and Executive Order 12968, as amended.

ICE continues to actively recruit and onboard personnel to ensure the agency reaches authorized staffing levels, accounting for natural attrition and retirements. While we saw a successful hiring surge last year made possible by President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill, our efforts to fill these positions in fulfillment of the President’s mandate continue.

Officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics. ICE law enforcement officers are trained to use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve dangerous situations to prioritize the safety of the public and our officers."

When asked specifically about Brouillette's training and conduct, DHS said it "does not comment on matters regarding personnel who are no longer with the agency."

According to military records, Brouillette served in the Maine National Guard from 2007 to 2010 as a quartermaster and chemical equipment repairer. He received an honorable discharge with the rank of private first class.

He then enlisted in the U.S. Army, where a spokesperson confirmed he served from 2010 to 2015 as a human intelligence collector. During his military service, Brouillette completed a nine-month deployment to Afghanistan and left the Army with the rank of sergeant.

Also read: 'My daughter asks for Papa': Family of Maine man killed by ICE agent speaks to media

After leaving active duty, state employment records show Brouillette was hired as a corrections officer at the Maine Correctional Center in Windham in 2015. Records indicate he resigned approximately one year later.

In 2019, Brouillette joined the Maine Department of Health and Human Services as a human services enforcement agent with the Division of Support Enforcement Recovery. A department spokesperson confirmed he resigned voluntarily after a little more than seven months.

The CBS13 I-Team also confirmed Brouillette served as a volunteer firefighter with the Manchester Fire Department for about a year. Town officials said he left the department for undisclosed medical reasons in 2024.

According to the Times, a former volunteer fire chief called Brouillette a “loose cannon” and described an incident in which Brouillette, after a training injury, allegedly yelled and threatened to punch him.

Brouillette later sued the college where the injury occurred, saying it affected his memory and cognitive abilities; the case was settled, according to the Times.

Court records also indicate Brouillette worked as a federal police officer at the Togus VA Medical Center.

State licensing records show Brouillette was also licensed as a Maine real estate agent for a period of time before that license ended last year.

Also read: ICE agent who allegedly killed man in Maine had military background, past government jobs

He was also let go from a pest control job over behavioral issues, according to the Times.

A review of Maine criminal court records found Brouillette has no criminal record in the state other than a traffic violation from about a decade ago.

The I-Team also obtained hundreds of pages of civil and family court records, which include allegations of domestic violence made by former partners. Court records show petitions seeking protection from abuse orders were either denied or later dismissed. None of those cases resulted in criminal convictions.

Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey’s office is investigating the shooting, as is the DHS inspector general.

The Times reports that cooperation between federal and state investigators has been limited.

The Times also noted that any racial bias could be relevant to an excessive-force inquiry, though federal prosecutors do not have to prove racial animus to bring such a case.

Benjamin Gideon, the attorney representing Guerrero’s wife, released a statement following the Times’ report, saying in part:

“It is appalling that our government handed David Brouillette a badge and a gun. Mr. Brouillette's threats, rage, and instability, have been covered in previous reporting. Liz Emen is the fourth member of Mr. Brouillette’s immediately family to state that he was unfit to work in law enforcement in any capacity, something a local Maine police department figured out when they turned him down for a job for ‘too many red flags.’

Today’s report adds to the long list of Mr. Brouillette’s disqualifying conduct open hostility toward immigrants, generally, and toward people from Colombia, specifically. Any reasonable background investigation would have uncovered who this man was and sent him home. Instead, the New York Times ‘could not find any employer or family member’ who was contacted about Mr. Brouillette before he was ‘fast-tracked’ for hire during a surge in which ICE lowered standards to rush new recruits out onto our streets. ICE then put Mr. Brouillette on the street without sending him to the standard ICE training course, which would have trained him on, among other things, the standards that govern use of deadly force and shooting into moving vehicles.

David Brouillette is the poster child for what happens when our government chooses to recruit agents to carry out a campaign of hate against immigrants, hires those agents without adequate screening and places them on the street without basic training. Johan Sebastián’s death was not an inevitable accident. It was a natural and predictable choices of the policies of our government and its political leadership.”

According to Gideon, the federal government has yet to tell Guerrero’s family if Brouillette has been disciplined, whether anyone who hired, trained, or supervised him has been held accountable, or what any federal investigation has found.

Congresswoman Chellie Pingree is also responding to the Times' report, saying part:

"ICE handed David Brouillette a gun and sent him into Maine communities before anyone at the agency had reviewed his background check. The agency restricted his access to certain computer systems because he had not been fully cleared, yet apparently saw no problem trusting him with the power to take someone’s life. That is an unconscionable betrayal of the public’s trust.

I have demanded answers from DHS about training and background checks in the days following Johan Sebastián’s death. This reporting makes a full, independent investigation even more urgent. DHS must release Brouillette’s hiring, vetting, training, and deployment records and cooperate fully with independent investigators.

ICE must be abolished and that is what I will continue to fight for. But perfect can’t get in the way of better. Until we can abolish ICE, this agency needs serious, immediate reforms. I am working on legislation to ensure federal agents are never armed and deployed into our streets without being fully vetted. Our communities’ safety cannot depend on whether this administration finds basic safeguards convenient."

Senator-elect Troy Jackson issued a statement as well:

"Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero should still be alive. ICE put an armed officer on Maine’s streets without fully reviewing his background. Now we’re learning about his disturbing history of anti-immigrant hatred. His family deserves answers and justice. Those responsible must be held accountable. ICE must be abolished. This is exactly why."

Governor-elect Hannah Pingree issued a statement, saying in part:

"[Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero'] family and the people of Maine deserve justice and a full accounting. I look forward to the results of the Maine Attorney General’s independent investigation into this shameful use of deadly force. As Governor, I will ensure there is no state cooperation that aids ICE operations in our communities and work with our federal delegation to demand answers from the Trump Administration about ICE’s appalling hiring and training practices. I have long believed that ICE must be abolished, and this tragedy underscores why. Maine families deserve to be safe in our own neighborhoods."

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement made five arrests Tuesday throughout San Mateo County, according to the county's Rapid Response Hotline and Office of Community Affairs.

Two arrests were reported in East Palo Alto, one around 6 a.m. at a Chevron gas station and another at 9:45 a.m. at Woodland Avenue.

Another arrest occurred at 10 a.m. in the parking lot of Dollar Tree and Home Depot in San Carlos.

Two additional arrests were made in the city of San Mateo, the first at 7:45 a.m. at Chavez Supermarket and another at 11 a.m. at South Idaho Street.

The arrests were confirmed by alerts from Faith in Action Bay Area, an organization that operates the Rapid Response Hotline for the county, a coalition of immigrant rights activists that connect people to resources who are impacted by immigration enforcement. The San Mateo County Office of Community Affairs also sent out a notice of the arrests.

Faith in Action Bay Area also says that ICE enforcement in the county has increased recently, with at least 16 people being detained by ICE in the last 10 days.

Additional arrests occurred Monday, with Faith in Action Bay Area reporting arrests at Hopkins Avenue and El Camino Real in Redwood City early in the morning, one arrest at a laundromat near Safeway in Half Moon Bay around 8 a.m., and another at Eighth and Main streets in Montara near Half Moon Bay.

The organization also said Tuesday that there has been an ICE presence outside the San Mateo County main jail, the Maguire Correctional Facility, in Redwood City every day since Friday.

ICE did not respond to a request for comment in time for publication.

Faith in Action Bay Area says it has identified and activated emergency legal support for the people detained and is in touch with their families.

text:
Former Mesa County Sheriff’s Deputy Alexander Zwinck appears to be working at Immigration and Customs Enforcement after facing discipline for collaborating with ICE last year in the arrest of Utah college student Caroline Dias Goncalves, according to federal data hacked and published by activists.

Zwinck is listed in the published data as a special agent at Homeland Security Investigations, an office that is part of ICE, in Grand Junction. The data, which includes the information of more than 41,000 employees at the Department of Homeland Security, was obtained by a group called Department of Peace and published in October by a nonprofit called Distributed Denial of Secrets as a searchable database.

The Washington Post verified the authenticity of the data with current and former DHS officials as part of an investigation the newsroom published this week.

It’s not clear when ICE hired Zwinck or if he is still employed there. Zwinck did not respond to a text message or email Tuesday.

ICE’s June 2025 detention of Dias Goncalves, then a 19-year-old University of Utah nursing student, sparked public outrage and led to a federal lawsuit in which a judge ruled ICE officers acted illegally in arresting Goncalves and others without warrants across the state. Most people arrested by ICE last year had no prior criminal convictions, according to data obtained from ICE and published by the University of California, Berkeley, School of Law’s Deportation Data Project.

When a Colorado Sun reporter called the phone number listed in the data for Zwinck this week and asked if this was him, he responded affirmatively before hanging up. The Sun attempted to independently verify the data by searching for records related to the person identified in the data as Zwinck’s supervisor in Grand Junction, that person’s supervisor in Denver, and that person’s supervisor in Montana. The Sun was able to confirm those people have addresses in those places.

In response to questions, a spokesperson at the Denver ICE public affairs office said in an email, “Due to employment privacy policies ICE does not confirm the employment status or personnel actions of any individual.” The emailer did not identify themselves.

Stopped on the way to Denver

As a Mesa County sheriff’s deputy, Zwinck pulled over Dias Goncalves on Interstate 70 near the town of Loma on June 5, 2025, for allegedly driving too close to a semi-truck as she was traveling to Denver.

During the traffic stop, Zwinck made Dias Goncalves get out of her car and walk to his car to input some of her information, body camera footage shows.

As Dias Goncalves was sitting in the front seat of Zwinck’s patrol car, he said, “Where are you from? You’ve got a little bit of an accent.”

“I’m from Utah,” Dias Goncalves responded.

“How long have you lived in Utah for?” Zwinck said.

“Uh, like 12 years,” Dias Goncalves responded

“Born and raised, or no?” Zwinck said.

“No, I was born in Brazil,” Dias Goncalves said.

“Oh, that’s cool,” Zwinck replied.

Zwinck released Dias Goncalves with a warning.

“All right, you’re good to go, you have safe travels, ok?” Zwinck said as Dias Goncalves exited his car.

In a subsequent lawsuit brought against Zwinck, Colorado Attorney General and governor-elect Phil Weiser alleged that Zwinck kept Dias Goncalves in his car as a way to stall while alerting officers from ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations office to her location in a chat on the app Signal.

Zwinck was part of a group of state and federal law enforcement working on drug interdiction.

Federal immigration agents arrested Dias Goncalves a few miles down the road and transported her to the immigration detention center in Aurora, where she spent the next 15 days before paying a $2,000 bond, according to her lawyers. She told The Salt Lake Tribune that her days at the facility were “the hardest of my life.”

Zwinck resigned after a lawsuit

Colorado law prohibits state and local law enforcement from asking people about their immigration status. State law also prohibits officers from aiding in federal immigration enforcement outside of their criminal enforcement duties.

A relative of Dias Goncalves told The Tribune that Dias Goncalves came to the United States with her parents in 2012, when she was 7 years old. The family had a six-month tourist visa, which they overstayed, and then applied for asylum several years later, the relative said.

Weiser sued Zwinck in July of last year, alleging this was not the first time Zwinck had shared information with federal immigration agents in the Signal chat in violation of Colorado law. According to the lawsuit, another officer in the chat commented on the day after Dias Goncalves’ arrest that “Zwinck is gonna get ERO interdictor of the year,” referring to ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations.

The Mesa County Sheriff’s Office removed Zwinck from his role in the interagency drug task force in July 2025 and put him on three weeks of unpaid leave as punishment for his involvement in the arrest. The office punished four other deputies after Dias Goncalves’ arrest. Zwinck resigned in September 2025. Weiser dropped his lawsuit shortly after.

Using the hacked and leaked DHS data, The Washington Post performed background checks on 300 newly hired ICE agents, a small sample of the 12,000 officers DHS had hired as of January.

text:
LEXINGTON, Ky. (LEX NEWS) — A Lexington man is now in ICE custody after going to Louisville for an immigration appointment.

David Reyes Mejia’s wife, Rhonda Whaley, says a prior deportation order surfaced during that appointment, leaving his family with questions about what happens next. We looked into what a prior order can mean while someone is pursuing a new immigration case.

Reyes Mejia’s friends describe him as the kind of guy who seems to know just about everyone.

“He can tell a good story. He makes everyone laugh,” Whaley said.

But for more than a week now, Reyes Mejia hasn’t been home.

Whaley says everything changed during the couple’s immigration appointment in Louisville, when she says federal immigration officials delivered unexpected news.

“They told me that ICE was going to come and get him because he had the deportation order,” Whaley said.

Whaley says the order itself wasn’t a surprise. She says Reyes Mejia had been open about his immigration history as they worked through the process.

“We kind of anticipated something because he was honest with everything, following the paperwork. Like he knew that he had the deportation order, but he was deported,” Whaley said.

LEX News reached out to ICE about Reyes Mejia’s detention. After a couple of days, ICE responded saying, “We will research this and respond as soon as possible.”

As Whaley works to understand her husband’s case, we asked immigration attorney Dallin Lykins what a pending immigration application means when there’s already a prior removal order.

“Just having another immigration application out there pending doesn’t necessarily eradicate or erase a prior removal order,” Lykins said.

What happens next in Reyes Mejia’s case remains unclear. Lykins says immigration cases can vary depending on a person’s history, prior orders and what legal options may be available.

“It doesn’t necessarily mean deportation is imminent. They have the ability to request a bond hearing and potentially be released on a bond. They also have the ability to defend and file applications while they’re in custody,” Lykins said.

As Reyes Mejia’s family waits for answers, his friends are waiting for something else: to have him back home.

“I love you, man, and I hope you’re doing well. We’re all thinking about you and just really can’t wait to get you back home,” Eric Dickerson said.

ICE has not yet provided additional details about Reyes Mejia’s detention or what comes next in his case. We will update this story once the agency responds.

text:
Attorneys and local observers say the first immigration detainees have been transferred to a large new detention center in western Minnesota.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement announced earlier this year that it planned to open the site this fall in Appleton, west of the Twin Cities. The facility, a former private prison, has sat vacant since 2010.

A spokesperson for the American Civil Liberties Union said attorneys there have received "credible and documented reports that at least one individual is currently being held at the facility."

A group of local advocates said they have also seen more activity around the facility this week, and believe detainees have been brought there. Observers said they spotted vans used to transport detainees drive into the facility early this week.

ICE has not responded to a request for comment from MPR News. The agency’s public list of detention facilities does not include Appleton.

ICE previously said the facility will be fully up and running by mid-2027. It has capacity for 1,600 detainees. Those people could be brought to the center from other county jails around the state, or flown in from other facilities around the country, as is the case at several of ICE's detention sites.

The center will be operated by CoreCivic, a company that used to own the jail and sold it to the U.S. government earlier this year for $495.6 million. A recent KARE 11 investigation found that was more than six times the price that CoreCivic asked from the state for the property a year earlier.

CoreCivic runs more than 70 detention centers around the country. Several have seen reports of poor living conditions, including the Dilley Immigration Processing Center in Texas.

John Boehler is the policy counsel at ACLU Minnesota. He said he’s concerned about the conditions at the Appleton facility, especially because it was vacant for more than 15 years before reopening. He’s tracked news from other immigration detention facilities around the country that opened quickly after long closures, and said he’s seen reports of health issues and lack of access to basic needs.

He said the federal government isn’t doing enough to make sure conditions are safe.

“What we've seen in the past two years is that the executive branch, the federal legislative branch, DHS, ICE, and their private partners have all been working in lockstep, so there hasn't been true oversight of these facilities,” Boehler said. “The lockstep has been to kind of obscure the conditions of these facilities get them up and running as fast as possible.”

Attorneys and clergy are legally allowed to access detention centers; Boehler said he’s watching to see any news that comes out of Appleton once more people are allowed to go in.

But Boehler said access at the Appleton site could be hard. It’s a three-hour drive from the Twin Cities, and attorneys have struggled to find out where ICE is bringing some of their clients.

And, he said, 1,600 additional immigration detainees in the state could put a strain on resources like mutual aid and attorneys. At the height of Operation Metro Surge, Boehler said, about 800 immigration detainees were being held in county jails around the state.

“Those resources were strained to the breaking point through Metro Surge,” Boehler said. “To take that and multiply it by three or four times, and to put them three hours outside the metro, where there are very few attorneys, let alone specialized immigration attorneys, you're going to make it quite difficult for these these individuals to get adequate representation.”

CoreCivic says the company expects to make about $75 million in revenue from the Appleton site annually, under its five-year contract with the U.S. government. They'll receive a fixed monthly payment and a daily payment based on the number of detainees held there.

The news of the new facility has gotten a divided response from Appleton residents. Some have organized protests against it, including a vigil and rally planned for Saturday afternoon.

Brian Wojtalewicz is a local resident who has been protesting the detention center. He said his main concern as the facility opens is for anyone who's released from there — possibly into the rural roads of Appleton, three hours from the Twin Cities and likely far from their lawyer or good transit options to a major city.

“Are they actually going to throw people out in the street?” he said. “You know, are we going to get any warning?”

He and other organizers have been attempting to plan to help any detainees released there. He said it’s hard to keep eyes on the facility, which is set far back off the main road and mostly surrounded by private farmland.

Wojtalewicz said he also knows people in town who are glad to see the site opening. Appleton's economy used to rely heavily on the prison there; some are hoping that the job opportunities and staff at the facility will give the town a boost.

“Anyone who's lived in little town America realizes how much little towns are on their knees for jobs, for higher incomes,” Wojtalewicz said.

And the jobs at the detention center, he said, pay higher than other jobs around the area.

Wojtalewicz said he and other opponents of the site are keeping eyes on it this week. Attorneys are waiting to see if other clients are transported to the site — and to see if they’re eventually allowed inside to see the conditions there.

text:
Yesterday’s argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards showed a court open to the possibility of a major limitation on the ability of agencies to impose fines or penalties under internal adjudicative processes, at least without ready review in court.

The constitutional problem is how to distinguish between the judicial power that is allocated to the judicial branch (in Article III of the Constitution) and the executive power that is allocated to the executive branch (in Article I of the Constitution). The Supreme Court always has recognized that it is permissible for officials in the executive branch – who don’t have the protections (including life tenure) that Article III gives to federal judges – to resolve questions in a proceeding that looks an awful lot like the kind of trial you might see in a federal court. And it also on several occasions has invalidated schemes that seemed to the court to go too far in that direction. To pick the most famous example, the justices invalidated the initial version of the Bankruptcy Code of 1978 because it gave undue adjudicative responsibility to bankruptcy “judges” that are not protected by Article III. What the court has never done well is explain exactly how far such powers can go. Nevertheless, recent decisions like Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo and Trump v. Slaughter show a great willingness to rein in the powers traditionally granted to the administrative state.

This case presents a dispute as to whether employers under the H-2A visa program (for temporary foreign agricultural workers) gave those employees certain things they were promised before being admitted to the United States. Conventionally, when the Department of Labor decided that an employer had failed to treat workers as it promised pre-admission, it imposed fines or penalties in an administrative proceeding, often handing the funds over to the employees as compensation in the nature of back pay. The question for the justices is whether Article III of the Constitution can tolerate that dispute being resolved internally by DOL employees rather than by judges in a federal court.

The government sees the dispute as squarely involving two categories of so-called “public rights” for which Article I treatment is permitted: the immigration power and public benefits. The immigration power is involved because the workers were permitted to enter the country on the condition that the employer treat them as agreed; the public benefit power is involved because the right to enter is a benefit almost entirely within the discretion of the executive.

Several of the justices found that argument rather weak. Chief Justice John Roberts, for example, commented early on that the leading case about the immigration power (Oceanic Steam Navigation v Mellor) “had to do very much with entry, a condition of entry, and loathsome diseases. This strikes me as significantly different. … You’re trying to leverage an entry several weeks, months … in the past to the particular condition of work that doesn’t seem to have much to do with the actual entry.” For the chief justice, the government was trying to “leverage what is a significant barrier to entry, where you have a lot of deference to the executive branch,” and “trying to … extend that broad authority beyond the justification for its application.” He repeatedly emphasized that the specifics of the case “look more like a condition of employment rather than … entry.”

In a similar vein, Justice Amy Coney Barrett stated to Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris (arguing for the government): “I think we agree that the aliens could be removed pursuant to our immigration tradition without an Article III court. But the fines, I’m wondering if they’re different. …. So I’m … wondering here why that wouldn’t be the case for the alien. If the alien violated some sort of condition on the H-2A visa, why wouldn’t the alien be entitled to an Article III court before the alien had to pay that kind of a fine?” At which point Justice Neil Gorsuch chimed in that he “thought [an earlier case had said that] confiscating property goes to an Article III court when you’re trying to confiscate property from aliens. … I thought we decided a long time ago that you’ve got to go to an Article III court. Are … you resisting that?”

Justice Brett Kavanaugh pointed to yet another precedent on civil penalties: “In Tull [v. United States], we said … and this is 40 years ago – a civil penalty was a type of remedy at common law that could only be enforced in courts of law. …. That’s a fairly definitive statement in our precedent. What … are we supposed to do with that?”

That’s not to say that all of the justices sided against the government. Justice Elena Kagan, for example, found the case well within the boundaries of existing doctrine. To Harris, she commented early on: “[I]sn’t there a condition of entry here? … [T]hey wouldn’t be admitted unless the employer had promised certain things.” To Robert Johnson arguing on behalf of the employer – a different Robert Johnson, not the blues singer – she was much more pointed:

[T]his is an admissions case. An employer has gone to the government and said: We’re going to make various certifications so that you allow us to bring in a boatload of foreign workers. … [A]nd what the government is now saying is those admissions requirements that we put on the admission of these workers have been violated. And just the same way that the admissions requirement in Oceanic has been violated, so too here, and so the same penalties can apply. … I feel that at the base of your argument, Mr. Johnson, you’re trying to get us to think that the H-2A program is not an immigration program. But it is an immigration program.

Offering a parallel perspective, Ketanji Brown Jackson emphasized that the court in numerous contexts has approved administrative adjudication of civil penalties. She repeatedly challenged Johnson to reconcile his argument with those decisions.

But ominous for the government was some repeated questioning of Harris about “the best way for you to lose” (as Justice Sonia Sotomayor put it). From early on in the argument, even the justices who seem most likely to accept the constitutionality of the arrangement were trying to help Harris identify the least damaging way for the court to rule against her. At the beginning of her argument and throughout it, Harris emphasized to the justices that a broad ruling against her on the constitutional question would unsettle programs in a wide variety of areas, ranging from Medicare, to government contracts, to student loans, but that did not seem to make any headway for her.

It is not at all clear from the argument how exactly the justices are going to come down. Clearly a significant group are considering the idea that an award of civil penalties is too far removed from the entry of the employee to be protected by the “public rights” doctrine that would protect administrative determination of the right to enter. My guess is that even those justices don’t yet know how far they would be willing to go – or how far they can go and secure five votes of agreement. I expect this case to come down late and be sharply divided.

authors: Laura Romero, Luke Barr, ABC News
description:
A deportation flight carrying Iranians was abruptly turned around shortly after takeoff Tuesday, according to the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund.
As promised, the Trump Administration is employing all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history.
There has been no public notice to the federal judge about the last two deportation attempts.
Judge Reyes, in last month's hearing, slammed the government over its plans to deport the Iranians back to their home country.

text:
A deportation flight carrying Iranians was abruptly turned around shortly after takeoff Tuesday, according to the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund.

The deportees on Tuesday's flight were scheduled to be flown to Pakistan, which was then set to transport them to Iran, but Pakistan declined to receive them, according to two sources familiar with the situation.

It's unclear why Pakistani authorities refused to accept the plane.

The diverted flight comes after a previous attempt to deport the same group was canceled Sunday while the plane sat on the tarmac in Arizona "ready for takeoff" and the detainees were moved back to detention, an attorney for the IALDF previously told ABC News.

Both flights come after a federal judge blasted the administration for planning to send people back to Iran -- "a declared enemy" -- during the ongoing war there.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said Wednesday that Tuesday's flight "contained criminal illegal aliens who have criminal histories that include arrests and convictions covering assaults, drug trafficking, child abuse, domestic battery, and illegal weapon possession."

"They all had final orders of removal," the DHS spokesperson said. "Every illegal alien has their claims heard and receives due process. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them. Period. As promised, the Trump Administration is employing all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history. Make no mistake, these criminals who committed heinous crimes will be deported."

According to Human Rights First, a nonprofit organization that tracks deportation flights, the small ICE Air jet carrying the Iranians departed Tuesday from Mesa, Arizona, at around 5 a.m. local time and returned within 30 minutes.

According to transcript unsealed last week of a hearing held on Oct. 15, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes ordered the government to provide at least five days' advance notice before any individual is "placed on a transport vehicle or plane bound for removal," along with 24 hours' notice of any finalized removal plan.

There has been no public notice to the federal judge about the last two deportation attempts.

"If anything happens that violates either of those two orders, I will hold every single person associated with violating it. I will start contempt proceedings," Reyes said during the hearing last month.

Judge Reyes, in last month's hearing, slammed the government over its plans to deport the Iranians back to their home country.

"We are talking about sending individuals in our care and custody to a country that we have bombed and we may continue bombing, and is a declared enemy of this country," Reyes said. "It is like saying we have individuals in 1942 in this country that we are going to send back to Nazi Germany. That is the equivalent of what you are telling me."

text:
WASHINGTON — Democrats and business leaders publicly lobbied the Trump administration Wednesday to prioritize work permits and other protections for long-term immigrants during the lame-duck session of Congress and beyond.

Citing the midterm elections, when Democrats flipped the U.S House and Senate, and President Donald Trump’s recent admission that his immigration crackdown hurt Republicans at the ballot box, Democratic lawmakers argued that voters were clear about wanting immigration reform before the start of the next Congress.

Congress has a lengthy to-do-list for the lame-duck session, possibly including government funding, the annual defense policy bill, the farm bill, a measure to regulate the college sports landscape and permitting reform to ease regulation on large construction projects.

“We owe it to these families to try anything, and I'm willing to try anything,” Arizona Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego said.

He was joined by American Business Immigration Coalition Action, which lobbies for work permits and legal pathways for long-term immigrants, and the South Texas Builders Association, a local trade group that represents the construction industry that has a workforce that is 30% immigrant nationwide, and Democratic U.S. House members from Texas.

Asked how receptive the White House would be to work permits for immigrants, which the administration has vigorously worked to limit, Gallego didn’t directly answer.

Trump’s mixed signals

The administration has revoked millions of immigrants’ work permits in the last two years. Many were workers in hospitality, healthcare and the construction industries.

But shortly after the midterm elections, the president said he was open to making a deal on work permits in certain industries.

At the same time, though, he elevated Stephen Miller, an official who has crafted some of the president’s harshest immigration policies, to White House chief of staff.

“I think right now the best thing the White House could do is to actually try to send some type of signal, besides talk, that they're serious about this, and the way to do that is to have some reforms already at (Immigration and Customs Enforcement),” Gallego said.

“Whether it's shutting down the detention centers, giving (a) certain level of protections, whether to veterans so they don't get deported, to maybe parents of U.S. students so they don't get deported, something to show that it's not just talk, and this isn't going to be a policy that's led by Stephen Miller,” he added.

The vice chair of South Texas Builders Association, Benny Melendez, had a pointed message for Miller.

“If you want to continue harassing our communities, prepare yourself not only to lose your job, but … these same communities you are now harassing will make sure you lose the White House” in 2028, he said.

Next Congress

If lawmakers are unable to get any major reforms through the crowded end-of-year session, Democrats are looking ahead to when they control both chambers next year.

House Republicans on Tuesday elected Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan, a staunch Trump supporter who has not supported immigration reform, to lead them in the minority.

Texas Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar, the incoming chair on the subcommittee that handles government funding for the Department of Homeland Security, said he’s not worried about Jordan because Democrats will have a majority in January.

Cuellar, whom Trump pardoned after he and his wife were indicted on charges of bribery, money laundering and conspiracy, said he’s going to use his subcommittee gavel to add guardrails on ICE and clear the backlog at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, which processes legal immigrants.

Gallego said he thinks the Senate will be able to get to 60 votes on some type of immigration reform legislation in the 120th Congress, when Democrats will have at least 54 and up to 56 seats depending on races that are still too close to call.

Whether that overhaul is in one bill or a series of increments is up for debate, Gallego said.

“If we can pass a big, beautiful conference immigration reform bill, the Trump immigration reform bill, and if that gets them on our side or not, then let's do that,” Gallego said. “But if that doesn't work, then I do think incremental passes to start protecting different communities I think is also an option. We should not avoid that either.”

title: After midterm elections, Trump said he was 'too tough' on immigration. Here's what he's done so far
description:
CBS News’ “60 Minutes” correspondent Ross Douthat asked Trump if his immigration crackdown hurt Republicans in the elections.
Trump, who said he had been “too tough” on immigration, said he would work out an immigration “deal” with Democrats, but provided no details.
Here’s a look at where Trump’s immigration promises stand.
A U.S. Border Patrol truck drives past a section of border wall, Sept. 17, 2026, in Mission, Texas.
During his first term, Trump used executive orders to impose travel bans on people from seven countries, suspending their visas for 90 days.
text:
In his first sit-down interview after the midterm elections where his party resoundingly lost control of both chambers of Congress, President Donald Trump both acknowledged that his immigration agenda might have turned away some voters and praised it.

CBS News’ “60 Minutes” correspondent Ross Douthat asked Trump if his immigration crackdown hurt Republicans in the elections.

“I think it both helped and hurt,” Trump said in the interview that aired Nov. 8. “I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out.” But the administration also removed “people that had good jobs” in landscaping or hotels, in some cases people who paid taxes, he said, and that hurt the party.

Trump, who said he had been “too tough” on immigration, said he would work out an immigration “deal” with Democrats, but provided no details.

After the Nov. 3 election, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin floated the idea of working with Congress on a legal pathway for immigrants who came to the U.S. illegally as children and who are protected from deportation under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, or DACA.

On Nov. 9, Trump told reporters “we’re not going to have amnesty or anything” for immigrants illegally in the country.

Trump has promoted Stephen Miller, his former deputy chief of staff, as his new chief of staff. Miller led Trump’s first-term hard-line immigration agenda, supporting policies that separated families arriving at the border and that banned the entry of people from several Muslim-majority countries.

During Trump’s second term, Miller has been a leading architect of Trump’s immigration strategy and has pushed the administration to arrest at least 3,000 immigrants a day.

Immigration experts doubt that Trump will cool down on enforcement as Miller embraces his new role.

“Promoting Stephen Miller hardly signals a retreat from the administration’s mass deportation agenda,” said Tom K. Wong, director of the U.S. Immigration Policy Center at the University of California, San Diego. “Until we see actual changes in enforcement priorities, the president’s remarks seem more like a change in political messaging than a change in policy.”

PolitiFact has tracked Trump’s progress on immigration campaign promises on our MAGA-Meter. Here’s a look at where Trump’s immigration promises stand.

Haitians deported from the United States deplane at the international airport in Cap-Haitien, Haiti, Aug. 27, 2026. (AP)

Promise: Carry out the largest domestic deportation operation in American history

This is In the Works.

The Department of Homeland Security said that as of October, the administration had deported about 1.2 million immigrants during Trump’s second term. Immigration experts say it’s hard to independently verify the scale of deportations, because the administration isn’t releasing monthly or comprehensive data.

The Migration Policy Institute, a nonpartisan think tank, analyzed DHS data and estimated that from January 2025 to July 31, the administration deported about 980,000 people. The institute said that on an annual basis, while the total deportations are up from the Biden and first Trump administrations, they remain below the levels from the early 2000s.

The Deportation Data Project at the University of California, Los Angeles, and the University of California, Berkeley, obtained data from ICE showing the agency arrested and detained about 42,000 people in July, a monthly record during this term.

A substantial proportion of those arrested within the country are people who lived in the U.S. for more than a decade, said Elizabeth Cohen, a Boston University political science professor.

“Trump‘s immigration agenda has dramatically expanded an already costly interior enforcement apparatus,” Cohen said, although most deportations continue to originate at the border, and border encounters have fallen sharply from Biden administration levels.

A U.S. Border Patrol truck drives past a section of border wall, Sept. 17, 2026, in Mission, Texas. (AP)

Promise: Finish the border wall

This is In the Works.

DHS reported Nov. 3 that from the beginning of Trump’s second term in late January 2025 through Oct. 30, U.S. Customs and Border Protection completed approximately 330 miles of new border barriers. This includes 139.5 miles of primary wall that faces Mexico, 73.9 miles of waterborne barrier, which are usually floating infrastructure placed in bodies of water along the southern border; and 116.2 miles of secondary wall, barriers behind the already existing primary walls to add an additional obstacle.

On Nov. 9, the Supreme Court ruled the Trump administration can continue with border wall construction along the southern border in the Big Bend region of Southwest Texas, which environmentalists say could harm wildlife and the area’s residents. It lifted a district judge’s order from October that halted construction.

Since Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act on July 4, 2025, which included funding to build the border wall, CBP has awarded 11 contracts to build segments of new wall and detection technology.

CBP says the money awarded in part is for building a “smart wall,” which is a mixture of steel walls, roads, detection technology, cameras and lighting.

CBP has designated $34.6 billion of the law’s funding for the border wall.

Promise: Revoke the temporary legal status of Haitians

This is In the Works.

In a 6-3 vote in June, the Supreme Court paved the way for the administration to revoke Haiti’s Temporary Protected Status designation, which protected hundreds of thousands of Haitians from deportation.

In recent months, about 1,000 of the 350,000 people with TPS have been deported to Haiti, according to Human Rights Watch, which cited Haiti’s National Migration Office. Haitians were also deported to Mexico in 2025 and 2026.

Trump made this promise in 2024 as he and his running mate JD Vance spread the lie that Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio, were stealing and eating people’s pets.

Promise: Restore and expand the travel ban

This is a Promise Kept.

During his first term, Trump used executive orders to impose travel bans on people from seven countries, suspending their visas for 90 days. After a legal battle, the Supreme Court ruled that the president can issue a travel ban under certain circumstances.

President Joe Biden revoked the ban; Trump resurrected it in his second term and expanded it to 19 countries.

Promise: Restore Remain in Mexico program

This is a Promise Broken.

Biden in 2021 terminated Trump’s first-term Migrant Protection Protocol, aka Remain in Mexico program. In January 2025, at the start of his second term, Trump signed an executive order to reinstate the program, which sent certain migrants seeking asylum to Mexico to await their U.S. immigration court proceedings.

On Oct. 7, a federal court ruled the program’s implementation is unlawful. The Trump administration has not appealed this decision.

Promise: Require proof of citizenship at the polls

This is a Promise Broken.

Trump lobbied for the passage of the SAVE America Act. The legislation would require people to provide documentary proof of citizenship, such as a passport or birth certificate, when registering to vote. It passed the House in February but stalled in the Senate. It’s unlikely that the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress will pass this legislation.

Federal law already says only U.S. citizens can vote in elections for Congress and president. When applying to register to vote, people sign a form attesting that they are U.S. citizens.

text:
David Brouillette fatally shot a Colombian migrant during an attempted traffic stop.

An ICE agent who fatally shot a Colombian migrant in Maine had previously spewed racist abuse about his sister’s Colombian partner in a series of vile emails.

David Brouillette, 38, called his sister Elizabeth Emen’s longtime partner—a Colombian-born graduate student who was living legally in the U.S. and with whom she shared two children—a “non citizen” who should return to his “third world” country in a 2021 exchange obtained by The New York Times.

He also attacked his “bloodline” and accused him of failing to embody American values.

“He can takes his non citizen a-- back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries,” Brouillette wrote in one email, riddled with typos.

In another, he attacked the man’s “bloodline,” claiming it knew nothing about what it took to “earn and then CHERISH the freedom America offers.”

“He does not emulate what it means to be an American” but “rather he emulates what it’s like to be entitled and think he has a seat” at a table “that has no room for his (or your ignorance),” he wrote.

He added that the man’s “bloodline knows nothing about what it takes to earn and then CHERISH the freedom America offers.”

Emen, who shared the emails with The Times, said her brother’s attacks had nothing to do with her partner’s immigration status, but rather his ethnicity.

“David had no basis for saying that my partner was undocumented,” she told The New York Times. “It was about how he saw him based on his race.”

Emen said the exchange began after she invited relatives to celebrate her son’s birthday.

Brouillette responded by condemning her relationship and accusing her partner of harboring “anti-American ideologies.”

He then turned his fury on his sister, telling her she had effectively lost him as a brother.

“Your choices have cost you a brother. I am so so so ashamed of you,” he wrote. “You’re dead to me Liz. Enjoy it. Dead to me. DEAD.”

Four years later, Brouillette fatally shot 25-year-old Colombian migrant Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero during an attempted traffic stop in Biddeford, Maine.

Guerrero was struck four times in the face and neck, the New York Times reported. He was killed in front of his wife and 3-year-old daughter, who stood crying in the street dressed in Bluey pajamas.

His wife was on her knees next to their daughter, screaming out in what one onlooker described as an agonizing howl.

“I heard agony,” resident Mary Hayes told The New York Times. “I heard a howl that came from your soul, that your whole life had just changed and it was never going to be the same.”

Guerrero was driving to work when ICE agents rammed his car while attempting to execute a warrant for a final order of removal.

The Department of Homeland Security claimed “the vehicle attempted to flee” and that Brouillette opened fire because he feared for public safety.

But evidence substantiating the department’s account has yet to emerge.

DHS initially claimed Guerrero had entered the country illegally, a statement it subsequently retracted, according to the office of Senator Angus King of Maine.

The Guerrero family’s lawyer said he was authorized to work in the U.S. and was not the subject of ICE’s investigation.

The shooting provoked widespread outrage in Biddeford, with elected officials from both parties criticizing ICE.

Republican Senator Susan Collins called on the agency to halt all non-urgent vehicle stops.

The shooting is now being investigated, and Brouillette’s emails could prove to be an important part of the investigation.

Michael Gennaco, a former federal prosecutor in California, told The New York Times that the emails could help support an argument that an officer used excessive force.

“Federal statute doesn’t require a prosecutor to prove racial animus, but such bias could support the idea that the officer used excessive force,” Gennaco said.

The Daily Beast has contacted DHS for comment.

text:
A University of San Francisco nursing professor who was granted protection from deportation to her native Nigeria has spent the last eight weeks in ICE detention in Louisiana, thousands of miles from her family.

Dr. Ann Lawani, 39, who has a valid U.S. work permit and no reported criminal history, was taken from her home in Lodi on Sept 16 by federal immigration agents. They placed her in shackles and took her to a holding facility in Stockton before she was transferred to El Paso. Her family reportedly spent days attempting to track her down before she called them from a processing center in southern Louisiana. Eight weeks later, she remains in ICE custody at the facility.

Her detention has prompted calls for her release from students, faculty and a California congressman, even as the Trump administration says it intends to deport her. The New York Times was the first to report the story (opens in new tab).

Lawani had lived in her Lodi home for 13 years, caring for her 83-year old father. She had previously applied for asylum, but her application was denied in 2013. However, the same judge ruled that she could not be deported to Nigeria because she faced a risk of persecution. Reached for comment Wednesday, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security called Lawani an “illegal alien” arrested during a targeted enforcement operation, adding that she will remain in ICE custody pending removal from the country.

“On June 7, 2007, Lawani legally entered the United States on a temporary basis, but in defiance of our laws overstayed her admittance by failing to depart by July 6, 2007,” the spokesperson said. “To be clear: work authorization does not confer legal status in the U.S.”

text:
It’s been 100 days since the Trump administration ended a contract with legal service providers working with immigrant children — effectively ending a federally funded program that’s been around for two decades and leaving thousands of children's asylum cases in limbo.

Advocates and attorneys say since then, the number of immigration court cases for children has shot up, proceedings are increasingly being done remotely, and the Trump administration is fast-tracking deportations for children.

A lawsuit filed last month challenges a series of changes at Citizenship and Immigration Services.

Melissa Crow is director of litigation for the Center for Gender and Refugee Studies, which represents the legal groups that filed suit.

She says children are usually given two weeks notice of an upcoming asylum appointment. A few months after the contract’s closure, attorneys began reporting their clients were sometimes getting as little as 24 hours.

“It was clear that USCIS was making a concerted effort to move kids through the system very quickly,” Crow said.

Crow says attorney requests to reschedule are also being routinely denied, even when attorneys can’t reasonably prepare a case in time, or even attend the interview at all.

“In one case we had a lawyer who I believe had five asylum interviews scheduled on the same day, at the same time,” Crow said.

A USCIS spokesperson said the agency does not comment on pending litigation.

At the end of last month, a federal judge ordered USCIS to stop enacting those changes until the case is heard in full.

In court this month, legal groups accused USCIS of continuing the policies despite that restraining order. Additional filings are due from both parties later this month.

text:
The Trump administration signaled it would respond aggressively to a Democratic-led Congress with a letter this week threatening to prosecute lawmakers for oversight efforts.

The letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf sent Monday to House Oversight and Government Reform ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., argued that members of Congress have limited authority to conduct oversight of a presidential administration and that some of the threats to issue subpoenas “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

The letter, obtained from a White House official, marks the latest escalation from the Trump administration ahead of Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress next year. It also dovetails with years of Trump’s threats to prosecute his critics.

“We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government,” the letter says.

Garcia, the likely committee chair next Congress, pushed back on the threat in a statement Wednesday, accusing the administration of having “something to hide” and that Congress has wide authority to investigate the executive branch.

“The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse,” Garcia said. “The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers.”

The letter came after Attorney General Todd Blanche previously refused to rule out criminal charges against members of Congress in response to investigations.

“It depends on what the crime is and what they have done,” Blanche told CNN over the weekend.

Last week, President Donald Trump himself said that threats of investigations and impeachment were “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

He also singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., calling for her to be imprisoned. The administration previously unsuccessfully attempted to indict Slotkin and other Democrats over a video she published calling for soldiers to disobey illegal orders.

And Trump last year publicly called for longtime critic Sen. Adam B. Schiff, D-Calif., to face unspecified charges in a post on Truth Social addressed to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi that also called for the prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James. Both have faced criminal charges, pleaded not guilty and fought them in court as political attacks.

Garcia and other Democrats have signaled they intend to pursue oversight aggressively in the new Congress. After Democrats won the House majority last week, Garcia put out an all-caps statement urging administration officials to “LAWYER UP” ahead of the new year.

Garcia, as well as other likely incoming chairs such as House Judiciary ranking member Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md.; Homeland Security ranking member Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss.; and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., have hinted at broad inquiries ranging from the handling of files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein to immigration enforcement and more.

Raskin told reporters last week that he thought Democratic oversight efforts could dovetail with the party’s broader effort to address affordability issues, including by addressing the Iran war, allegations of corruption within the Trump administration and more.

“We’re going to get all the information that we need in order to restore the rule of law in American constitutional democracy,” Raskin said.

The letter also echoes a previous fight the administration pitched with the House in the first Trump administration, where officials resisted in court allowing former White House Counsel Don McGahn to testify to the House Judiciary Committee for years.

text:
WASHINGTON — The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the Trump administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress -- may amount to "blatant criminality."

White House counsel Will Scharf issued the warning in a letter dated Monday to Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee.

Garcia most likely would chair the powerful panel in the new Democratic-controlled Congress that is seated in January. Garcia warned Trump officials to "lawyer up" as his party was on the way to stunning victories in last week's midterm election.

In response, Scharf wrote that "threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality." The letter's existence was first reported by Punchbowl News.

Garcia said in response to the letter that "it appears Donald Trump has something to hide" and stressed that Congress' investigative powers do not need the "permission of the White House."

"Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate," Garcia said. "The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse."

Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. The Republican president and his White House have long denied any wrongdoing.

Garcia also wants to look at the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations. Other targets include Trump's White House ballroom and other construction projects, as well as the Trump family's role in mineral deals and Trump's crypto dealings with special envoy Steve Witkoff.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a CNN interview that aired Sunday that "there could be" a crime to investigate if rhetoric from Democrats turned threatening. He appeared to strike a more conciliatory tone during an appearance in Missouri this week, saying "Congress has oversight authority. It always has, it always will. The Department of Justice, the federal government, works with Congress to address questions they have — whether it's through subpoenas or letters — so we're not going to stop working with Congress."

"Nothing I've said this weekend, or in the past, should suggest otherwise," he added.

Some lawmakers cautioned Democrats as well as the White House against overreaching.

Outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a Trump critic, said he hopes Democrats don't squander their new powers on "stupid things."

"I hope they have real hearings about real things, not another Russiagate," he said, referring to a previous congressional inquiry into ties between Trump's first presidential campaign in 2016 and Russia. Trump repeatedly denounced that investigation as a "hoax."

"I think there is some real corruption there around the fringes," Massie said about Trump and some of those around the president. Massie lost his primary election to a Trump-backed GOP challenger.

Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., who is expected to be the next House Ethics Committee chairman, said he would not back down from any investigations because of warnings from the White House.

"If they're trying to intimidate, at least for me, it's not going to get me," said DeSaulnier, who was a Republican before he switched to the Democratic Party in 2000. "I don't work for a mafia, a mob organization."

description:

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers put a man on the ground in Hillcrest, New York, in late October, put their knees into his back and shot him with a Taser, according to the Human Impact Project.

The incident is one of more than 300 reports tracked by the project in which immigration officials injured someone to the point that they needed medical treatment.

Run by nonprofit Human Security Initiative, Human Impact Project scrapes court records, media reports, self-reported social media posts and GoFundMe accounts for information about the impacts of the Trump administration’s immigration policies. Though the project uses AI for the initial data gathering, human rights researchers fact-check those findings before adding them to the project website, according to organization founder Julia Neusner.

“The idea was to try to understand the scope of enforcement impacts across all these different sources with a focus on individual people,” Neusner said. “Other folks are tracking numbers. We wanted to track the stories and the impact on people.”

ICE did not respond to a request for comment from Capital & Main.

The project recently surpassed 5,000 published reports, and Neusner and her team began analyzing trends in the data. The results serve as a reminder of the immigration-related news stories that have come out in the past two years — arrests of U.S. citizens, detention of pregnant people in inhumane conditions, deportations to third countries of people who won protection in the U.S. and arrests at courts.

Even though the headlines may be familiar, Neusner said, the volume of stories and the extent of the abuses they describe still shock her.

That includes an Instagram post of a family detained in Key Largo, Florida. The woman, a U.S. citizen who is also pregnant, and her husband were on their way to vote in the recent midterm election when agents detained them and separated them from their young child, according to the database. They remained in custody for about a week.

Neusner said the project also reveals stories that the public — and even journalists — may have missed.

“There’s so many everyday abuses, people being beat up in arrests, horrendous conditions in detention,” Neusner said. “The sheer volume of these stories was quite shocking, and the things happening that don’t make it to mainstream press.”

She said the report of an incident involving ICE officers detaining a father who went to visit his son at a jail in Santa Ana, California, recently caught her attention. The father, a 69-year-old construction worker from Mexico, was the primary caregiver for another one of his sons who is only 13.

She also pointed to several stories where ICE officers mistook someone they detained for someone else or identified them by the wrong name.

That includes a Florida woman originally from Guatemala who is arguing in court that ICE detained her under a name she has never used.

The database also includes the story of a Coachella Valley, California, farmworker whom immigration officials mistakenly detained in December and who — 10 months later — is still in ICE custody.

In both cases, judges have denied their petitions for release from custody, according to the database.

Neusner said people can use the database to learn more about stories happening in their area. It features a map showing where the different incidents took place.

The greater Los Angeles area has the most of any geographic location, with more than 500 stories logged there.

An entry from Nov. 1 there pulls information from an online fundraiser asking for help to pay legal fees for a detained grandfather. Another from Oct. 30 details how ICE officers dragged a Venezuelan man outside his North Hollywood apartment and shot him with a Taser. Witnesses said the officers attempted to hogtie him. One of the officers shoved a nearby dog walker into some bushes and pointed a gun inches from the person’s face.

In another online fundraiser from Oct. 30 cited by the project, a family asks for help after ICE detained the father, a truck driver with a pending application for a U visa, a type of visa given to crime victims. The mother has cancer and has started working as a delivery driver to take care of their children on her own, the database says.

An Instagram post from Oct. 27 documents ICE arresting a food truck vendor operating Emin’s Kebab in the Echo Park neighborhood of Los Angeles.

Neusner and her team supplement the information found online with their own research on the ground. They recently went to Tapachula and Villahermosa in southern Mexico to speak with people from other countries sent there by U.S. immigration officials.

Neusner said she sees several ways that people could use the database. She said when her cousin’s wife had a green card appointment approaching, the family searched to see whether ICE officers were detaining people at the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services office in their area. Neusner said she was able to determine that those arrests had happened in other areas, including in San Diego, but not where her family member would soon have the interview.

That information helped allay the family’s worry leading up to the appointment, and the family member now has a green card, Neusner said.

She also hopes the database will connect people, including journalists, to what’s happening near them. Lawyers can look at pages compiled for specific detention centers to pull information about reported conditions to include in habeas corpus petitions to try to get their clients out of custody, she said. The database has catalogued the complaints in more than 1,200 habeas petitions, she said.

In the future, she also hopes the database will serve as a historical record for potential reparations. She said the database archives all of the source documents it uses.

“If there is some sort of future accountability process, these stories will be preserved,” Neusner said.
