The Trump administration canceled those protections for new grantees and renewals of the special status, effective May 10, 2026.
The Beacon is not identifying the Kansas City youth by name or complete biography, but attorneys and therapists outlined some of their circumstances.
Many of the Kansas City children are Honduran or Guatemalan, but they also come from Vietnam, Mexico and several countries in Africa.
“We really need this next Congress to put a stop to this egregious treatment of unaccompanied children,” Giovagnoli said.
text:
They’re the immigrant children long considered to be the most vulnerable.

Many traveled to the U.S. alone, unaccompanied by a parent or guardian. Some were trafficked for labor or sex. A state judge has ruled that each of them has experienced serious abuse, neglect or abandonment and is in need of the state’s care.

For decades, the U.S. treated these foreign-born youth from a child protection perspective. Policy, law and federal funding acknowledged their unique needs.

A special immigration status was available for them, which opened up the pathway to a green card. And while their cases moved through the country’s clogged-up immigration system, policy gave them protections from being deported.

But many of those protections have disappeared under President Donald Trump’s administration, affecting up to 150,000 children nationwide.

And now, at least two dozen such children in the Kansas City area are in active removal proceedings and could soon be ordered deported. And the organizations supporting the children have lost the federal funding that helped provide counseling and legal representation.

Hearings before immigration judges have been abruptly pulled from 2027 dockets. Some have been rescheduled for mid-November, leaving attorneys scrambling to jam six months or more of legal work into a matter of weeks.

“It’s nonsensical and it’s cruel because these children had already been told by the government that they wouldn’t be pursued for deportation,” said Aly Englander, senior staff attorney at the Asylum Clinic Kansas City.

Englander manages 113 immigration cases, about 80% of which are for children, including those whose deportations are being expedited.

The Trump administration maintains that it is focused on countering what it characterizes as Biden-era fraud within programs for unaccompanied children, and decreasing backlogs in immigration proceedings.

In a statement to The Beacon, federal officials with the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) said they’re just doing their job.

“Prior leadership may have allowed certain cases to languish indefinitely in violation of the law, and EOIR is working hard to correct those violations,” the statement read. “However, there is nothing novel about EOIR trying to ensure that cases are resolved as expeditiously as possible.”

October change-ups

The Kansas City-area children most at risk of being ordered deported have either been granted or have a case pending to receive special immigrant juvenile status, a humanitarian designation for abused or neglected children that can lead to a permanent legal status, Englander said.

Previously, children with this legal classification were granted deferred action, an aspect of immigration law that allows for a suspension of deportation proceedings while cases progress. Since 2022, the children were also allowed to legally work, which provided them a government-issued identification as they waited for a green card to become available.

The Trump administration canceled those protections for new grantees and renewals of the special status, effective May 10, 2026.

In October, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. issued statements saying changes had been necessary to counter Biden-era fraud within the unaccompanied children programs.

Also in October, the government began offering $3,000 to unaccompanied children who are willing to self-deport, an increase of the $2,500 the administration set in 2025.

Around that same time, some of the children’s cases handled by the Asylum Clinic and assigned to the Kansas City immigration court were abruptly shifted to the docket of a Chicago immigration judge, worrying the children’s lawyers.

In addition, some of the families housing the youth, considered sponsors, have been put under heightened scrutiny by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

”They’ve started sending ICE to the houses of sponsors,” Englander said. “A lot of our clients have experienced ICE just going up to their house.”

The escalating tensions have left the local immigration attorneys, caseworkers and therapists scrambling.

”We took about 24 hours to freak out, and then we have not stopped since,” said Meaghan Fanning, youth program manager at Jewish Vocational Service, or JVS, which is coordinating with the Asylum Clinic to provide case management and therapy for some of the children.

“They’re kids,” Fanning said. “Either their life is unsafe, the people in their lives are unsafe, or they don’t have anybody else in their life at this point.”

The attorneys were told to appear with the youth in court in Kansas City on Oct. 29, despite the fact that such hearings were typically conducted virtually.

At the hearing, Judge Shawn Abraham appeared by teleconference and said he couldn’t access the Kansas City case files, pushing the cases back several weeks. Abraham agreed that at future hearings, the children could appear by video.

Court challenges to many of the administration’s new policies have also been filed.

Who are Kansas City’s kids at risk of deportation?

The Beacon is not identifying the Kansas City youth by name or complete biography, but attorneys and therapists outlined some of their circumstances.

One teenage girl lives in a Kansas City homeless shelter. She escaped what her attorney described as “intense labor trafficking.”

The girl doesn’t have steady access to food, an outcome of the Trump administration eliminating SNAP benefits for many immigrant classifications. Advocates deliver gift cards to her every two weeks, so she can purchase meals at Walmart.

One boy was homeless in Honduras from the ages of 6 to 10. He walked and hitched rides to the U.S. with a group of friends who were also homeless. The trip took several months until they approached Homeland Security agents at the southern border.

The boy was detained for a year in a U.S. government shelter for youth.

He’s 11 now, living with a relative and thriving at a local middle school.

Others among the children came to the U.S. as siblings. Older siblings often care for younger brothers and sisters as they walk across borders.

Some of the children have worked long hours in construction, roofing, drywalling and restaurants, with an adult confiscating their wages. A few have been unpaid nannies. Lawyers say at least five have been sexually exploited.

Many of the Kansas City children are Honduran or Guatemalan, but they also come from Vietnam, Mexico and several countries in Africa. The youngest is 6, and the oldest is 18.

Several are disabled, physically or intellectually. Some do not have a parent or other close relative in the U.S. and are in foster care.

For most, formal schooling was severely interrupted because of the abuse they fled or the exploitation they endured after entering the U.S.

A departure from the status quo

The situation these children and their lawyers are navigating marks a major shift in how the government handles such cases, according to Mary Giovagnoli, a Kansas City native who is the former ombudsperson for unaccompanied children at the Department of Health and Human Services.

Giovagnoli, whom Trump removed from his administration last year, said she worries that the government is disregarding some of the children’s rights.

“They’re pushing these kids out the door so fast, there needs to be some attention paid to ensuring that their return to their home countries is safe,” Giovagnoli said.

That is not happening, she said, which comes up against provisions of the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008.

The act expanded protections for trafficking victims, including setting standards to ensure they would not be persecuted or experience trafficking again if returned to their native countries.

In September 2025, Giovagnoli testified before a Senate subcommittee in oral and written comments. Her testimony outlined changes under the Trump administration that have shifted the care of vulnerable children from child welfare strategies to immigration enforcement.

In particular, she testified that decades-old positive approaches to funding work to protect children from trafficking were “all but abandoned in the provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025.”

The Asylum Clinic is part of a network of agencies nationwide that received federal grants to represent abused and neglected children during their immigration cases. Those grants have been canceled by the Trump administration.

Similarly, some federal allowances for medical treatment for the children, therapy for trauma and help with food and housing have also been rescinded.

“The Trump administration’s policies pose the greatest risk to unaccompanied children in the U.S. today, as it systematically eliminates the protections and resources put in place by Congress to keep unaccompanied children safe,” reads a portion of Giovagnoli’s submitted testimony.

She accuses the Trump administration of “using children as pawns in its mass deportation agenda,” echoing a common charge by legal associations, nonprofits and some members of Congress.

“We really need this next Congress to put a stop to this egregious treatment of unaccompanied children,” Giovagnoli said. “It should be, as with so many immigration issues, something that’s nonpartisan that everybody can agree on.”

The administration, in reply to such criticism, has released statements, often arguing that changes are necessary to correct fraud.

A statement released Oct. 1 said the government found fraudulent documentation, manipulated photographs, misrepresented or unverifiable addresses, problems with fingerprints and ages submitted and a failure to disclose household members of homes where the unaccompanied children were living.

“The Biden Administration failed in its most basic responsibility: protecting vulnerable children in federal care,” said Kennedy in a news release. “It weakened safeguards and prioritized speed over scrutiny, leaving children exposed to fraud, exploitation, and abuse.”

Looking toward an uncertain future

Many of the children around Kansas City understand what is happening in their legal cases, or at least that their future is less certain, advocates told The Beacon.

“They can’t actually dream ahead because they either have lost their status or could lose their status at any time,” Fanning said.

Fanning said some of the students she worked with had a hard time starting school this fall.

Young people had absorbed the daily drum of news, she said, seeing video of ICE agents arresting people, sometimes in violent confrontations. Some of the children isolated themselves during the summer months, hesitant to be too far from home.

The administration’s actions upended how JVS therapists help the children process trauma.

“We work with kids on the stuff that they don’t want to say out loud,” Fanning said.

Talk therapy guides the youth in telling the story of their lives. They learn to speak about the abuse, the neglect, everything that they have faced until they arrive at surviving all of it, versus suffering.

Then they can set goals: graduating high school, obtaining a green card, planning for college.

The process also prepares the children for immigration hearings, where they’ll need to share details to an immigration judge and be ready to answer the questions of government attorneys.

“But how do you heal from your past when you cannot see a future?” Fanning said. “Now, it’s so unstable for them.”

Many of the youth lean into faith, often saying that God brought them this far in their lives and he will see them through, even if they don’t like the eventual legal outcome.

One child recently said this to Fanning: “‘I went through way too much to get here to just give up now.’”

title: Op-ed | The midterm elections were a rebuke of Trump and ICE's tactics - PoliticsNY
description:
President Trump bet that his deportation agenda would win the day for him and his party; he lost that bet resoundingly.
Americans at the ballot box made clear that their concerns focused on affordability, inflation and the Trump administration’s tactics on immigration.
The midterm election results are a referendum on the Trump Administration and its policies.
The same voters who gave Republicans a narrow edge on immigration issues rejected how this administration has carried out its agenda.
They should produce laws that protect families and make clear no agency is above the law.
text:
Democrats swept both chambers of Congress last week. President Trump bet that his deportation agenda would win the day for him and his party; he lost that bet resoundingly. Americans at the ballot box made clear that their concerns focused on affordability, inflation and the Trump administration’s tactics on immigration.

The midterm election results are a referendum on the Trump Administration and its policies. The same voters who gave Republicans a narrow edge on immigration issues rejected how this administration has carried out its agenda. Exit polls found that 57% of voters said Trump’s enforcement has gone too far, and 59% disapprove of ICE. Voters aren’t asking Democrats to abandon immigration. They’re asking them to bring order and decency back to a system that has lost both.

Democrats now have the tools to do it. Starting in January, they should use three.

The first is oversight. ICE has operated with too little transparency and too few consequences. A Democratic House now has subpoena power. It should investigate enforcement practices, detention conditions, deaths in custody, and how the agency spends its money.

Accountability can’t stop at agency leadership. When agents or contractors violate people’s rights, Congress must make clear there will be consequences. And hearings aren’t the goal. They should produce laws that protect families and make clear no agency is above the law.

text:
Beata Siemionkowicz, a Polish immigrant, green card holder and immigration detainee who sued the Campbell County jailer and several federal officials in September has been released.

Siemionkowicz’s daughter, Gabi Siemionkowicz, confirmed with LINK nky that Siemionkowicz’s family picked her up from the detention center Tuesday afternoon.

Siemionkowicz was detained by ICE in August 2025 in Illinois and transported to Campbell County Detention Center, which houses immigration detainees. She spent more than a year being detained there.

Siemionkowicz sued Campbell County Jailer James Daley and several federal officials in September of this year, alleging the federal government and detention center violated constitutional habeas corpus protections. It was filed with the aid of attorneys from the ACLU of Kentucky and Illinois, who demanded authorities furnish a reason for her detention or release her.

Siemionkowicz has been living legally in the United States since 1995. She got her green card in 2003. Gabi told LINK nky that her mother tried twice to go through the naturalization process but was unsuccessful.

DHS issued an order for her removal last summer, citing her criminal history. Siemionkowicz has two misdemeanor charges on her record, both in Lake County, Illinois. One occurred in 2005, and another occurred in 2011. Both charges were for retail theft, for which she was fined and subject to either supervision or conditional release. DHS characterized these crimes as crimes of “moral turpitude,” a somewhat vague term for which someone can be deported under federal law.

Siemionkowicz has not been convicted of any crimes since then, and the amounts for the retail theft were both less than $300, according to court documents. Federal Immigration Court denied Siemionkowicz a hearing for bond, which would have allowed her avoid long term detention, in late August 2025. The court then later denied her application to cancel her removal orders. Siemionkowicz has appealed these decisions, according to court documents.

Siemionkowicz’s lawsuit from this year was filed in the U.S. District Court Eastern District of Kentucky — a separate court from federal immigration court, which is a special administrative court under the DOJ, rather than a court in the conventional judicial system. Siemionkowicz alleged that she had a right to a bond hearing and that the immigration court had failed to meet its burden of proof necessitating her detention.

United States District Judge Karen Caldwell issued an opinion on Nov. 3, which you can read here, granting Siemionkowicz a bond hearing and arguing that her detention had violated her constitutional rights to due process under the law. The District Court ruled the Immigration Court had to hold a bond hearing within seven days of Nov. 3.

LINK nky will update this story as we learn more.

title: U.S. boycotts U.N. human rights review for second year running | WGCU News
description:
The aim is to ensure that every country, however powerful, undergoes a peer review of its human rights record.
Jamil Dakwar, the ACLU's human rights director, told journalists that the current U.S. administration was continuing to violate human rights "unabashed," citing the treatment of immigrants, student protesters and the LGBTQ community as examples.
Dakwar said the U.N. must hold the U.S. accountable, warning that the Trump administration wanted to "dismantle human rights."
In a written response, the State Department pointed out that Washington had already formally withdrawn from the U.N. Human Rights Council, accusing it of "pushing anti-American rhetoric."
Rights groups would like the U.N. to hold the review anyway, and take evidence about alleged violations in the U.S.
text:
Updated November 10, 2026 at 8:46 PM EST

GENEVA, Switzerland — The United States has left an empty chair at a key United Nations human rights review for the second year running, becoming the only U.N. member state ever to do so.

The review, known as the universal periodic review, is meant to be just that: universal. Each state is reviewed every four to five years by fellow member states. The aim is to ensure that every country, however powerful, undergoes a peer review of its human rights record.

As well as diplomats from countries under review, civil society groups are allowed to submit evidence too. Several made the trip to Geneva, led by the American Civil Liberties Union.

Jamil Dakwar, the ACLU's human rights director, told journalists that the current U.S. administration was continuing to violate human rights "unabashed," citing the treatment of immigrants, student protesters and the LGBTQ community as examples.

Dakwar said the U.N. must hold the U.S. accountable, warning that the Trump administration wanted to "dismantle human rights." In a written response, the State Department pointed out that Washington had already formally withdrawn from the U.N. Human Rights Council, accusing it of "pushing anti-American rhetoric."

In fact, leaving the council, which has 47 elected members, does not mean the U.S. can easily get out of the review process, which is obligatory for all 193 U.N. member states. Human rights groups see Washington's stance as part of a pattern of disengagement and even active opposition to multilateral organizations, pointing to U.S. sanctions on the International Criminal Court and the decision to leave the World Health Organization.

So what happens now? The U.N. has few sanctions against a country that does not cooperate with the review process. Israel skipped one review back in 2013 in protest at what it said was anti-Israel bias, but returned nine months later after the U.N. rescheduled. Until today's no-show by the U.S., no country has ever failed to turn up twice.

Rights groups would like the U.N. to hold the review anyway, and take evidence about alleged violations in the U.S. Member states had already drawn up a list of questions for Washington's diplomats, including questions about the use of the death penalty and restrictions on abortion.

But U.N. insiders fear that holding the review when there is no one to answer those questions could set a risky precedent. Even authoritarian regimes such as North Korea take part in the review process. If the U.N. allows a review to go ahead without U.S. participation, it could encourage other member states to stay away, too, leaving rights groups to present their evidence, as one put it, "in a vacuum."

For now, the U.N. has decided to postpone tricky deliberations about how to react until early next year. In the meantime, a process regarded as a last resort for the victims of human rights violations is not available to U.S. citizens. It is, one rights activist said in Geneva, "a crisis of accountability."

text:
SCARBOROUGH, Maine —

Vandalism and the presence of near-daily protesters, some of them armed, have led to increased security at the Scarborough ICE facility, according to a spokesperson for the agency.

There has been a small group of protesters outside the Scarborough facility ever since ICE agent David Brouillette shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian father, when he was leaving for work in Biddeford last July.

According to the lawyer for Guerrero's widow and members of Maine's congressional delegation, Guerrero was not the intended target of the ICE operation and was in the U.S. under a valid federal work authorization.

Nearly four months after his death, ICE observers still have a presence outside the agency's facility on Manson Libby Road in Scarborough. Some are monitoring the movements of agents in and out of the facility and sharing that information on social media. Others are calling for the prosecution of Brouillette and "abolishing" ICE entirely, arguing that the Trump administration's immigration crackdown is unlawful and is spreading fear within immigrant communities in Maine.

Those fears were cited by the Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition on Monday, when the organization notified community members that recent sightings of "several new vehicles" arriving at the Scarborough facility were assigned to building security, not immigration enforcement.

"We understand that any increase in immigration enforcement presence can cause fear and uncertainty," wrote Ruben Torres, the director of advocacy and policy at the Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition. "We are sharing this update to provide context and help community members distinguish this change in Scarborough ICE building security from broader enforcement activity."

Democratic congresswoman Chellie Pingree took to Facebook to share a similar message, writing that security had increased specifically because of armed protesters.

"Mainers deserve to know what’s happening in their communities and I’m continuing to monitor the situation closely," wrote Rep. Pingree. "Maine has endured too much chaos and violence at the hands of this rogue, unaccountable agency already."

On Tuesday, at least one protester could be seen outside the Scarborough facility with a firearm. Open carry is legal in Maine, assuming the firearm holder is legally allowed to possess one.

A spokesperson for ICE told Maine's Total Coverage Tuesday that the agency's officers are "under constant threat from violent agitators." The spokesperson claimed that there have been six different occasions of vandalism at the Scarborough facility in the past three months.

ICE would not disclose whether the agency had plans for increased enforcement operations in Maine, citing "operational security purposes."

text:
By Emma Farge

GENEVA, Nov 10 (Reuters) – The United States spurned a UN meeting on Tuesday where its human rights record under President Donald Trump was due to be examined, drawing criticism from rights groups who say ​violations have surged to levels not seen in decades.

Washington disengaged from the ‌Geneva-based UN Human Rights Council last year, citing an anti-Israel bias, and this is the second year in a row that it has skipped its own review — a process that even authoritarian states take part in.

The US left its seat on the stage of the UN meeting empty and the ‌council decided to ​postpone the event until January.

A US State Department spokesperson ⁠said participation would imply endorsement ⁠of the council’s work.

“This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own ‘values’ as it pushes anti-American rhetoric,” the spokesperson said, without responding to allegations about the US record.

The 47-member council has not directly ​criticised Washington’s rights record but its appointed experts have, such as over migrant deportations. Washington said deportations were carried out in accordance with US immigration law.

QUESTIONS ON ⁠ABORTION AND DEATH PENALTY

The Universal Periodic Review asks all ⁠193 UN member states to submit a rights report every ​few years and these are reviewed by other states, which provide non-binding recommendations.

UN documents show ​countries had planned on Tuesday to raise issues such as abortion and ‌the death penalty.

US and international non-governmental organisations also sent nearly 200 UN submissions covering topics from migration to racial discrimination.

“We’ve seen attacks on fundamental human rights and civil liberties unprecedented in generations,” Jamil Dakwar, of the American Civil Liberties Union, told reporters in ⁠Geneva. “Enough is enough.”

Fourteen countries are due to take part in the review process in Geneva this month. In Trump’s first term in office, the US submitted its UPR report.

Noor Abdalla, wife ⁠of pro-Palestinian student activist Mahmoud ‌Khalil, who was held in immigration detention last year, is ⁠among campaigners pressing UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker ​Turk ‌to promptly hold a briefing on the US rights situation, ​even in Washington’s ⁠absence.

“When the most powerful government in the world is not held accountable, they think that they can do whatever they want,” Abdalla told reporters.

However, diplomats were sceptical given that few states want to confront Washington.

“The view is to leave the door open and hope they come back in two years,” said a diplomat.

(Reporting by Emma Farge; Editing by Peter ​Graff and Alex Richardson)

authors: Laura Romero, Osej Serratos, ABC News

text:
In a first for the Trump administration in its ongoing immigration crackdown, some immigrant families who are not in detention are being scheduled to appear for their immigration hearings inside Texas' controversial Dilley detention center -- raising concerns among immigration advocates that people could be scared away from attending their hearings out of fear of being detained.

According to advocates and attorneys, non-detained families began receiving notices last week for in-person court hearings inside Dilley's South Texas Family Residential Center.

Standard procedure, according to immigration attorneys, has been for families who received court appearance notices to appear at their local immigration court. While some detention facilities house immigration courts, they typically only hear cases for detained individuals.

"We really did not think that it was real," said Kristin Etter, the Director of Policy and Legal Services at the Texas Immigration Law Council. "We've never heard of a detained docket, like Dilley, a detention center, having non-detained court appearances."

Congressional Democrats have accused the Dilley facility of having "horrendous conditions," with food that is allegedly "contaminated with worms and mold," drinking water that leaves detainees feeling sick, lights that stay on through the night and inadequate medical care that has led to "severe depression, hopelessness and suicidal ideation amongst their children."

Advocates told ABC News the move could make immigrant families ever more fearful of appearing for their hearings.

Casey Revkin, the co-founder of Each Step Home, a group that raises funds for detained families, told ABC News that one immigrant mother who received a notice was "filled with fear and anxiety when she saw the location."

"She was horrified," Revkin said. "She is so scared that after her hearing she and her children will be immediately detained. She is also worried about getting to court. Dilley is over an hour's drive from San Antonio and she doesn't have a car."

"Dilley is a very odd choice because it's not just a remote location, it has become synonymous with family immigration detention, isolation," Etter said. "It's the only place in the country that detains children and families, and so there's absolutely just like a symbolism of it and the message that it's sending to people."

The Department of Homeland Security has previously denied any allegations of poor conditions and the lack of access to medical care at Dilley.

In a statement to ABC News, a spokesperson for the DOJ said that the agency overseeing immigration courts conducts hearings "in a variety of locations throughout the country," including "DHS detention facilities."

"There is nothing novel about EOIR maximizing available space options to ensure aliens receive their day in court in a timely manner," the spokesperson said.

In a notice obtained by ABC News, the agency that oversees immigration courts warns people that they could be ordered removed from the U.S. if they fail to appear at a hearing, if DHS proves that a notice of the hearing was delivered.

text:
It’s business as usual for President Donald Trump's deportation offensive despite the Republican wipeout in the midterm elections.

In Los Angeles, masked immigration officers in body armor blocked a hospital emergency room driveway in a heavily Latino neighborhood early Saturday. In central Alabama, twin 19-year-old brothers from Venezuela were arrested while driving back to college a day after the election.

Advocates reported arrests from California to Michigan to Massachusetts.

After Democrats trounced the GOP and won control of the next Congress, Trump said his immigration crackdown may have been “too tough” and suggested it was time to sit down with the rival party.

“I’d love to do something on immigration,” he said in an interview with CBS “60 Minutes” recorded Friday.

Hours later, he named Stephen Miller, the architect of his hardline immigration agenda, as his new chief of staff. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, meanwhile, said his orders had not changed.

“Deportations will continue,” Mullin wrote in an online post the day after the election, warning that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement takes no days off and that “this includes on Thanksgiving, Christmas, and Election Day.”

María Bilbao, a campaign coordinator for the American Friends Service Committee in Miami, said she has received at least one call a day from someone detained in South Florida since the election.

“Everything remains exactly the same. The arrests have not ceased at all,” Bilbao said.

Florida Highway Patrol officers and ICE agents have detained people in their cars, as well as places including supermarkets, pharmacies and gas stations. Immigrants under supervision have also been arrested when they showed up at ICE's Miami office for their appointments.

Erick Gasca, 31, got home Friday night after an evening playing board games with friends. He lives near Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center in Los Angeles.

An “unprecedented” number of vehicles with tinted windows and no license plates were parked near the hospital's emergency room entrance, he said.

“I thought they were going to raid the hospital or something,” he recalled.

The Department of Homeland Security declined to explain the officers’ presence there, though Bill Essayli, the top Justice Department prosecutor in Los Angeles, said they were bringing a detainee for medical treatment. Essayli said two people were arrested for assaulting federal agents.

“ICE does not target hospitals, schools, or churches,” DHS said in a statement.

The agents' presence attracted some 30 residents and passersby. Footage shot by Gasca’s cousin, Michelle Rivera, shows protesters shouting and officers pinning someone down.

The hospital said it wasn't involved.

“White Memorial does not participate in immigration enforcement,” hospital president Daniel Fontoura said in a statement, adding it would not let such activities "compromise our commitment to patient care and safety.”

A married couple from Orlando, Florida, was arrested Saturday at the airport in Phoenix while traveling to a funeral.

Gustavo Romanello and Agustin Baccega, both from Argentina, have work permits while they seek asylum after entering the United States about six years ago, according to Jonathan Batchelor, a family friend.

Batchelor was on the phone with them at the time. A mutual friend died Friday and the couple was visiting for the funeral Saturday. As the couple left the airport, two casually dressed officers asked if one was Agustin Baccega. Batchelor heard the officer say, “Asylum seekers are not in the United States legally.”

Batchelor said he could hear Romanello walking alongside his husband during the arrest and asking the officers how to collect his things. Batchelor said they then asked what his name was, "and then the guard said, ‘Oh, do you have another set of handcuffs? This is another one.’”

The voices grew distant, and the call then ended.

Both men remain in detention centers. They worked as acrobats in Florida and had no criminal record, Batchelor said.

“This is just taking good people who have been following the rules out of their lives and out of the lives of those who rely upon them and care about them,” Batchelor said.

DHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the arrests.

The brothers were headed back to college after visiting their parents when they were stopped in a small city in central Alabama.

Luis and Carlos Orta-Santoro, 19-year-olds born in Venezuela and living in the U.S. for four years, are soccer players at Wallace State Community College in Hanceville, Alabama.

Relatives say they have pending asylum applications, valid work permits, and no criminal records. Both are now in an immigration detention facility.

“Our family is devastated,” said their aunt, Carolina Orta.

DHS said that while they had entered the country legally, they had “overstayed in defiance of our laws,” and their case would be heard by an immigration judge. It said pending asylum applications do not confer legal status in the U.S.

The school said in a statement, “Both young men are valued members of the Wallace State community, and our thoughts are with them during this difficult time. We sincerely hope for a positive resolution to their situation.”

An 8-year-old Haitian boy had been living with his uncle in San Diego since his father was deported last year. The uncle, who is not a legal guardian, took him to an ICE office when the boy was summoned Nov. 4 and taken into custody.

That left the boy “without the support of their family, community and their school,” according to a letter to top administration officials from San Diego Unified School District Superintendent Fabi Bagula and school board members.

“Children should not lose access to education simply because of circumstances unfolding around them,” they wrote.

ICE has defended its actions.

Johny Oxeda, pastor of the Fairmount Haitian Community Church, which helped get legal representation for the boy, said he’ll ultimately benefit by going through legal channels.

Activists, though, were furious.

“This is not child protection,” said Guerline Jozef of Haitian Bridge Alliance, adding, "this is state-inflicted trauma.”

___

Associated Press reporters Gisela Salomon in Miami and Elliot Spagat in San Diego contributed.

text:
Transcript

LEILA FADEL, HOST:

The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday allowed the Trump administration to keep building a wall along the southern border in Texas, including within a national park. As Carlos Morales reports, the decision comes despite an ongoing legal battle in a lower court over the project's legality.

CARLOS MORALES, BYLINE: The Supreme Court's order reverses a decision from a federal judge in El Paso that had halted the construction of 30-foot-tall steel barriers and patrol roads through desert shrubland and sweeping canyons carved by the Rio Grande.

LAIKEN JORDAHL: This decision greenlights the contractors. It allows the dynamiting of national park canyon walls, the bulldozing of pristine desert.

MORALES: Laiken Jordahl is with the Center for Biological Diversity, one of the groups that brought forward a lawsuit, along with a landowner who fears losing his property through eminent-domain proceedings. In the justices' five-page ruling, the court wrote that federal law allows the Trump administration to waive environmental protections. And as a result, there's a, quote, "clear preference for expeditious border construction" over the harms of the plaintiffs.

STEVE VLADECK: The ruling, I think, is unfortunately all too typical.

MORALES: Steve Vladeck is a law professor at Georgetown University and studies the Supreme Court.

VLADECK: The court has taken the position over the last 21 months that the executive branch suffers irreparable harm anytime a lower court stops it from doing something it wants to do, whether or not the thing it wants to do is illegal.

MORALES: In a statement to NPR, U.S. Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott said the agency will now be moving forward with critical border-security construction. Scott said the agency has met with local residents and has readjusted their plans for Big Bend National Park to preserve its unique landscape. The Trump administration has maintained barriers are needed in the Big Bend region to stop illegal crossings. Hillary Pierce is with the group Conserve Big Bend.

HILLARY PIERCE: The truth is, we do not have an immigration emergency in the Big Bend sector.

MORALES: The Big Bend sector is a nearly 500-mile stretch patrolled by CBP. Historically, it sees the fewest numbers of encounters along the Texas border, according to CBP data. The lawsuit at the center of the Supreme Court's intervention still needs to be ruled on in full. Meanwhile, landowners have lodged a separate lawsuit to stop the federal government from taking their properties.

For NPR News, I'm Carlos Morales in Marfa, Texas.

title: Immigration arrests go on unabated despite Trump's misgivings after the GOP's midterm wipeout
authors: Valerie Gonzalez And Tim Sullivan, Associated Press
description:

Hours later, he named Stephen Miller, the architect of his hardline immigration agenda, as his new chief of staff.
Officers assembled outside a Los Angeles hospital Erick Gasca, 31, got home Friday night after an evening playing board games with friends.
He lives near Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center in Los Angeles.
text:
It’s business as usual for President Donald Trump's deportation offensive despite the Republican wipeout in the midterm elections.

In Los Angeles, masked immigration officers in body armor blocked a hospital emergency room driveway in a heavily Latino neighborhood early Saturday. In central Alabama, twin 19-year-old brothers from Venezuela were arrested while driving back to college a day after the election.

Advocates reported arrests from California to Michigan to Massachusetts. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has not released numbers.

After Democrats trounced the GOP and won control of the next Congress, Trump said his immigration crackdown may have been “too tough” and suggested it was time to sit down with the rival party.

“I’d love to do something on immigration,” he said in an interview with CBS “60 Minutes” recorded Friday.

Hours later, he named Stephen Miller, the architect of his hardline immigration agenda, as his new chief of staff. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, meanwhile, said his orders had not changed.

“Deportations will continue,” Mullin wrote in an online post the day after the election, warning that ICE takes no days off and that “this includes on Thanksgiving, Christmas, and Election Day.”

María Bilbao, a campaign coordinator for the American Friends Service Committee in Miami, said she has received at least one call a day from someone detained in South Florida since the election.

“Everything remains exactly the same. The arrests have not ceased at all,” Bilbao said.

Florida Highway Patrol officers and ICE agents have detained people in their cars, as well as places including supermarkets, pharmacies and gas stations. Immigrants under supervision have also been arrested when they showed up at ICE's Miami office for their appointments.

Officers assembled outside a Los Angeles hospital

Erick Gasca, 31, got home Friday night after an evening playing board games with friends. He lives near Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center in Los Angeles.

An “unprecedented” number of vehicles with tinted windows and no license plates were parked near the hospital's emergency room entrance, he said.

“I thought they were going to raid the hospital or something,” he recalled.

The Department of Homeland Security declined to explain the officers’ presence there, though Bill Essayli, the top Justice Department prosecutor in Los Angeles, said they were bringing a detainee for medical treatment. Essayli said two people were arrested for assaulting federal agents.

“ICE does not target hospitals, schools, or churches,” DHS said in a statement.

The agents' presence attracted some 30 residents and passersby. Footage shot by Gasca’s cousin, Michelle Rivera, shows protesters shouting and officers pinning someone down.

The hospital said it wasn't involved.

“White Memorial does not participate in immigration enforcement,” hospital president Daniel Fontoura said in a statement, adding it would not let such activities “compromise our commitment to patient care and safety.”

A couple is arrested at the Phoenix airport

A married couple from Orlando, Florida, was arrested Saturday at the airport in Phoenix while traveling to a funeral.

Gustavo Romanello and Agustin Baccega, both from Argentina, have work permits while they seek asylum after entering the United States about six years ago, according to Jonathan Batchelor, a family friend.

Batchelor was on the phone with them at the time. A mutual friend died Friday and the couple was visiting for the funeral Saturday. As the couple left the airport, two casually dressed officers asked if one was Agustin Baccega. Batchelor heard the officer say, “Asylum seekers are not in the United States legally.”

Batchelor said he could hear Romanello walking alongside his husband during the arrest and asking the officers how to collect his things. Batchelor said they then asked what his name was, “and then the guard said, ‘Oh, do you have another set of handcuffs? This is another one.’”

The voices grew distant, and the call then ended.

Both men remain in detention centers. They worked as acrobats in Florida and had no criminal record, Batchelor said.

“This is just taking good people who have been following the rules out of their lives and out of the lives of those who rely upon them and care about them,” Batchelor said.

DHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the arrests.

Twin brothers seized while driving back to college

The brothers were headed back to college after visiting their parents when they were stopped in a small city in central Alabama.

Luis and Carlos Orta-Santoro, 19-year-olds born in Venezuela and living in the U.S. for four years, are soccer players at Wallace State Community College in Hanceville, Alabama.

Relatives say they have pending asylum applications, valid work permits, and no criminal records. Both are now in an immigration detention facility.

“Our family is devastated,” said their aunt, Carolina Orta.

DHS said that while they had entered the country legally, they had “overstayed in defiance of our laws,” and their case would be heard by an immigration judge. It said pending asylum applications do not confer legal status in the U.S.

The school said in a statement, “Both young men are valued members of the Wallace State community, and our thoughts are with them during this difficult time. We sincerely hope for a positive resolution to their situation.”

A Haitian boy is taken into custody, drawing protests in San Diego

An 8-year-old Haitian boy had been living with his uncle in San Diego since his father was deported last year. The uncle, who is not a legal guardian, took him to an ICE office when the boy was summoned Nov. 4 and taken into custody.

That left the boy “without the support of their family, community and their school,” according to a letter to top administration officials from San Diego Unified School District Superintendent Fabi Bagula and school board members.

“Children should not lose access to education simply because of circumstances unfolding around them,” they wrote.

ICE has defended its actions.

Johny Oxeda, pastor of the Fairmount Haitian Community Church, which helped get legal representation for the boy, said he’ll ultimately benefit by going through legal channels.

Activists, though, were furious.

“This is not child protection,” said Guerline Jozef of Haitian Bridge Alliance, adding, “this is state-inflicted trauma.”

___

Associated Press reporters Gisela Salomon in Miami and Elliot Spagat in San Diego contributed.

text:
A Chicago area-man who had no criminal record and suffered from multiple chronic health conditions died shortly after a deportation flight to Pakistan, his lawyer said Tuesday.

Sixty-one-year-old Ayaz Ahmed of Morton Grove was arrested in June by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and faced deportation for having an expired visa, said his attorney Hashim Siddique. Siddique said Ahmed’s family hired him to expedite his deportation because they feared his health would deteriorate in custody.

Ahmed needed a breathing device, nasal spray and medication for chronic conditions, according to Siddique, who also mentioned high blood pressure and a possible heart condition.

Prior to the July flight to Pakistan, Ahmed had been detained at the Clay County Detention center in Indiana, according to Siddique.

Around June 10, Siddique contacted the detention center after Ahmed’s family raised concerns about whether he was receiving prescribed medication. A jail officer, Siddique shared, assured him Ahmed was receiving them.

Siddique also spoke directly with Ahmed, who told him he was getting the medication at that time but he could not confirm whether this was being done consistently.

“He may have been [receiving his medication] when I spoke to him, but I don’t know if he was receiving it daily,” he said. “That I don’t know.”

He said he notified ICE of Ahmed’s medical needs and was told those concerns would be forwarded to the detention center.

Siddique said Clay County officials repeatedly told him that detainees could request medical care through electronic tablets. But Ahmed was not fluent in English and Siddique questioned whether he was able to properly use the system.

On June 18, Siddique learned Ahmed had been placed in medical isolation. He said a Clay County officer cited claustrophobia but the circumstances surrounding the isolation remain unclear. He described medical isolation as similar to solitary confinement, with Ahmed alone in a cell.

Clay County officials confirmed Ahmed was in detention there but would not answer questions about his medical care.

In the days before his deportation, Ahmed was transferred through several detention facilities, according to Siddique. On July 24 Ahmed was moved to Jackson Parrish Correctional Center in Louisiana; three days later, he was transferred to Camp East Montana in El Paso, Texas, and on July 29 to Prairieland Detention Center in Alvarado, Texas.

Siddique said he does not know whether Ahmed received his prescribed medication at each facility or during the deportation flight.

“He keeps getting transferred, and then I’m not sure if everything went with him, “Siddique said.

Alexa Van Brunt, director of the Illinois office of the MacArthur Justice Center, is part of a legal team that recently filed a class-action lawsuit challenging conditions at Miami Correctional Facility, an Indiana prison that also holds ICE detainees. The lawsuit alleges inadequate medical care, delays in receiving prescribed medications, prolonged solitary confinement and unsanitary conditions.

Van Brunt said frequent transfers between detention facilities pose another risk for people with chronic illnesses.

“That’s another impediment to proper care because there’s no continuity of care for people with chronic diseases like cancer or diabetes,” she said.

Siddique said he tracked Ahmed’s transfers between detention facilities through ICE notifications but received no flight itinerary or updates during the journey.

ICE officials said Ahmed was medically cleared for travel and was no longer in their custody when he died.

“No medical emergencies occurred during the flight, no signs of medical distress were observed, and no individuals required hospitalization upon landing,” the agency said in a statement.

ICE said Ahmed received all his scheduled medication during the flight.

“Any claims of neglect or mistreatment are categorically FALSE,” the agency said.

But after the plane landed, Ahmed allegedly collapsed on the tarmac in Pakistan.

Siddique said Ahmed’s son emailed him saying his father died seven hours after landing in Islamabad.

ICE officials said once Ahmed was transferred to the custody of the Pakistani government, they no longer had “authority over their care or access to their medical or official records.”

Ahmed’s family is exploring legal action, according to Siddique.

Some Chicago advocates are calling for an independent criminal investigation into Ahmed’s death and ICE’s medical standards.

“This heartbreaking and entirely preventable tragedy lays bare the harrowing human cost of rushed, aggressive immigration enforcement,” Ahmed Rehab, executive director of CAIR-Chicago, said in a statement.

The Pakistan Consulate in Chicago and the Pakistani Embassy did not respond to requests for comment.

text:
By Bill Ojile, Carrie Schaffer, and Hannah Wolf

On October 19, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari to decide what evidence a plaintiff must present to demonstrate that a facially race-neutral admissions policy is intentionally discriminatory.1 The federal courts of appeals are evenly divided, two circuits to two, on how a plaintiff must show harm. The First and Fourth circuits require proof that the racial group allegedly targeted was disadvantaged as a whole, measured against that group’s share of the applicants.2 The Second and Third circuits allow a claim to go forward on evidence of how the policy affected individual applicants, using a more individualized approach.3

The grant is significant because the Court previously turned away a similar petition following its decision to strike down affirmative action and bar race-conscious admissions in higher education.4

Background

A. The Legal Framework for Racially Neutral Policies

In Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, the U.S. Supreme Court held that the race-conscious admissions programs at Harvard College and the University of North Carolina violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.5 That decision left open a separate and increasingly contested question: When does an admissions policy that is facially neutral violate the Equal Protection Clause? Under Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Housing Development Corp., a facially neutral policy violates the Equal Protection Clause only if it was adopted with a discriminatory purpose; disparate impact alone is not enough, although impact is a starting point in the Arlington Heights intent inquiry.6 Courts also consider the historical background of the decision, the specific sequence of events leading up to it, departures from normal procedures or substantive criteria, and contemporaneous statements by decision makers.7

B. How the Circuit Split Arose

The circuit split began with Coalition for TJ, in which the Fourth Circuit concluded that a policy was race-neutral and imposed no unconstitutional disparate impact because Asian American students received offers “notably in excess of” their share of the applicant pool.8 The Supreme Court declined review, with Justice Alito, joined by Justice Thomas, warning that the rule “effectively licenses official actors to discriminate against any racial group with impunity as long as that group continues to perform at a higher rate than other groups.” In the years since, the First Circuit has adopted the Fourth Circuit’s approach, while the Second and Third Circuits have rejected it, opting instead to allow racial discrimination challenges to school admissions policies based on individualized evidence, producing the split now before the Court.

C. The Montgomery County Litigation

The Association for Education Fairness (AFEF), a parent-led coalition, sued the Montgomery County Board of Education in September 2020, after the Board adopted a new admissions policy for the county’s four magnet schools.9 The policy screened every student in the county for possible admission rather than only applicants and changed how student potential was assessed.10 AFEF alleged that under the policy, the share of Black and Hispanic students admitted increased while the share of Asian American students decreased, amounting to unconstitutional discrimination against Asian American students in violation of the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.11

A Maryland federal district court initially allowed the case to proceed, finding that AFEF had plausibly alleged discriminatory intent.12 However, after the case was allowed to proceed, the county adopted a new policy because of COVID-19 restrictions.13 Under this new policy, all students who met certain criteria, such as grades and standardized test scores, were placed in a pool and selected at random by lottery.14 The district court dismissed the case because Asian American admissions did not fall below their share of the applicant pool under this new policy, and the Fourth Circuit affirmed.15

What the Supreme Court Will Consider

The Court has not agreed to consider whether Montgomery County’s specific policy is constitutional. Instead, it will address the threshold legal question of what plaintiffs who challenge facially race-neutral admissions criteria must establish to demonstrate discrimination — specifically, whether aggregate, group-wide disparate impact measured against the applicant pool is required.

The stakes are considerable. If the Court adopts the applicant-pool benchmark, plaintiffs will face a higher threshold showing, and some claims may be dismissed before courts examine evidence of intent. If the Court endorses a more individualized approach, more challenges to race-neutral criteria are likely to survive early motions and proceed to discovery on intent.

Practical Implications

Until the Court rules, institutions should assume their race-neutral admissions criteria may be challenged, and should plan for either result. As a first step, institutions should identify and document the reasons behind each race-neutral measure they use. A clear record of non-racial rationales is a strong defense against a claim of discriminatory intent.

An applicant-pool benchmark would not end the need for careful recordkeeping. Groups admitted below their share of the applicant pool could still bring claims, so institutions should continue to keep thorough records of how and why their admissions criteria were adopted. If the Court instead adopts an individualized approach, institutions should expect more claims to survive early motions and be ready to defend the merits of intent through discovery.

Finally, a ruling for AFEF would remove the applicant pool barrier, but plaintiffs would still have to prove discriminatory intent under Arlington Heights. However, more challenges would likely reach discovery, and the institution’s internal records and documents would become central to the defense. Institutions should be ready to show that their policies are neutral on their face and that their adoption reflects legitimate, non-racial objectives.

The Court will hear oral argument early next year, with a decision expected by the end of the Court’s current term in mid-2027.

text:
The CEO of Brentwood-based CoreCivic is urging Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials to act with speed in inking contracts for immigration detention centers after Democrats scored big wins in last week’s elections.

“We would urge the ICE administration to move quickly,” President and CEO Lucibeth Mayberry said during a quarterly earnings call on Thursday. “They have a need for capacity. We have the capacity. There’s no reason to wait.”

The private prison and immigration detention center operator netted $1.3 billion in its most recent quarter from the sales of four detention centers to the Department of Homeland Security as the second Trump administration ramped up immigrant detentions nationwide. The sales helped bolster the publicly-traded company’s better-than-predicted profits in the third quarter of this year.

Mayberry said the company is hoping to sell more.

“We continue to have discussions with ICE about the potential acquisition of additional CoreCivic detention facilities,” she said, noting the discussions remain preliminary. “However, we do believe additional facility acquisitions continue to be a key element of ICE’s detention strategy.”

Historic Democratic victories on Nov. 3 could put a damper on future ICE deals after members of the newly-elected Democratic majority in the U.S. House and Senate are sworn into office in January. Democratic candidates across the country campaigned on reining in controversial ICE enforcement tactics that have led to unprecedented numbers of immigrants being detained.

Democrats have pledged scrutiny, investigations and accountability for ICE’s enforcement tactics, which have resulted in tens of thousands of immigrants with no criminal backgrounds held in detention centers, the arrests of U.S. citizens and the deaths of two Americans.

CoreCivic has drawn scrutiny for its own role in the administration’s immigration crackdown, with reports about poor and unsafe conditions at its detention centers and new questions about its sales.

A recent investigation by a Minneapolis television news station showed CoreCivic offered to sell a shuttered prison in Appleton, Minn. to the State of Minnesota for $75 million in 2025. A year later, ICE paid $485.6 million for the facility, which is to be used as an immigration detention center. Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison has called for a Congressional investigation into the sale.

ICE, however, remains the highest-funded law enforcement agency in the nation, boosted over the past two years by more than $240 billion in appropriations to the agency and the U.S. Border Patrol by a GOP-controlled Congress. President Donald Trump, in the days since his party suffered big losses in the election, has offered mixed signals about plans for the agency going forward.

Trump on Sunday said his administration’s aggressive detention deportation policy may have been “too tough” and contributed to the GOP election losses during an interview with “60 Minutes” on Sunday. However, the president also promoted the architect of his immigration policy, Stephen Miller, as his Chief of Staff. And key administration leaders have signaled the administration will stay the course on its immigration detention and deportation plans.

text:
Less than six months ago, University of Maryland student Maria Flores Garcia, 19, delivered her valedictorian speech at Parkdale High School’s graduation in Prince George’s County.

Today, she sits in ICE custody in Louisiana with her mother.

Flores Garcia and her mother drove to an annual immigration check-in in Baltimore last Thursday, an appointment that in the past has taken about 30 minutes, Flores Garcia’s boyfriend, Cesar Saavedra, said.

At the appointment, ICE officers asked Flores Garcia if she wanted to remain with her mother or leave, Saavedra said. Flores Garcia chose to stay and the two were taken into ICE custody. They’ve since been transported to a facility in Louisiana.

Saavedra, a graduate of DuVal High School, has spoken to his girlfriend over the phone multiple times since she was detained. The two have been together since the eighth grade and celebrated their five-year anniversary the week of her detention.

“Sometimes she’s very hopeful, sometimes she’s very helpless,” Saavedra said of his girlfriend’s spirits during these conversations.

He has raised over $25,000 for the mother and daughter’s legal fees via GoFundMe. The two are being represented by immigration lawyers from Murray Osorio PLLC, who didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Prince George’s County Executive Aisha Braveboy said in a statement that she is “outraged and deeply concerned” by the detention of Flores Garcia and her mother, whom she called a “law abiding county resident.”

“Maria and her mother should know they are not alone: the people of Prince George’s County stand firmly with them,” Braveboy’s statement said. “We are calling for Maria’s immediate release and safe return home.”

After graduating from Parkdale, Flores Garcia received a scholarship that covered her tuition at the University of Maryland, where she is studying public health and hopes to become a doctor. She commuted to classes from her family’s Prince George’s County home and worked at a nearby elementary school.

Flores Garcia loves kids and is “a very caring person” who loves to listen to others. Her mother is the same way and “likes to joke around,” said Saavedra.

Saavedra said he has been reaching out to lawmakers and “anyone with power” to plead his girlfriend’s case.

The university in a statement said that it is aware one of its students has been detained.

“We are working to connect our student’s loved ones with elected officials, including members of our Congressional delegation who are offering assistance to their constituent,” the university said.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen said in a statement that Flores Garcia’s detention “puts a clear lie to ICE’s claim that they are going after ‘the worst of the worst.’

“They are not. They are going after whoever they please, and it’s clear they’re not making our communities any safer,” Van Hollen said.

ICE did not respond to The Banner’s request for comment.

Flores Garcia immigrated to the U.S. when she was 9.

“I was the new girl who struggled to understand words and had to wait for someone to translate even the simplest instructions,” she said during her valedictory address.

She recalled spending “countless” hours translating her homework with her dad before becoming the star student who earned college scholarships.

“It is crucial that you never underestimate the power of determination,” Flores Garcia said in her speech.

text:
MADISON, Wis. (WBAY) - Security videos released to Action 2 News shows an off-duty Wisconsin state trooper being taken into custody by agents from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) last week.

What the videos show

One video shows two agents in plain clothes, including hooded sweatshirt jackets and baseball caps, waiting for Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe at the Dane County Regional Airport on Nov. 5.

They approach him and there’s a short discussion. The security video is silent. Van Der Merwe, 21, appears to pull identification out of his wallet and he walks off with the two agents.

In the second video, Van Der Merwe can be seen putting his hands together in front of him and one of the agents handcuffing him. A short time later, he’s led outside the airport.

A news release from Van Der Merwe’s attorneys say he told the officers he had a work permit and a pending asylum application.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) says Van Der Merwe was taken into custody in a targeted enforcement operation because he overstayed his legal time in the country. DHS says he entered the country in March 2019 and had legal permission to stay for six months.

Attorneys cite work permit and asylum application

The law firm representing the trooper said he came to the U.S. from South Africa as a child, and his family has been waiting for an asylum hearing for seven years. text:
Family members, colleagues and a U.S. congressman are demanding the immediate release and return of Dr. Ann Lawani, a highly regarded Bay Area nurse and USF professor who is being held in a federal immigration detention center.

Lawani, 39, a native of Nigeria who has lived and worked in the United States for 21 years on a valid work permit, was taken from her Lodi home in shackles by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement eight weeks ago.

Colleagues say Lawani was initially transported from a detention center in Stockton to El Paso, Texas, and subsequently transferred across the country to the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center, where she remains detained.

"Dr. Lawani has spent her entire career in service to our community, and ICE shows up on her doorstep while her elderly father is asleep in the home, whisks her away from her family, and then transports her across the entire part of the country," said U.S. Rep. Josh Harder, D-Calif.

Harder noted that Lawani had been granted a legal status known as "withholding of removal" due to the threat of persecution in Nigeria, allowing her to live and work in the U.S. legally. Harder sent a letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin demanding Lawani's immediate return to California and her family.

"This goes against everything ICE has publicly said," Harder said. "They're saying they are keeping our community safe and prioritizing folks who are threatening public safety. This is exactly the opposite."

Colleagues and university leaders expressed deep frustration over the arrest of Lawani, who oversees the master's nursing program at USF and works weekends in the cardiovascular stroke unit at John Muir Health. They noted that she has spent her career caring for vulnerable patients, including serving on the front lines throughout the COVID-19 pandemic. Her specialty is palliative and hospice care.

"I'm shocked. I'm angry. Here's a person who has committed herself to caring for others. In fact, the most vulnerable, in that her specialty is palliative and hospice care, and yet she's in this situation now. I find it unfathomable," said Eileen Fry-Bowers, dean of the USF School of Nursing.

"I'm appalled that an individual like Dr. Lawani is in this circumstance. She's one of the finest nurses that I know," Fry-Bowers added, speaking alongside other supporters. "I get really upset thinking Anne is alone right now in a place where she's not safe, and she needs to come home to us."

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

text:
LAFAYETTE – On November 9, 2026, United States District Judge Jerry Edwards Jr. sentenced Chandrakant “Lala” Patel, 40, of Oakdale, to 120 months in federal prison for Conspiracy to Commit Visa Fraud and Engaging in Monetary Transactions in Property Derived from Unlawful Activity. Patel previously pled guilty to the charges on May 28, 2026. Upon completion of his sentence, Patel will be removed from the United States.

Four other defendants were also sentenced for their roles in the visa fraud conspiracy.

On September 2, 2026, Tebo Onishea, 39, of Glenmora, was sentenced to 60 months in federal prison for Conspiracy to Commit Visa Fraud, followed by two years of supervised release. Onishea previously pled guilty to the charge on May 28, 2026.

On September 15, 2026, Chad Doyle, 56, of Oakdale, was sentenced to 60 months in federal prison for Conspiracy to Commit Visa Fraud, and ordered to pay a $30,000 fine, followed by two years of supervised release. Doyle previously pled guilty to the charge on May 20, 2026.

On September 16, 2026, Michael Slaney, 65, of Oakdale, was sentenced to 60 months in federal prison for Conspiracy to Commit Visa Fraud, and ordered to pay a $30,000 fine, followed by two years of supervised release. Slaney previously pled guilty to the charge on May 12, 2026.

Finally, on November 9, 2026, Glynn Dixon, 63, of Forest Hill was sentenced to 60 months in federal prison for Conspiracy to Commit Visa Fraud, and ordered to pay a $30,000 fine, followed by two years of supervised release. Dixon previously pled guilty to the charges on June 30, 2026.

According to court documents, the scheme occurred between about November of 2020 and July of 2025. Patel, then a local businessman, recruited foreign nationals who were seeking legal status in the United States, and accepted payments to have them falsely identified as victims in fictitious armed robbery reports. Patel then paid Onishea, Doyle, Slaney, and Dixon—all public servants acting in leadership roles in their communities—to prepare false police reports and certify immigration documents used to support fraudulent U-Visa applications. (A U-Visa is an immigration benefit available to certain noncitizens who are victims of qualifying crimes and who assist law enforcement in investigating or prosecuting those crimes.)

Court evidence showed that Onishea, Doyle, Slaney, and Dixon used their respective positions in law enforcement to certify the false police reports. At the time of the conspiracy, Onishea was the Chief of Police for the City of Glenmora; Doyle was the Chief of Police for the City of Oakdale; Slaney was the Marshal of the Ward 5 Marshal's Office in Oakdale; and Dixon was the Chief of Police for the City of Forest Hill.

Records also show that the conspirators transmitted fraudulent documents through the U.S. mail and other interstate carriers to advance the scheme.

U.S. Attorney Zachary A. Keller for the Western District of Louisiana made the announcement.

Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Internal Revenue Service-Criminal Investigation, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services – Fraud Detection and National Security Division, investigated this case as part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) under Operation Take Back America.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys John W. Nickel and Danny Siefker, with assistance from Paralegal Specialists Joanne Henry-Mills and Denise Duhon.

HSTFs and Operation Take Back America, established by President Trump in Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion, are joint operations led by the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security. Operation Take Back America is a nationwide federal initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations and protect communities from perpetrators of violent crime. Operation Take Back America streamlines efforts and resources from the Department's Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Forces and Project Safe Neighborhoods.

You may find a copy of this press release (and any updates) on the website of the United States Attorney's Office for the Western District of Louisiana at www.justice.gov/usao-wdla.

Related court documents and information may be found on the website of the District Court for the Western District of Louisiana at www.lawd.uscourts.gov or at https://www.lawd.uscourts.gov/cmecf-pacer, under Case Number 1:25-cr-00173.

text:
A Northern California lawmaker is calling on federal immigration officials to release a University of San Francisco nursing professor after she was detained in September and transferred thousands of miles away to Louisiana.

Rep. Josh Harder, D-Stockton, sent a letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Oct. 20, demanding the immediate return of Lodi resident Dr. Ann Lawani — who, Harder said, is living in the U.S. legally under judicial protection.

He also sounded the alarm that Lawani’s whereabouts are not reflected in ICE’s online detainee locator system — as part of a new policy for people with final deportation orders — leaving Lawani’s family and attorney struggling to locate her.

“ICE has also reportedly pursued her removal to an undisclosed third country without providing her or her attorney with the relevant documentation,” Harder wrote. “These circumstances raise serious concerns about due process, transparency, and the justification for her continued detention.”

Lawani, a nurse and educator, oversees 230 nursing students at the University of San Francisco and practices nursing at John Muir Health. She also serves as a caregiver for her 83-year-old father, who is currently hospitalized, according to a statement from USF.

Eileen K. Fry-Bowers, dean of USF’s School of Nursing and Health Professions, said Lawani was deeply embedded in the university community.

“Her continued absence causes real and mounting harm to the students and faculty who rely on her mentorship, to our accreditation-mandated curriculum work, and to the safety-net partnerships she has built,” Fry-Bowers said.

In his letter, Harder called Lawani’s continued detention unjustified, citing her lack of criminal history, longstanding compliance and strong ties to her community. He said the case raises broad questions about the department’s priorities, such as why significant taxpayer resources are used to target and transport people like Lawani.

“Her case illustrates the troubling consequences of an enforcement approach that fails to adequately distinguish between individuals who threaten our communities and those who help sustain them,” Harder wrote.

He asked ICE to release Lawani under an order of supervision and arrange her immediate return to California. He also requested that DHS provide Lawani and her attorney with information about her proposed country of removal, supporting travel documents and an explanation for her continued detention.

Lawani’s detention has also raised concerns at USF, where her absence has disrupted campus operations and affected nursing students and faculty. An email from USF President Salvador Aceves on Tuesday said that while Lawani and her family initially wanted to keep her detention private, they would now like the community to know.

Her brother, Samuel Lawani, also called for her return, describing her as an accomplished nurse, educator and caregiver whose work has a significant impact on patients and students.

“My family and I want to see my sister returned home safely and as soon as possible,” he said.
