text:
The human cost of the Trump administration’s immigration surge has been staggering, measured in detained parents, deported neighbors, and people held for months without ever seeing a bond hearing. There’s a second casualty, too: a Justice Department that no longer has the lawyers to keep up with the mess its own policy created.

In an October 26 letter to Chief U.S. District Judge David Estudillo of the Western District of Washington, the self-styled Acting U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd told the court that his office just doesn’t have the lawyers to keep defending the immigration detentions the administration keeps churning out. Per Floyd, the office “unfortunately does not have the available resources, at this juncture, to continue entering AUSA appearances in every one of the dozens of § 2241 Immigration Petitions filed each week.”

Floyd opens by praising the district’s streamlined habeas procedures, which he helped craft, as working “to the benefit of petitioners, the government, and the public interest.” Then comes the “however”:

Since the General Order was first issued, however, the influx of § 2241 Immigration Petitions has continued to increase. The large volumes of petitions that are being filed, often copying from other petitions, has severely impacted the government’s ability to respond to specific petitions that require appreciable attorney time from the USAO to investigate and analyze. It has also negatively impacted the government’s ability to respond to other civil litigation filed against the government in the District.

Among the burdens Floyd lists: having to “oppose EAJA motions,” which are the fee requests from the lawyers who beat the government. He also complains about responding to “motions and orders to show cause stemming from what are often technical violations of the scheduling order.” Way to downplay the government missing court deadlines.

So the government will be sitting a lot of these out. “Thus, going forward, in order to conserve resources, there will be many habeas cases in which the USAO will no longer assume responsibility for providing a defense on behalf of the respondents,” Floyd wrote.

If no government lawyer appears within seven court days of a scheduling order, the court can rule on the petitioner’s papers alone. In those cases, Floyd wrote, the office “will take no responsibility for facilitating the processing of the case through the District Court nor will it serve as a conduit for communications between the District Court and respondents in the case.” So the government’s lawyers won’t defend ICE, and they won’t pass along the judge’s messages to ICE either. Release orders can instead be emailed straight to the Northwest ICE Processing Center. Floyd’s assessment is that the “change is expected to significantly streamline and expedite the resolution of most habeas petitions, providing more discretion to the District Court.”

Meanwhile, the office he’s running is itself a legal mess. Floyd got the top job in Seattle after Attorney General Todd Blanche fired Roger Rogoff, the court-appointed U.S. Attorney, within an hour of his appointment. A federal judge has since ruled that Rogoff is the rightful officeholder, which is how we ended up with two guys in Seattle calling themselves US Attorney, neither confirmed by the Senate. The government has appealed.

None of this should surprise anyone who’s been watching the department empty out. More than 10,000 federal lawyers have left the government since the start of 2025, and DOJ alone has shed 21% of its attorneys. The department’s answer has been to recruit AUSAs over Twitter, lean on forward-this-to-a-friend referrals, lower its hiring standards, and offer $25,000 signing bonuses to anyone willing to take on immigration cases. The lawyers who stayed are so buried that one handling habeas petitions in Minnesota asked a judge to hold her in contempt so she could get some sleep. Border czar Tom Homan recently told Fox News that the courts are dealing with roughly 85,000 immigration habeas cases. About 2,000 of them have been filed in western Washington since January 2025, and when Floyd took over last year, DOJ said he’d be leading an office of about 85 attorneys.

Seattle is just the first office to put the impact of the brain drain in writing. As the DOJ’s anti-migrant surge keeps wiping out what’s left of the department, it won’t be the last.

The flood of habeas petitions didn’t come out of nowhere. It exists because the administration has been holding people without bond hearings, a policy Floyd helped pioneer. As an immigration judge in Tacoma, he was one of four judges who started denying bond hearings in 2022, years before the Trump administration took the theory nationwide. When U.S. District Judge Tiffany M. Cartwright ruled the practice unlawful last year, Floyd, by then U.S. Attorney, dismissed her decision as “an advisory opinion.” The question is now before the Supreme Court.

The letter became public when it was filed as an exhibit in the case of Baljit Singh, an asylum seeker from India. Singh was detained in September after he and some friends accidentally ended up at a Canadian border exit while visiting a state park. On Saturday, the same Judge Cartwright labeled his petition “intentionally unopposed” and ordered him released within 24 hours.

Which, for Singh, is great news. As a statement about the United States Department of Justice, it’s mortifying, and it *should* make the government rethink its catastrophic immigration policy. It won’t, but it should.

title: 7th Circ. Orders BIA To Reconsider Deported Man's Visa Bid - Law360
description:
-- A Seventh Circuit panel has ordered immigration officials to reconsider a Jamaican man's bid to reopen his deportation case.
But the opinion said immigration officials began the process of removing him to Jamaica the day he left the prison.
The panel said Panton needed proof that he met the statutory requirements for the visa and officials in New York for confirmation.
The panel noted that the Supreme Court will decide in Roney v. Barbosa da Cunha whether this court's holding in Cirrus Rojas is correct.
Circuit Judges Frank H. Easterbrook, Michael Y. Scudder, and John Z. Lee sat on the panel for the Seventh Circuit.
text:
-- A Seventh Circuit panel has ordered immigration officials to reconsider a Jamaican man's bid to reopen his deportation case.

The panel said in a seven-page opinion filed Tuesday that the Board of Immigration Appeals ignored Jamaican-born Robert Panton's request to excuse a missed deadline and confused his request for a waiver with a pending visa application.

"When an agency's rationale is deficient, and counsel advances new arguments, the normal course is a remand so that the agency can reconsider," the panel said in the opinion. "We follow that approach here."

Panton came to the United States in 1970 as a lawful permanent resident when he was 4 years old. He was involved in a large-scale drug conspiracy during the 1980s and was convicted and sentenced to life in prison in 1992.

A district court then granted Panton's bid for compassionate release in 2020. But the opinion said immigration officials began the process of removing him to Jamaica the day he left the prison.

Panton argued that he would face harm in his native country, but an immigration judge disagreed and ordered his removal. The Seventh Circuit then denied his petition for review of the removal order in 2023.

Panton applied to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security secretary for a U visa, which is available to victims of crime who assist law enforcement. The panel said his application, which remains pending, didn't prevent the judge from issuing the removal order.

The opinion noted that his drug conviction and removal order made him inadmissible, so he needed a waiver of inadmissibility to remain in the country and benefit from the visa if he ever got it. Panton attempted to increase his chances by seeking a waiver from DHS and the U.S. Department of Justice.

The panel said Panton needed proof that he met the statutory requirements for the visa and officials in New York for confirmation. But they took around three years to respond.

"Finally, on December 11, 2023, the New York Police Department certified that Panton had been the target of an attempted murder, had assisted with the investigation of that crime, and had positive equities," it said.

But it noted that the response came too late to be presented to the immigration judge, so Panton asked the BIA to reopen his case and remand with instructions to take the new information into account. But the board denied it, and Panton sought judicial review of the decision.

"The board might have denied that request on the ground that New York's certification is not as vital as Panton depicts, or perhaps that Panton is not entitled to a favorable exercise of discretion," the opinion said. "What the board said instead is hard to fathom — and, to the extent we can fathom it, impossible to accept."

The panel noted that the board said that because Panton sought relief more than 90 days after its decision, only reopening the matter sua sponte, or of their own accord, was an option.

"The board ignored the possibility of equitable tolling, even though Panton had requested that relief explicitly," the panel said. "Its statement that Panton had not even 'claimed' an exception to the 90-day limit is false."

It added that the board's claim that only U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services can issue a U visa is true, but noted that it had nothing to do with Panton's request. It noted that his request was for a judge to waive his inadmissibility and not to issue a U visa, adding that the board "seemingly equated" them.

The panel said that Panton had asked for an additional remedy that the board did not mention as a possibility.

"The agency's lawyer in this court has confessed error on the board's decision, recognizing that it was mistaken in part (conflating a visa with a waiver of inadmissibility) and nonresponsive in full," the panel said. "Still, counsel contends that the board's errors were harmless."

The opinion said that the brief recognized that the court has found that immigration judges and other officials in the DOJ can issue waivers of inadmissibility. It also noted that the brief argued that Panton can't obtain from the DOJ the kind of waiver that was addressed in other cases.

The panel said the agency's brief did not try to reconcile the Justice Department's position in Cirrus Rojas v. Olson — that inadmissible noncitizens in the country must be deemed to be seeking admission — with its position here that inadmissible noncitizens in the country cannot be deemed to be seeking admission.

The panel noted that the Supreme Court will decide in Roney v. Barbosa da Cunha whether this court's holding in Cirrus Rojas is correct. But it added that since Panton isn't in the country right now, the resolution of the tension in the agency's positions may not matter to him.

"The Board of Immigration Appeals must address and resolve the arguments that Panton advances and any response that the agency's lawyer presents," the opinion said.

But the panel said the board does not need to reconsider the possibility of reopening sua sponte as it has already declined to follow it and the decision is not judicially reviewable.

Panton's counsel, Graham White of Mayer Brown, called the decision "an important check on the government's rush to deport immigrants before their cases have been fully heard" and said it was a critical step in bringing him back "where he belongs."

"The Seventh Circuit recognized that the Board of Immigration Appeals cannot deny relief without engaging with the arguments in front of it," White added. "Due process requires the government to listen before it acts, particularly when it seeks to separate a person from his family and community."

Counsel for the government did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday.

U.S. Circuit Judges Frank H. Easterbrook, Michael Y. Scudder, and John Z. Lee sat on the panel for the Seventh Circuit.

Panton is represented by Charles Roth of The National Immigrant Justice Center and Graham White of Mayer Brown.

The government is represented by Gregory Michael Kelch of the U.S. Department of Justice.

The case is Robert Savio Panton v. Todd W. Blanche, case number 25-2528, in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit.

text:
A viral arrest during Operation Metro Surge is now at the center of a new lawsuit against the government.

Lawsuit challenges Metro Surge arrest

What we know:

In the court file, Aliya Rahman says immigration officers assaulted her, wrongly detained her, retaliated against her, and were negligently supervised during Operation Metro Surge. Photos and video of the arrest that spread in January are now part of the court record.

Timeline:

The court record includes images and video showing agents breaking Rahman’s car window, elbowing her neck and back and later carrying her by her arms and legs.

In one video from the arrest, less than a week after federal agents killed Renee Good a couple of blocks away, Rahman says, "I am an autistic disabled person, and I'm trying to go to the doctor."

"This didn't change my world view, but it definitely changed everything about how I move around the world. I am still dealing with lasting injuries," said Rahman on Tuesday. She says the physical and emotional damage is still with her 10 months later.

Government response and broader fallout

Dig deeper:

Rahman’s is at least the third lawsuit filed against the government tied to Operation Metro Surge, and several more people have filed claims that could become lawsuits.

Attorneys expect the cases to take several months to develop and a fight over whether they should go to trial.

Rahman says what happened to her was horrible, and she did not want to be a public figure, but she plans to use the case to highlight efforts to change the way law enforcement approaches minority communities.

"Aliya's lawsuit is an act of resistance and a demand for accountability. It challenges not only what happened to her, but the systems that made that possible in the first place," said Elizer Darris.

The other side:

"We are aware of the lawsuit and look forward to vigorously defending ourselves in court," a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson told FOX 9.

Just hours after the arrest, DHS posted on the site formerly known as Twitter that its officers have immunity in the conduct of their duties.

Rahman’s attorneys say the law does not work that way in every case and that a discretionary-function finding could lead to dismissal.

"They should be accountable. They did not follow their training. They did not follow their rules," said Al Gerhardstein.

What we don't know:

The Department of Justice and ICE told FO X 9 they have no comment on the pending lawsuit, so it is not clear how they plan to fight the case in court.

It is also not clear whether this case or the other Operation Metro Surge claims will reach trial.

ICE posted about the case in February as Rahman testified before Congress, saying it "have the receipts" showing she impeded or interfered with federal officers.

But federal prosecutors never charged Rahman with a crime after hours in custody, and ICE has since deleted the post.

text:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton dropped a lawsuit seeking to shut down FIEL, a Houston immigrant-rights organization the state had accused of violating nonprofit restrictions by criticizing President Donald Trump and Gov. Greg Abbott’s immigration policies.

On Monday, Paxton’s office filed a notice withdrawing the claims “with prejudice,” which means the state can’t bring the same lawsuit against the organization again. The two-page notice, which was filed in a state court in Harris County, didn’t say why Paxton’s office dropped the lawsuit.

“This lawsuit has been very burdensome for us as an institution,” said Cesar Espinosa, executive director of Familias Inmigrantes y Estudiantes en la Lucha. “Now that this is over, we can return to committing 100% of our time and energy to protecting, educating, and empowering our community.”

Paxton had filed the lawsuit against FIEL in July citing social media posts encouraging people to vote against Trump’s immigration proposals. The group opposed a 2023 law, Senate Bill 4, that would let Texas police arrest people suspected of having entered the country illegally.

The decision to drop the lawsuit against FIEL came the same day Paxton’s office dropped similar legal efforts to shut down Annunciation House, an El Paso nonprofit network of migrant shelters that has worked with Border Patrol to house immigrants who have been processed and released.

description:

Throughout his career, Miller has advocated for authoritarian, racist policies that mirror the goals of white nationalists.
Image at top: Illustration by the SPLC Citations 1 David Smith, “Stephen Miller, Architect of Trump’s Immigration Crackdown, To Become White House Chief of Staff,” The Guardian, November 6, 2026; CBS News, “Stephen Miller, Driving Force Behind DHS Overhaul, Looking To Revive the Family Separation Policy,” April 9, 2019; Sabrina Siddiqui, “Meet Stephen Miller, Architect of First Travel Ban, Whose Words May Haunt Him,” The Guardian, March 15, 2017.

text:
President Donald Trump’s appointment of Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff portends the dangerous escalation of an extremist agenda that includes attacks on immigrants, their allies and U.S. democracy. Throughout his career, Miller has advocated for authoritarian, racist policies that mirror the goals of white nationalists. With this appointment, Miller now has the potential to influence the direction of the country and policy on a global scale.

Miller is credited, by the Southern Poverty Law Center and others, with shaping the racist and inhumane immigration policies of both Trump administrations.1 This includes policy goals derived from anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim ideologies, such as the initial Muslim travel ban and efforts to end the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program. His goals also include the zero-tolerance policy that resulted in family separations, draconian immigration policies and attempts to ban birthright citizenship.2 In May 2025, Miller pushed Immigration and Customs Enforcement to make at least 3,000 immigration arrests per day.3

But he can wield the unbridled influence of this new role well beyond his hard-line immigration policy.4 Many civil rights leaders and democracy advocates have sounded the alarm, warning that Miller’s installation as chief of staff has significant negative implications for the rule of law, the concentration of executive power and institutional checks. They also warn of the implications for the rights and safety of Black and Brown people and other perceived political opponents or allies standing in the way of a white nationalist authoritarian agenda.5

In a statement to the news site TheGrio, NAACP President and CEO Derrick Johnson wrote of Miller: “He belongs before a judge. He’s a thug who will be remembered as the architect of Trump’s vile and authoritarian regime.”6

Miller has advocated broadening presidential power, expanding federal enforcement authority and suspending habeas corpus — a legal procedure requiring those who are detaining a person to justify the detention in court — to accelerate deportations. Through the Department of Government Efficiency, Miller influenced the removal of nonpartisan federal government civil servants, some who were baselessly considered part of a “deep state” plot to obstruct the Trump administration’s authoritarian plans.7

Following the electoral rebuke to the administration by midterm voters, Trump appeared to acknowledge that his deportation policies were “too tough.” However, Miller’s appointment signals that the administration is doubling down on its anti-immigrant extremist positions rather than moderating its approach.8

For more on the SPLC’s analysis of Miller, please see our Miller extremist file and the Hatewatch investigation of more than 900 emails between Miller and Breitbart News editors.

title: Maine State Library limits ICE access under new policy
description:
The Maine Library Commission unanimously adopted a policy Monday prohibiting anyone “acting on behalf of the state library” from voluntarily granting law enforcement officers access to nonpublic library areas for immigration enforcement.
The administrator would then review the documents or orders and, if necessary, consult with legal counsel before advising library staff members on how to respond.
The Maine Library Commission adopted a second policy Monday providing free notary services by appointment when the Maine State Library reopens.
Commissioners approved the new guidelines as the state prepares to reopen the Maine State Library inside the Cultural Building in Augusta.
The building, which also houses the Maine State Museum and the Maine State Archives, closed in early 2020 for a $3 million renovation.
text:
AUGUSTA — Public libraries across the country are determining how to respond to potential encounters with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement as the agency ramps up deportation enforcement this year.

The Maine Legislature passed three laws in 2026 restricting federal immigration actions: ICE Out of Policing, ICE Out of Our Homes and ICE Out of Schools and State Health Care.

All three took effect July 29. ICE Out of Schools and State Health Care covers Maine’s public libraries.

The Maine Library Commission unanimously adopted a policy Monday prohibiting anyone “acting on behalf of the state library” from voluntarily granting law enforcement officers access to nonpublic library areas for immigration enforcement.

If a law enforcement officer demands access to nonpublic areas, the policy instructs staff members to first ask why the officer needs entry.

The policy calls for library staff members to contact the designated administrator on duty if the officer possesses a court-issued warrant or any other official documents authorizing immigration enforcement activity.

The administrator would then review the documents or orders and, if necessary, consult with legal counsel before advising library staff members on how to respond.

The policy also instructs library staff members not to physically interfere with a law enforcement officer who attempts to access nonpublic library areas before this review process occurs.

The guidelines also address access to library records. Staff members cannot voluntarily offer protected patron records to officers seeking information for immigration enforcement.

As with nonpublic space access, library staff members must ask law enforcement officers requesting patron records for immigration purposes to produce a court-issued warrant or official authorization.

An administrator would then review the documents and consult legal counsel.

The policy also sets mandatory compliance guidelines if federal statutes authorize ICE or other law enforcement officers to interview noncitizens frequenting the library or access records as part of an official investigation.

Under these circumstances, the library must designate a nonpublic area where interviews or record reviews can take place.

The Maine Library Commission adopted a second policy Monday providing free notary services by appointment when the Maine State Library reopens.

The commission also unanimously reaffirmed policies on computer use, internet safety, photocopying and bulletin boards.

Commissioners approved the new guidelines as the state prepares to reopen the Maine State Library inside the Cultural Building in Augusta. The building, which also houses the Maine State Museum and the Maine State Archives, closed in early 2020 for a $3 million renovation.

Delays in elevator repairs and public computer deliveries forced the commission to push back the reopening to mid-December. The Maine State Museum reopened Oct. 24.

title: Justice Department prosecutors in Washington can't keep up with all the cases of ... - CNN
description:
Thousands of detainees have challenged their detention in federal court, requiring Justice Department prosecutors to formally respond to all the filings in the cases before a judge can rule.
The Justice Department also frequently has to follow-up in court even after the judge rules for the detainee to be released.
Prosecutors in other states across the country have previously expressed their frustration with the volume of immigration detention cases they’re facing.
Spokespeople for the US Attorney’s Office in Seattle and the Justice Department in Washington, DC, didn’t respond to requests for comment on Tuesday.
Immigrant rights officials have also been highly critical of how the Trump administration prompted the onslaught of habeas cases.
text:
Federal prosecutors in Seattle and surrounding areas of Washington state are forfeiting court fights over detained immigrants because they don’t have the resources to keep up with the flood of cases.

Thousands of detainees have challenged their detention in federal court, requiring Justice Department prosecutors to formally respond to all the filings in the cases before a judge can rule. The Justice Department also frequently has to follow-up in court even after the judge rules for the detainee to be released. While the filings are voluminous across the country, the Western District of Washington is effectively removing itself from arguing the cases in court.

The mounting case load has led to “protracted litigation” that “consumes substantial AUSA time,” the US attorney’s office said recently.

“The USAO unfortunately does not have the available resources, at this juncture, to continue entering AUSA appearances in every one of the dozens of [habeas petitions] filed each week,” Seattle’s acting US Attorney Charles Floyd wrote to Chief Judge David Estudillo on October 26.

The change in policy captures an admission by the Trump administration that its hard-line immigration detention policies are still overwhelming the court system, and the Justice Department itself. Prosecutors in other states across the country have previously expressed their frustration with the volume of immigration detention cases they’re facing.

The shift in Seattle and Tacoma also puts more control in the court’s hands to prompt the release of detainees. Floyd’s letter even encourages the court to “directly” email an ICE detention facility in Tacoma, Washington, when an immigrant housed there is to be released.

Spokespeople for the US Attorney’s Office in Seattle and the Justice Department in Washington, DC, didn’t respond to requests for comment on Tuesday.

Earlier in President Donald Trump’s second term, the administration changed its policy so that immigrant detainees didn’t have immediate resources to be released through the immigration system. Instead, they would have to file court cases, called habeas corpus petitions, asking for federal judges to approve their releases from detention. This applied to even non-violent immigrants who were detained by ICE. The number of habeas cases skyrocketed in federal courts across the country.

Nearly 100,000 of these cases have been filed in federal district courts since January 2025 — representing hundreds of thousands of undocumented people who are in detention awaiting further immigration proceedings, according to data collected by ProPublica.

The Western District of Washington has had about 2,000 of those cases as of earlier this month, according to ProPublica.

“The large volumes of petitions that are being filed, often copying from other petitions, has severely impacted the government’s ability to respond to specific petitions that require appreciable attorney time from the USAO to investigate and analyze,” the US Attorney in Seattle wrote. “It has also negatively impacted the government’s ability to respond to other civil litigation filed against the government in the District.”

The letter was made public by a different judge this weekend.

“The Government has full access to the relevant facts concerning Petitioner’s detention, yet it has offered no factual or legal basis to rebut his petition,” federal District Judge Kymberly Evanson in Seattle wrote on Saturday in one of the habeas cases where the Justice Department never responded. “The Government’s failure to oppose the petition constitutes forfeiture of the arguments it could have made.”

Judges have released many detained immigrants who file habeas cases. Some districts, like Minnesota, have been so bogged down by the habeas cases, the judges became highly critical of the Justice Department and the Trump administration’s inability to keep up with court orders.

Immigrant rights officials have also been highly critical of how the Trump administration prompted the onslaught of habeas cases.

“Because of the Trump administration’s unlawful detention policies, the federal district courts have been inundated with thousands of habeas petitions over the last two years,” Mark Fleming, the director of policy at the National Immigrant Justice Center, said on Tuesday. “This is just the latest indication that U.S. attorney resources are being distracted from important matters that communities rely on, all to defend unlawful ICE detentions.”

text:
A Minneapolis woman who was dragged from her vehicle by ICE agents while on her way to a doctor's appointment is now suing the federal government over her arrest.

ICE arrest lawsuit filed

What we know:

In a lawsuit filed against the United States government Tuesday morning, Aliya Rahman alleges misconduct by federal agents during her Jan. 13 arrest in Minneapolis.

The lawsuit includes claims of assault, battery, false arrest and imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and negligence.

Rahman is seeking compensatory damages for her physical and emotional injuries.

Arrest recounted

The backstory:

Rahman says she was driving to a doctor's appointment for a traumatic brain injury when she encountered ICE agents blocking traffic near Park Avenue and East 34th Street in Minneapolis.

The Department of Homeland Security said that agents were attempting to make an arrest when a "significant crowd" gathered, impeding the operation. Rahman says she unknowingly drove into the chaotic situation.

Rahman's confrontation occurred in the midst of the federal immigration surge launched by the Trump administration and a week after Renee Good was shot and killed in Minneapolis.

Local perspective:

According to the lawsuit, agents surrounded her vehicle and shouted conflicting commands as she attempted to get through the intersection.

Rahman says she tried her best to comply with agent demands after being engulfed in the crowd, but ultimately, agents broke her window, pulled her from her car, and dragged her from her vehicle.

Requests for accommodations ignored

Dig deeper:

While being arrested, Rahman told agents she was disabled. As she was being taken to the Whipple Federal Building, the lawsuit states that Rahman asked for accommodations for her disabilities.

In response, however, the lawsuit states that agents "responded by laughing and accusing Ms. Rahman of lying." Rahman also says she asked for a lawyer and her requests were ignored.

The lawsuit says despite Rahman's physical symptoms worsening while in custody, agents didn't seek help until after she passed out. At that point, Rahman feared she would not make it out of custody alive.

According to the lawsuit, when ICE officers did call 911, about 30 minutes after Rahman's cellmates alerted them, she was unresponsive. The lawsuit claims agents told 911 Rahman was suffering from chest pain and anxiety – which did not fit her symptoms. She was ultimately hospitalized.

What they're saying:

The lawsuit follows an administrative complaint filed by Rahman in April which Rahman says the Department of Homeland Security never responded to.

"We followed their process," Rahman's attorney, Jessica Gingold, said. "They didn't respond. And so here we are today, taking them to court."

"This didn't change my worldview, but it definitely changed everything about how I move around the world," said Rahman. "I am still dealing with lasting injuries. But I'll be honest, the hardest thing for me is knowing that this is part of a much, much longer trajectory that we can do something about."

"That is what ICE accountability means to me," continued Rahman. "That is the only thing that matters to me at this point. The rest of it, I'll figure it out. But, these are going to be lifelong injuries."

ICE statements

The other side:

Rahman was never charged with a crime for the altercation. However, in a post on X, the Department of Homeland Security called her an "agitator" and accused her of ignoring multiple commands to move her vehicle away from the scene.

text:
CHICAGO (WLS) -- A Chicago family is asking the Trump administration to reconsider the deportation of a mother of three who has been held in immigration detention centers for more than nine months despite having lived legally in the United States for decades.

The family of Martha Gutierrez said she was born in Mexico but has lived in Chicago since 1990 as a legal permanent resident. According to her relatives, Gutierrez traveled to Mexico in February and has been detained in the United States ever since.

ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch

Her family said she is facing deportation to Mexico because of two retail theft charges in Illinois that they say had already been resolved.

The detention has taken a significant toll on her daughters, who say they have been forced to navigate daily life without their mother's support.

"I ask the judge to please free her. Please let her return home with us. I ask the judge to see her as a person," daughter Irma Serrano said.

Gutierrez's daughter, Nathalie Vargas, recently celebrated her 10th birthday without her mother. Nathalie and her two sisters are now appealing to federal officials to allow Gutierrez to remain in the United States.

"It's just lonely and dull, and you can tell the sadness in everybody. We've been through a lot, but my mom has always been there for us, helping us, making sure we knew how to be independent," daughter Mariaelena Serrano said.

Gutierrez is scheduled to appear before an immigration judge Tuesday morning in Tennessee for what the family described as her final hearing.

Relatives contend that Gutierrez is not a criminal and note that she has traveled to Mexico several times over the past few decades without incident.

Pastor Julie Contreras of United Giving Hope said she is filing a clemency request with Gov. JB Pritzker in an effort to intervene in the case. She is also urging President Donald Trump to reconsider the scope of his immigration enforcement policies.

"I love my sovereign nation. I'd pick up an arm to defend it, but I would never do it at the cost of destruction of families. Only God has that right. And if you're listening to this, sir, free Martha Gutierrez," Contreras said.

The family's plea comes after Trump said during a recent interview with "60 Minutes" that some people believe immigrants who are working and contributing to society should be allowed to remain in the country.

"And there's a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes. And a large group of people think that they should be allowed to stay," Trump said.

Gutierrez's immigration hearing is scheduled for Tuesday morning in Tennessee, where a judge will determine the next step in her case.

title: Appeals court panel overturns pause on chemical weapons use near Portland ICE facility
description:
A panel of judges in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit spiked a temporary ban on chemical munitions use outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Portland.
They separately sought to limit federal law enforcement from using tear gas, pepper balls and other chemicals as a means of crowd control.
The protesters had argued the frequent tear gas usage was unlawful because it infringed on their First Amendment rights.
Neighbors of a nearby apartment complex separately argued that the tear gas, which seeped into their homes, violated their civil liberties.
Residents have talked of tear gas being so pervasive that they’ve had to wear gas masks to sleep, among other precautions.
text:
A panel of judges in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit spiked a temporary ban on chemical munitions use outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Portland.

The parallel decisions, released Tuesday, deal a legal blow to protesters and residents of an apartment complex near the facility. They separately sought to limit federal law enforcement from using tear gas, pepper balls and other chemicals as a means of crowd control.

Two federal judges in the Oregon district had originally agreed to ban the weapons, but the appellate panel paused the ban this summer. The Tuesday decisions officially overturn both bans.

The twin lawsuits emerged from the clashes outside the facility, which mostly occurred in late 2025. Federal officers stationed at the facility repeatedly clashed with protesters who opposed President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda.

While the intersection outside the South Waterfront facility has been relatively quiet for most of the year, there is a nonzero chance large protests could return as Trump enters the final two years of his presidency.

The outcome of both lawsuits will guide federal law enforcement’s strategies for deploying tear gas, flash-bang grenades and other munitions against crowds, should they reappear.

The protesters had argued the frequent tear gas usage was unlawful because it infringed on their First Amendment rights. Neighbors of a nearby apartment complex separately argued that the tear gas, which seeped into their homes, violated their civil liberties.

Earlier this year, a pair of Oregon district judges agreed to immediately, but temporarily, restrict the federal government’s tear gas use until a full hearing can be held.

The U.S. Department of Justice appealed and has found their arguments more convincing to the appeals court panels. In July, the appellate panel tentatively paused the Oregon district judge’s ruling. Their opinions on Tuesday made it official.

In a 2-to-1 ruling, the appeals court wrote that neighbors — collectively called REACH Community Development in their lawsuit — haven’t made a convincing argument that the Constitution protects them from exposure to tear gas when federal officers are using the munitions for crowd control.

The neighbors live in Gray’s Landing, an affordable-housing complex that sits kitty-corner to the ICE facility. Residents have talked of tear gas being so pervasive that they’ve had to wear gas masks to sleep, among other precautions. Some neighbors have said the chemicals have exacerbated pre-existing medical conditions.

“We are deeply disappointed by this decision, which leaves Gray’s Landing residents without the protections they sought after chemical munitions deployed by federal agents repeatedly polluted their homes and disrupted their daily lives,” Sky Perryman, of the legal group Democracy Forward, wrote in a statement.

The decision, however, merely ends the Oregon district judge’s injunction. It does not end the full lawsuit and attorneys can continue to pursue it.

In a separate 2-to-1 ruling, the appeals panel also disagreed that federal law enforcement violated protesters’ and independent journalists’ freedom of speech by deploying tear gas.

The protesters and independent journalists — represented by the American Civil Liberties Union’s Oregon chapter — had said agents wantonly used tear gas and other devices against crowds that posed no physical threat.

“Law enforcement agents may use nonlethal force to clear crowds and restore order — they need not wait until they face ‘an imminent threat of physical harm,’” Circuit Judge Kenneth K. Lee wrote.

Attorneys for the ACLU did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

description:

Dakwar said the U.N. must hold the U.S. accountable, warning that the Trump administration wanted to "dismantle human rights."
In a written response, the State Department pointed out that Washington had already formally withdrawn from the U.N. Human Rights Council, accusing it of "pushing anti-American rhetoric."
Rights groups would like the U.N. to hold the review anyway, and take evidence about alleged violations in the U.S.
text:
Updated November 10, 2026 at 8:46 PM EST

GENEVA, Switzerland — The United States has left an empty chair at a key United Nations human rights review for the second year running, becoming the only U.N. member state ever to do so.

The review, known as the universal periodic review, is meant to be just that: universal. Each state is reviewed every four to five years by fellow member states. The aim is to ensure that every country, however powerful, undergoes a peer review of its human rights record.

As well as diplomats from countries under review, civil society groups are allowed to submit evidence too. Several made the trip to Geneva, led by the American Civil Liberties Union.

Jamil Dakwar, the ACLU's human rights director, told journalists that the current U.S. administration was continuing to violate human rights "unabashed," citing the treatment of immigrants, student protesters and the LGBTQ community as examples.

Dakwar said the U.N. must hold the U.S. accountable, warning that the Trump administration wanted to "dismantle human rights." In a written response, the State Department pointed out that Washington had already formally withdrawn from the U.N. Human Rights Council, accusing it of "pushing anti-American rhetoric."

In fact, leaving the council, which has 47 elected members, does not mean the U.S. can easily get out of the review process, which is obligatory for all 193 U.N. member states. Human rights groups see Washington's stance as part of a pattern of disengagement and even active opposition to multilateral organizations, pointing to U.S. sanctions on the International Criminal Court and the decision to leave the World Health Organization.

So what happens now? The U.N. has few sanctions against a country that does not cooperate with the review process. Israel skipped one review back in 2013 in protest at what it said was anti-Israel bias, but returned nine months later after the U.N. rescheduled. Until today's no-show by the U.S., no country has ever failed to turn up twice.

Rights groups would like the U.N. to hold the review anyway, and take evidence about alleged violations in the U.S. Member states had already drawn up a list of questions for Washington's diplomats, including questions about the use of the death penalty and restrictions on abortion.

But U.N. insiders fear that holding the review when there is no one to answer those questions could set a risky precedent. Even authoritarian regimes such as North Korea take part in the review process. If the U.N. allows a review to go ahead without U.S. participation, it could encourage other member states to stay away, too, leaving rights groups to present their evidence, as one put it, "in a vacuum."

For now, the U.N. has decided to postpone tricky deliberations about how to react until early next year. In the meantime, a process regarded as a last resort for the victims of human rights violations is not available to U.S. citizens. It is, one rights activist said in Geneva, "a crisis of accountability."

name: Policy
title: The biggest loser on Election Day: Stephen Miller.
description:
Among Hispanic voters, 48 percent voted for Trump in 2024, compared to only 36 percent in 2020.
Similar gains were seen among Black voters, as 15 percent voted for Trump in 2024, compared to only 8 percent in 2020.
In California, ICE agents targeted farmworkers, many of whom had been living in the U.S. for decades and had no criminal records.
These results should not be shocking to anyone, as the writing was on the wall heading into Election Day.
And yet, President Trump doesn’t seem to get it—or simply doesn’t care.
text:
President Donald Trump has plenty of lessons he could take from the results of the 2026 midterm elections, but one might top the list: Stop mass deportations, now. Two years ago, the president ran on tightening up America’s immigration system, and voters overwhelmingly bought the message he was selling, so much so that he won over key voting blocs like young men and Hispanic people in margins the GOP had never experienced before. But in the two years since, voters have been watching Trump’s immigration promises turn into a cruel law-enforcement scheme that has killed U.S. citizens and set off a violent detention and deportation operation. Last week, millions of Americans indicated they had seen enough and chose Democrats over Republicans to represent them in what can only be interpreted as a full-scale repudiation of Trump’s—and his newly promoted chief of staff Stephen Miller’s—mass deportation agenda.

“We’re going to have the largest deportation in the history of our country,” Trump proudly announced while campaigning for president two years ago, against the backdrop of his Los Angeles golf club. “And we’re going to start with Springfield [Ohio] and Aurora [Colorado].” It was around this time that he also unleashed a bizarre and racist attack on Haitian immigrants, many of whom live in Springfield, Ohio, who he claimed were “eating the dogs” and “eating the cats.” He also exaggerated claims that Aurora was suffering from Venezuelan gangs whose members were “destroying our country.”

The sentiment behind these at times grotesque claims resonated with many voters who said they were tired of watching the Biden administration simply give in to the mass migration hitting the U.S. southern border. Trump’s hard-on-immigration stance led to massive swings from a more racially and ethnically diverse coalition of voters than Trump had earned in 2016 and 2020. Among Hispanic voters, 48 percent voted for Trump in 2024, compared to only 36 percent in 2020. Similar gains were seen among Black voters, as 15 percent voted for Trump in 2024, compared to only 8 percent in 2020. Asian voters also increased their support for Trump, with 40 percent backing him in 2024, compared to 30 percent in 2020.

The president and his anti-immigrant “hatemonger” sidekick Miller wasted no time taking these electoral wins—boosted in large part by the sons and daughters of immigrants—and using them to justify a full-throated assault on America’s immigrant communities. The day of Trump’s inauguration, Customs and Border Patrol shut down its CBP One mobile app, shutting out thousands of people who had been waiting to apply for asylum through the only legal mechanism allowed. Hours later, Trump went on to sign an obscene number of executive orders, including one attempting to strike down birthright citizenship. From there, things would only get exponentially worse—and deadly.

Shortly after the inauguration, the Trump administration would begin what can only be described as a national manhunt for Black and brown immigrants. In one of its most egregious acts of cruelty, the administration targeted over 200 Hispanic men with tattoos, claiming they were gang members, then went on to expel them to the world’s largest prison camp in El Salvador—violating a federal judge’s order. “We lived through hell,” one prisoner said to describe his four month stay at CECOT. Further showcasing the administration’s cruel intentions, when a Department of Justice lawyer admitted they had mistakenly deported Kilmar Abrego Garcia on one of those El Salvador flights, they fought tooth and nail for over a year to keep him locked up, taking his case all the way to the Supreme Court and filing a dubious indictment against him.

Soon, Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents descended upon Democrat-led cities, followed by National Guard troops, leading to mass arrests and protests. In California, ICE agents targeted farmworkers, many of whom had been living in the U.S. for decades and had no criminal records. During one raid of a local car wash, federal agents tackled the 79-year-old owner, breaking several of his ribs, injuring his elbows, and causing a traumatic brain injury. It turned out that he was a U.S. citizen.

In Chicago, a raid was executed on an apartment building where adults and children were yanked from their beds in a military-style attack in the middle of the night. Tenants said agents were arresting everyone, regardless of their citizenship status. “Federal agents reporting to [now former] Secretary Noem have spent weeks snatching up families, scaring law-abiding residents, violating due-process rights, and even detaining U.S. citizens. They fail to focus on violent criminals and instead create panic in our communities,” Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said at the time. Soon it was public knowledge that Miller had tasked federal agents with arresting 3,000 immigrants a day, leading to pure lawlessness, including bogus indictments and near-deadly shootings.

No one will ever forget what ICE then did to Minneapolis. Agents killed not one, but two U.S. citizens in the span of a month while terrorizing the entire community. To this day, the Trump administration has refused to accept accountability for the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, instead taking part in more killings, like those in Texas and Maine this past summer. This behavior created a systemic culture of fear among America’s immigrant communities, many of whom were keeping their children home from school in fear of ICE targeting them during school dropoff or pickup. Others simply stopped showing up to work after ICE began conducting workplace raids, upending industries that rely heavily on immigrant labor.

The list of the Trump administration’s lawless immigration policies goes on and on. Not only has it been weaponizing federal agents, its Justice Department has been finding novel ways to undermine America’s immigration laws. If they could not forcibly remove Black and brown immigrants who had been here lawfully and peacefully for decades, they were happy to eliminate legal protections allowing them to live and work here through ending temporary protected status and enforcing mandatory detention.

The very voters who in 2024 swung decisively toward Trump have spent the last year and half with targets on their backs. A UCLA analysis found that Latinos accounted for 9 out of 10 ICE arrests during the first six months of 2025, and the number of arrests rose drastically after Miller announced his arrest quota. Texas, Florida, California, Georgia, and Virginia experienced the highest volume of immigration enforcement in the country, and on Election Day, voters in all of these states pushed back.

In Florida, Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar tried to warn the president, filming a campaign ad that called Trump out directly. “Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” she said. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.” Last week, Salazar held on to her seat by less than a percentage point.

Texas was not as kind to the president. In Webb and Hidalgo counties, which hold Hispanic majorities, voters overwhelmingly cast their ballots for Democrat James Talarico for Senate—by roughly 50 points. And in a closely watched race down in the Rio Grande Valley, Democrat Bobby Pulido pulled off a decisive win with 62 percent of the vote over incumbent Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, in a district that Trump carried by 18 percentage points in 2024. Not to mention that Texas voters elected the state’s first-ever Latina governor, ousting Republican Greg Abbott, who has served in that role since 2015 and has been happily having Texas law enforcement cooperate with Trump’s ICE crackdowns.

Similar scenes played out in California, where roughly three-quarters of Latino voters voted for Democrats in the House, a 29-percentage-point shift from 2024. That includes California’s 22nd Congressional District, where Latinos make up 64 percent of the population. Here, progressive Democrat Randy Villegas ousted six-term incumbent Republican Rep. David Valadao. In Kansas, Hispanic-majority counties Finney and Seward shifted roughly 50 percentage points to Democrats, while Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Pennsylvania also saw sizable shifts toward Democrats in their Latino populations that in 2024 had swung to Republicans.

These results should not be shocking to anyone, as the writing was on the wall heading into Election Day. Poll after poll indicated Republicans were beginning to lose support on immigration while Democrats were beginning to gain ground on the issue. ICE has been ramping up its immigration enforcement so aggressively, with upward of 40,000 people arrested per month, that at this point there are plenty of Americans who personally know someone impacted by the president’s deportation agenda. And even those who don’t watched the clips of immigrants being violently thrown to the ground, shot in their cars at point-blank range, and having children torn from their family members—horrifying images no voter would want their elected officials to be associated with.

And yet, President Trump doesn’t seem to get it—or simply doesn’t care. Less than one week after Republicans suffered debilitating losses at the polls, he announced Miller would be promoted to being his new chief of staff. The man whose rise in politics was largely fueled by racist, xenophobic beliefs is now being given the green light to not just continue his punitive immigration policies, but to lean into his anti-immigrant fervor even more.

Meanwhile, Democrats, with their newly minted majorities in the House and Senate, have a mandate to make serious changes to the Trump administration’s immigration agenda. They can seek to use Congress’ power of the purse to defund ICE and force guardrails on agents, including penalties for those who recklessly violate federal law. They can also initiate investigations, ensuring Americans get to see exactly how Miller’s inhumane policies are hurting people.

Voters did their part; now we wait and see if the newly elected members of Congress will do theirs.

title: Justice Department prosecutors in Washington can't keep up with all the cases of ... - ABC17NEWS
description:
Thousands of detainees have challenged their detention in federal court, requiring Justice Department prosecutors to formally respond to all the filings in the cases before a judge can rule.
The Justice Department also frequently has to follow-up in court even after the judge rules for the detainee to be released.
Prosecutors in other states across the country have previously expressed their frustration with the volume of immigration detention cases they’re facing.
Spokespeople for the US Attorney’s Office in Seattle and the Justice Department in Washington, DC, didn’t respond to requests for comment on Tuesday.
Immigrant rights officials have also been highly critical of how the Trump administration prompted the onslaught of habeas cases.
text:
By Katelyn Polantz, CNN

(CNN) — Federal prosecutors in Seattle and surrounding areas of Washington state are forfeiting court fights over detained immigrants because they don’t have the resources to keep up with the flood of cases.

Thousands of detainees have challenged their detention in federal court, requiring Justice Department prosecutors to formally respond to all the filings in the cases before a judge can rule. The Justice Department also frequently has to follow-up in court even after the judge rules for the detainee to be released. While the filings are voluminous across the country, the Western District of Washington is effectively removing itself from arguing the cases in court.

The mounting case load has led to “protracted litigation” that “consumes substantial AUSA time,” the US attorney’s office said recently.

“The USAO unfortunately does not have the available resources, at this juncture, to continue entering AUSA appearances in every one of the dozens of [habeas petitions] filed each week,” Seattle’s acting US Attorney Charles Floyd wrote to Chief Judge David Estudillo on October 26.

The change in policy captures an admission by the Trump administration that its hard-line immigration detention policies are still overwhelming the court system, and the Justice Department itself. Prosecutors in other states across the country have previously expressed their frustration with the volume of immigration detention cases they’re facing.

The shift in Seattle and Tacoma also puts more control in the court’s hands to prompt the release of detainees. Floyd’s letter even encourages the court to “directly” email an ICE detention facility in Tacoma, Washington, when an immigrant housed there is to be released.

Spokespeople for the US Attorney’s Office in Seattle and the Justice Department in Washington, DC, didn’t respond to requests for comment on Tuesday.

Earlier in President Donald Trump’s second term, the administration changed its policy so that immigrant detainees didn’t have immediate resources to be released through the immigration system. Instead, they would have to file court cases, called habeas corpus petitions, asking for federal judges to approve their releases from detention. This applied to even non-violent immigrants who were detained by ICE. The number of habeas cases skyrocketed in federal courts across the country.

Nearly 100,000 of these cases have been filed in federal district courts since January 2025 — representing hundreds of thousands of undocumented people who are in detention awaiting further immigration proceedings, according to data collected by ProPublica.

The Western District of Washington has had about 2,000 of those cases as of earlier this month, according to ProPublica.

“The large volumes of petitions that are being filed, often copying from other petitions, has severely impacted the government’s ability to respond to specific petitions that require appreciable attorney time from the USAO to investigate and analyze,” the US Attorney in Seattle wrote. “It has also negatively impacted the government’s ability to respond to other civil litigation filed against the government in the District.”

The letter was made public by a different judge this weekend.

“The Government has full access to the relevant facts concerning Petitioner’s detention, yet it has offered no factual or legal basis to rebut his petition,” federal District Judge Kymberly Evanson in Seattle wrote on Saturday in one of the habeas cases where the Justice Department never responded. “The Government’s failure to oppose the petition constitutes forfeiture of the arguments it could have made.”

Judges have released many detained immigrants who file habeas cases. Some districts, like Minnesota, have been so bogged down by the habeas cases, the judges became highly critical of the Justice Department and the Trump administration’s inability to keep up with court orders.

Immigrant rights officials have also been highly critical of how the Trump administration prompted the onslaught of habeas cases.

“Because of the Trump administration’s unlawful detention policies, the federal district courts have been inundated with thousands of habeas petitions over the last two years,” Mark Fleming, the director of policy at the National Immigrant Justice Center, said on Tuesday. “This is just the latest indication that U.S. attorney resources are being distracted from important matters that communities rely on, all to defend unlawful ICE detentions.”

Questions about the economic accessibility of legal counsel for immigrant detainees is also before the Supreme Court this year.

text:
This is the transcript version of our EB-5 webinar discussing I-829 denials. Join our Immigration News Digest Newsletter for more immigration updates.

By Joey Barnett, Angelica Rice and Phillip Kuck.

🎧 Available on YouTube & Spotify

In this EB-5 webinar, WR Immigration Partner Joey Barnett is joined by WR associates Angelica Rice and Phillip Kuck to discuss EB-5 I-829 denials and the options available to investors facing removal proceedings. They examine the increasing number of I-829 denials, the reasons behind them, and how investors can challenge adverse decisions and protect their permanent residency.

1. Understanding I-829 Denials and Removal Proceedings

I-829 denials are becoming an increasing concern for EB-5 investors. To help clarify some of the terminology used throughout the discussion, the attorneys explain several key terms and their significance in the I-829 denial and removal proceedings process:

I-829 Denial: USCIS notifies the investor that their petition has been denied and explains the available options.

Notice to Appear (NTA): The government files a charging document with the immigration court, formally commencing removal proceedings.

Master Calendar Hearing: The initial procedural hearing before an immigration judge.

Immigration Judge (IJ): The judge responsible for presiding over removal proceedings and reviewing the investor’s case.

Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA): The appellate body that can review decisions made by immigration judges.

The timing between an I-829 denial and the issuance of an NTA varies. It may take weeks, months, or longer. The attorneys explain that recent cases have seen NTAs issued relatively quickly following denials.

Importantly, receiving an NTA does not mean deportation is imminent. It is the beginning of the removal proceedings process, during which investors have an opportunity to present their case.

2. Understanding I-829 Denials

The attorneys discuss several reasons USCIS may deny an I-829 petition, including:

Failure to demonstrate job creation.

Insufficient evidence showing how investment funds were spent.

Issues involving the sustainment of investment.

Source of funds and currency transfer concerns.

National security concerns.

The attorneys emphasize the importance of understanding the specific factual and legal allegations behind each denial. The reason for denial will influence the available legal strategies, the evidence required, and how the case should be presented in immigration court.

3. The Importance of Building a Strong Evidentiary Record

Investors preparing to file their I-829 petitions should proactively obtain documentation from their regional centers. This includes:

Evidence of job creation and economic model inputs.

Documentation showing how investment funds moved from the new commercial enterprise (NCE) to the job creating entity (JCE).

Bank statements and expenditure records showing how funds were used.

Copies of relevant regional center reporting, including Form I-956G.

Joey explains that regional centers should maintain documentation supporting their annual reporting obligations. Investors should request relevant records early rather than waiting until USCIS issues a request for evidence or denies their petition.

The attorneys also discuss national security concerns and the importance of challenging inaccurate factual allegations. Evidence may include personal declarations, employment and educational histories, expert witness reports, and documentation establishing the historical context of an investor’s activities or affiliations.

4. Motions to Reopen and Reconsider

Following an I-829 denial, investors may have the opportunity to file a Motion to Reopen (MTR), a Motion to Reconsider, or both. The attorneys explain the key differences:

Motion to Reopen: Introduces new, material evidence that was not previously considered and could affect the outcome.

Motion to Reconsider: Argues that USCIS made an error in applying the law or interpreting the facts already in the record.

Filing both motions can allow investors to present additional evidence alongside legal arguments challenging the denial.

Joey and the attorneys emphasize that these motions serve another important purpose: preserving the evidentiary record for potential immigration court proceedings.

However, investors must pay close attention to filing deadlines for MTRs, which are generally 30 days, with an additional three days in certain circumstances involving service by mail.

Filing a motion does not prevent the government from issuing an NTA. If an NTA is issued while a motion remains pending, the case may proceed in immigration court without waiting for USCIS to decide the motion.

5. Federal Litigation and Unreasonable Delays

The attorneys also discuss federal litigation as another potential strategy following an I-829 denial.

An Administrative Procedure Act (APA) challenge may be available when USCIS has made an arbitrary or capricious decision, abused its discretion, or otherwise acted contrary to law.

However, jurisdiction is an important consideration. If an NTA has already been issued, a federal court may determine that the immigration court is the appropriate forum to review the I-829 application.

Joey also discusses unreasonable delay lawsuits, including mandamus actions, which seek to compel USCIS to adjudicate a pending petition.

Importantly, a mandamus lawsuit seeks an adjudication, not necessarily an approval. The attorneys also address concerns that filing federal litigation could lead to retaliatory action by USCIS, noting that such action would be improper.

6. De Novo Review: A Fresh Opportunity in Immigration Court

One of the most important aspects of EB-5 removal proceedings is the opportunity for de novo review.

De novo review means the immigration judge considers the I-829 application anew (with “fresh eyes”) and reviews the record in totality, rather than simply reviewing whether USCIS made the correct decision.

This provides investors with an opportunity to submit:

New and supplemental evidence.

Additional source of funds documentation.

Updated evidence of job creation and investment sustainment.

Expert reports and personal declarations.

Legal arguments challenging the original denial.

Angelica explains that the immigration judge can consider the complete record, including evidence submitted previously to USCIS and new evidence introduced during court proceedings.

The attorneys also highlight an important distinction involving the burden of proof. Depending on the grounds for denial and the allegations in the removal proceedings, the government may bear the burden of establishing that the investor is not eligible.

Phil emphasizes that this can be a significant advantage for EB-5 investors, particularly when the government fails to present sufficient evidence supporting its allegations.

The attorneys share an example of successfully representing investors whose I-829 petitions had previously been denied. Despite multiple unsuccessful motions and a further motion still pending, they were able to obtain approval through de novo review in immigration court.

7. Cancellation of Removal as an Alternative

For certain investors, cancellation of removal may provide another potential path to permanent residency.

The attorneys focus on LPR cancellation of removal, commonly referred to as 42A.

To qualify, an investor generally must demonstrate:

At least five years as a lawful permanent resident. Conditional permanent residence counts toward this requirement.

At least seven years of continuous residence in the United States after admission in any status.

Phil explains that these requirements must be carefully evaluated because even being a few days short of the continuous residence requirement could affect eligibility.

The attorneys emphasize that cancellation of removal is an alternative form of relief, only available in immigration court, not a substitute for pursuing de novo review of the I-829 application.

Where appropriate, investors may pursue both forms of relief, allowing the immigration judge to consider alternative options depending on the circumstances.

8. Frequently Asked Questions: Maintaining Status, Working and Traveling

The attorneys address several important questions from EB-5 investors facing I-829 denials.

Do investors have to leave the United States immediately after an I-829 denial?

Not necessarily. Investors may have options to challenge the denial, including filing motions and defending their case in immigration court.

Can investors continue working?

The attorneys explain that an I-829 denial does not automatically mean an immigration judge has terminated the investor’s permanent resident status. Investors may be able to obtain an I-551 stamp from USCIS to continue documenting their status and employment authorization.

Can investors travel internationally?

The attorneys strongly caution against international travel following an I-829 denial. Even with an I-551 stamp, investors may encounter difficulties returning to the United States, particularly if an NTA is issued while they are abroad.

How can investors prove their status?

Investors may request an appointment with USCIS to obtain an I-551 stamp in their passport, which can serve as evidence of their continued status.

Can children continue attending school?

The attorneys explain that children can generally continue attending school, including college, while their immigration proceedings are pending.

The attorneys stress that each situation is different and that investors should obtain legal advice before making decisions involving employment, travel, or their immigration status.

Final Takeaways

An I-829 denial does not necessarily mean the end of an investor’s EB-5 journey. There may be several options available, including motions to reopen and reconsider, federal litigation, de novo review in immigration court, and alternative forms of relief.

Joey, Angelica and Phillip emphasize the importance of acting quickly after a denial, reviewing the original I-829 filing, gathering supporting documentation, and understanding the legal and procedural options available.

With more EB-5 investors reaching the I-829 adjudication stage, understanding how to respond to a denial and navigate potential removal proceedings is increasingly important for investors and their families.

About the Authors

Joey Barnett is a partner at WR Immigration and a member of the firm’s EB-5 and Business Immigration practices. He has extensive experience representing immigrant investors seeking U.S. permanent residency through Regional Centers and direct investments, as well as advising businesses and developers on EB-5 Regional Center projects. He serves on AILA’s EB-5 Committee and IIUSA’s Editorial Board. Recognized as a Top 25 Immigration Attorney by EB-5 Magazine from 2023 to 2025, he was also named a Top 5 Rising Star in EB-5 in 2019 and selected for inclusion in The Best Lawyers in America® in 2023. Joey also co-hosts our monthly Chatting with Charlie: EB-5 Investor Outlook webinar series alongside Charlie Oppenheim, providing insights into visa availability, Visa Bulletin developments, and their implications for EB-5 investors.

Angelica Rice is an attorney at WR Immigration with experience in business immigration, litigation, and removal defense. She previously served as an Assistant Chief Counsel with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS/ICE) in Los Angeles, where she litigated hundreds of cases before immigration courts. In private practice, she handles all manner of complex litigation cases and employment-based petitions including EB-5, EB-2 NIW, EB-1A, and O-1. She was recently selected for inclusion in the 2027 edition of The Best Lawyers in America®in the Ones to Watch awards category and served as a Speaker/Panelist at the 39th Annual AILA CA Chapters Conference. She is a member of The Florida Bar and earned her Juris Doctor from St. Thomas University School of Law after graduating cum laude from the University of Florida.

text:
A Minneapolis woman who was dragged from her car and detained by ICE agents last winter has filed a lawsuit alleging her constitutional rights were violated.

Aliya Rahman said she was trying to get to a doctor's appointment on Jan. 13 when she encountered federal agents near the intersection of 34th Street and Park Avenue in south Minneapolis. She said she was given contradictory orders by agents to continue driving or exit the vehicle.

Videos of the incident went viral. They show agents smashing Rahman’s car window and aggressively pulling her out of the car, even though she told them she was a U.S. citizen. Four agents then carried her by her legs and arms to an unmarked SUV and transported her to Whipple Federal Building.

Rahman said she told the agents she was autistic and had a traumatic brain injury, so she needed accommodation, but she was disregarded. She said her health worsened until she fell unconscious in her cell, only to wake up at Hennepin County Medical Center. She was never charged with a crime.

Rahman said she wants to highlight the long history of state violence in the United States, especially toward Indigenous and Black people.

“Since Metro Surge, we have watched ICE continue to shoot people in their cars, leave the grieving families of Keith Porter and Victor Diaz and so many others waiting for answers, expand their budget and footprint, and detain dramatically more people per month,” Rahman said. “These things happened because it was already culturally normal for law enforcement to operate without accountability.”

Rahman is alleging that federal agents engaged in battery, assault and false imprisonment, as well a number of other charges.

Local counsel Al Gerhardstein called the agents’ behavior “outrageous and illegal.”

MacArthur Justice Center Senior Attorney Jessica Gingold said the lawsuit is one more step towards holding the federal government accountable for behavior during immigration enforcement efforts across the country.

“What happened to Aliya is not a result of just a couple of rogue officers,” Gingold said. “It is the result of a lawless and negligent government, encouraging and egging on officers who were recklessly and systemically violating the rights of individuals.”

The agents involved in Rahman’s detention have not yet been publicly identified.

A spokesperson for ICE said it “does not comment on or discuss matters involving ongoing litigation.”

Other Minnesotans — including a Minneapolis Roosevelt High School educator and a nurse from St. Peter — have also filed lawsuits tied to ICE agents' conduct.

title: Supreme Court grapples with Labor Department case involving migrant worker fines
description:
The Supreme Court grappled on Tuesday with a case involving poor working and living conditions for migrant workers at a New Jersey farm and how the federal government can collect damages for violations of the migrant worker program.
The high court heard oral arguments in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, a case involving a dispute with H-2A migrant agriculture workers.
Recommended Stories The Labor Department ordered the farm to pay $211,800 in civil penalties and $344,945.80 in back wages for the alleged violations.
The farm sued the Labor Department in federal court, alleging that the department could not enforce those fines on its own and needed instead to take them to federal court.
At the heart of the arguments on Tuesday was whether the immigration component of the violations meant the claims needed to go to federal court for fines to be collected.
text:
The Supreme Court grappled on Tuesday with a case involving poor working and living conditions for migrant workers at a New Jersey farm and how the federal government can collect damages for violations of the migrant worker program.

The high court heard oral arguments in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, a case involving a dispute with H-2A migrant agriculture workers. Sun Valley Orchards, a New Jersey farm that grew vegetables and fruit, had applied for and been granted permission to import 96 noncitizen workers via the H-2A program in 2015, which included certain requirements and parameters to avoid undercutting domestic workers. The Labor Department’s Wage and Hour Division found that Sun Valley Orchards had violated several of the program’s requirements, including false promises about the living facilities, unacceptable housing and transportation, and improper deductions from workers’ wages.

Recommended Stories

The Labor Department ordered the farm to pay $211,800 in civil penalties and $344,945.80 in back wages for the alleged violations. The farm sued the Labor Department in federal court, alleging that the department could not enforce those fines on its own and needed instead to take them to federal court. At the heart of the arguments on Tuesday was whether the immigration component of the violations meant the claims needed to go to federal court for fines to be collected.
