text:
HOUSTON – In a major victory for Houston’s immigrant rights community, the State of Texas dismissed its lawsuit against FIEL Houston Inc. on November 9, 2026, bringing an end to a legal battle that had threatened to dissolve the nonprofit’s charter.

Previous story: Appeals court allows Paxton to move forward with case against FIEL Houston

What Was the Lawsuit About?

Attorney General Ken Paxton filed suit against FIEL Houston — accusing the nonprofit of violating federal 501(c)(3) rules. Specifically, the state alleged FIEL crossed legal lines by urging people not to vote for former President Donald Trump and by opposing border-security legislation.

Under Texas law, the state can seek to dissolve a nonprofit’s charter if it believes the organization violated federal or state requirements — even though revoking federal tax-exempt status is handled separately by the IRS.

The case gained momentum in October 2025, when a Texas appeals court reversed a lower-court ruling that had blocked Paxton from moving forward. That decision sent the case back to state district court, where FIEL — represented by the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund (MALDEF) — prepared to fight back.

The Dismissal: “We Are on the Right Side of History”

More than a year after the appeals court ruling, the state dropped the case entirely.

FIEL Executive Director Cesar Espinosa responded with a statement:

“History will remember who was on the right side and on the wrong side of it. Today proves once again that we continue to be on the right side of History. This lawsuit has been very burdensome for us as an institution. Now that this is over, we can return to committing 100% of our time and energy to protecting, educating, and empowering our community. We want to thank MALDEF for their unwavering support and all of our supporters who have never left our side.”

Why This Case Mattered Beyond FIEL

Constitutional law professor Josh Blackman of South Texas College of Law Houston had previously noted the case could set a significant precedent for nonprofits and advocacy organizations across the state.

“There are two things nonprofits usually can’t do: endorse political candidates and lobby for or against legislation,” Blackman explained during the case. “Groups engaging in public advocacy have to be very clear about not crossing those lines.”

Faith communities were also watching closely. Reverend Heather Tolleson of First Christian Church in Katy said the uncertainty extended to churches engaged in advocacy work. “It feels like some groups are held to one standard and others to another,” she said.

With the dismissal, those concerns — at least in this case — are now resolved.

What’s Next for FIEL Houston

FIEL says it’s ready to refocus entirely on its mission. The organization advocates for just immigration laws, access to higher education regardless of immigration status, and the rights of people in vulnerable situations.

“There’s better things to do out there than to go into legal battles,” Espinosa had said during the height of the case — and now, the organization can do exactly that.

text:
FOREST HEIGHTS, Md. — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Monday that he and President Donald Trump haven’t yet discussed any concrete immigration policy changes in the aftermath of the midterm elections as the president shifts his tone on deportations and says he’s open to working with Democrats on the issue.

Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a conference near Washington, D.C., Mullin also said he is strongly opposed to any amnesty for people living in the U.S. illegally — long a red line for Republicans that has contributed to the intractableness of the immigration issue.

The midterms highlighted voters’ disaffection toward the administration’s hard-line immigration enforcement activities and Trump has since said not only that he could work with Democrats on immigration but also, during an interview with “60 Minutes” Sunday, said that his deportation policy was too aggressive for voters.

Mullin on Monday reiterated Trump’s willingness to work with Democrats on the issue.

Mullin, who was a senator and house representative before becoming Trump’s Homeland Security secretary earlier this year, said after the election he’s been fielding calls from Democrats that he worked with in Congress on bipartisan issues.

“I’ve let the president know that those calls are coming in. And the president has said, you know, let’s start working with them and then let’s meet at some point. So that’s the extent of the conversation,” Mullin said in a briefing with reporters. “We haven’t had any conversation just on policy.”

Trump since the election has elevated Stephen Miller, the key architect of his immigration crackdown, to be his chief of staff, raising questions about how cooperation with Democrats might look so long as enforcement remains strict. Mullin called him in a post on social media last week an “excellent choice.”

Mullin, who said he worked with Democrats while he was in Congress including on immigration reform, said he thought a bipartisan approach was the only way to get anything done. But the secretary also pushed back decisively against any type of agreement that would include amnesty for people living illegally in the U.S.

“I was working on immigration reform when I was in the House and when I was in the Senate. I think the only way you can actually get it is by a bipartisan approach. But amnesty’s never going to be a solution. We’re never gonna allow amnesty to happen. So that’s a full stop,” said Mullin.

The Homeland Security secretary raised the issue of DACA — a form of protection from deportation for children brought to the country illegally by their parents. He said figuring out a way to legalize their status would be up to Congress.

“Now, if we wanna have an immigration reform to where we can look at DACA and figure out a way that these individuals can become maybe legal permanent citizens or something like this, that’ll be up to Congress to do that,” Mullin said.

Mullin spoke on the sidelines of a conference about drones and counter-drone technologies in the Washington, D.C., suburbs.

text:
The Mamdani administration is “evaluating next steps” after a federal judge ruled City Hall must comply with a federal subpoena seeking information about certain residents of a South Bronx shelter for migrant men, according to spokesperson for the mayor.

Ivonne Rodriguez, spokesperson for Mayor Zohran Mamdani, had no further comment after U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan in Manhattan ruled the city must provide to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement the names and birthdates of any shelter residents who had “serious criminal histories.” That includes residents charged with any of eight crimes: murder, manslaughter, rape, robbery, assault, grand larceny, burglary or assault of a law enforcement officer.

An ICE official previously stated in a sworn affidavit that the agency is aware of 20 immigrant residents of the shelter who have entered the country illegally and 12 who had been charged with a “serious” criminal offense.

City attorneys have fought the subpoena, arguing the request would require the city to conduct an unduly broad and burdensome investigation to produce the information.

The Department of Homeland Security declined to comment on the matter, citing ongoing litigation.

The legal action focuses on the last emergency shelter for migrants in the city. During the peak of the “migrant crisis,” as former Mayor Eric Adams termed it, the city maintained more than 260 shelters, including in sprawling tent cities and hotels across the five boroughs and in upstate communities, to house an influx of more than 240,000 migrants and asylum seekers.

Over 1,400 single adult migrant men resided at the Bronx shelter as of the end of June, according to City Hall data provided to City Council. The Bronx shelter's population has slowly shrunk over the course of this year, down from 1,670 residents in February, according to the data. The shelter was originally designed to hold up to 2,200 residents.

As of the end of June, shelters across the city were housing 27,120 migrants and asylum seekers, the vast majority of whom are families with children, according to the City Council data. That’s down from a peak of nearly 68,000 in January 2024, according to city comptroller data.

The ruling comes amid a drop-off of in visits by federal immigration officers to city shelters, seeking access to and information about immigrant residents. Federal immigration officers visited city shelters six times in the second half of last year and four times in the first half of this year, according to quarterly city reports.

That follows a surge in such visits in the first six months of President Donald Trump’s second term, a trend first reported by Gothamist. The Gothamist analysis of those visits found that federal immigration officers were able to enter private areas of city shelters or obtain resident information without presenting judicial warrants at least five times earlier this year, raising questions about whether both federal officers and local shelter employees were following the law.

The Bronx shelter opened in February 2025. Soon after taking office Jan. 1, 2026, Mamdani announced plans to close the shelter by the end of the year.

While thousands of other migrants and asylum-seekers continue to reside in the city’s shelter system, the Bronx shelter is unique in that it’s the only shelter specifically designated for migrants and operating outside of the normal Department of Homeless Services system. That allows the city to operate outside the framework of laws governing city shelters, including restrictions on size. City law currently prohibits most shelters larger than 200 people.

The shelter is currently run by the mayor’s office of Housing Recovery Operations. It is the last official Humanitarian Emergency Response and Relief Center, generally large-scale migrant shelters first announced by former Mayor Eric Adams’ administration in September 2022.

The Bronx shelter has been plagued by concerns of bed bugs and poor food, as reported by local news outlets the City Reporter and Documented. Before opening, the shelter also garnered the ire of local residents and officials, who saw the placement of the shelter in their borough as further representation that the Bronx was unfairly shouldering the city’s undesirables.

name: Human Rights
title: Aliya Rahman Wants To Unmask the ICE Agents Who Dragged Her From Her Car
authors: Sophie Hurwitz, Kiera Butler, Michael Mechanic, Madison Pauly, Alex Nguyen, Emily Jones, Rachel Santarsiero, Satchel Walton
description:
Aliya Rahman, the disabled Minneapolis resident dragged out of her car and detained by federal immigration agents last January, has tried over and over to get some accountability from the government that harmed her.
In February, Rahman testified before Congress that ICE agents smashed her windows, pulled her out of her car, ignored her assertions that she is a US citizen, taunted her for her disability, and withheld medical care until she blacked out on the floor of a cell.
Then, in June, Rahman filed a complaint with DHS’ internal Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties.
The federal government has chosen to hide.” The names of the officers who hurt Rahman are currently unknown.
“When I see ICE Out signs, I wonder what they mean now,” Rahman said Tuesday.
text:
Aliya Rahman, the disabled Minneapolis resident dragged out of her car and detained by federal immigration agents last January, has tried over and over to get some accountability from the government that harmed her. Today, she filed an assault and false imprisonment lawsuit against the federal government—one she hopes could be “copy and pasteable” onto other people’s cases.

“What happened to me is not just about ICE, and lawsuits are only one tool for fixing what is really going on,” Rahman said at a press conference Tuesday. “These things happened because it was already culturally normal for law enforcement officers to operate without accountability.” The day Rahman was arrested, the Department of Homeland Security’s X account posted a message “to all ICE officers,” telling them “you have federal immunity in the context of your duties.” In the following months, Rahman tested every possible strategy to prove that statement false.

In February, Rahman testified before Congress that ICE agents smashed her windows, pulled her out of her car, ignored her assertions that she is a US citizen, taunted her for her disability, and withheld medical care until she blacked out on the floor of a cell.

She filed a tort claim against ICE and DHS this April, seeking personal injury damages through one of the few avenues an individual can legally use to sue an otherwise-unaccountable federal agency. Then, in June, Rahman filed a complaint with DHS’ internal Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties. But that office was gutted after Trump’s return to office, so Rahman didn’t expect much of a response. “It’s hard to imagine that sending a letter to DHS to ask them to respect our civil rights will do anything,” she told me at the time.

Rahman’s tort filing from April also went unanswered. As the six-month timeline for a government response ran out, she filed a new lawsuit today, alleging assault and false imprisonment—and joining a growing number of people who are demanding legal restitution for violence done by ICE and DHS. Carlos Jimenez, a US citizen from Southern California who was shot in the back and shoulder by an ICE agent, sued the government for $25 million yesterday; in August, 54 people represented by the ACLU filed tort claims over harm done by ICE agents nationwide.

“We followed their process; they didn’t respond,” Jessica Gingold of the MacArthur Justice Center, Rahman’s lawyer, said Tuesday, referring to Rahman’s previous attempts at accountability. “Nearly seven months later, we have heard nothing. The federal government has chosen to hide.” The names of the officers who hurt Rahman are currently unknown. Through the lawsuit process, Gingold said, they will be unmasked.

“We have their pictures; we have a right to know their names. We have a right to depose them. We have a right to get their records.” Images of the six masked officers who were there that day are attached to the lawsuit as an exhibit.

Almost a year since the beginning of Operation Metro Surge, Rahman is far from the only Twin Cities resident still dealing with the repercussions of ICE’s months-long occupation. As the global NGO Human Rights Watch wrote in June, the ICE operation—which left two civilian protesters dead and entire communities traumatized—was a “humanitarian crisis.” The city of Minneapolis estimates that the surge caused $700 million in damages; the Department of Homeland Security says 4,000 people were detained.

But months after the ouster of former Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino and ICE’s partial retreat from Minnesota, Rahman says the fight isn’t over. Less than two weeks ago, an investigation by KARE 11 revealed that the Trump administration used taxpayer funds to purchase a detention center in Western Minnesota from CoreCivic—for $420 million more than the building was worth.

“When I see ICE Out signs, I wonder what they mean now,” Rahman said Tuesday. Getting rid of ICE in Minnesota, she said, means addressing the cash bail industry, extractive prison labor, and qualified immunity for police. “I desperately hope that beyond pushing Greg Bovino out of town, we will fight the things that gave rise to Metro Surge. Those are the body parts ICE is made of.”

The other legal challenge was filed by Reach Community Development, which owns Gray’s Landing, an apartment complex near the ICE facility.
Residents who live there said tear gas deployed by federal agents seeped into their homes, causing health issues.
text:
New federal appeals court rulings will change how protests and crowd control are handled around the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) building in south Portland, and what rights demonstrators, journalists and nearby residents hold under the law.

A panel of Ninth Circuit judges vacated major preliminary injunctions that previously barred federal officers’ use of non-lethal crowd-control measures like tear gas or pepper balls. It also applied strict limits on when and how they could deploy munitions near the Portland ICE facility.

In both decisions handed down Tuesday, the judges sided 2-1 with the Trump administration.

KATU has been following this unfolding legal battle, which began after a year of frequent and sometimes chaotic protests outside the facility.

PAST COVERAGE | Landlord, residents sue federal government over tear gas use near Portland ICE building

COVERAGE FROM FEBRUARY 2026:

One of the cases against the government was filed by Jack Dickinson, known as the “Portland Chicken,” and journalists. Back on March 9, U.S. District Judge Michael H. Simon issued a preliminary injunction that prohibited federal agents from deploying tear gas against the protesters unless there was a life-threatening situation.

On appeal, the Ninth Circuit panel disagreed with several key points in the lower court’s ruling, saying that based on established legal precedent, officers do not need to wait for an imminent threat of physical harm before deploying non-lethal force to disperse disorderly crowds or restore order.

They also found no broad pattern or unwritten policy that targeted protesters or reporters for their viewpoints, instead describing those affected as “unfortunate collateral casualties” amid attempts to manage unruly and sometimes violent crowds.

“The plaintiffs have not shown an unwritten policy, pattern, or practice of First Amendment retaliation and the record does not support the plaintiffs’ claim that federal agents retaliated against them for exercising their First Amendment rights,” one of the decisions reads.

The other legal challenge was filed by Reach Community Development, which owns Gray’s Landing, an apartment complex near the ICE facility. Residents who live there said tear gas deployed by federal agents seeped into their homes, causing health issues.

U.S. District Judge Amy Baggio issued a preliminary injunction that prohibited federal agents from using chemical munitions that had the likelihood of reaching the complex.

PAST COVERAGE | Federal judge limits tear gas use near Portland ICE Facility in lawsuit filed by neighbors

The Ninth Circuit also vacated the injunction in that case, ruling that neither longstanding tradition nor constitutional text supported a substantive-due-process right to be free from government use of crowd-control chemicals, even when neighbors are incidentally affected.

The court stated that “such devices have long been a common tool of law enforcement to disperse crowds that have turned disruptive and violent,” and found no legal basis for new rights as described by the plaintiffs.

While one judge dissented in part and would have kept some restrictions in place, like a ban on officers intentionally firing munitions at the head, neck or torso without justification, the majority opinion vacated the injunctions entirely.

The rulings mean that, for now, federal law enforcement can continue to use non-lethal force under guidelines already established for crowd dispersal and public safety and that broader class protections for demonstrators and observers at the Portland ICE facility do not apply.

text:
A federal judge has ordered Immigration and Customs Enforcement to release a UC Berkeley student and asylum seeker detained at San Francisco International Airport on Oct. 30.

ICE agents arrested Paula Valentina Albornoz Hernandez, a 23-year-old business administration student from Colombia, while she was waiting to board a flight with her boyfriend for a vacation in Oregon.

Her attorneys argued that the detention of Albornoz Hernandez, who had a pending asylum case and current work permit, violated the U.S. Constitution because she was deprived of her liberty without an opportunity to challenge it in court.

The Department of Homeland Security told Berkeleyside last week that Albornoz Hernandez was deportable because she had overstayed a visa in 2023, that her work authorization and pending asylum application did not confer legal status, and that “being in detention is a choice” because immigrants have the opportunity to self-deport.

On Monday, U.S. District Court Judge Dena Coggins agreed with Albornoz Hernandez, writing that “due process forbids the government from detaining the noncitizen unless they are first provided with adequate notice and a pre-deprivation hearing before a neutral arbiter.”

She ordered that Albornoz Hernandez be released immediately, and forbade the agency from requiring her to wear an electronic monitor unless it proves in a future court hearing that it is necessary.

ICE had placed Albornoz Hernandez in deportation proceedings and her asylum case will continue to make its way through immigration court, said Lizzie Fulton, the attorney representing her in that case.

In a statement Monday, DHS called Coggins “a Biden-appointed activist judge” before saying the agency “complies with all lawful court orders.” The department also defended its policy of detaining immigrants at airports, saying, “This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.”

MORE: ICE activity prompts concerns outside Elmwood Correctional Facility in Milpitas

UC Berkeley mounted an all-out effort to obtain Albornoz Hernandez’s release in the week since she was detained, with administrators rallying support from elected officials and students demonstrating on Sproul Plaza.

“I feel relieved, happy, so many positive emotions,” Liliana Iglesias, the director of UC Berkeley’s Undocumented Students Program, wrote to Berkeleyside Monday morning upon hearing the news.

Attorney Niko De Bremaeker of Centro Legal de la Raza, which filed the petition challenging Albornoz Hernandez’s detention, said Monday morning he expected it to take between a few hours and a day for her to be released. She has been held at ICE’s California City detention center, a facility in the Southern California desert.

“Federal judges have overwhelmingly found these arrests unlawful, and ICE keeps making them,” De Bremaeker said. “They need to stop, and Congress needs to investigate.”

While Albornoz Hernandez’s immigration case is still pending, Fulton said it will now be easier to pursue because she will be able to meet privately with her lawyers and prepare evidence, something that’s difficult to do while detained. Besides reuniting with her family and boyfriend, she is eager to return to her schoolwork, Fulton said.

“One of her big concerns while she was detained was missing classes,” Fulton said. “She called her graduate student instructor and asked how she can jump right back in when she’s released.”

Albornoz Hernandez’s boyfriend, Anthony, said he hit the road as soon as he heard the news, and was on his way to Bakersfield late Monday morning, where he hoped to reunite with his girlfriend after a weeklong separation that, he said, “felt like months.”

“I didn’t doubt for a second that she was going to get released,” he said. “I was ready at any time to hop in the car and just go.”

text:
Faced with an influx of petitions by people alleging they’re being unlawfully detained by federal immigration authorities, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Washington said Monday that it no longer has the staffing to defend every case and will let judges rule without government opposition.

Acting U.S. Attorney Charles Floyd said in a letter to U.S. District Judge David Estudillo that habeas corpus cases initiate “protracted litigation” with numerous hearings, briefings and motions that consume prosecutors’ resources.

“Thus, going forward, in order to conserve resources, there will be many habeas cases in which the USAO will no longer assume responsibility for providing a defense on behalf of the respondents,” Floyd wrote.

The backlog has “severely impacted the government’s ability to respond” to immigration petitions and prevented prosecutors from dealing with other unrelated civil litigation, he said. As a result, his office will decline to defend “many” habeas cases. He didn’t specify how many cases could be affected.

Judges have often ruled against the administration in cases filed by tens of thousands of detainees arguing that they were being held illegally by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It has been a source of great frustration to administration officials — and to judges and advocates who say ICE has trampled on individual rights amid the Trump administration’s hardline immigration agenda.

Last week, U.S. border czar Tom Homan told Fox News that courts have been weighed down by about 85,000 immigration habeas cases as the government carries out a sweeping crackdown.

Floyd is a former judge who, along with three other Washington judges, advocated for prohibiting immigration courts from granting bond to detainees — a question that is now before the U.S. Supreme Court.

The justices will consider whether immigrants who have been living in the U.S. have a right to a hearing to determine if they should remain detained while challenging their possible deportation.

text:
Federal immigration agents continue to obtain Maryland driver information to make arrests despite state lawmakers’ efforts to curtail access, according to a new report.

Researchers at the University of Washington’s Center for Human Rights found that laws in four states, including Maryland, intended to prevent U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection from accessing state motor vehicle data “may not be as airtight as they appear.”

Maryland has some of the strongest such laws in the nation, including a new data privacy law that took effect in July. But the state is stumbling to implement it effectively, said Angelina Godoy, the report’s author.

The report comes nearly two years into President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown that has led to more arrests of immigrants residing in Maryland than ever. Its findings spotlight how states are limited in their attempts to curb federal enforcement efforts.

ICE officers have used vehicle stops as an enforcement tool for a long time. But they have faced increased scrutiny since last year as videos of some traffic stops that turned violent have gone viral across the country.

In an emailed statement, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, wrote that its officers are highly trained and conduct vehicle stops in accordance with federal law. The statement did not, however, directly address questions regarding the report and agents’ access to Maryland data.

In 2021, local immigrant advocates hailed the passage of the Driver Privacy Act, which prohibited Maryland’s Motor Vehicle Administration from directly sharing driver’s license or vehicle registration information with immigration agents.

However, ICE continued to access that information through a back channel called the International Justice and Public Safety Network, an independent nonprofit organization that facilitates information sharing across law enforcement agencies. All 50 states participate in the system, and ICE is one of several federal agencies with membership.

In practice, the system’s users have an agency identifier code, which functions like a username, to submit queries for specific information. The query — like an ICE agent requesting the name associated with a license plate number — pings a corresponding state system that houses a variety of data, like motor vehicle records and individuals’ criminal histories. Godoy’s report indicates that this is where the leaks are.

Del. Lorig Charkoudian, a Montgomery County Democrat who sponsored the state’s most recent data privacy law, said the legislation was meant to close that loophole in cases involving immigration enforcement. It put strict guardrails on when Maryland could respond to data queries and which agencies could receive the information.

Charkoudian said that tracking and responding to ICE’s operations requires “constant vigilance” from the state and indicated she may return to the General Assembly in January with another bill that tightens the state rules further if necessary.

In an email, Yianni Varonis, spokesperson for the Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services, the state administrator of information that is accessible through the national database, wrote that Maryland is “fully committed” to the Data Privacy Act and has taken several steps to implement it.

The Department now has a screening process that asks those requesting data if their request is for immigration enforcement. If so, they must upload proof of a valid judicial warrant.

Robyne McCullough, spokesperson for the MVA, wrote in an email that the data requests may be fulfilled or denied after official review of the warrant.

Varonis highlighted that the unauthorized sharing of MVA data “can prompt immediate criminal investigations” and that officers receive regular training on how to prevent disclosures.

The MVA has already blocked over 250,000 attempts to access its records by federal agents conducting immigration enforcement, McCullough wrote. Varonis wrote in an email that both the correctional services department and the MVA are working to block system usernames associated with immigration enforcement agencies.

Godoy, however, said that immigration agents have access to tens of thousands of different usernames for the system. And evidence across various states suggests that shutting them down in a “whack-a-mole” approach isn’t entirely effective.

The MVA is also requiring all third parties who purchase its data to sign privacy agreements that prohibit its disclosure for immigration enforcement, McCullough wrote. Still, data brokers like LexisNexis are private organizations, and Godoy’s team has been unable to access and review any evidence regarding ICE purchasing MVA data through them.

Federal agents continue to get driver information “in precisely the ways these laws seek to prohibit,” the University of Washington report states.

Godoy’s team combed through federal court records in which immigration agents detail how they obtained and relied on MVA data to make arrests. The report includes cases like that of Tiago Alexandre Sousa-Martins, whom ICE accused of overstaying his visa. Federal agents shot him during a Christmas Eve arrest that began with running his license plate in a parking lot.

But it also includes cases of arrests made after July 1, when the new Data Privacy Act took effect, adding to a growing body of evidence suggesting state records continue to play a role in ICE activity.

Through public records requests, Godoy’s team obtained reports of MVA data queries made on vehicles involved in ICE traffic stops during the first two weeks of July. In an interview, Godoy also pointed to an August arrest in Laurel in which an ICE agent later testified in court to having queried law enforcement databases about a license plate to identify the registered owner.

And on Oct. 31, Alfredo Herrera, a 56-year-old New Carrollton resident who DHS said had entered the U.S. illegally, was arrested in Ellicott City by ICE after agents scanned his license plate, according to Herrera’s family.

Ninfa Amador-Hernandez, policy manager for We Are CASA, Maryland’s largest immigrant advocacy organization, wrote in an email that these data security lapses have led to Maryland families being separated by ICE enforcement.

In September, We Are CASA sued the Trump administration for what it called a pattern of indiscriminate and illegal arrests across the state, at times made during traffic stops that turned violent.

“Maryland has made a promise to protect its residents. We Are CASA is here to work closely with state officials to safeguard that promise and to remind them of the harrowing consequences of when that promise is broken,” she wrote.

text:
(The Center Square) — U.S. Supreme Court justices appeared divided on Tuesday over whether administrative agencies or federal courts should adjudicate migrant farm worker disputes.

The high court heard arguments in U.S. Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, a case challenging a more than $550,000 fee against a New Jersey farm for allegedly not providing required amenities to migrant farm workers as part of the H-2A visa program.

The H-2A visa program allows employers to recruit seasonal migrant farmworkers to address worker shortages. The businesses must provide adequate housing, fair pay, transportation and job protections to recruit workers. The requirements are designed to prevent depriving U.S. citizens of a job.

An administrative judge within the Labor Department assessed the fine over improper living conditions and unfair wages for the migrant workers against Sun Valley Orchards. The New Jersey farm later went out of business following the fine.

Sarah Harris, a principal Deputy Solicitor General, argued for the Labor Department. She said the dispute was primarily over the public rights issue of immigration, although private rights over housing and pay were involved in the case.

“That classic public rights dispute doesn’t convert to private rights just because the government requires those programs to be embedded,” Harris told justices on the court.

Several justices on the high court appeared to push back on Harris’ arguments. Justice Clarence Thomas said the case cannot solely rely on the immigration authority granted to the federal government.

“You can’t rely on immigration as a basis for this,” Thomas said. “[There are] plenty of civil penalties in the immigration process.”

Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Amy Coney Barrett appeared cautious about allowing the executive branch to have broad, sweeping powers in its adjudication of farm worker programs.

“It seems to me you’re trying to extend broad authority beyond the justification of its application,” Roberts told Harris.

Harris said Congress authorized the administrative state to handle a wide range of adjudications because federal judges do not have the resources to handle the array of issues present. She pointed to the thousands of welfare claims adjudicated by executive branch agencies on a regular basis.

“If you’re outsourcing and transferring everything that has been in agencies to federal courts [there] is resource constraints,” Harris said.

Harris said Congress gave authority to the secretary of labor to “impose” fines against businesses that employ migrant workers.

Robert Johnson, a lawyer for Sun Valley Orchards, argued that the dispute rests on differences in a contract and should be adjudicated by a federal court.

“The government invokes the idea of immigration but does not issue a judgment imposing breaches of contract at a labor issue here,” Johnson told justices on the high court.

However, justices on the high court appeared to sharply disagree with Johnson. Justices Elena Kagan, Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson said immigration was a central issue in the case regardless of the contractual disagreement.

“You’re trying to get us to say the H-2A program is not an immigration program, but it is an immigration program,” Kagan told Johnson. “It’s about the admission of foreign workers.”

Kagan said businesses that do not provide adequate pay, living conditions and other necessary resources to the government are committing visa fraud. She said the contracts are required to ensure fairness to American workers when migrants are recruited.

“We allowed these people to be brought in on a certain set of conditions,” Kagan said. “It’s a condition of admission, the condition has been violated.”

Sotomayor posed a hypothetical situation where a business broke its contract by placing a farmworker in a factory. She said, under Johnson’s proposal, the government executive branch would not be able to adjudicate it.

“You’re seriously suggesting that that could not be administratively adjudicated?”

Johnson pushed back. He said the specifics in this case do not pose that question.

“What you’re suggesting is a hypothetical where the statements would be made under false pretenses,” Johnson retorted. “Look at the nature of the allegation to see why that is not the case [here].”

Harris urged justices on the high court to issue a narrow ruling in the case. She cautioned against a ruling that would allow any issue regarding civil penalties to immediately be handled by the federal judiciary.

“It would be a big deal for the government to lose, a bigger deal to have no clarity on what public rights look like,” Harris said. “The government cannot live like that.”

name: Policy
title: The Court Against the Courts - Harvard Law Review
authors: Mira Yu, Shalev Gad Roisman, Amanda Frost, Rachel E. Rosenbloom, Aaron L. Nielson, Stephen I. Vladeck
description:
Formally, the Constitution bestows only limited “original” jurisdiction on the Court, jurisdiction that Congress, at least according to the Supreme Court, cannot constitutionally expand.
The story of the Supreme Court since early 2025 is, in the main, a story about the Court against the courts.
Justice Kavanaugh has done the most to explicate the distinction between the relative powers of district courts and the Supreme Court.
To unpack these arguments, Part I surveys the challenges district courts have encountered in litigation involving the Trump Administration.
Continue Reading in the Full PDF * Agnes Williams Sesquicentennial Professor of Federal Courts, Georgetown University Law Center.
text:
The majority can reach the result it does . . . only by arrogating to itself [the district] court’s rightful function. We know better, the majority declares today. I cannot think of a reason why.

— Justice Elena Kagan

The Supreme Court of the United States sits at the apex of a judicial system in which it is deeply dependent upon the courts beneath it. Formally, the Constitution bestows only limited “original” jurisdiction on the Court, jurisdiction that Congress, at least according to the Supreme Court, cannot constitutionally expand. And practically, the Court lacks the capacity to hear appeals in all but a tiny fraction of the total cases filed in state and federal trial courts. Even in the (dwindling) subset of cases the Justices do consider, they are necessarily reliant upon the “inferior” courts within the federal system to develop the record, sharpen the legal issues in dispute, manage the litigation, and enforce compliance with coercive orders and adverse mandates.

For all of those reasons, the Supreme Court is not just — and never has been — a standalone tribunal; it sits atop a system for which it is a steward. John Roberts isn’t the “Chief Justice of the Supreme Court”; he is the “Chief Justice of the United States.” And as Chief Justice Roberts himself recently reminded us, ensuring and preserving the proper functioning of the federal judiciary writ large has been understood for more than a century as one of the Chief Justice’s (and, through him, the Court’s) most important and enduring responsibilities.

Since shortly after President Trump returned to office in January 2025, that judicial system has been subjected to a sustained, multifront assault without precedent in American history — most of which has been directed toward federal district courts, specifically. With thousands of lawsuits filed challenging executive orders on immigration, agency spending (or not), workforce cuts, and the targeting of disfavored law firms, district judges appointed by Presidents of both parties have temporarily halted or paused well over one hundred of those initiatives. The President has responded by publicly branding individual judges “radical left lunatic[s],” “crooked,” and “rogue”; by publicly attacking their spouses and families; and by publicly urging the impeachment of D.C. District Court Chief Judge Boasberg after he blocked the government’s effort to summarily remove hundreds (if not thousands) of Venezuelan nationals under the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 (AEA).

Senior Administration officials have echoed and amplified the President’s rhetoric, and congressional Republicans have moved in parallel, taking up the President’s call to impeach federal district judges whose rulings have done nothing other than cross the Administration. In the House, Representative Derrick Van Orden filed articles of impeachment against Judge Engelmayer after he blocked the Department of Government Efficiency’s access to Treasury payment systems, and Representative Brandon Gill and other conservative members have lodged similar articles against judges accused of political bias solely for ruling against the President. Articles of impeachment have been introduced against a total of twelve different district judges since January 2025 — the only common theme among them is that their rulings angered the White House and its allies.

The Senate has also amplified this campaign. On January 7, 2026, the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Federal Courts, chaired by Senator Ted Cruz, devoted an entire hearing to the impeachment charges against Chief Judge Boasberg (D.D.C.) and Judge Boardman (D. Md.). Senator Cruz used the hearing to urge the House to advance impeachment articles, declaring that “[b]oth of these judges, I believe, meet the standard for impeachment and for conviction and removal from office.” In the same hearing, Senator Eric Schmitt referred to Chief Judge Boasberg as “the embodiment of a rogue judge” who “wears, in fact, a blue jersey.”

These executive and legislative attacks have coincided with a documented and dangerous escalation of harassment and threats directed at federal judges and their families. According to the U.S. Marshals Service, there were 564 threats against federal judges in fiscal year 2025, with 275 already logged in just the first four months of 2026 and an additional 131 since the new fiscal year had begun the previous October; the Service has asked Congress for an additional $34 million in funding, noting that “the threat environment” is “unlikely to decrease in the foreseeable future.” Beginning in late February 2025, at least a dozen federal judges received anonymous pizza deliveries — some sent in the name of Daniel Anderl, the murdered son of Judge Salas — an intimidation campaign that prompted Senator Richard Durbin to demand an FBI investigation. Chief Judge McConnell of the District of Rhode Island and Judge Coughenour of the Western District of Washington have reported sustained harassment after rulings against the Administration, with Chief Judge McConnell alone receiving more than 400 “vile” voicemails, including wishes for his imprisonment and assassination. More than 150 retired federal and state judges, joined by the newly formed Article III Coalition of some sixty former federal judges, have publicly warned that the Administration’s rhetoric is creating conditions in which, as former Judge Jones of the Middle District of Pennsylvania put it, “if we’re not careful we’re going to get a judge killed.”

All of this is happening while the federal courts have been flooded — and, in some cases, overwhelmed — by an unprecedented volume of lawsuits challenging allegedly unlawful policies and other actions by the Trump Administration. To take just one example, consider habeas petitions filed by immigration detainees. According to ProPublica, in the entire seventeen-year period from January 1, 2008, through December 31, 2024, there were 15,884 such cases filed nationwide. From January 1, 2025, through the end of August 2026, plaintiffs have filed 75,648 more — many of which have arisen from a single specific shift in the DHS’s interpretation of when noncitizens arrested and detained pending removal proceedings are entitled to be released on bond. In other words, we’ve gone from fewer than 1,000 such cases nationwide each year to more than 3,700 per month. That flood has inundated even courts far afield from the locations of targeted enforcement “surges.” The Southern District of Indiana, for instance, reported zero immigration habeas cases in 2023, one in 2024, and 484 between January 1, 2025, and August 31, 2026.

If the volume of litigation is unprecedented, so too is the rate of executive branch defiance of federal court orders — including more than fifty documented instances in New Jersey and more than 200 in Minnesota. And beyond direct noncompliance, Professors Daniel T. Deacon and Leah M. Litman have also documented the far broader and subtler rise of what they call “legalistic noncompliance,” that is, when “the executive deploys specious arguments,” uses tactics to impede courts from verifying whether their orders have been complied with, or uses alternative means to reach the same end that a court has deemed unlawful. Wherever the line may be between legalistic noncompliance and outright defiance, the upshot is that it is far more difficult for federal judges to restrain the executive branch — and to see their orders against the executive branch carried into force — than it has ever been before.

With the federal judiciary under siege from without, one might expect the Supreme Court, led by the Chief Justice of the United States, to be its shield. Yet in the story told so far, the Court appears only by its absence. And the reality is worse: In multiple distinct respects, the Court bears significant responsibility for the travails of the courts beneath it — through its own behavior, through the direct and indirect effects of its rulings, through its rhetoric, and through its refusal to meaningfully push back against these broader attacks on district courts. The Court as an institution has not explicitly endorsed the executive and legislative efforts to undermine lower courts, but its behavior has enabled them; its rulings have hamstrung those courts’ ability to hold the executive branch accountable; and, as a result, its interventions are regularly cited in support of the specious and dangerous attacks coming from elsewhere. The story of the Supreme Court since early 2025 is, in the main, a story about the Court against the courts.

Through an accelerating series of emergency docket interventions since April 2025, the Court has repeatedly stayed, narrowed, or vacated district court orders blocking executive action — often without full briefing, oral argument, or reasoned explanation. Those rulings have signaled to litigants, the public, and the lower courts that the considered factfinding and legal conclusions of trial judges (and their colleagues on the courts of appeals) are provisional placeholders to be revisited at the Justices’ discretion.

And two of those grants of emergency relief — in Trump v. J.G.G. and DHS v. D.V.D. (D.V.D. I) — came in cases in which the government had overtly defied the underlying district court rulings. In both, the majority declined to even acknowledge the government’s defiance, let alone explain why the government’s unclean hands didn’t preclude relief. As Justice Sotomayor warned in dissent, the Court thereby signaled that the government would suffer no consequences from the Justices for such misbehavior below.

Although this pattern hasn’t been limited to cases challenging federal executive branch action, it has been most pronounced in that context. Over and over again, district courts exercising their traditional equitable powers to enjoin allegedly unlawful conduct by the federal government have found their orders paused (and, in some cases, set aside) on truncated records, sometimes within days of the district court’s initial intervention. The cumulative effect has been not just doctrinal but also institutional: When reasoned trial court opinions are displaced by unsigned, unexplained stays, the public is invited to view district judges less as Article III adjudicators entitled to deference within their sphere and more as preliminary functionaries whose work matters only insofar as it survives appellate triage.

Supporters of the current Administration and of the Supreme Court have pointed to the Justices’ interventions as proof of systemic lower court errors — and of bias, malice, or simply rank incompetence on the part of (a substantial number of) district judges from across the political and ideological spectrum. Of course, that claim wholly ignores the majority of cases in which the Trump Administration is losing in lower courts and not appealing to the Justices. But even in the cases that are reaching the Supreme Court, when the Justices aren’t actually identifying the errors to which they are purportedly reacting, it’s hard to reach any objective conclusion about how, why, or even if the district courts went wrong.

If anything, these developments have been exacerbated by the Court’s newfound practice of treating even orders with no explanation whatsoever as a form of precedent that lower courts are bound to follow. The crystallization of that move in July 2025 was soon followed by an August 2025 concurring opinion in which Justice Gorsuch, joined by Justice Kavanaugh, directly accused three different district judges of “defy[ing]” the Court for failing to adequately divine the meaning of earlier, thinly (or entirely un-)explained interventions. Justice Gorsuch’s concurrence provoked strong (and unusually public) responses from a wide array of lower court judges. And yet, the Court has seemingly only dug in on the point since.

Beyond these signaling effects, the Court in recent years has also imposed new, formal limits on what district courts can actually do in suits challenging federal government action. Most visibly, in June 2025, the Court used the birthright citizenship cases to heavily circumscribe the ability of district courts (but not itself) to issue “universal” injunctions.

Two months earlier, it had barred usage of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) to bring facial challenges to immigration-detention policies — based on the view that those kinds of cases must be brought as (district-specific) habeas petitions. The 5–4 majority’s cryptic and unsigned opinion in Trump v. J.G.G. never even tried to reconcile that holding with the Court’s 2020 holding that challenges to final removal orders are not part of the historical “core” of habeas corpus. The result of this inconsistent logic has been to effectively limit district courts to district-wide (and, in some contexts, individual) relief in most immigration-detention cases, even when the challenges are all to the same nationwide policy, and even when there are tens of thousands of such cases.

And in a pair of thinly explained rulings, the Justices have also significantly narrowed the ability of district courts (as opposed to the Court of Federal Claims (CFC)) to entertain challenges to the government’s refusal to spend contractually obligated money. That difference might seem purely procedural, except that the CFC generally lacks the power to issue prospective relief. When the only consequence of refusing to honor a contract is an eventual order to honor it, a government that’s not internally committed to legal constraints has every incentive to keep refusing — delaying, in many cases, irreparably, the ability of plaintiffs to be made whole from the direct and indirect effects of the government’s unlawful behavior.

Those new constraints have come alongside broader existing limits — including decades-old statutory constraints on the jurisdiction and scope of relief district courts can provide in immigration cases; and Court-made limits on damages suits for constitutional violations by federal officers and suits for injunctive relief challenging unconstitutional law enforcement practices. Some of those limits may have predated the second Trump Administration, but they have been expanded, and their implications have been embodied, in the cases that have arisen since last spring.

All the while, the Supreme Court has neither identified nor imposed any comparable limits on its own powers. To the contrary, one can find numerous examples since April 2025 of the Justices going out of their way to protect (and even expand) their power to strike down a wide range of government actions, including through relief benefiting nonparties. Justice Kavanaugh has done the most to explicate the distinction between the relative powers of district courts and the Supreme Court. In his June 2025 concurring opinion in Trump v. CASA, Inc., he argued that it is entirely appropriate for the Supreme Court — rather than any subset of the lower courts — to provide “nationally uniform interim answer[s]” in cases challenging federal executive action. Yet in that same case, he voted not only to prevent district courts from providing those answers but also to stay three district court rulings that had provided such an answer in the birthright citizenship cases, all while refusing to provide such an answer himself.

The Court also appeared, in June 2026, to introduce a subtle but significant distinction into its approach to emergency applications in election-related disputes — suggesting that the “Purcell principle” (that federal equitable power should generally not be deployed to change the rules of an election as Election Day draws nigh) applies to lower federal courts, but not to the Justices. Likewise, a four-Justice plurality in the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) cases asserted that the Supreme Court can exercise a form of hypothetical jurisdiction to reach the merits in “interim relief” cases — never mind the Court’s emphatic rejection of such a concept in 1998.

Ultimately, this Foreword argues that the Supreme Court since early 2025 has done significant damage to the formal, practical, and moral authority of federal district courts to hold the federal government to account — while arrogating some of those same courts’ powers to itself. The cumulative effect has been to transform the district judge from an Article III adjudicator whose orders bind the parties before her, including the United States, into something closer to an adjunct of the Justices. In a growing category of cases, the Court no longer sits in review of the district courts so much as in their place, even though there are myriad reasons why even a Court that’s more willing to check the executive branch than the current one cannot go it alone.

None of this is to suggest that district courts are infallible or that they should enjoy unbounded power to halt executive action nationwide. I’ve long criticized “judge-shopping” and the broader drift that has made it too easy for a single, cherry-picked judge to bind the entire federal government. Nor is my claim that the Court was wrong on the merits of every case discussed below — or even most of them. Rather, the argument is deeper: Whatever one thinks of recent substantive results, the way the Court has reached them has worked a systematic transfer of authority away from the trial courts — a transfer that should trouble even those who applaud the outcomes. I bracket the merits not out of diffidence, but because my claim is largely orthogonal to them: The transfer of authority documented below has come through the Court’s procedural choices, and would be just as troubling if every substantive result the Court reached turned out to be correct.

To unpack these arguments, Part I surveys the challenges district courts have encountered in litigation involving the Trump Administration. Part II shows that the Supreme Court is not only undermining the lower courts’ formal and practical power but arrogating much of it to itself — with respect to factfinding, law-finding, the timing and scope of appellate review, and the balancing of equities. Despite insisting it is “a court of review, not of first view,” the Court today acts as if it is a court of first impression.

Using seven sets of cases from the past eighteen months, Part II demonstrates that lurking beneath the headlines of some of the Court’s biggest rulings are moves the Justices made to directly or indirectly undermine district courts’ ability to resolve the same types of claims. Whereas top-line analyses of rulings like Trump v. Barbara and Trump v. Slaughter have focused on the substantive merits, the way those cases reached the Supreme Court has produced ominous ramifications for district courts’ formal and moral authority going forward. The same is true if the aperture expands beyond litigation against the federal government; it is impossible to understand the significance of Louisiana v. Callais without telling the stories of the Court’s machinations in the Texas, New York, and Alabama redistricting cases, too.

Finally, Part III turns to why the daylight the Court has created between its authority and that of the lower federal courts poses a significant threat to our constitutional order. Part III identifies (1) how the Court’s moves have made it much harder for federal courts to hold the executive branch accountable; (2) how those developments have further enabled executive branch lawlessness; and (3) why restoring the authority of district courts ought to be central to any meaningful court-reform measure. These moves, as Part III develops, are best understood as one expression of what Professors Rebecca Brown and Lee Epstein call “autocratic judging” — a Court that aggrandizes its own authority at the expense of the institutions on which constitutional government depends.

This was the closing argument of Justice Jackson’s CASA dissent: “[T]h[e] Court’s complicity in the creation of a culture of disdain for lower courts, their rulings, and the law (as they interpret it) will surely hasten the downfall of our governing institutions, enabling our collective demise.” Professor Richard Re (the author of last year’s Foreword ) suggests that events of the October 2025 Term have not only dispelled the CASA dissenters’ concerns; they’ve proven that their “doomsaying” was “both falsifiable and falsified.”

Justice Jackson closed her CASA dissent by invoking Justice Robert Jackson’s celebrated concurrence in Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer :

With all its defects, delays and inconveniences, men have discovered no technique for long preserving free government except that the Executive be under the law, and that the law be made by parliamentary deliberations.

Such institutions may be destined to pass away. But it is the duty of the Court to be last, not first, to give them up.

In reaching back to Justice Robert Jackson, the third Justice Jackson was insisting that the responsibility to keep the Executive “under the law” — and to be “last, not first” to surrender it — falls on the whole federal judiciary, not just the Supreme Court. A holistic assessment of what has happened over the past eighteen months suggests both that Justices Jackson were close to the mark, and that reports of the CASA dissenters’ “falsification” are premature. The gravest threat to that shared duty today comes not from the Executive alone but also from the Supreme Court — which has set itself against the courts beneath it.

* Agnes Williams Sesquicentennial Professor of Federal Courts, Georgetown University Law Center. I am grateful to Grace Kiple, Abby Liman, Ava Singh, and Mackenzie Webb for truly extraordinary research assistance; to Will Baude, Joan Biskupic, Maureen Carroll, Michael Dreeben, Jack Goldsmith, Ryan Goodman, Irv Gornstein, Sherrilyn Ifill, Kate Klonick, Alli Orr Larsen, Marty Lederman, Sandy Levinson, Marin Levy, Abby Liman, Leah Litman, Alyssa Negvesky, Richard Re, David Reiser, Judith Resnik, Kate Shaw, Brad Snyder; and to participants in a faculty workshop at Georgetown and in the Public Law Workshop at Yale, especially Robert Post and Reva Siegel, for their immensely helpful feedback.
