title: Berk v. Choy - Harvard Law Review
description:
Berk then sued Dr. Choy and Beebe Medical Center in Delaware federal court for medical malpractice.
Relying on Third Circuit precedent treating similar affidavit requirements as substantive state law, the court held that Delaware’s requirement applied in federal diversity cases.
The scope a court gives to a Federal Rule affects the likelihood that state law will survive.
In state court, a defendant may obtain an early ruling, avoid discovery, and recover fees if the claim lacks merit.
A defendant may receive the protections of anti-SLAPP laws in state court yet lose those protections solely because the plaintiff filed in federal court.
text:
At some point every year, wide-eyed 1Ls are taught the difference between substance and procedure in Civil Procedure — and sooner or later, they learn that the distinction is easier stated than applied. In 1934, Congress built that distinction into the Rules Enabling Act (REA), authorizing federal courts to apply uniform rules of “practice and procedure” so long as those rules do not “abridge, enlarge or modify” substantive rights. Last Term, in Berk v. Choy, the Supreme Court held that Rule 8 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure displaced a Delaware law requiring an expert affidavit of merit to be filed by plaintiffs bringing a medical malpractice lawsuit. After conducting a textual analysis of Rule 8, the Court concluded that the Rule’s requirement of a “short and plain statement” showing that a plaintiff is entitled to relief precluded Delaware from demanding additional evidence at the start of litigation in federal court. In so doing, the Court adopted a broad view of Rule 8’s reach and a narrow view of the REA’s protection of substantive rights. Together, those moves make it easier for federal courts to find conflicts with — and ultimately displace — state laws that protect substantive interests through procedural mechanisms, including anti–Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation (SLAPP) statutes.

In August 2020, Harold Berk fractured his ankle in Delaware. According to his complaint, hospital employees repeatedly manipulated his injured leg while attempting to fit it into a protective boot, thereby aggravating the fracture. He further alleged that his doctor, Dr. Wilson Choy, failed to order additional imaging and that later imaging revealed a severe fracture that required surgery. Berk then sued Dr. Choy and Beebe Medical Center in Delaware federal court for medical malpractice. The district court dismissed his claims without prejudice because Berk had not filed the expert affidavit of merit required by Delaware law. Relying on Third Circuit precedent treating similar affidavit requirements as substantive state law, the court held that Delaware’s requirement applied in federal diversity cases.

The Third Circuit affirmed. It reasoned that Delaware’s affidavit requirement did not conflict with the Federal Rules governing pleading and certification — Rules 8, 9, 10, 11, or 12 — because the affidavit was separate from the complaint and served a different function from those Rules’ pleading and certification requirements. The court also relied on prior Third Circuit decisions holding that materially similar Pennsylvania and New Jersey requirements occupied a separate sphere from the Federal Rules. Having found no conflict, the court proceeded to the Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins inquiry. Under Erie, federal courts sitting in diversity apply state substantive law, and the determination of whether a rule is substantive or procedural is informed by Erie’s twin aims: “discouragement of forum-shopping and avoidance of inequitable administration of the laws.” The Third Circuit held that the state’s requirement was outcome determinative and that failing to apply it would frustrate Erie’s twin aims. It therefore concluded that the requirement was substantive.

The Supreme Court reversed. Writing for the Court, Justice Barrett first explained that “when a valid Federal Rule of Civil Procedure is on point, a federal court bypasses Erie’s inquiry altogether.” A valid Federal Rule displaces contrary state law even if that law would otherwise qualify as substantive under Erie. The Court therefore asked first whether a Federal Rule “answers the question in dispute” and, if so, whether that Rule exceeds the authority granted by the REA.

The Court held that Rule 8 answered the disputed question. Rule 8 requires only “a short and plain statement of the claim,” which the majority read to establish, “implicitly, but with unmistakable clarity,” that “evidence of the claim is not required.” According to the Court, Rule 8 therefore “sets a ceiling on the information that plaintiffs can be required to provide about the merits of their claims.” Although the affidavit was formally separate from the pleading, the Court found it “fair to infer” that Rule 8’s specification of what information must appear in a pleading excluded any requirement that additional evidence accompany it. The Court explained that Rule 12 reinforced that conclusion because it “provides only one ground for dismissal based on the merits,” namely, “failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted,” and generally prohibits courts from considering “matters outside the pleadings.” Because Delaware required plaintiffs bringing medical malpractice claims to provide an expert affidavit in addition to factual allegations, the Court concluded that the state law demanded more information about the merits than Rule 8 permitted.

The Court rejected the respondents’ argument that the affidavit is a “free-floating evidentiary requirement that can serve as the basis for an early dismissal” rather than a pleading requirement. If the affidavit merely required Berk to produce proof early in the case, the majority reasoned, Rule 56 already supplied “a mechanism for putting a plaintiff to his proof: a motion for summary judgment.” The Court also rejected respondents’ argument that Rule 11 incorporated Delaware’s requirement. Rule 11 governs representations made by attorneys and unrepresented parties, requiring them to certify after reasonable inquiry that their legal and factual representations are warranted. Its affidavit proviso, the Court explained, concerns verification by parties before the court, while Delaware required an affidavit from a third-party medical professional.

Finally, the Court held that Rule 8 was valid under the REA. Applying Sibbach v. Wilson & Co., the majority asked only whether Rule 8 “really regulates procedure.” Because Rule 8 governs “the manner and the means” by which litigants enforce their rights — specifically, what a plaintiff must present at the outset of litigation — rather than the underlying rights, remedies, or rules of decision, the Court concluded that it did. The majority further rejected respondents’ argument that the Court should separately consider whether Delaware’s affidavit requirement protected state substantive rights, stating that “the substantive nature of [a state] law, or its substantive purpose, makes no difference” to the validity of the Federal Rule. Rule 8 therefore governed, and Delaware’s affidavit requirement did not apply in federal court.

Justice Jackson concurred in the judgment but disagreed that Rule 8 supplied the conflict. In her view, Delaware’s statute conflicted instead with Rules 3 and 12 because it required more than a complaint to commence and preserve the action and created an additional merits-based dismissal mechanism. She therefore agreed that the Delaware requirement could not apply in federal court.

Berk makes it easier for federal courts to displace state laws that protect substantive rights through procedural mechanisms. It does so in two ways. First, by reading Rule 8 broadly, Berk makes it easier for courts to find that a Federal Rule answers the question in dispute and thereby avoid considering Erie’s twin aims altogether. Second, by treating Sibbach’s “really regulates procedure” test as the conclusive REA inquiry, Berk allows courts to displace state laws without considering whether their procedural mechanisms define or protect a state-created substantive right. The decision therefore threatens state laws that protect substantive rights through procedure, such as anti-SLAPP statutes.

The scope a court gives to a Federal Rule affects the likelihood that state law will survive. When no Federal Rule governs, courts look to Erie’s twin aims. But when a Federal Rule does govern, Hanna v. Plumer instructs courts to apply it unless it exceeds the authority granted by the REA or violates the Constitution. The scope a court gives to a Federal Rule therefore is important: A narrow reading may leave room for state law to survive and be evaluated under Erie, while a broad reading that creates a conflict moves the inquiry to the Rule’s validity under the REA, a more constrained inquiry that leaves less room for state law to survive.

Berk reached the Federal Rule inquiry by reading Rule 8 broadly. Rather than confining Rule 8 to what must (minimally) appear within the four corners of a complaint, the Court read the Rule as “set[ting] a ceiling on the information” required at the outset of litigation, even when the state requirement takes the form of a separate filing. That route forecloses any inquiry into whether disregarding Delaware’s law would encourage forum shopping or produce inequitable administration of the laws — the unfairness Erie is meant to guard against.

That breadth was not inevitable as a matter of precedent. In Walker v. Armco Steel Corp., the Court declined to displace Oklahoma’s service-based statute of limitations by reading Rule 3’s statement that an “action is commenced by filing a complaint with the court” broadly. The Rule and the state law, the Court explained, could “exist side by side,” each operating within its own sphere. Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp. reflected a similar approach. Although Rule 23.1 regulated derivative suits, the Court did not read it to displace a New Jersey law requiring certain shareholder-plaintiffs to post security for the defendants’ litigation expenses, because Rule 23.1’s provisions “neither create nor exempt from liabilities,” and “[n]one conflict[ed] with the statute in question.” Gasperini v. Center for Humanities, Inc. later reproduced the same impulse, noting that the Court had “continued since [Hanna] to interpret the federal rules to avoid conflict with important state regulatory policies.” While none control Berk, these cases elucidate how the first step of Hanna — whether the Federal Rule governs the disputed issue and thus conflicts with state law — depends on how expansively courts frame a Rule. Berk chose the expansive reading.

But Berk did so without clarifying when courts should read a Federal Rule broadly. In treating Rule 8 as setting a ceiling on information required to initiate litigation, the Court did not explain why that reading was appropriate in the face of cases like Cohen, Walker, and Gasperini, which read other Federal Rules more narrowly to leave room for state law. Lower courts are therefore left with two competing lines of authority: one set of cases supporting broad readings of Federal Rules and another supporting narrower readings, without much guidance to reconcile the two. By failing to explain when a broad reading is warranted, Berk leaves lower courts more room to find conflicts between Federal Rules and state laws.

The second inquiry — whether the Federal Rule may displace state law — is governed by the REA, and Berk’s approach to that inquiry further reduces the protection afforded to state substantive interests. Congress enacted the REA in 1934 with the goal of creating “a uniform system of legal procedure.” The REA contains two commands. First, § 2072(a) grants the Supreme Court the authority “to prescribe general rules of practice and procedure and rules of evidence” in federal courts. Second, § 2072(b) dictates that “such rules shall not abridge, enlarge or modify any substantive right.” The difficulty, of course, is that the REA draws a line between procedural and substantive rights without instructing courts how to apply it.

The Supreme Court’s first major answer to this difficulty came in Sibbach. Sibbach argued that applying Rules 35 and 37 — which authorize a court to order a physical examination of a plaintiff in a personal injury suit — would abridge her right to bodily autonomy and therefore violate § 2072(b) of the REA. The Court rejected the argument that § 2072(b) turns on the “importance of the alleged right,” warning that such a standard would “invite endless litigation and confusion worse confounded.” Instead, it announced that “[t]he test must be whether a rule really regulates procedure,” meaning “the judicial process for enforcing rights and duties recognized by substantive law.” Because Rules 35 and 37 met that test, the Court upheld them.

The meaning of Sibbach’s test divided the Court in Shady Grove Orthopedic Associates, P.A. v. Allstate Insurance Co. There, the Justices disagreed over whether Rule 23, which governs class actions, displaced a New York statute barring class actions seeking statutory penalties. Justice Scalia’s opinion read Sibbach’s test broadly: Once a court determines that a Federal Rule answers the question in dispute, the REA’s validity inquiry focuses on the nature of the Rule itself and not the state law it displaces. As he put it, “it is not the substantive or procedural nature or purpose of the affected state law that matters, but the substantive or procedural nature of the Federal Rule.” The possibility that New York’s law embodied substantive policy made “no difference.” Justice Stevens agreed that Rule 23 applied because New York’s class action bar was “a procedural rule that [was] not part of New York’s substantive law,” but rejected Justice Scalia’s rule that a Federal Rule’s procedural character ends the inquiry. In his view, although the REA “does not mean that federal rules cannot displace state policy judgments,” it does mean “that federal rules cannot displace a State’s definition of its own rights or remedies.” This is because a state rule that is “‘procedural’ in the ordinary sense of the term” may be “so bound up with the state-created right or remedy that it defines the scope of that substantive right or remedy.”

Sibbach, however, leaves § 2072(b) doing little work. As commentators have observed, “[t]he Sibbach analysis is skewed.” “Sibbach asks only whether a Rule is procedural.” It therefore “puts all the REA eggs in the § 2072(a) basket and gives no independent heft to § 2072(b).” Justice Scalia himself acknowledged in Shady Grove that “[t]here is something to” the criticism that Sibbach gives “short shrift to” § 2072(b)’s text, conceding that its exclusive focus on the Federal Rule “is hard to square with § 2072(b)’s terms.” While a court might determine “whether a Federal Rule ‘enlarges’ substantive rights without consulting state law,” he explained, “it is hard to understand how” a court could decide whether a Rule “abridges” or “modifies” substantive rights without first asking what state-created rights would apply in the Rule’s absence. The Court nonetheless retained Sibbach’s test because it was settled and administrable. Berk follows that approach, instructing courts not to ask what state-created rights would apply in the Federal Rule’s absence.

By treating Sibbach’s “really regulates procedure” formulation as the whole REA inquiry, Berk left little room to consider what state-created protection Rule 8 would displace. Its brief discussion of § 2072(b) focused entirely on Rule 8’s procedural character. Because Rule 8 governs what plaintiffs must present at the outset of litigation, the Court concluded that it regulates only the process for enforcing rights, even if it has “some ‘practical effect on the parties’ rights.’” But § 2072(b) asks whether a Federal Rule abridges, enlarges, or modifies a substantive right, which at least calls for considering whether the state law embodies substantive rights that the Federal Rule would affect. The Court did not meaningfully examine Delaware’s law or the interests it served. Quoting Shady Grove, it reasoned instead that Rule 8 “regulates ‘only the process for enforcing’” rights, not “the rights themselves, the available remedies, or the rules of decision.” That omission may not have changed the outcome in Berk, but it matters for state laws that, through procedural mechanisms, protect substantive rights or remedies. Under Berk, such laws may be displaced without examining the state-created interests they serve, rendering § 2072(b) effectively moot.

Anti-SLAPP statutes are an example of such laws and are especially vulnerable to displacement in federal court. These statutes target SLAPP suits brought “not to win on the merits, but rather to discourage the defendant’s right to free speech through the prospect of ruinously expensive litigation.” Anti-SLAPP statutes do so through mechanisms that are procedural in form — like a special motion to dismiss, an early merits showing, or a discovery stay — but that implement a substantive judgment about who should bear the costs of meritless litigation over speech. To be sure, most procedural rules have some effect on substantive rights. But anti-SLAPP statutes present a different problem because avoiding the burdens of litigation is itself part of the protection they confer. Their special motion, discovery stay, and fee provisions protect defendants from undergoing the ordinary litigation process in the first place, rather than simply offering another (procedural) means of reaching the same ultimate result. By the time a defendant has gone through discovery and pretrial litigation, the statute has already failed to provide much of the protection it was meant to offer — even if the defendant eventually wins.

Courts have recognized that anti-SLAPP statutes protect substantive interests. Sitting en banc this term, a Ninth Circuit judge explained that California’s fee-shifting and special-motion provisions “provide defendants with a pretrial claim for attorneys’ fees for plaintiffs’ abuse of the judicial process by filing a meritless SLAPP suit,” and that “[n]o federal rule controls or directly collides with that right.” Still, other courts have held that Rules 12 and 56 “answer the same question” as an anti-SLAPP statute’s dismissal mechanism without considering what the displaced state law protects.

Berk makes that result easier to reach in two ways: by encouraging a broad reading of the Federal Rules that creates conflicts with state laws and by narrowing the REA’s protection of the substantive interests those state laws serve. Once a court reads Rules 12 and 56 broadly enough to govern the disputed issue, the state statute’s substantive character “makes no difference.” Anti-SLAPP statutes may therefore lose much of their force in federal court even though “they create a right to avoid the burdens of litigation.” In contrast, had the Berk Court adopted Justice Stevens’s approach in Shady Grove, that result would have been less likely. His approach requires courts to consider the substantive rights and remedies those statutes protect. Under that framework, if the right to avoid the burdens of litigation is part of the state-created protection, the statute’s procedural mechanisms may be “so bound up with the state-created right or remedy that [they] define[] the scope of that substantive right or remedy.” On that view, a Federal Rule could not displace them.

Displacing anti-SLAPP statutes would undermine both of Erie’s twin aims. It would encourage plaintiffs to choose a federal forum and enable them to subject defendants to burdens they avoid in state court.

First, the absence of anti-SLAPP protections encourages the kind of vertical forum shopping Erie sought to prevent. A plaintiff bringing a suit aimed at burdening protected speech has reason to prefer federal court if the state’s anti-SLAPP law does not apply there. In state court, a defendant may obtain an early ruling, avoid discovery, and recover fees if the claim lacks merit. In federal court, a plaintiff may avoid those consequences and use the costs of ordinary litigation as leverage — the exact harm anti-SLAPP statutes are enacted to prevent. As the Ninth Circuit explained, without the state protections, “a litigant interested in bringing meritless SLAPP claims would have a significant incentive to shop for a federal forum.” The availability of anti-SLAPP protection can therefore influence a plaintiff’s choice of forum: The federal courthouse offers a way to pursue the same state law claim without the safeguards the state adopted to deter it.

Second, displacement also treats similarly situated defendants differently depending on where they are sued. A defendant may receive the protections of anti-SLAPP laws in state court yet lose those protections solely because the plaintiff filed in federal court. That difference is especially important in the anti-SLAPP context, where the burden of defending the suit is often the point of a plaintiff bringing it. Even a defendant who ultimately prevails may have already expended the resources the statute was designed to protect after undergoing discovery and ordinary pretrial litigation and costs. The Ninth Circuit thus concluded that a defendant “otherwise entitled to the protections of the Anti-SLAPP statute would find considerable disadvantage in a federal proceeding,” and that withholding those protections would “run squarely against the ‘twin aims’ of the Erie doctrine.” The same state law claim therefore carries materially different consequences depending on which courthouse hears it.

Whatever the proper result on Berk’s facts, the Court’s reasoning extends beyond affidavit-of-merit statutes. By reading Rule 8 broadly, the Court made it easier for courts to avoid Erie’s twin aims altogether. For state laws like anti-SLAPP statutes, which use procedural mechanisms to protect substantive judgments about litigation burdens, that approach is hard to square with § 2072(b)’s text and Erie’s concern with forum-based inequality. And by treating Sibbach’s “really regulates procedure” test as the whole of the REA inquiry, the Court weakened § 2072(b) as an independent limit on Federal Rules.

text:
The UN’s top human rights body on Tuesday postponed a regular review of the U.S. human rights record until January in hopes of persuading the Trump administration to reverse its decision to become the first government to snub the process.

The move by the Human Rights Council buys it more time to try to coax Washington to take part in the review. The council’s 47 member countries adopted without a vote the decision to delay the U.S. review – amid “continued non-cooperation” with its process.

The Geneva-based council regularly examines the rights records of all 193 UN member states – generally about every four to five years – as part of a process known as the universal periodic review.

The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump last year pulled the U.S. out of the council, accusing it of an anti-U.S. and anti-Israel bias, and alleging that it didn’t uphold the very values it promotes.

The U.S. government has drawn criticism for its policies including strong-arm deportations and targeted killings of alleged drug-runners in the Caribbean and Pacific – which the administration has said are designed to protect U.S. workers and help keep the country safe.

The European Union, a key U.S. ally, and other supporters of the review process say it’s needed to keep tabs on human rights in all UN member states.

“The EU regrets any situation in which full engagement with the mechanism does not occur, including the decision by the United States again not to participate in their review today,” Simone van der Post, a Dutch envoy speaking on behalf of EU council members, said after Tuesday’s decision.

“All states are subject to the scrutiny of their human rights situation by the international community,” she added.

The U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to an e-mailed request for comment from The Associated Press.

The United States, under Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago. The scheduled November 2025 review was pushed back until Tuesday in hopes that the U.S. government might change its mind. It did not.

“[W]e give no credibility to the agency,” the State Department said in an e-mailed statement before Tuesday’s decision.

“This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own ‘values’ as it pushes anti-American rhetoric,” the statement said, alleging the council’s “persistent failure to condemn the most egregious human rights violators.”

The council requires participation of the country in question for any national review to take place.

As part of such reviews, national delegations – which at times can include a dozen officials or more – make a presentation, face questions and hear recommendations from other national envoys. It’s supposed to be a sweeping and constructive process, akin to holding up a mirror to governments to improve their human rights policies.

Rights advocates say U.S. deserves scrutiny, like every other country

Critics of the U.S. snub warn that the walkout could encourage other countries – many of which bristle about intense scrutiny from human rights monitors – to follow suit.

Phil Lynch, executive director of advocacy group International Service for Human Rights, said the U.S. deserves scrutiny for its recent record on “migration, LGBT rights, racial discrimination and civic freedoms, like the right to protest,” as well as wars in the Middle East and “extrajudicial executions” in the Pacific and Caribbean.

“What has Washington got to hide?” he said.

Jamil Dakwar, director of the American Civil Liberties Union’s human rights program, said: “The administration is saying to the world, ‘we don’t care about whether you would review us or not, we’re going to continue to violate human rights unabashed’.”

He said the ACLU and allies have called on the UN human rights chief to respond by presenting an update on rights in the United States early next year.

Eric Tistounet, a visiting professor at the Geneva Graduate Institute who was the council’s first secretary, said the U.S. walkout could affect the credibility of the council’s review system.

“If the predominant global power – which has always claimed to adhere to the human rights norms – doesn’t show up and doesn’t even justify why, then you are in big trouble,” he said.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton dropped a lawsuit seeking to shut down FIEL, a Houston immigrant-rights organization the state had accused of violating nonprofit restrictions by criticizing President Donald Trump and Gov. Greg Abbott’s immigration policies.

On Monday, Paxton’s office filed a notice withdrawing the claims “with prejudice,” which means the state can’t bring the same lawsuit against the organization again. The two-page notice, which was filed in a state court in Harris County, didn’t say why Paxton’s office dropped the lawsuit.

Paxton had filed the lawsuit against FIEL in July citing social media posts encouraging people to vote against Trump’s immigration proposals. The group opposed a 2023 law, Senate Bill 4, that would let Texas police arrest people suspected of having entered the country illegally.

text:
The Supreme Court is paving the way for the Trump administration to resume border construction throughout the Big Bend region in Texas, including inside Big Bend National Park.

The Supreme Court ruled 8-1 Monday that the government “is exceedingly likely to prevail” in its argument that a district court lacked jurisdiction to pause construction when it issued a preliminary injunction in October.

The Trump administration’s plans to build a combination of physical walls, access roads and vehicle barriers in the Big Bend region have sparked bipartisan backlash.

In May, ABC News spoke with Charlie Angell, a resident and landowner in Redford, Texas, who said he received a letter from U.S Customs and Border Protection (CBP) alerting him that the government wanted access to his land for border construction purposes and may want to take ownership of it if he declined to agree.

Angell runs an outdoor expedition company out of his property on the banks of the Rio Grande. According to a map of the administration’s plans, his property would be split in half and he’d be cut off from the river, where he often launches kayaks for his business.

“It's devastating for me. I'm almost 60 in August, so that's almost at the end of my career. And I've faced all my life savings and everything into retiring right where I'm at,” he told ABC News.

The plans for Big Bend National Park initially included a physical wall, but after public outcry, the plans were changed to include only a combination of vehicle barriers, roads and surveillance technology.

In their petition to the Supreme Court, the government reiterated its claims that the Big Bend Sector, the largest along the southern U.S. border, is an area of “high illegal entry.” However, opponents of the administration’s plans have expressed doubt about those claims.

According to CBP statistics, only about 1% of encounters with migrants happen in the sector. The rugged, remote and dangerous terrain has long been thought to be one of its most deterring factors.

Plaintiffs challenging the construction in court argued in part that DHS exceeded its authority when it waived several environmental and conservation laws to expedite the construction.

On Monday, the Supreme Court reaffirmed that the Department of Homeland Security secretary has wide discretion to waive certain laws in the interest of border security and ruled that the preliminary injunction prevented the government from “advancing its ‘compelling interests’ in border security and integrity.”

The court also appeared swayed in part by the Trump administration’s claim that stalling construction was costing nearly half-a-million dollars a day.

Some residents of the Big Bend region worry that the construction will cut off access to the Rio Grande, destroy the natural habitats and beauty that draw thousands of people to the region, and would decimate their local economies, which reply heavily on tourism.

“The Trump administration and its contractors are hellbent on destroying one of America’s greatest national parks, and the Supreme Court just gave them the green light,” said Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity. “This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal. They’re signing off on the permanent destruction of the wildest place in Texas, and the theft of a great American river from all of us.”

text:
In Brief

Supreme Court lifts injunction on Big Bend border project.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissents from majority ruling.

Trump administration cites Illegal Immigration Reform Act.

Big Bend Sector includes 150 miles of 30-foot border wall.

The Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for construction to resume on one of the longest and most controversial sections of President Donald Trump’s security project along the Mexican border.

The more than 500-mile stretch of road, cameras, vehicle barriers and sensors planned to cut through Texas‘s iconic Big Bend National Park has generated significant backlash. It includes segments where a 30-foot border wall will be built, although the administration has backed off plans for a wall inside the park.

The justices’ ruling allows work to continue while a legal challenge filed by an environmental group, preservationists, and a river guide and landowner plays out in court. Only Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson noted her dissent.

“Respondents claim that construction in the Big Bend Sector will diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area,” the majority wrote. But the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 “reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert.”

A federal judge in Texas halted work on the project in October, siding with the challengers, who argued that the Trump administration violated the Constitution by waiving dozens of laws to speed construction. The high court lifted that block after the Trump administration appealed.

U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone had ruled that the administration would have to comply with the laws before construction could resume.

“As Plaintiffs have demonstrated, without an injunction, they and the public at large stand to permanently lose protected wilderness that benefits tourism, recreation, farming, ranching, spirituality, aesthetic sensibilities and education,” Cardone wrote in her opinion.

In its appeal of that ruling to the Supreme Court, the Trump administration said the project was urgently needed to stop the flow of migrants and illegal drugs across the border.

“Plaintiffs’ environmental, recreational, and aesthetic interests do not outweigh the harm to the public,” the government wrote in court filings.

More than 89,000 people were apprehended trying to enter the United States between 2021 and 2025 in the area known as the Big Bend Sector, according to government court filings. About 15 percent of drugs seized along the border in recent years were recovered in the sector.

Citing the flow of migrants and drugs, then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi L. Noem found earlier this year that the administration did not have to comply with dozens of mostly environmental laws because there was “an acute and immediate need” for the barrier.

The plaintiffs questioned whether the accelerated timeline was necessary.

They pointed out that the Big Bend Sector had by far the least number of migrant apprehensions of any of the border’s six sectors, accounting for about 2 percent of the total number. The drug seizures amount to less than 1 percent of all non-marijuana drugs.

Anna Claire Beasley of No Big Bend Wall, one of the groups opposed to the project, said she was dismayed by the high court’s decision.

“The consequences of this decision are not theoretical. Every road cut into the desert, every stretch of land cleared, and every barrier built changes this landscape in ways that may never be undone,” Beasley said. “Big Bend is not an empty stretch of border waiting for development. It is a living landscape, home to communities, wildlife, cultural history, and a globally significant natural environment.”

Asked for comment on the decision, the White House referred to a message Department of Homeland Security General Counsel James Percival posted on X celebrating the victory.

‘When we filed in the Supreme Court, I called the district court’s order halting wall construction ‘as unprecedented as it is flawed.’ We just won,” Percival wrote.

The Trump administration is building hundreds of miles of new border wall across California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas, after Congress included $46.5 billion in funding in last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill. The Big Bend sections total $1.7 billion.

Conservationists fear that the administration’s move to bypass environmental laws during construction will damage otherwise remote wilderness and irreversibly alter iconic landscapes enjoyed by outdoor enthusiasts.

The wall expansion originally included plans to build a barrier through Big Bend National Park, the most-visited national park in Texas with more than half a million people entering in 2025.

The park, which consists of 800,000 acres in southwest Texas, is renowned for its views of the mountains and steep cliffs that descend to the Rio Grande, drawing hikers and kayakers.

But in the face of outcry from local landowners, tourism businesses and politicians, the administration reversed course, opting instead to build patrol roads through the park and install vehicle barriers and additional surveillance technology.

Conservation advocates argue that even building a road would require blasting through the mountains with dynamite, although Customs and Border Protection denies that.

In the wider Big Bend region, the administration still plans to build more than 150 miles of the 30-foot wall, according to the CBP website.

The construction has moved forward rapidly in many areas thanks to the 2005 Real ID Act, which granted the Department of Homeland Security the ability to waive some environmental laws for building a border wall. That has allowed it to forgo reviews of potential damage to the environment and archaeological sites, which can often delay projects months or years.

Inside the national park, contractors in August began bulldozing scrubland along the Rio Grande to clear a path for the new patrol road. That land would typically be protected by the Endangered Species Act as the Fish and Wildlife Service has designated it as critical habitat for the yellow-billed cuckoo.

Following local outcry, CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott paused that work to consult with local stakeholders.

Efforts to oppose the wall elsewhere have been less successful. In Arizona, activists blocked wall construction for more than two months by occupying a giant tree along the border, before a dramatic raid by more than 50 CPB agents ousted them and downed the tree. Construction preparations are also moving ahead on Arizona’s nearby Tohono O’odham Nation, after a judge denied the Native American reservation’s request for a preliminary injunction.

text:
A disabled Minneapolis resident whom Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers violently arrested in January is suing the federal government over her arrest and subsequent detention.

Aliya Rahman, whose treatment fueled outrage over the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota, filed a lawsuit Tuesday accusing the officers of unlawfully arresting her, using excessive force to do it and failing to provide adequate medical care during her detention, despite her repeated pleas.

Rahman’s attorneys submitted an administrative complaint against the Department of Homeland Security in April under the Federal Tort Claims Act, the first step toward suing the government. Civilians cannot sue a federal employee for civil rights violations the way they can a police officer, but the FTCA allows people to sue the United States for a federal employee’s actions.

Rahman’s legal team also separately filed a complaint to the department’s Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties in June.

Jessica Gingold, Rahman’s attorney and senior counsel at the MacArthur Justice Center, told MS NOW that those complaints had gone unanswered. She said that to her knowledge, DHS had taken no action against the officers — whose identities are still unknown.

“Perhaps they can ignore our administrative complaint, but once we go to court, they have to answer,” Gingold said. “And we have all the tools at our disposal to get discovery, to depose the agents that were involved in this incident and to demand that there is some accountability for what happened.”

Rahman was arrested Jan. 13 during the Trump administration’s “Operation Metro Surge” in the Minneapolis area while she was driving to a doctor appointment. Video captured by a bystander shows ICE officers surrounding her car before dragging her out, restraining her with her arms behind her back and then carrying her by the arms in that position.

According to the complaint, Rahman encountered the officers while driving, and they banged on her car windows and yelled at her as she tried to move out of the intersection as ordered. Rahman grew frustrated and told the officers that “they needed to learn how to respect human beings,” the complaint states, at which point an officer broke her car window.

“Though an officer had just smashed her window without any legal basis, covering her with broken glass, other officers immediately yelled at Ms. Rahman to ‘go,’ ‘get out,’ and ‘get out of here,’ gesturing eastward on East 34th Street,” the complaint states. “Terrified and in shock, Ms. Rahman attempted to comply and drove forward, eastbound on East 34th Street. But at this point, officers stopped her, reaching through her windows at Ms. Rahman and pulling open her car doors.”

Rahman was then detained at the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building in Fort Snelling, where she was denied medical care even though her condition was deteriorating, according to the complaint.

More articles

DHS disputed Rahman’s account at the time, calling her an agitator who “ignored multiple commands by an officer to move her vehicle away from the scene.”

The department did not immediately respond to MS NOW’s request Tuesday for comment about the lawsuit.

Rahman, who has said she has autism and a traumatic brain injury, said she continues to experience severe stress and anxiety as a result of the encounter.

“She had been going to the traumatic brain injury center on the day that this happened, and this kind of rerouted her whole healing journey,” Gingold said. “And she had to spend the last several months mostly focused on physical therapy for her shoulders after being carried like an animal through the street for 215 feet.”

Rahman’s arrest took place just days after an ICE officer shot and killed a Minneapolis resident, Renee Good, and it further stoked outrage among local residents over the administration’s immigration crackdown.

Less than two weeks after Rahman’s ordeal, ICE officers shot and killed another Minneapolis local, intensive care unit nurse Alex Pretti.

text:
New York Times highlights Dr. Ann Lawani’s life in the Valley threatened by aggressive ICE policies(link is external)

Image

Harder wrote to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin demanding Dr. Lawani be returned to California for legal proceedings after being abruptly transferred across the country

WASHINGTON – Today, Rep. Josh Harder (CA-09) sounded the alarm on outrageous new deportation tactics by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) that caused a local constituent to be detained, arrested, and abruptly transported across the country. Dr. Ann Lawani – a nurse, caregiver, and 13-year resident of Lodi in the U.S. legally under judicial protection – was sent thousands of miles away to Louisiana in violation of a federal court order. In response, Harder wrote to U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin to demand Dr. Lawani’s immediate return to California for any further legal proceedings.

Dr. Lawani lives in Lodi, where she is a caregiver for her 83-year-old father. She also oversees the education of 230 nursing students at the University of San Francisco, and she practices as a nurse at John Muir Health. Her abrupt absence has already caused significant disruptions on campus and pulled yet another healthcare worker away from a community facing severe shortages. Dr. Lawani’s story(link is external) was featured this morning in the New York Times.

“Given her longstanding compliance, lack of criminal history, and substantial community ties, there is no apparent public safety justification for keeping Dr. Lawani detained thousands of miles from home while her case proceeds,” wrote Rep. Harder. “Our immigration enforcement system should focus on protecting communities from danger, not removing the individuals who dedicate their lives to serving them. Dr. Lawani's continued detention undermines that mission while imposing unnecessary harm on her family and the countless people who depend on her.”

In his letter, Harder demanded that ICE release Dr. Lawani under an order of supervision and facilitate her immediate return to California, and that DHS provide her and her attorney with the proposed country of removal, supporting travel documentation, and an explanation of the basis for her continued detention.

“My sister is an amazing caregiver, healthcare leader, and educator in our community, and I was devastated not just at her unacceptable arrest, but the decision to send her across the country and detain her unnecessarily. Not only is Dr. Ann a scholar in her profession, but an extremely skilled nurse with unmatched dedication to her patients and students alike. She gives everything she has, daily, to save lives and train the nurses of the future to be as trained, ready and dedicated as she is. As a recognized expert in palliative care as well, I can assure anyone, countless lives have been lost due to her absence, since her wrongful detainment. For someone that vital to the community to be tracked, abruptly vacuumed into an abyss and moved across the country, is simply EVIL and consequential. My family and I want to see my sister returned home safely and as soon as possible, and like so many families in our community, we want an end to the chaos caused by these agencies. I want to thank Congressman Harder for his work to bring Ann home as well as the USF family for their relentless support,” said Samuel Lawani, brother of Dr. Lawani.

“I speak with confidence to what I know firsthand: Dr. Ann Lawani is a person of exceptional professional accomplishment and moral character, deeply embedded in our university community, with responsibilities that hundreds of nursing students and, in turn, the patients they will someday care for, depend upon her fulfilling. Her continued absence causes real and mounting harm to the students and faculty who rely on her mentorship, to our accreditation-mandated curriculum work, and to the safety-net partnerships she has built,” said Eileen K. Fry-Bowers, Dean of the School of Nursing and Health Professions.

Read Harder’s full letter to DHS Secretary Mullin here.

Harder has been pushing for reforms at ICE and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for months, including successfully calling for former Secretary Kristi Noem’s firing. Following her departure, Harder demanded the new Secretary Markwayne Mullin prioritize clear standards for enforcement, bans on face coverings, mandatory identification, new use-of-force policies, and bans on racial profiling. Harder has also continued to oppose any new federal funding for ICE until these reforms are enacted, and he has repeatedly conducted oversight investigations at the Stockton ICE facility.

text:
The US Supreme Court’s conservative majority appeared skeptical that the Labor Department’s in-house judges could order a New Jersey farm to pay penalties for violating a seasonal worker visa program.

During oral argument Tuesday, several Republican-appointed justices seemed to doubt that the H-2A program’s requirements on employers fell within the “public rights” exception to adjudication in federal court.

Justices critical of agency tribunals drew a distinction between denying entry or ordering deportation — a clear instance of public rights in the immigration space — and enforcing a visa program’s mandates through monetary penalties. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump appointee, took the most aggressive stance during argument, calling into question the power of the government to seek any such penalties outside of court.

The case could have serious ramifications for agency power by further limiting what they can enforce in administrative proceedings. Enforcement actions before agency tribunals generally move faster and more efficiently compared to federal court.

Justice Elena Kagan, an Obama appointee, asked the government’s lawyer what’s at stake in the case for immigration enforcement.

“If the proposition were that the only types of things that could be in executive adjudication are things that happened at the border, I think it would be catastrophic,” Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris told the justices. “Just the volume of immigration-related cases for the aliens themselves, things that make you inadmissible after you enter the country — huge.”

The high court holding that civil penalties across the board can only be imposed in court would be the “nuclear option,” Harris said.

The Supreme Court is reviewing a decision by the US Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit overturning an administrative order against Sun Valley Orchards LLC to pay more than $500,000 in penalties and back wages for violations of the visa program.

Regulating Farmworker Visa Rules

The court’s three liberal justices seemed to embrace the government’s argument that the H-2A program imposes obligations on employers to protect domestic workers being undercut by foreign labor, and adjudicating alleged violations of those promises is a classic public right.

Harris buttressed that argument by repeatedly citing the Supreme Court’s 1909 decision in Oceanic Steam Navigation Co. v. Stranahan, which permitted $100 administrative fines on shipping companies for every immigrant they brought to the US who suffered from a contagious disease.

But Oceanic Steam seems “significantly different,” said Chief Justice John Roberts, a George W. Bush appointee. There’s no justification to extend the broad authority the executive branch gets for the admission of immigrants to H-2A workers who’ve been in the country for months, he said.

Justice Clarence Thomas, a George H.W. Bush appointee, said “kicking someone out” of the program for violating its requirements would be a “clear way” of regulating it.

The Supreme Court made a “fairly definitive statement” in its 1987 decision in Tull v. US that civil penalties can only be enforced in courts of law, Kavanaugh said.

There’s already judicial review of enforcement actions, so the main differences for courts if agencies can’t penalize in administrative proceedings would be the standard of review they use and their volume of cases, he said.

title: U.S. Supreme Court Allows Continued Big Bend Border Construction - The Texan
description: “The Government’s interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents,” the court said.
text:
“Our next 9/11 is coming,” one witness warned the Committee …

Officials allege that cartels could use them as staging area…



In a major judicial development, the Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) issued a decision Monday allowing President Donald Trump’s administration to continue border construction in Texas’ Big Bend region.

The decision follows a lower court’s order to halt construction last month .

A lawsuit filed by Friends of the Ruidosa Church in April — the current crux of the Big Bend border dispute — alleges that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's waiving of federal rules in order to precipitously build border infrastructure in the region violated a swath of federal rules. The federal rules waived deal mostly with environmental and conservation-related protections.

Last month, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone granted a preliminary injunction in the matter, stating that the plaintiffs were “likely to succeed on the merits” of at least one of their allegations in the lawsuit.

On Monday, SCOTUS reached a different conclusion, staying the preliminary injunction as requested by the federal government and allowing continued construction in the Big Bend region.

U.S. Senator-elect and state Rep. James Talarico (D-Austin) commented on SCOTUS’ decision, “They’re allowing out-of-state contractors to get rich by destroying the crown jewel of Texas. We can work with President Trump to fix this broken immigration system without desecrating our sacred land.”

Associate Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that she would deny the stay.

In the administration's decision to build border infrastructure in the area, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) relied on Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA). These sections of the IIRIRA allow for particular legal requirements to be waived in pursuit of border security.

Plaintiffs invoked the “major-questions doctrine,” arguing that the lack of congressional approval invalidates DHS’ use of these waivers, according to the SCOTUS decision. The lower court found that the plaintiffs would “suffer serious, irreparable harm without an injunction, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest weigh in their favor,” U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone previously said.

The judge’s order suspended the DHS’ waivers and halted construction. The lower court also found that the major questions doctrine claim would likely succeed because of the absence of congressional approval.

SCOTUS, however, found the lower court “lacking jurisdiction," and agreed with the federal government’s request to stay the preliminary injunction.

SCOTUS argued that the plaintiffs' claim was not constitutional but statutory, saying, “Although styled as constitutional, that claim simply alleged that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority in issuing the waivers.”

“There is no such thing as a ‘constitutional’ major-questions claim,” the court stated.

The court also concluded that the injunction “impedes” the federal government from advancing its interests in “border security and integrity.”

The court’s decision also cites a Customs and Border Protection employee's claim that the government is “incurring nearly half a million dollars” in irrecoverable costs per day if the injunction “prevails at the end of this litigation.”

The court concluded, “The Government’s interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents.”

Hillary Pierce, director of communications for No Big Bend Wall and a board member of Conserve Big Bend, two organizations both advocating against Big Bend sector border construction, stated about the legal developments in an emailed press release, “This isn't the end of our fight. The justices didn't decide whether Big Bend actually qualifies as an area of high illegal entry.”

Conserve Big Bend filed a lawsuit in September claiming the U.S., in calling the region a "high entry” zone, did not accurately designate the area.

“The government's own numbers show Big Bend has the fewest Border Patrol apprehensions along the southern border. That's exactly what we're challenging in our lawsuit in Washington,” Pierce added in the emailed press release.

U.S. Senator John Cornyn released an op-ed on Monday in the San Antonio Express-News, stating, “Big Bend deserves border security that reflects the realities of its geography, the input and experience of local law enforcement, and the rights of the people who live there.”

He argued that the area was not a region of “high illegal entry,” but that the sector “recorded the lowest number of apprehensions among the nine Border Patrol sectors along the southern border.”

Cornyn contended for better use of technology, rather than physical border construction, in the area.

While yesterday marked a major development in the judicial branch on the issue, the Texas Legislature also began moving to weigh in.

State Rep. Eddie Morales (D- Eagle Pass) filed a bill on Monday, the first day of pre-filing, related to “a prohibition on the installation or construction of border security infrastructure on state park property.” He was joined by state Rep. John Bucy III (D-Austin), who, in addition to filing various Medicaid bills on Monday, filed a bill related to “a prohibition on agreements to use state park property for border security infrastructure or related improvements.”

Texas Democrats are hitting the ground running after their historic flip of the Texas House and every statewide office on Election Day. Texas’ 90th Legislative Session will begin on January 12, 2027.

text:
A federal judge on Monday pressed the acting head of Denver's U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement field office over an order to quickly re-arrest immigrants a court had ordered released from detention. She is now deciding whether contempt proceedings are appropriate.

U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney called the re-arrests concerning, both for due process and for the fear they instill among immigrant detainees.

Court testimony revealed at least 18 detainees were released and then quickly re-arrested over about a week at the GEO facility in Aurora. The arrests prompted a series of protests outside the detention center and led to Monday morning's hearing.

Nathan Rasper, acting director of ICE's Denver field office, testified that beginning October 27, he told his team that detainees subject to release following habeas corpus proceedings could be re-arrested "based on our statutory authority." Rasper, who became acting director on October 14, said he was under the understanding that some detainees had been arrested without the proper paperwork, so serving them with those warrants after their release would solve the issue.

Rasper said he believed such arrests would not violate court orders but told the judge the practice has stopped, saying he ordered an end to the practice on November 4.

The American Civil Liberties Union said ICE's actions have a specific aim "where cruelty seems to be the point."

"What we're seeing is instructions from Washington that amount to abuses, and it's happening day in and day out," said Tim Macdonald, Legal Director for ACLU of Colorado. "With the elevation of [Stephen] Miller, we should all be concerned that this administration didn't get the message from the midterms and they're going to continue their abusive practices."

Last week, an unnamed Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told CBS Colorado that ICE complies with lawful court orders and that prohibiting the re-arrests is "nothing short of sabotage."

At Monday's hearing, the assistant U.S. attorney quickly distanced himself and his office from that statement, saying they did not know it was being submitted to the press.

Sweeney is now weighing whether contempt proceedings are appropriate.
