title: Minneapolis woman sues feds for dragging her from car during Metro Surge - Sahan Journal
description:
South Minneapolis resident Aliya Rahman can’t leave her house without being reminded of what happened on Jan. 13 when several federal agents broke into her vehicle and dragged her out during Operation Metro Surge.
She was on the way to a doctor’s appointment at the time, and was caught in a traffic jam while federal agents were conducting arrests nearby.
Rahman chose to continue living in south Minneapolis despite seeing constant reminders of her arrest.
Federal agents shouted conflicting orders at her, telling her to “move” or “get out,” according to her lawsuit.
According to the lawsuit: Federal agents transported her to the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building.
text:
South Minneapolis resident Aliya Rahman can’t leave her house without being reminded of what happened on Jan. 13 when several federal agents broke into her vehicle and dragged her out during Operation Metro Surge.

“This is not an event that changed my world view, but it definitely changed my day-to-day interaction with this world,” she told Sahan Journal Monday.

Rahman’s arrest went viral after multiple bystanders posted videos of the incident showing several federal agents surrounding her vehicle on Park Avenue near East 34th Street in south Minneapolis. They swore at her, cut her seatbelt and pulled her out of the vehicle as she yelled that she was disabled, according to the videos and a lawsuit she’s filing against the federal government.

Rahman, 44, filed a tort claim in April, which allows individuals to sue the U.S. government in federal court for personal injury, death and property damage. She filed a civil lawsuit in federal court Tuesday after the U.S. government did not respond to her tort claim within six months.

Rahman continues to suffer mental and physical pain from her arrest, the lawsuit says. She was on the way to a doctor’s appointment at the time, and was caught in a traffic jam while federal agents were conducting arrests nearby.

She alleges assault, battery, false imprisonment and negligence against the federal government, and is seeking an unspecified amount of damages.

“It’s very clear that my story is really common, even though the attention it got might be uncommon,” she said. “It’s very clear that we don’t have a thick enough line around what somebody who calls themselves law enforcement is allowed to do to another person in this country. So for me, that’s one of the points of the lawsuit. We always have to keep thickening those lines to establish what is okay to do to anyone.”

“This is a federal lawsuit, but I think that it’s important to do these things for the cultural impact they can have all the way up and down the criminal justice system.”

Rahman said she has visited her doctor more regularly because of injuries she suffered in the arrest. She continues to deal with double vision and reduced peripheral vision, according to her lawsuit. She also suffers from pain in her neck, shoulders and head.

Another major change in her life is that strangers often approach her and share their thoughts about what happened to her, or, share deeply personal stories about Operation Metro Surge. Her presence sometimes triggers traumatic memories for people, she said, and some respond with vulgar language.

These conversations initially felt disorienting, she said, adding that she now tries to make people who share vulnerable stories feel respected and “whole” by listening to their stories.

Rahman has had trouble sleeping since her arrest, and often sees the faces of other people who were detained with her at the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building, which houses immigration court and local U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement offices.

“I wake up every morning hoping that beyond pushing ICE officers off of our street to the extent we did – they’re not all gone – that we actually uproot the reasons they were here in the first place,” she said. “I think that’s the only thing that would feel like healing to me.”

Rahman was born in northwestern Wisconsin, and spent most of her childhood in Bangladesh. She moved back to the United States in 1999 when she was 17 to attend Purdue University in Indiana.

Rahman chose to continue living in south Minneapolis despite seeing constant reminders of her arrest. Her close-knit neighborhood feels similar to the small town she lived in in rural Wisconsin, and the community that raised her in Bangladesh. Her family taught her the value of hard work, — her mother worked in a grain elevator and her stepfather was a railroad worker — to build infrastructure for stable communities.

Rahman said she was a block away from an immigration enforcement operation that had caused a traffic jam when she was detained. Federal agents shouted conflicting orders at her, telling her to “move” or “get out,” according to her lawsuit. Videos went viral of her arrest, where she is seen loudly yelling that she is disabled.

The Department of Homeland Security called Rahman an “agitator” at the time and accused her of obstructing ICE agents conducting arrests in the area.

Rahman was never criminally charged in the incident.

“My body is different. The injuries are unresolved. I’m at the doctor a lot. And what happened on January 13th, it didn’t stop that day, right?,” Rahman said. “These folks engaged in a disinformation campaign as well, which has also transformed what it’s like to interact with the public.”

Rahman, said she has autism, and was recovering from a traumatic brain injury at the time of her arrest.

“Ms. Rahman remains deeply distressed and traumatized that her own government, after assaulting and falsely arresting her, continues to make statements through its official social media channels and to the press that identify her, use threatening language about her, and spread lies,” says her lawsuit.

According to the lawsuit: Federal agents transported her to the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building. Rahman grew increasingly more sick in her cell, and after several attempts to notify federal agents of her condition, she eventually passed out.

Rahman was transported to a hospital a few hours later, where she was treated for a concussion and injuries “consistent with assault.” She was released from the hospital and allowed to go home.

“There isn’t a reason to think that’s not going to happen again to me or to somebody I love,” she said of her motivation for the lawsuit.

Rahman was also arrested and injured while attending President Donald Trump’s State of the Union address in February as a guest of Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar. She was standing silently in the gallery when she was arrested. Capitol police said at the time that she refused orders to sit down, and was taken into custody for unlawful conduct. She was released, and never faced charges.

title: Reported ICE activity sparks tense confrontation in Huntington Park
description:

“That is what protesters want to do, they want to create enough noise that ICE doesn’t feel comfortable and that they can leave,” said Jonathan Sanabria, Huntington Park Vice Mayor.
Huntington Park officials and community activists have expressed opposition to federal immigration enforcement activity in the city.

text:
Tensions escalated outside the Huntington Park Police Department on Monday morning after federal immigration agents reportedly arrived in the area, prompting community activists to confront them, blow whistles and demand that they leave.

According to Huntington Park officials, the agents were allegedly waiting for someone being held in police custody.

Community members quickly gathered outside the police department, using whistles and protests to voice their opposition to the agents' presence.

“I am really proud of our community, how they protected and how they did everything possible for them to leave,” said a witness who asked not to be identified, citing concerns for their safety.

The witness said residents sprang into action as soon as they noticed the federal agents.

“That is what protesters want to do, they want to create enough noise that ICE doesn’t feel comfortable and that they can leave,” said Jonathan Sanabria, Huntington Park Vice Mayor.

Sanabria said the agents were waiting for someone in police custody and explained that federal agencies can access information entered into the police department's database.

“We don’t tell them if we are releasing anyone, we don’t tell them any information. That’s why they were just sitting and waiting,” said Sanabria.

Huntington Park adopted a sanctuary city ordinance last year that prohibits the use of city resources to assist with federal immigration enforcement and protects residents' personal information, including their immigration status.

“We’re on the side of the community, and we want to make sure that the community is safe,” said Sanabria.

The federal agents eventually left without detaining anyone, according to city officials.

Huntington Park officials and community activists have expressed opposition to federal immigration enforcement activity in the city. Activists say they plan to continue protesting and alerting residents whenever they spot immigration agents in the area.

“We just want to make our community safe for parents and other hardworking people in Huntington Park. If you see anything, you know, alert, let people know they are around,” said the witness.

Sanabria said community members have been communicating with one another to share information about the presence of immigration agents.

“They’rall communicating with one another to let them know where ICE is. Because what ICE is doing, to me, is not lawful. If they were going after the criminals, that’s one thing. But we have seen time and time again that they’re targeting anyone,” said Sanabria.

NBC4 reached out to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Customs and Border Protection to ask why federal agents were in the area Monday morning but had not received a response.

text:
Bulldozers may soon tear into the rock cliffs and desert sand in Big Bend National Park to erect parts of the Trump Administration’s controversial border barrier.

On November 9, the U.S. Supreme Court gave the federal government the green light to resume construction on barriers, fences, and surveillance equipment along the U.S.-Mexico border in a remote corner of Texas that includes Big Bend National Park.

In an unsigned opinion, the court ruled that Congress has expressed “clear preference for expeditious border construction.” The government’s desire to limit immigration overrules any “aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm,” the court added.

The court ruled 8-1. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented with the decision.

The Center for Biological Diversity, one of the plaintiffs in a lawsuit that challenged the construction, blasted the decision in a statement.

“The Trump Administration and its contractors are hellbent on destroying one of America’s greatest national parks, and the Supreme Court just gave them the green light,” Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity, said on Facebook.

A Major Court Decision After Months of Legal Battles

The ruling marks a groundbreaking decision in a months-long game of political football between the Trump Administration and a growing number of advocates, Texas locals, and lawmakers who opposed the construction.

Officials with the U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the Department of Homeland Security have said that the barriers along stretches of the Rio Grande and Big Bend National Park are needed to curb illegal immigrants from entering the U.S. from Mexico.

Advocates and local property owners in Texas have argued that the number of illegal crossings in the Big Bend region is negligible, and that construction would irreparably damage the pristine landscape, hurt local flora and fauna, and destroy local businesses that rely on the landscape for tourism and agriculture. In April, a coalition of opponents to the project filed suit to block the construction.

In August, construction crews arrived in the Big Bend region and began clearing swaths of desert for bollards and fencing. But construction ground to a halt after state politicians put pressure on Trump administration officials. And on October 2, a federal judge overseeing the legal case ruled that the construction should stop because it threatened to harm a group of plaintiffs who had sued to stop it.

The border wall plan drew ire from officials on both sides of the political spectrum. On November 9, Texas Senator John Cornyn, a Republican, published an op-ed in the San Antonio Express-News titled “The Case Against the Big Bend Border Wall.”

“Texans should not have to bear another unnecessary financial burden caused by building a 30-foot wall atop a 1,000-foot riverbank cliff,” Cornyn wrote.

Groups Condemn the Supreme Court Decision on Big Bend National Park

After the Supreme Court decision on November 9, environmental groups and other opponents voiced their disapproval on social media.

“We are outraged by the Supreme Court’s decision allowing Trump’s border wall construction to resume in Big Bend National Park,” the Sierra Club posted on X. “This destructive project threatens irreplaceable wildlife habitat, sacred cultural sites, and one of America’s most treasured landscapes.”

In a statement, Cary Dupuy, Texas Regional Director for the National Parks Conservation Association (NPCA), said the decision would have “profound consequences.”

“Our national parks are meant to be set aside from harmful development and safeguarded under the highest standard possible under American law,” Dupy said. “Regardless of the court’s decision, we urge the administration to implement alternatives to damaging border barriers and other heavy infrastructure in this wild place. There is still a chance for us to save Big Bend, and there is still an opportunity for the administration to change course.”

Meghan Riley, senior attorney with the environmental advocacy group Earthjustice, called Big Bend a “national treasure.”

“allowing the administration to bulldoze through these fragile and protected ecosystems puts irreplaceable land at risk,” Riley said in a statement. “Once this damage is done, there is no simply putting Big Bend back together.”

Dave Cortez, director of the Sierra Club’s Lone Star chapter, pointed out the bipartisan anger at the border construction within Texas.

“Millions of Texans turned out to vote for change last week, and Republicans, Democrats, and Independents alike have spoken out against the Trump administration’s reckless and destructive plans to bulldoze the treasured borderlands of Far West Texas and the greater Big Bend region,” Cortez said in a statement. “This Supreme Court decision ignores the bipartisan opposition to a project that threatens some of Texas’s most cherished landscapes.”

This is a developing story.

title: Arizona freshmen Shah, Mendoza and Lamb eye costs, border and Trump
authors: Joey Chenoweth, Arizona Capitol Times, Sophia Braccio, Ellis Preston and Eileen Mamaghani, Cronkite News, Joey Chenoweth, Arizona Capitol Times
description:

When the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, at least 109 House members will be newcomers.
JoAnna Mendoza Mendoza is the first female Marine elected to the House.

text:
Key Points:

JoAnna Mendoza, Amish Shah and Mark Lamb took part in freshman orientation at the U.S. House of Representatives

Members of Congress are adjusting to the dynamics of a new Democratic majority and Republican minority

More than a quarter of the House will be new faces after a midterm where voters chose change at the federal level

WASHINGTON – Arizona’s three newest members of Congress arrived at the Capitol for freshman orientation Monday eager to deliver on their promises to voters.

Democrats JoAnna Mendoza and Amish Shah, who flipped GOP-held seats, and Republican Mark Lamb, who’ll replace gubernatorial runner-up Rep. Andy Biggs, are part of the largest House freshman class in decades.

Between closed-door orientation sessions on such topics as how to set up a congressional office, the three spoke with Cronkite News about their approaches to affordability and oversight of the executive branch, and their hopes for committee assignments.

When the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, at least 109 House members will be newcomers. That’s more than a quarter of the 435-member House.

Democrats will vastly outnumber Republicans after voters handed President Donald Trump and his party a stinging rebuke. Democrats attributed the result to high gas prices, corruption, executive overreach and Trump’s immigration and tariff policies.

As Arizona’s members get acquainted with Washington, they are each preparing for the opportunities of the 120th Congress with their own policy goals.

JoAnna Mendoza

Mendoza is the first female Marine elected to the House. She said she hopes to land a seat on the House Armed Services Committee, calling the Iran war a “huge concern.”

She ousted two-term Rep. Juan Ciscomani, R-Tucson, by about 28,500 votes in a district that includes Tucson and the southeast section of the Arizona-Mexico border.

She’s also interested in the Homeland Security Committee.

“In the military, you don’t ask people if they’re Republicans, independents or Democrats,” she said. “What you do is you build relationships, you earn trust, and then you accomplish the mission, and that’s exactly what I plan to do here.”

Like other Democrats, she said she intends to focus on affordability through reversing Medicaid cuts, a problem she heard about from many of her soon-to-be constituents.

The cuts under Trump, she said, are “going to be so devastating.”

Democrats also promised accountability and oversight in the midterms. Mendoza emphasized issues with tangible impact on her district, including healthcare, job security and cost of living.

“There’s going to be plenty of time for oversight and accountability,” she said. “But I think we can do both because people really need us to.”

Amish Shah

Shah, an emergency room physician and former state House member, defeated Trump-backed Jay Feely by just under 25,000 votes.

“Core function in medicine is to care for people,” he said. “We have to care for those people back at home in our district. Make sure we deliver.”

He’ll replace Rep. David Schweikert, R-Fountain Hills, who gave up his seat to run for governor. Biggs defeated him in the GOP primary.

The district includes northeast Phoenix, Scottsdale and Paradise Valley and had been trending more purple. Schweikert carried it by less than 4 percentage points two years ago.

Shah said he met with Schweikert after winning the seat.

“He was gracious, he was kind,” Shah said. “We’ve got to do the best we can for the constituents.”

Apart from the usual Democratic emphasis on affordability and healthcare, Shah also cited water policy. He campaigned in part on working across party lines but said that doesn’t mean shying from tough oversight of the Trump administration.

“Corruption is directly tied to cost-of-living increases and all the other issues that we’re facing back at home,” he said, referring to the Iran war, Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill tax overhaul, and the tariffs the president has slapped on major trading partners.

“Those things are going to be a focus for us to try to move costs in the right direction for the people,” he said.

As for a third impeachment of Trump, as some in the party’s progressive wing are demanding, Shah said: “We’ll see.”

“Impeachment is in the Constitution as a remedy, put in there by the founding fathers for high crimes, misdemeanors and egregious actions, and that is the law, and we will follow the law,” Shah said. “ It’s our constitutional duty.”

Mark Lamb

Lamb, the former Pinal County sheriff, put border security at the top of his list and said the fact he’ll be in the minority won’t change his priorities.

He narrowly won the 5th District with 51.7% of votes – a big drop from Biggs’ 60% tally in 2024.

“The border still needs to be fixed long term. That’s not an issue that has solidified,” he said before Monday morning’s orientation outside the Capitol Visitor Center auditorium. “While we’re doing great with it, I think a lot of Americans forgot how bad it could be – and it was – and we need to get back to fixing it again.”

A longtime Trump supporter, Lamb campaigned on closer cooperation between local law enforcement and federal immigration authorities, though he also offered an implicit critique of Trump administration policy, calling for prioritizing people who have committed crimes while in the country illegally.

He said he wants to “pare down big-government,” make life more affordable by cutting taxes – unlikely with Democrats in control – finding ways to lower energy costs and “getting inflation under control.”

The $40.5 trillion national debt puts the U.S. economy on a “collision course,” he said.

GOP leaders haven’t yet made committee assignments.

Lamb said he believes his background would serve him well on Homeland Security or Judiciary.

name: Human Rights
title: The border without boundaries: human rights in digital immigration enforcement
description:
But the United States reveals another dimension of this transformation: the border is moving inward.
Expansion of the digital border and federal databases Federal immigration databases are increasingly expanding their scope beyond biometric and identification technologies.
Integrating data collected in everyday civic life into the machinery of immigration control extends the digital border beyond the nation’s physical boundaries and into the routine activities of people throughout the United States.
In the United States, the border is no longer confined to the place where people cross it.
As the reach of the digital border continues to expand, so too must the protections of due process, transparency, and human rights.
text:
Imagine walking down the street of a country where you are a citizen and suddenly being stopped by federal immigration officials, questioned about your movements, and asked to prove your identity. For Jesus Gutiérrez, a 23-year-old US citizen in Chicago, this was not a hypothetical situation. Gutiérrez, who had not committed a crime or acted in any way that required intervention, told immigration agents that he was a US citizen, but they ignored and proceeded to arrest him simply because he was unable to immediately prove his legal status. They did not set him free until a face scan process through an internal federal database confirmed his citizenship.

Gutiérrez passed no physical checkpoint. No border crossing was involved. But a database, biometric scan, or algorithm may now be enough to bring the border into ordinary encounters well within the United States. Petra Molnar has argued that the creation of “smart borders” through technological surveillance, biometrics, and artificial intelligence is transforming migration governance, often at the expense of fundamental human rights. But the United States reveals another dimension of this transformation: the border is moving inward. It is now a barrier that can follow people rather than one they cross.

From border security to digital governance

Traditional border enforcement is geographically defined. Federal immigration authorities operate at ports of entry, along land borders, and within designated areas where federal law provides particular enforcement powers. Digital systems, like internal biometric databases, complicate that geographic model by allowing information collected in one place to be retrieved and analyzed in another.

The federal government maintains extensive biometric and biographical databases for immigration enforcement and other domestic operations. One example is the Department of Homeland Security’s Automated Biometric Identification System (IDENT), begun in the 1990s, which is being replaced by the Homeland Advanced Recognition Technology (HART) system. HART is designed to store and process fingerprints, facial images, iris scans, and other identifiers submitted by immigration agencies like US Customs and Border Protection and US Citizenship and Immigration Services.

Significantly, these systems do not simply make identification faster; instead, they fundamentally change the nature of an immigration encounter. A government official who previously needed a document or direct access to a particular record can now use a biometric identifier to establish a person’s identity and retrieve information associated with it. In some cases, individuals may not even be aware that a database search has occurred or which system or systems influenced an officer’s decision.

Federal information-sharing practices further expand this capacity. One example is the 287(g) program, which effectively embeds immigration screening into routine policing by allowing state and local law enforcement agencies to collaborate directly with federal immigration authorities.

The result of all this is that immigration enforcement does not necessarily begin with an individual presenting themselves at a border. It can begin with a traffic stop in Arizona, a booking procedure in a county jail in Texas, or a routine identity check in a city hundreds of miles from any international boundary.

Due process in the age of unknown databases

Moreover, individuals may have difficulty identifying, accessing, or correcting the information used to make decisions about them as part of these digital immigration-enforcement processes.

Government databases can easily produce erroneous results even when the technology performs as designed. A facial recognition system can correctly match a person to a record, but the underlying record itself may be outdated or inaccurate. In more extreme cases, the record may be associated with an entirely different individual who simply has a similar name or biometric profile. These risks are not distributed equally. Studies of facial recognition systems have found higher error rates for certain demographic groups, particularly women and people with darker skin tones, creating a greater risk for mistaken identification and government scrutiny.

An inaccurate or misapplied database is not merely an administrative inconvenience if it contributes to detention, removal proceedings, or the denial of an immigration benefit. Yet the person affected may not even know which database was consulted, what information generated the government's decision, or which agency is responsible for correcting it.

Immigrants, regardless of legal status, are entitled to due process of law, a fundamental right outlined in the Fifth Amendment of the US Constitution and repeatedly affirmed by the Supreme Court. Due process generally requires procedural safeguards designed to mitigate the risk of erroneous decisions and proportionate to their consequences. But the US government is not strengthening these procedural safeguards—a danger recognized by federal agencies themselves. Instead, it is increasingly and actively expanding digital immigration enforcement mechanisms with known errors that tend to fall disproportionately on already vulnerable populations.

Expansion of the digital border and federal databases

Federal immigration databases are increasingly expanding their scope beyond biometric and identification technologies. Information originally generated for purposes largely unrelated to border enforcement (including taxation, air travel, social media, healthcare, and other ordinary interactions with government institutions) is increasingly incorporated into immigration enforcement systems.

Integrating data collected in everyday civic life into the machinery of immigration control extends the digital border beyond the nation’s physical boundaries and into the routine activities of people throughout the United States.

Molnar warns that making migration increasingly subject to biometric identification, automated decision-making, and data collection creates new frontiers of surveillance and contributes to the erosion of human rights. In the United States, the border is no longer confined to the place where people cross it. The government’s technologies, databases, and information-sharing systems increasingly operate throughout domestic society, far beyond the state’s physical boundaries.

As the reach of the digital border continues to expand, so too must the protections of due process, transparency, and human rights.

Durbin: “Americans, from one end of this nation to the other, exercised their right to vote last Tuesday, and in doing so, they changed the course of America and its politics for years to come.”

WASHINGTON – In a speech on the Senate floor, U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, highlighted last Tuesday’s historic election wins—which included flipping both chambers of Congress.

“Americans have fought and died to protect the Constitution—they have marched and bled to change this document so that the promise of a more perfect union would be available to all men and women, not just a few. Was it perfect? By no means… Does the Constitution still work? I think anyone watching the results of last Tuesday’s election would say that it does… Americans, from one end of this nation to the other, exercised their right to vote last Tuesday, and in doing so, they changed the course of America and its politics for years to come. What happened on that day renewed my faith in this country,” said Durbin.

“The midterm elections were a repudiation of the toxic brand of politics we have faced for the past 10 years… Americans made it clear that our nation prefers love over hate and community over cruelty. We saw that message on full display in my home state of Illinois,” Durbin continued.

During his speech, Durbin offered his congratulations to Illinois’s Senator-elect, Juliana Stratton, noting that she has served Illinois as a member of the General Assembly and Lieutenant Governor and that he looks forward to seeing her success in her new role. In addition to Stratton, Illinois Democrats won every statewide race that was on the ballot, and they won in deep red counties like McHenry County, which had not voted for a Democrat for governor since 1852.

Durbin then highlighted how voters rejected the chaos, corruption, and cruelty of the Trump Administration’s policies.

“Those results are unsurprising for anyone who has had a chance to speak to Illinois families over the past two years, who have all too often faced the brunt of the cruelty, chaos, and corruption of this Administration. They saw the cruelty firsthand on our streets during ‘Operation Midway Blitz,’ when immigration agents raided and terrorized our communities in Illinois—jailing and beating immigrants and U.S. citizens alike… They saw chaos in our hospitals when patient after patient witnessed their health insurance premiums dramatically increase, if they even still had insurance at all, after this Administration’s health care cuts. And they saw the corruption in the White House when families struggled to afford groceries and gas while the President and his cronies enriched themselves beyond their wildest dreams… Illinoisans made it clear on Tuesday that they do not have confidence in this Administration’s leadership—and tens of millions of Americans across the country joined them in that effort,” said Durbin.

Durbin then highlighted the historic and diverse wins from the 2026 midterm election. Next Congress, 159 women will serve across the two chambers. In addition, voters elected the first Muslim American, the first Native American woman, and the first openly gay man to serve in the United States Senate. Senator Duckworth and Senator-elect Stratton will be the first women of color to serve a state simultaneously.

“In governors’ races, voters elected more women, and more women of color, to the highest state office than we have ever seen before. While there is still more to be done to ensure that the composition of our elected officials reflect the people who put us here, Tuesday brought us one step closer to a world where every American can see themselves in their representatives,” said Durbin.

Durbin then slammed President Trump for promoting Stephen Miller to serve as the White House Chief of Staff after the election.

Durbin continued, “As fortunate as Tuesday was, it was only the first step. Americans made it clear they demand change, and it is up to those in Washington to give it to them. You would think after this clear and resounding defeat, the President would listen to the voters. But what was one of his first decisions in the aftermath of this historic election? To choose Stephen Miller, architect of this Administration’s cruel mass deportation campaign, as his new chief of staff.”

Following American voters’ massive rejection of the Trump Administration’s immigration policies, Durbin concluded his speech by urging Congress and the President to pass his Dream Act, bipartisan legislation which would allow noncitizens without lawful status who were brought to the United States as children and meet certain education, military service, or work requirements to earn lawful permanent residence. These young people, known as Dreamers, have lived in America since they were children, built their lives here, and are American in every way except for their immigration status. However, under current law, there is often no chance for them to ever become citizens and fulfill their potential.

Environmental groups and tribal organizations urged lawmakers to pause consideration of the permitting bill until the next Congress, when Democrats will take control of the House and the Senate.

In a media advisory, organizers from the New York Public Interest Research Group, Food & Water Watch, and New York Communities for Change, who led Monday’s protest and a previous one at Schumer’s apartment on Friday, called the bill an “aggressive attack on federal environmental protections in order to facilitate rapid, unregulated development of fracked gas power plants, dirty fossil fuel pipelines, and expensive hyperscale data centers.”

The motion needs 60 votes to advance, so some Democrats will have to support holding a final vote. The bill’s leading Democratic sponsor, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), said he believes supporters “have the votes to proceed.”

The bill faces longer odds in the US House of Representatives, especially after Tuesday’s Democratic blowout in the midterms, when voters across the country also backed restrictions on data centers.

Sponsors have revised the bill, but David Watkins, director of government affairs for the Climate and Energy programs at the Union of Concerned Scientists, argued that the amendment “fails to address the fundamental imbalance of the legislation” in favor of polluting energy.

“To get bipartisan support for negligible reductions in emissions,” he said, “this deal would convert compliance with the National Environmental Policy Act, Endangered Species Act, National Historic Preservation Act, and Clean Water Act into largely voluntary exercises.”

While some Democratic proponents of the bill have argued that these compromises are necessary to speed up permits for clean energy infrastructure, Watkins said existing law already allows much of that work and saw no need to enact “the most significant legislative reversal in environmental and community protections in decades.”

A coalition of conservation groups, including Earthjustice Action, Defenders of Wildlife, and Friends of the Earth, sent a letter to the Senate on Monday urging members to delay the vote until newly elected members of the US Congress—some of whom made opposition to data centers central to their campaigns—can be sworn in.

As questions mount about whether Democratic leaders will use their new mandate to pursue a bold legislative agenda, some see BAAJA as a worrying sign that Schumer and other party leaders may squander the moment by reverting to business as usual.

The majority ruled that construction can continue as the lower court considers its legality, finding that Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is permitted by the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 to waive environmental laws and has “broad authority to construct border barriers and roads."

In August, despite a separate coalition's lawsuit, bulldozers appeared at Big Bend and began leveling part of the national park before the October ruling halted construction.

Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity, told The New York Times he was "completely devastated" by the ruling.

Customs and Border Protection has indicated the agency plans to build vehicle barriers and patrol roads across the national park, including in the remote Mariscal Mountain region, which would require "extensive dynamite blasting," according to CBD.

“The Trump administration and its contractors are hell-bent on destroying one of America’s greatest national parks, and the Supreme Court just gave them the green light,” Jordahl said in a statement. “This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal. They’re signing off on the permanent destruction of the wildest place in Texas, and the theft of a great American river from all of us.”

Sierra Club also expressed outrage, and US Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) said the decision would only "destroy the nature and wildlife that we love at Big Bend."

"The corrupt and far-right Supreme Court just gave [President Donald] Trump the OK to rip up Big Bend with a border wall. No one will be safer or freer," said Casar. "Democrats, Republicans, Texans of all backgrounds all agree: Leave Big Bend alone."

Jordahl emphasized that the court had ruled in favor of the Trump administration less than a week after two Texas Democrats, Sen.-elect James Talarico and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, stunned the Republican Party with their electoral victories in the longtime GOP stronghold.

Texans “roundly rejected the destruction of this national park and border wall destruction at large," Jordahl told the Times, adding that Mullin's agency “would be wise to listen to Texans and pump the brakes on this project.”

In a statement, he warned that "Americans care deeply about this extraordinary national park and they won’t stand by quietly if its irreplaceable landscapes are butchered and paved over."

"The damage done to Big Bend will be felt for future generations of Texans and Americans," he said, "and this administration will bear responsibility for the natural heritage we lose.”

Hillary Pierce, director of communications for the group No Big Bend Wall, which also sued the administration in September, noted that officials haven't "answered why the government is building a wall in one of the least-crossed stretches of the southern border."

“Once the bulldozers cut through a canyon or a family's ranch gets walled off from the Rio Grande, there's no undoing it," said Pierce. "This isn't the end of our fight. The justices didn't decide whether Big Bend actually qualifies as an area of high illegal entry. That matters because the administration used that designation to justify building the wall and bypassing environmental protections. The government's own numbers show Big Bend has the fewest Border Patrol apprehensions along the southern border. That's exactly what we're challenging in our lawsuit in Washington.”

text:
The Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for a Trump administration wall construction project along the U.S.-Mexico border in Texas, over dissent from Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson.

The high court majority said that a lower court was wrong to halt the project because it likely lacked jurisdiction to block the government action.

The administration sought to waive environmental and conservation laws in order to facilitate construction in a region it called the “Big Bend Sector.” The Homeland Security secretary said the area was “an area of high illegal entry” that required more protection.

That prompted a lawsuit from a river guide, an environmental nonprofit and a nonprofit dedicated to preserving a historic church in Ruidosa, Texas. They argued that the secretary exceeded his authority. A federal district court in West Texas granted a preliminary injunction.

More articles

Lifting that injunction while further litigation proceeds, the Supreme Court said, in part, that the government’s interest “outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged” by the plaintiffs.

Unsuccessfully opposing the action the court took on Monday, the plaintiffs said that granting the government’s request “would result in the permanent alteration of an irreplaceable landscape that includes Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, and nearly 200 miles of the congressionally designated Rio Grande Wild and Scenic River corridor.”

The court’s reasoning came in an unsigned “per curiam” opinion, which is how the justices have been handling some emergency litigation lately instead of simply issuing an unexplained order.

Jackson, a Biden appointee, only noted without explanation that she would have denied the administration’s application.

text:
Read a PDF of our statement here.

On November 6, 2026, a federal judge ordered the City of New York to provide Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) with the names and dates of birth of certain male residents in a Bronx shelter.

Previously, ICE requested this information of all 2000+ residents in the shelter.

In response, Legal Defense Fund (LDF) Director of Strategic Initiatives Jin Hee Lee issued the following statement:

“ICE’s initial attempts to indiscriminately obtain identifying and personal information of all of a Bronx shelter’s residents, the vast majority of whom are Black and Brown, exposes a dangerous and troubling strategy of targeting some of the most vulnerable in our communities for immigration enforcement. Shelter residents already are at significant risk of violence and experiencing life-threatening health and economic conditions. Adding an additional fear of ICE enforcement may deter residents from seeking the supportive services that are vital to their health and well-being, especially as we experience colder weather.

“We caution against the unnecessary disclosure of information that would prevent vulnerable, unhoused people from seeking the life-saving services they need. ICE’s large scale and indiscriminate request for information about shelter residents has been substantially narrowed, but the risk of harm and the threat communicated by their targeting of unhoused people remain very real.

“While accountability is necessary and important, we should never accept the dehumanization of any person, including those who are unhoused and those who have become enmeshed in our criminal legal system. Everyone, regardless of their housing status or past conduct, are entitled to humane treatment and the full due process of our laws.”

###

Founded in 1940, the Legal Defense Fund (LDF) is the nation’s first civil rights law organization. LDF’s Thurgood Marshall Institute is a multi-disciplinary and collaborative hub within LDF that launches targeted campaigns and undertakes innovative research to shape the civil rights narrative. In media attributions, please refer to us as the Legal Defense Fund or LDF. Please note that LDF has been completely separate from the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) since 1957—although LDF was originally founded by the NAACP and shares its commitment to equal rights.

Carlitos Ricardo Parias, also known as Richard, is a citizen journalist who reports on issues impacting his community in Los Angeles, California. In October 2025, masked immigration agents shot and injured Richard while attempting to arrest him outside his home for immigration purposes. While in hospital he was subsequently charged with assault against a federal agent and taken into US Marshals custody, despite needing ongoing medical care.

A federal judge ultimately dismissed the assault charge against Richard on the grounds that the government failed to uphold Richard’s right to a fair trial. Richard continues to suffer severe pain and swelling from his gunshot wound. His lawyers say he has not received adequate medical care, and his family fears he could suffer lasting damage or worse.

Richard is a father of two who loves spending time with his family, whether going for walks or simply watching television together. Instead, Richard has spent a year separated from them. He should be free and receiving urgent medical treatment.

text:
FOREST HEIGHTS, Md. – After suggesting he was open to negotiating a deal with Democrats on an immigration policy that he described as too tough, President Donald Trump on Monday defended his administration’s deportation policy and said he was opposed to any immigration deal that would include “amnesty” for immigrants living in the U.S. illegally.

The comments from Trump came after Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin earlier Monday also said that while he has been fielding calls from Democrats interested in working on immigration policy, he was adamantly opposed to any deal that would include amnesty.

The midterm elections highlighted voters’ disaffection toward the administration’s hard-line immigration enforcement activities. But the comments from both Trump and Mullin reflected the mixed messaging from the administration in the aftermath of the election and emphasized how complicated it will be for a new Congress controlled by Democrats to find any common ground when it comes to the issue of immigration.

Immigration has long been one of the most intractable issues facing Congress, with any deal that gives people in the country illegally a pathway to resolve their status often characterized by anti-immigration critics as amnesty. But advocates have said that longtime immigrants who've lived in the U.S. for years and worked and raised families here deserve a way to come out of the shadows and legalize their status.

“There won’t be amnesty,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “Somebody suggested, will there be amnesty? No, but — they came in. They knew the law.”

Trump defended his administration’s deportation policy as “very strong.” Asked if he had spoken with Stephen Miller, his newly promoted chief of staff who was the architect of his immigration crackdown, about immigration changes, Trump said no.

“My policy hasn’t changed,” he said, adding that the focus will be on removing “the worst of the worst.”

In comparison, during an interview that aired Sunday with “60 Minutes,” Trump said “killers” and “drug dealers” in the country illegally should be deported, but suggested he was open to the idea of a deal that would let others stay “if they’re good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes.”

Trump rode back into power with a promise to crack down on immigration. During the first two years of his second term, arrests of immigrants surged, including through high-profile operations in large U.S. cities that sometimes turned violent.

And voters appeared to disapprove of the tactics. Nationally, about 6 in 10 voters said the Trump administration’s actions on immigration enforcement had “gone too far,” according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters. A similar share disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement was doing its job.

Mullin earlier Monday reiterated Trump’s willingness to work with Democrats on the issue, although he said that he and the president haven’t yet discussed any concrete immigration policy changes in the aftermath of the midterm elections.

Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a conference near Washington, D.C., Mullin also said he is strongly opposed to any amnesty for people living in the U.S. illegally.

Mullin, who was a senator and House representative before becoming Trump’s Homeland Security secretary earlier this year, said after the election he’s been fielding calls from Democrats that he worked with in Congress on bipartisan issues.

“I’ve let the president know that those calls are coming in. And the president has said, you know, let’s start working with them and then let’s meet at some point. So that’s the extent of the conversation,” Mullin said. “We haven’t had any conversation just on policy.”

Trump since the election has elevated Miller, raising questions about how cooperation with Democrats might look so long as enforcement remains strict. Mullin called Miller in a post on social media last week an “excellent choice.”

Mullin, who said he worked with Democrats while he was in Congress including on immigration reform, said he thought a bipartisan approach was the only way to get anything done. But the secretary also pushed back decisively against any type of agreement that would include amnesty for people living illegally in the U.S.

“I was working on immigration reform when I was in the House and when I was in the Senate. I think the only way you can actually get it is by a bipartisan approach. But amnesty's never going to be a solution. We’re never gonna allow amnesty to happen. So that’s a full stop,” said Mullin.

The Homeland Security secretary raised the issue of DACA — a form of protection from deportation for children brought to the country illegally by their parents. He said figuring out a way to legalize their status would be up to Congress.

“Now, if we wanna have an immigration reform to where we can look at DACA and figure out a way that these individuals can become maybe legal permanent citizens or something like this, that’ll be up to Congress to do that,” Mullin said.

___

Associated Press writer Collin Binkley in Washington contributed to this report.

text:
An internationally wanted crook with a lengthy rap sheet, including the admitted murder of his girlfriend, was arrested in New York City for illegally entering the country, federal immigration officials said.

Sobirjon Sobirov Khusen Ugli, from Uzbekistan, was cuffed near his Brooklyn home on Oct. 14, after having illegally crossed over the border into the United States through Lukeville, Arizona over three and a half years ago, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement announced Monday.

The illegal immigrant, 35, had been living freely in the United States, even after he admitted to murdering his girlfriend in Thailand in 2013, ICE officials said.

Sobirov was arrested for the crime and told cops that he’d stuffed his beau’s body in a suitcase before dumping it in a canal, according to press reports cited by ICE. It’s not immediately clear if he was convicted and served any time for the murder.

The crook was later found guilty of felony theft in his native Uzbekistan in 2020 and was hit with a prison sentence of five years, the agency said.

Then in April 2023, he illegally crossed into the United States and was detained with a group of 110 border crossers, authorities said.

Sobirov was released into the US with a notice to appear for immigration proceedings in New York City – reporting only once in May 2024, according to immigration officials.

The confessed killer’s reign of terror continued while he lived in New York City, ICE said.

Sobirov was arrested by the NYPD for harassing communication and given a restraining order by a Kings County Criminal Court judge in 2024, officials said.

ICE’s New York City Field Office Director Kenneth Genalo said that the agency “particularly” goes after dangerous threats to public safety such as Sobirov.

“Our officers work every day to identify, arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens before they can cause further harm in our communities,” Genalo said in a statement.

Sobirov is being held in ICE custody, and removal proceedings are underway, officials said.

text:
UPDATE: Termination of Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and Syrians

On Tuesday, June 25, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled that the Trump administration could move forward with its plans to rip legal status away from nearly 350,000 current Haitian and Syrian Temporary Protected Status (TPS) holders. Following this decision, the Department of Homeland Security announced the termination of TPS for Haitians and Syrians, effective July 27, 2026.

Individuals who have lost TPS may be impacted in different ways, including loss of protection from deportation and loss of work authorization. However, there may be alternative legal pathways to remain and work in the United States. To learn more about what the end of TPS means for you and your family:

All TPS holders regardless of designation should visit the USCIS website for the latest updates on their TPS status.

text:
SAN ANTONIO – The future of the proposed immigration warehouse facility on the East Side is uncertain as the City of San Antonio and the U.S. Department of Justice discuss potential agreements following a lawsuit.

The city sued the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Acting ICE Director David Venturella in October to try to block the conversion of a 640,000-square-foot warehouse into an immigration processing facility.

The city said the federal government skipped over an environmental review process required under the National Environmental Policy Act and violated the Administrative Procedure Act.

After the U.S. Department of Justice was made aware of the lawsuit, federal officials reached out to the city of San Antonio to discuss plans to come up with an agreement and comply with the environmental review, according to the City Attorney’s Office.

The agreement, according to the city, would pause the lawsuit while environmental reviews are conducted. Additionally, work to convert the warehouse into a detention facility would also be on pause. However, the city said the agreement is still in the works.

KSAT reached out to ICE and DHS for comment Monday evening.

In late August, ICE awarded a $17.3 million contract to GardaWorld Federal Services LLC to renovate the East Side warehouse into a processing and detention facility and provide wraparound services to operate it.

Federal records show the contract has since grown to $61.8 million.

The immigration agency also paid $51 million for a pair of office leases at Brooks in October.

The 1,500-person facility, located at 542 SE Loop 410, is projected to open as early as next spring, according to ICE.

title: Lack of cultural and linguistic understanding lead to unfair immigration decisions
description:
Where Home Office decision-makers and First-tier Tribunal judges lack cultural understanding and sensitivity, this often materially alters case outcomes and results in errors of law.
The study analysed 271 decisions of the Upper Tribunal (Immigration and Asylum Chamber) promulgated between 2023 and 2025.
The Upper Tribunal hears appeals against decisions of the First-tier Tribunal (Immigration and Asylum).
The Upper Tribunal found that, given the appellant’s age and cultural background, such evidence was unlikely to exist.
In multiple decisions, Upper Tribunal judges found that First-tier Tribunal judges confused sexuality with being sexually active (UI-2025-000550; UI-2023-000932).
text:
A new report by Public Law Project examines how people’s socio-cultural and historical-political background shapes the way they experience and communicate issues relating to relationships, sexual identity and trauma. Where Home Office decision-makers and First-tier Tribunal judges lack cultural understanding and sensitivity, this often materially alters case outcomes and results in errors of law. Below we outline three main issues and the recommendations that follow.

The study analysed 271 decisions of the Upper Tribunal (Immigration and Asylum Chamber) promulgated between 2023 and 2025. The Upper Tribunal hears appeals against decisions of the First-tier Tribunal (Immigration and Asylum). We also observed tribunal hearings and interviewed legal representatives, interpreters and an intermediary. This is the second of two reports on why cultural and linguistic sensitivity matters in immigration and asylum tribunals. The first examined translation and interpretation services, contextual evidence and procedural culture.

The recommendations focus on what to consider when preparing and conducting a case. They emphasise the need to weigh each case’s individual circumstances against the broader socio-cultural context.

The report is organised around three themes: family and relationships; LGBTQ+ identity and community; and trauma, vulnerability and mental health. Each section explains why cultural understanding and translation are particularly relevant and reviews the key patterns or issues observed in the decisions. This approach enables institutional learning by drawing on the reasoning of highly experienced and qualified Upper Tribunal judges to identify preventable errors in earlier decision-making.

Family and private life and its varied forms

The Upper Tribunal has highlighted examples in which First-tier Tribunal judges held rigid expectations about what constitutes a family relationship. These are often rooted in eurocentric conceptions of the nuclear family and hierarchical assumptions about which relationships deserve protection. The judiciary also had unrealistic expectations about the documentary evidence appellants should produce.

In one case, the First-tier Tribunal judge expected an appellant to produce records of conversations and telephone calls showing that she had ‘fallen out’ with members of her family in India after her husband’s death (UI-2024-001328). The Upper Tribunal found that, given the appellant’s age and cultural background, such evidence was unlikely to exist. Even if telephone records existed, they might indicate amicable contact rather than the openly hostile nature of the underlying family conflict.

We recommend in our report that the Home Office and the judiciary recognise varied forms of family life and adopt a more culturally sensitive approach to evidencing it.

Lack of understanding of sexuality and LGBTQ+ identity

The report notes that the judiciary had even greater difficulty understanding sexuality. In numerous First-tier Tribunal decisions, judges understood sexuality through narrow, homogenising assumptions and expectations about relationships, coming out, emotionality and openness.

In one decision, an Upper Tribunal judge found that it was inappropriate for a First-tier Tribunal judge to comment on or draw conclusions about someone’s sexuality based on their body language (UI-2024-003100). In multiple decisions, Upper Tribunal judges found that First-tier Tribunal judges confused sexuality with being sexually active (UI-2025-000550; UI-2023-000932).

Some First-tier Tribunal judges expected appellants to provide a clear, linear account of discovering and disclosing their sexuality (UI-2022-005697; UI-2024-003100). Others appeared to place particular weight on whether an appellant had been in a same-sex relationship (UI-2025-000550; UI-2023-000932). This assumes a universal trajectory of LGBTQ+ identity.

In one case, the Upper Tribunal judge found that an appellant who adduced higher-quality evidence over time was not a sign of dishonesty, contrary to the reasoning at the First-tier. Instead, this reflected how they had come to feel safer disclosing their sexuality (UI-2024-003100).

One interpreter interviewed described an appellant who became distressed while discussing their sexuality because the interpreter spoke the appellant’s language and might have been from the same community.

We recommend improved training and guidance for Home Office decision-makers and the judiciary from organisations run by, for or with LGBTQ+ communities, and culturally sensitive approaches to interpreting LGBTQ+ cases.

Trauma, vulnerability and mental health

The report identifies that judges repeatedly made assumptions about trauma and mental health issues. In particular, they expected people to experience and describe trauma in coherent, linear and recognisably clinical terms. However, evidence shows that trauma often goes unrecognised, or that speaking about it openly may conflict with someone’s cultural or religious beliefs.

An Upper Tribunal judge ruled that decision-makers should not assume that a person whose condition has improved will not relapse, especially where they have a history of relapses and may re-experience symptoms on returning to a situation of distress or violation (UI-2022-004295). Another judge emphasised that whether mental health treatment is available in a person’s country of origin is a different question from whether they can access or engage with it (UI-2022-004295). In one case, the Upper Tribunal found that the First-tier Tribunal had made an error of law by failing to take vulnerability into account when assessing credibility (UI-2025-000293).

Trauma also affects a person’s ability to remember and recall, which is often central to evidencing an asylum claim. One legal representative interviewed described clients who said they felt ‘tired and exhausted’ or that their ‘head is getting hot’, without acknowledging that they could have mental health issues. By working closely with these clients over time, the experienced and attentive representative recognised signs of anxiety, depression and complex trauma.

Interpreters play an important role when working with vulnerable participants. One interpreter recalled interpreting for a 13-year-old unaccompanied asylum seeker and victim-survivor of sexual violence. The girl asked the interpreter to hold her hand, which is against professional rules for interpreters. The interpreter stayed beyond her paid hours because the girl asked her to, despite the social worker’s disapproval. For vulnerable people, an interpreter’s role goes beyond interpretation. That role is not always recognised and underscores why culturally sensitive support for vulnerable participants matters.

Intermediaries are not widely used in practice yet, but they can play an important role. They can explain the process to vulnerable participants, help people emotionally regulate, identify when someone needs a break or more time to respond, and help appellants communicate effectively. The intermediary we interviewed stressed that appellants are not the only people who experience trauma. Home Office employees and legal representatives can experience vicarious trauma, a concern that needs further attention.

We recommend that the judiciary recognise how context and social factors, including culture, shape mental state and wellbeing, and how people perceive and talk about these issues. This includes recognising the varied ways people experience trauma, how vulnerability affects participation in a hearing, vicarious trauma and the social stigma around mental health in some societies.

We also recommend raising awareness of intermediary services and adopting a more flexible approach to official diagnosis. Finally, judges need to understand not only whether mental health treatment and support are available, but whether people can access them in practice.

Conclusion

The decisions examined in the new report demonstrate that immigration and asylum is not only one of the most complex and high-stakes areas of law, but also requires decision-makers to navigate diverse political, socio-cultural and linguistic contexts. Translating these contexts requires a holistic, collaborative approach involving numerous professionals, especially on issues as complex as identity, vulnerability and relationships.

The report is published amid public scrutiny of the tribunal system, exemplified by the Home Office’s consultation on proposed changes that would create an Independent Appeals Body within the Home Office, and the Immigration and Asylum Bill. Public Law Project’s stance on the proposed changes, also echoed in the report, is that the proposals lack detail and are unsupported by evidence; they risk undermining judicial independence and the rule of law; and will not achieve their aims of reducing delays, backlogs, and multiple appeals.

As the report highlights, rather than scrutinising the judges, the reform should focus on better decision-making at earlier stages (notably, the Home Office’s decision-making), which would reduce appeals in the longer term, and a greater linguistic and socio-cultural understanding of the context and individual circumstances of applicants would help contribute to this.
