title: Building an archive of deaths in Greek immigration detention centres | Oxford Law Blogs
description:
Over 112 foreign nationals have died while held in Greek detention centres and police stations in the last 26 years.
People have been dying inside Greece’s police stations and immigration detention centres for decades.
The archive, published on Detention Landscapes in English, Greek and Arabic, was developed by University of Oxford researchers working on the Greek immigration detention system, and gathers years of documentation by activists, NGOs, journalists and monitoring bodies.
The announcement directly conflates legal status with criminality, and raises concerns that people could be transferred directly from their homes to immigration detention centres.
NGOs do not have guaranteed, regular access to immigration detention centres in Greece, limiting opportunities for independent monitoring of detention conditions and the documentation of deaths and other abuses.
text:
Blog post by Andriani Fili, Stergios Magkriotis and Alice Troy-Donovan. The researchers are based at the University of Oxford, working on Andriani’s project ‘Medicalising Immigration Detention’. The project is funded by the Wellcome Trust.

Over 112 foreign nationals have died while held in Greek detention centres and police stations in the last 26 years. These are some of their names:

Jadeous Kotseva. 38, Polish. Died in 2004 in Vyronas police station, Athens, while awaiting his deportation. According to reports he was suffering from chronic alcoholism.

Nezam Hakimi. Age unknown, Afghan. Died in 2013 in Corinth detention centre. The Afghan community said he had cancer which was left untreated for four months in detention.

Fata Abdul. 23 years old, Yemeni. Died in 2015 in a detention centre in Thessaloniki by suicide. Reports said he was held in isolation for a month prior to his death.

Mohammed Kamran. 37 years old, Pakistani. Died in 2024 in Agios Panteleimonas police station, Athens, likely as a result of police violence.

Hashir Latif. 30 years old, Pakistani. Died in 2025 after being declared brain dead following a suicide attempt in Amygdaleza detention centre, Athens.

Name unknown. Age unknown. Nationality unknown. Police report that this person died in 2024 in an unknown location and on an unknown date.

People have been dying inside Greece’s police stations and immigration detention centres for decades. Yet there is no reliable public record of these deaths. Greek authorities do not routinely publish statistics showing how many foreign nationals have died in immigration or police detention, who they were, where they died, or under what circumstances.

Drawing on police data obtained through Freedom of Information requests (FOIs), as well as reports by international monitoring bodies, media archives and interviews with formerly detained people, we have documented at least 112 deaths of foreign nationals in police and immigration detention in Greece since 2000 (read our methodology for researching deaths of foreign nationals in detention). Since Greece’s first pre-removal detention centre opened in 2012, 27 deaths have been reported in these facilities. Media coverage of deaths is typically limited to brief reports that reproduce information provided by the police, with little detail about the individuals concerned or the circumstances of their deaths. The perspectives of families, friends and fellow detainees are frequently absent.

Most of those whose deaths we documented were men (82), although four were women and the gender was not recorded in 26 cases. Among the 70 individuals whose age was known, the median was 33.5 years, with 45 aged under 40. Albanian and Pakistani nationals were the largest identified nationality groups (13 each), although nationality was unspecified in 32 cases. Suicide was the most frequently recorded cause of death in official (police or governmental) sources (44 cases), followed by pathological causes (20), while no cause was reported by the authorities in 36 cases. Non-governmental sources also raised concerns about medical neglect and physical abuse in some cases. These gaps in basic information, alongside the limited documentation of the circumstances of death, are particularly striking given that the individuals died in state custody, where their identities and personal details would ordinarily be expected to be recorded.

The archive, published on Detention Landscapes in English, Greek and Arabic, was developed by University of Oxford researchers working on the Greek immigration detention system, and gathers years of documentation by activists, NGOs, journalists and monitoring bodies. Beyond counting deaths, the project seeks to situate individual cases – which have previously been presented as isolated tragedies – within a broader context of violence and medical neglect in Greece’s immigration detention system.

Deaths occur across a range of sites, including in police stations in towns and cities, and in pre-removal detention centres, which are typically located in remote areas outside cities. In documenting these deaths, our research draws attention to the links between hostile immigration policies, violence against racialised people and repressive policing in Greek society.

The project adds to long-standing efforts elsewhere to document border and immigration control related deaths where reliable government data is not available. The most extensive existing database of this kind is the UNITED List of Refugee Deaths which contains data on deaths related to Fortress Europe since 1993, including deaths in custody. Other research has highlighted the urgency of making prisoner deaths visible, neglect as a form of power, and how the mental despair created by detention and intentional organisational failure push detained people to suicide and self-harm in immigration detention.

One year on from new criminalisation measures

We publish this archive now, one year after Greece passed legislation (Law 5226/2025) which further criminalised migration via the categories of ‘illegal entry’ and ‘illegal stay’. This law also expanded the grounds and duration of detention. People apprehended without documents may now face a maximum of 48 months in administrative detention as well as a prison sentence of at least two years. In June 2026, 311 people were reported to be behind bars for this charge.

These changes are part of a wider attack on migrants’ existence in Greece, and come alongside a recent announcement that police will raid migrants’ homes in central Athens neighbourhoods. The announcement directly conflates legal status with criminality, and raises concerns that people could be transferred directly from their homes to immigration detention centres. Meanwhile, people detained in the country’s newest detention centre in Sintiki have spoken out against their conditions of detention, declaring that “death is preferable to this”. Their words highlight the importance of examining deaths in detention in relation to broader conditions of confinement, rather than as isolated incidents.

What counts as a death in detention?

The archive includes deaths of foreign nationals in police stations and immigration detention centres, during transportation under police custody, and in hospitals where individuals remained in police custody at the time of death. It covers people detained for immigration-related reasons as well as foreign nationals held in police facilities following arrest or detention on criminal grounds. Deaths occurring after release, even where health conditions may have developed or worsened during detention, are excluded. This reflects our decision to focus specifically on deaths occurring while individuals remained in police custody, rather than the wider health consequences of detention, which may extend well beyond release. The archive therefore captures only part of the broader impact of detention on people's lives and health.

Deaths missing from the official record

Our attempts to reconstruct these deaths revealed significant gaps and inconsistencies in the information provided by the Hellenic Police. Gaps were found in statistics on suicides in police stations (2000-2024), all deaths of foreign nationals in police stations (2000-2024), deaths during or following transfer to hospital (2012-2024), and deaths in pre-removal detention centres (2013-2024). The police responses to our Freedom of Information requests are available in full through the Detention Landscapes database (see our FOI requests and the documents we were provided).

Thirty-four deaths documented by journalists, civil society organisations and monitoring bodies were absent from the police statistics disclosed to us through FOIs. In other cases, different sets of official statistics appeared to contradict one another. For example, police statistics concerning suicides recorded the death of a foreign national in Athens in 2002, while another set of statistics concerning all deaths of foreign nationals in police custody reported no deaths for the same year.

Elsewhere, the police provided aggregate figures without sufficient information to establish who had died, when or under what circumstances. For 25 cases, police statistics provided little more than the year and region in which the deaths occurred. These discrepancies raise fundamental questions about how deaths in police custody are recorded and made available for public scrutiny. Moreover, in our follow-up requests, the Hellenic Police refused to share more information due to confidentiality of ongoing investigations. After the intervention of the Greek Ombudsman, the police claimed that the requested information is not kept in digital databases and as a result providing detailed data would cause excessive administrative burden to the authorities. As a result, we know that data inconsistencies do not necessarily mean that the deaths were never recorded internally, but they reveal the limitations of the official information disclosed.

The true number of deaths in detention is likely to be higher than 112. Independent monitoring of detention facilities is limited, while access for lawyers, families and civil society organisations is highly restricted. NGOs do not have guaranteed, regular access to immigration detention centres in Greece, limiting opportunities for independent monitoring of detention conditions and the documentation of deaths and other abuses. Although the Council of Europe's Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT) and the Greek Ombudsman conduct visits to detention facilities and investigate concerns about their operation, their monitoring is periodic or case-specific. It therefore cannot substitute for systematic, ongoing and publicly accessible reporting of deaths in police custody. We also know that the Hellenic Police have previously ignored requests for data on deaths in custody, while independent human rights bodies have raised concerns about transparency and the investigation of deaths in police detention.

Detained people's ability to communicate with the outside world and report violations or deaths is also severely restricted in both pre-removal centres and police stations. Restrictions include the confiscation of phones in police holding cells, the destruction of phone cameras and confiscation of phones as punishment in some detention centres, as well as limited access to Wi-Fi and charging facilities. Limited visiting hours and the remote location of some facilities further restrict contact with the outside world. Documented intimidation practices, including verbal threats and police checking detained people's messages to identify their contacts with organisations, can also discourage people from reporting abuses.

Presence of medical staff does not prevent deaths

Of the deaths documented, 84 occurred in police stations, where there are no medical staff at all, and 27 in pre-removal detention centres, where healthcare is formally provided by the publicly-owned company AEMY, with EU funding. Yet the presence of healthcare professionals does not necessarily mean that detained people can access timely or adequate medical treatment.

Testimonies gathered through our research describe difficulties accessing doctors, requests for medical assistance being ignored or delayed, and police acting as intermediaries between detained people and healthcare services. This role of the police is also embedded in the formal organisation of detention: the EU-funded AMIF 018 project provides salaries for 97 fixed-term border guards at Amygdaleza pre-removal detention centre whose responsibilities include ‘ensuring [...] medical examination [of detained people] and the transfer to hospitals and health centres when such needs arise’. At Amygdaleza, the latest statistics, from April 2026, recorded seven healthcare professionals (two doctors, two nurses, two health visitors and one dentist) for 666 detainees. When we requested information regarding when medical staff positions in pre-removal centres were vacant during the years 2018-2025, the Hellenic Police did not provide any substantial information.

Our interviews with healthcare professionals who have worked for AEMY reveal further problems in the organisation of care, including inadequate supervision, high staff turnover, difficulties obtaining equipment and limited continuity of treatment. Some workers also described police officers obstructing access to the doctors, while others reported a lack of effective mechanisms for raising concerns with management and reported instances in which staff who challenged established practices were marginalised by colleagues or subsequently reassigned to other facilities. AEMY employees have lodged claims totalling over €350,000 against the company, including for overtime and dangerous and hazardous working conditions, according to the company’s financial statements.

These accounts suggest that barriers to healthcare are shaped not only by staffing levels but also by the organisation of detention and the control exercised by police over access to treatment. Interviews with formerly detained people reveal similar patterns. As one man who spent two and a half years in Amygdaleza put it: "[In Amygdaleza], there are doctors, but no care". For several deaths documented in the archive, non-governmental sources have also raised allegations of medical neglect.

Taken together, these accounts point to the need to examine not only whether healthcare is formally available, but whether detained people can access it, particularly given the documented conditions in Greek detention centres and the wider evidence that immigration detention contributes to deteriorating physical and mental health.

Why documenting these deaths matters

The archive is, by nature, incomplete. There are people whose names we have been unable to recover, deaths whose circumstances remain unknown, and others that may have left no publicly accessible trace at all. The 112 deaths documented should therefore be understood as a minimum, rather than a comprehensive account.

This incompleteness is revealing. Our research shows that even basic information about deaths in police custody can be difficult to obtain, that official statistics are not always consistent, and that the circumstances surrounding individual deaths remain obscure. These gaps raise questions not only about how people die in detention, but also about how the Greek state accounts for deaths occurring under its authority.

By bringing together official records, media reports, testimonies and documentation produced by civil society organisations and solidarity groups, the archive seeks to make visible deaths that might otherwise remain isolated or forgotten. It cannot establish the circumstances of every death, but it can provide a basis for further investigation and demands for accountability.

Note: The archive is an ongoing project. We will continue to update and correct entries as new information becomes available and welcome additional documentation that may help establish the circumstances of individual deaths. Please reach out via our contact form: https://detentionlandscapes.uwazi.io/en/page/3nx7gbdjqra/contact-us

name: Litigation
title: Faced with influx, prosecutor in Washington says he lacks resources to defend immigration cases
description:
Acting U.S. Attorney Charles Floyd said in a letter to U.S. District Judge David Estudillo that habeas corpus cases initiate “protracted litigation” with numerous hearings, briefings and motions that consume prosecutors' resources.
The backlog has “severely impacted the government's ability to respond” to immigration petitions and prevented prosecutors from dealing with other unrelated civil litigation, he said.
As a result, his office will decline to defend “many” habeas cases.
Judges have often ruled against the administration in cases filed by tens of thousands of detainees arguing that they were being held illegally by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Last week, U.S. border czar Tom Homan told Fox News that courts have been weighed down by about 85,000 immigration habeas cases as the government carries out a sweeping crackdown.
text:
TACOMA, Wash. -- Faced with an influx of petitions by people alleging they're being unlawfully detained by federal immigration authorities, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Washington said Monday that it no longer has the staffing to defend every case and will let judges rule without government opposition.

Acting U.S. Attorney Charles Floyd said in a letter to U.S. District Judge David Estudillo that habeas corpus cases initiate “protracted litigation” with numerous hearings, briefings and motions that consume prosecutors' resources.

“Thus, going forward, in order to conserve resources, there will be many habeas cases in which the USAO will no longer assume responsibility for providing a defense on behalf of the respondents," Floyd wrote.

The backlog has “severely impacted the government's ability to respond” to immigration petitions and prevented prosecutors from dealing with other unrelated civil litigation, he said. As a result, his office will decline to defend “many” habeas cases. He didn't specify how many cases could be affected.

Judges have often ruled against the administration in cases filed by tens of thousands of detainees arguing that they were being held illegally by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It has been a source of great frustration to administration officials — and to judges and advocates who say ICE has trampled on individual rights amid the Trump administration’s hardline immigration agenda.

Last week, U.S. border czar Tom Homan told Fox News that courts have been weighed down by about 85,000 immigration habeas cases as the government carries out a sweeping crackdown.

Floyd is a former judge who, along with three other Washington judges, advocated for prohibiting immigration courts from granting bond to detainees — a question that is now before the U.S. Supreme Court.

The justices will consider whether immigrants who have been living in the U.S. have a right to a hearing to determine if they should remain detained while challenging their possible deportation.

title: Wisconsin trooper released after ICE arrest draws public backlash - WISN
description:
MADISON, Wis. — Wisconsin State Trooper Carel Van Der Merwe, a South African immigrant, was briefly jailed last week after ICE agents arrested him at the Madison airport while he was traveling to visit family in New Mexico.
Van Der Merwe's attorney questioned the approach taken by ICE agents.
President Donald Trump appeared to reference cases like Van Der Merwe's during a Sunday interview on CBS's "60 Minutes."
Van Der Merwe's attorney responded to the president's remarks.
Van Der Merwe is expected to return to his State Patrol duties while awaiting an immigration court hearing in the coming months.
text:
MADISON, Wis. —

Wisconsin State Trooper Carel Van Der Merwe, a South African immigrant, was briefly jailed last week after ICE agents arrested him at the Madison airport while he was traveling to visit family in New Mexico.

Van Der Merwe, who immigrated to the U.S. seven years ago at age 14, has been working legally under a permit issued by the Department of Homeland Security while his family’s asylum case remains pending since 2019.

"He's risked his life to help out people in our community, and when you're going to indiscriminately pick him up, detain him, especially when he's done everything correctly that he can do. I think that people just found that to be an extreme overreach," said his attorney Marc Christopher Monday in an interview with WISN 12 News.

Van Der Merwe's attorney questioned the approach taken by ICE agents.

"I would ask their agency why didn't you simply write him a letter or contact him; he would have presented himself. What is the utility of shackling him and throwing him behind bars?"

President Donald Trump appeared to reference cases like Van Der Merwe's during a Sunday interview on CBS's "60 Minutes."

"I get very good marks for getting the bad ones out. But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation for breaking of the law, and that was they came into the country illegally. I think it might be too tough, yeah," Trump said.

Van Der Merwe's attorney responded to the president's remarks.

"To say that maybe this is an overreach would be a massive, massive understatement."

The trooper was released Friday night, a move his attorney credited to public pressure and the efforts of Wisconsin Congressman Derrick Van Orden, who he said spoke directly to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin about the case.

Van Der Merwe is expected to return to his State Patrol duties while awaiting an immigration court hearing in the coming months.

"We're gonna try to use every tool that's available to us to try to get this young man his lawful permanent resident status," Christopher, said.

text:
EL PASO, Texas (KVIA) -- The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), through Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), said Michell German, an El Paso High student, was arrested along with her family due to their illegal status in the country.

ABC-7 reported on Friday that U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro was calling ICE to release the family who are currently detained at the Dilley Immigration Processing Center, which is located in South Texas and is designed to house families.

DHS and ICE responded to our media request for information on Saturday with the following written statement:

“While conducting targeted enforcement arrests on October 22 in El Paso, Texas, ICE arrested Pablo Jose Guerrero-Pimentel, an illegal alien from Venezuela. Guerrero-Pimentel admitted he was in the U.S. illegally and had no documentation to remain in the U.S. legally. He was arrested along with a 17-year-old female passenger also in the country illegally.

During a separate targeted enforcement on the same date, ICE arrested Dolores Emilia Zarraga-Colina, an illegal alien from Venezuela. Zarraga-Colina admitted she was in the U.S. illegally and had no documentation to remain in the U.S. legally. She was arrested along with an 11-year-old female passenger also in the country illegally.

The family unit entered the U.S. illegally August 12, 2022, and under the Biden Administration they were released into the country. They are in ICE custody, together, at the Dilley Immigration Processing Center pending a hearing before an immigration judge. They will receive due process.

Detention is a choice. We encourage all individuals without lawful status to take control of their departure through the CBP Home app. The United States is offering $3,000 and a free flight to self-deport. We encourage every person here unlawfully to take advantage of this offer and preserve the opportunity to return to the United States lawfully in the future. Otherwise, they may be arrested and removed without the opportunity to return.”

ABC-7 reached out to the attorney representing the family, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, who says the family has been living in very difficult conditions at the Dilley Processing Center.

"The youngest girl, Paula, who's only 11 years old, has already lost weight because she's not eating the food. Michelle was nominated as the lady in waiting at her high school over the weekend, and she was unable to attend the game," Lincoln-Goldfinch said. "Their Mom, Dolores, has been having medical issues and she's not receiving adequate treatment from them."

"What's hardest on the family and these kids is that they went from living a very normal life where they were in an immigration process, but following all the rules, there are no criminal issues," she added.

"That's one of the cruelties of this administration, is that the children and the families that are impacted are people who have been living in this country for years and who are living normal lives and have friends and jobs and communities and school and all of a sudden everything changes and children find themselves in prison; that is just never acceptable, it's never okay," attorney Lincoln-Goldfinch added.

title: ICE agents arrested 4 people in Oakland on Saturday
description:
Several videos circulated over the weekend on social media appearing to show a man being arrested by federal agents on 81st Avenue.
Since the operation began, federal agents have arrested at least five people in Oakland, one at San Antonio Park, who was violently arrested according to De Bremaeker.
Fortunato Bas told The Oaklandside on Sunday afternoon that it has been “incredibly frustrating” to see federal agents in Oakland.
Uptick in ICE arrests across Alameda County The arrests by federal agents were not limited to Oakland.
On Nov. 3, ICE agents arrested a 23-year-old UC Berkeley student and asylum seeker, Paula Valentina Albornoz Hernandez, at San Francisco airport.
text:
Agents from the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, made several arrests in Oakland over the weekend.

ACILEP, the Alameda County Immigration Legal Education Partnership, a county program launched last year in response to the Trump Administration’s escalation of immigration enforcement, confirmed on social media that four back-to-back arrests took place on Saturday, Nov. 7.

According to information shared by ACILEP, the first person was arrested between 5 and 6 a.m. after being pulled over on I-980. The next Oakland arrest occurred around 10 a.m. on Golf Links Road near Cosgrave Avenue. Around 11:30 a.m., federal agents detained another person near 51st Avenue and East 12th Street, and a fourth arrest took place around 1:30 p.m. on the 1300 block of 81st Avenue. ACILEP said it has connected three of the people arrested with legal support. The organization has yet to identify the individual arrested near 51st Avenue.

Several videos circulated over the weekend on social media appearing to show a man being arrested by federal agents on 81st Avenue. The Oaklandside could not independently corroborate if it was the same person.

The Oaklandside reached out to ACILEP for comment about the arrests. Nikolas De Bremaeker, ACILEP’s managing attorney, responded on Sunday night that the organization “can’t share more info at this time other than what was shared in our ACILEP post.”

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comment.

In early October, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement announced the launch of “Operation Safe California,” a 45-day operation across the state to arrest immigrants without legal status.

Since the operation began, federal agents have arrested at least five people in Oakland, one at San Antonio Park, who was violently arrested according to De Bremaeker. He was released from ICE custody upon his discharge from the hospital.

A sixth person, arrested by ICE in Emeryville, was taken to Highland Hospital in Oakland to get treated. He was released back into ICE custody upon his discharge, a decision that sparked outrage on the part of Alameda County supervisor Nikki Fortunato Bas.

Fortunato Bas told The Oaklandside on Sunday afternoon that it has been “incredibly frustrating” to see federal agents in Oakland.

“I’m in touch with other supervisors across the Greater Bay Area, from Monterey to Santa Clara and elsewhere, and we are all seeing more immigration arrests,” she said.

According to Fortunato Bas, at the Oct. 27 board meeting where the Alameda County Board of Supervisors met jointly with the Board of Trustees of the Alameda Health System, which operates Highland Hospital, the board requested a thorough investigation into what happened at Highland. The report, she said, should be available in the coming weeks.

“I am not waiting for the report or a hearing to take action,” she said. “I’ve already successfully connected Alameda Health System’s legal team and our legal services community partner; they’re already starting to work together to improve the protocols and training, so that even before that report is published, we are hoping to get much stronger protocols and training at the hospital.”

She said the report will be presented to the board’s Alameda County Together for All ad hoc committee, which oversees the county’s policy to welcome immigrants, Monday, Dec. 7, at 3 p.m., at 1221 Oak St. 5th floor. The meeting is also broadcasted virtually.

Uptick in ICE arrests across Alameda County

The arrests by federal agents were not limited to Oakland. On Nov. 3, ICE agents arrested a 23-year-old UC Berkeley student and asylum seeker, Paula Valentina Albornoz Hernandez, at San Francisco airport. Attorneys at Centro Legal de la Raza have filed a habeas corpus petition challenging her detention. On Nov. 9, a federal judge ordered her release. On Nov. 4, ACILEP confirmed another arrest outside the Residence Inn by Marriott in Berkeley. On Nov. 5, four people were arrested in Livermore, and on Oct. 25, someone was arrested near the Santa Rita County Jail in Dublin, according to ACILEP.

“Recently, the Sheriff’s Office has observed federal immigration enforcement take place outside of Santa Rita Jail,” the Alameda County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement released on Saturday night. Sheriff Yesenia Sanchez, the statement said, wants to “reassure our community of our commitment to protecting the constitutional rights, safety, and dignity of everyone we serve remains unwavering. These responsibilities do not change with the political climate or the circumstances of the moment. Our mission to serve and protect all members of our community remains constant.”

“We want to be clear about our role and responsibilities: The Alameda County Sheriff’s Office does not participate in federal civil immigration enforcement or honor administrative immigration warrants.”

Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee told The Oaklandside by email, “I am deeply concerned to see Oakland residents detained by ICE and am actively coordinating with officials in Washington, D.C. about actions we can take. Oakland remains a sanctuary city. The Oakland Police Department does not work with ICE, and our residents should never hesitate to call 911 when they need help.”

Fortunato Bas and Lee both said that Oakland residents who see suspected ICE activity in their neighborhood should call the ACILEP hotline at 510-241-4011. The ACILEP team can help verify the sightings and provide legal help.

A protest in Fruitvale

On Sunday, Nov. 8, several dozen protesters gathered at Fruitvale Plaza to protest the recent spate of Oakland arrests. Amy Wong, a college professor, arrived with her 8-year-old child, who carried a homemade sign that said, in rainbow colors, “Immigrants belong here.” Wong said she and her daughter have gone to other anti-ICE protests but this one was personal, because Albornoz Hernandez, the UC Berkeley student who was arrested, was the student of a friend of hers. “It’s important that we show up for immigrants,” she said.

Edgar Sanchez, a history teacher at Coliseum College Prep Academy in East Oakland, showed up because he’s seen the impact of the crackdowns at his school. “They’re very aware of the history of attacks on immigrant communities,” he said of his students. He said he’s grateful that “the district is doing a lot” and that his school has set up a rapid response system.

Valarie Bachelor, the vice-president of the Oakland Unified School District school board, was the only elected official who spoke. “We need to put pressure on the city to take action right now,” she said. “And we are demanding immediate action from the Alameda County Sheriff and the board of supervisors over the ICE activity at the Santa Rita Jail parking lot.”

“Sanctuary cannot exist on paper,” she said. “It means taking real action in the community.”

This morning, ACILEP confirmed more immigration federal enforcement activity in Oakland — this time near Seminary Avenue and Tevis Street, in what appeared to be a targeted enforcement operation. ACILEP said no arrests were reported.

text:
Montana Attorney General Austin Knudsen’s administrative seizure of the Gallatin County Attorney’s office is “unenforceable” and he exceeded his authority in attempting to do so, the Montana Supreme Court said in a unanimous opinion issued late last week.

Knudsen and newly re-elected Gallatin County Attorney Audrey Cromwell have been in a 13-month legal battle about the status of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement as it operates in Montana and how it stands in state law – either as a “criminal justice agency” as it’s termed in state code, or an agency that also includes civil enforcement components.

“I’m grateful for the court’s clarification of the law, and look forward to continuing my duties to the people of Gallatin County,” Cromwell said in a statement to the Daily Montanan.

The dispute centers on whether state law enforcement, including county attorneys offices, must turn over “confidential criminal justice data” to other agencies in civil matters. In some circumstances, immigration arrests are civil in nature.

Knudsen took over the office on April 30. He has argued ICE is always a criminal justice agency under Montana law, and therefore can have access to any data it pleases.

Montana has strong privacy laws, and Cromwell has argued ICE is not a criminal justice agency in all contexts, and therefore should have to follow rules and processes that are dependent on how that information will be used by the federal agency.

While the state supreme court ruled that Knudsen exceeded his authority in an attempted administrative take-over of the Gallatin County Attorney’s Office, it did not decide where ICE sits in Montana law, instead asking both sides to answer two questions for further deliberation:

The parties have until Dec. 7 to submit their respective briefs.

“The Attorney General does not supervise the county attorney in her representation of her local government, and cannot override the local government client’s direction of a lawsuit,” the Supreme Court opinion, written by Justice James Jeremiah Shea said. “If that were the case, the Attorney General could deprive a local government of due process by directing a county attorney to dismiss any civil suit against the State and prohibit a county attorney from representing a county on an issue.”

The state Department of Justice did not respond to questions about the case, or give a response to the high court’s ruling.

title: AG Ken Paxton drops Annunciation House lawsuit - The Texas Tribune
authors: El Paso Matters, Joshua Fechter, Terri Langford, Alex Nguyen, Acacia Coronado Austin Current, Uriel J. García, Carlos Nogueras Ramos, Natalia Contreras, The Texas Tribune, Cindy Ramirez
description:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has dropped a suit seeking to shut down Annunciation House after demanding two years ago to examine the records of the nonprofit network of migrant shelters in El Paso, including information about the people it served.
It’s over,” Ruben Garcia, founder and executive director of Annunciation House, told El Paso Matters.
The AG’s Office first delivered a demand letter to examine Annunciation House records on Feb. 7, 2024.

text:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has dropped a suit seeking to shut down Annunciation House after demanding two years ago to examine the records of the nonprofit network of migrant shelters in El Paso, including information about the people it served.

“It’s very gratifying that this has now ended. It’s over,” Ruben Garcia, founder and executive director of Annunciation House, told El Paso Matters. “What I would want next is for the state Legislature to say, ‘We have to find a way to prevent this from happening.’”

The Attorney General’s Office on Monday filed a notice of nonsuit with prejudice, meaning the office will never again file a lawsuit with similar allegations against the organization in the future. Paxton’s office didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The move comes as Paxton, a Republican who unsuccessfully sought a U.S. Senate seat in the Nov. 3 midterm election, prepares to leave the AG’s Office in mid-January. Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson, a Democrat who now serves in the Senate, has said he intends to review cases brought by Paxton.

The AG’s Office first delivered a demand letter to examine Annunciation House records on Feb. 7, 2024. The next day, the organization sued Paxton challenging the demand. Within days, Paxon sought to revoke the Annunciation House’s nonprofit registration in Texas and shut down its operation, alleging harboring, human smuggling and stash-house activity.

Garcia vehemently denied the claims, stating the organization serves migrants processed and released by U.S. immigration authorities.

The case wound its way through the courts, with an El Paso district judge blocking the AG’s attempt, and Paxton appealing to the Texas Supreme Court. In May 2025, the Texas Supreme Court reversed the lower court’s decision and later denied Annunciation House’s request for a rehearing.

Annunciation House was among more than a handful of organizations that Paxton targeted using consumer protection laws.

“This whole process of suing organizations like Annunciation House puts a blanket, a wet blanket, over the work of all of these organizations and many others that were not sued but feared they might be,” Garcia said. “It makes everybody go about their daily work looking over their shoulder, asking themselves, ‘Are they going to come after me?’”

The case was set to go to court again in March, with a hearing in an El Paso district court. Garcia noted that he was scheduled to be deposed later this week as the case had picked up pace before the midterms.

U.S. Rep. Veronica Escobar, D-El Paso, said Paxton dropping the lawsuit was “long overdue good news.” “This is what happens when the people use our collective voice at the ballot box,” she said in a statement to El Paso Matters. “Under Democratic leadership, our state will be redirecting its time, energy, and resources to issues that matter instead of the partisan bullying we’d grown accustomed to under Republicans.” Garcia agreed, saying that he’s confident dropping the suit is a result of the midterm elections that saw Democrats sweep key seats across Texas.

“We’re tremendously grateful that that it it gives back a certain level of of voice to organizations and in their ability to more freely speak out on the issues that are affecting refugees in terrible, terrible ways,” he said.

Annunciation House was established in February 1978 by Garcia and four other young adults who began meeting in 1976 searching for ways to serve El Paso’s poor and homeless, particularly undocumented immigrants who were turned away from other shelters.

The organization has served more than a half a million people, and in 2023 was the focal organization providing shelter to thousands of migrants who arrived in El Paso during a major influx.

text:
Faced with an influx of petitions by people alleging they're being unlawfully detained by federal immigration authorities, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Washington said Monday that it no longer has the manpower to defend every case and will let judges rule without government opposition.

Acting U.S. Attorney Charles Floyd said in a letter to U.S. District Judge David Estudillo that habeas corpus cases initiate “protracted litigation” with numerous hearings, briefings and motions that consume prosecutors' resources.

“Thus, going forward, in order to conserve resources, there will be many habeas cases in which the USAO will no longer assume responsibility for providing a defense on behalf of the respondents," Floyd wrote.

The backlog has “severely impacted the government's ability to respond” to immigration petitions and prevented prosecutors from dealing with other unrelated civil litigation, he said. As a result, his office will decline to defend “many” habeas cases. He didn't specify how many cases could be affected.

Judges have often ruled against the administration in cases filed by tens of thousands of detainees arguing that they were being held illegally by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It has been a source of great frustration to administration officials — and to judges and advocates who say ICE has trampled on individual rights amid the Trump administration’s hardline immigration agenda.

Last week, U.S. border czar Tom Homan told Fox News that courts have been weighed down by about 85,000 immigration habeas cases as the government carries out a sweeping crackdown.

Floyd is a former judge who, along with three other Washington judges, advocated for prohibiting immigration courts from granting bond to detainees — a question that is now before the U.S. Supreme Court.

The justices will consider whether immigrants who have been living in the U.S. have a right to a hearing to determine if they should remain detained while challenging their possible deportation.

Most appeals courts to have considered the issue have found that it violates federal law to detain immigrants, including those living in the U.S. illegally, without a bond hearing. Those decisions conflict with rulings by the 5th and 8th circuits, which held that immigrants accused of illegally entering and remaining in the U.S. must be detained while their deportation cases are pending.

text:
President Donald Trump acknowledged that his administration's immigration policies may have been "too tough" during an interview with "60 Minutes," while emphasizing that his border policies remain strong.

The president's comments have been interpreted by some as signaling a possible willingness to work with Democrats on immigration reform. While he did not provide specifics, Trump suggested that some immigrants who have been working and contributing to their communities could be allowed to stay.

Meanwhile, immigrants navigating the legal process continue to face detention. Miguel Angel Rios, who has been in the United States for nearly three decades, has been waiting for his immigration visa for eight years.

"We did expect maybe two or three years, but never eight years ongoing to now," said Janeth, a family member of Rios. "We don't know when he's going to get his appointment or even be let out on bond."

Since September 2025, Rios has been waiting for one final step: his immigration interview. However, before that could happen, he was taken into ICE custody.

"He's just waiting for an appointment to go to his final interview," said Douglas Lehrman, Rios' attorney. "The man has high blood pressure, he's never spent a night in jail, and now he's trying to do things legally and he's been taken into custody just so ICE can keep their numbers up."

Lehrman said Rios has been actively trying to obtain legal status, but his detention highlights the challenges faced by immigrants pursuing legal pathways.

According to documents provided to KCRA 3 by Rios's attorney, his Petition for Alien Relative (Form I-130) was approved in November 2019, followed by approval of his provisional unlawful presence waiver (Form I‑601A) in August 2024. On September 18, 2025, he was notified that his case was qualified and ready for a final green card interview in Ciudad Juárez, México. However, no interview date had been scheduled before he was taken into ICE custody.

Julian Sanchez Mora, another attorney at Immigrant Crime and Justice, said, "He hasn't really acted on immigration via legislation, so if he's willing to do something positive in immigration, he doesn't need the Democrats just yet."

For families like Janeth's, the impact of ICE detentions is deeply personal. Her stepfather, a landscaper for over 20 years, was detained in West Sacramento last Thursday after depositing money at a bank.

"It does look like they're racially profiling," Janeth said. "My stepdad has been a landscaper for over 20 years, so in that moment, my dad was going to go deposit money from Bank of America, so he was in his work truck. He had his [equipment] in his truck."

Lehrman says Rios' only known violation was a 2010 citation for driving without a license, which he says is not a deportable offense.

"My heart dropped immediately," Janeth said. "My dad is our world. He's head of household. He's a family guy. He does no wrong."

The family is now waiting for his next court hearing, scheduled for Nov. 18.

The Department of Homeland Security is defending ICE officers who took custody of an 8-year-old Haitian child at an immigration hearing in San Diego last week.

Video of the boy being led away by ICE agents quickly spread online.

“The immigration officials took the child from the uncle and at that point, that’s when a lot of panic set in,” Sean Elo-Rivera, a San Diego Councilmember, told Scripps News San Diego.

In a letter to the secretaries of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services, the San Diego Unified School District said the child was "having to endure the emotional toll of being separated from their family, the interruption to their schooling and the stability of their daily routine."

“Unfortunately, the simple mistake as an Uber driver crossing into the US-Mexico border, that led to a family separation” Gaetan told Scripps News San Diego.

The Department of Health and Human Services is caring for the child, but has not said where he is being held.

“Due to the U.S.' aggressive enforcement of immigration, we no longer have this boy in school as we speak,” Gaetan said.

text:
The US supreme court has allowed Donald Trump to continue his administration’s construction of a border wall in Texas’s Big Bend region, including parts of Big Bend national park.

In an unsigned, five-page ruling, the nation’s highest court granted the Trump administration’s emergency request to suspend a lower court order that had temporarily stopped the project last month.

Liberal justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only member of the nine-member court to dissent from the ruling.

The justices wrote that the case’s plaintiffs, which include the Center for Biological Diversity, a Big Bend river guide and a church preservation group, “claim that construction in the Big Bend sector will diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area”.

However, they noted: “But Congress’s enactment of [immigration law] – which permits the secretary [of homeland security] to waive the requirements of environmental-protection and other conservation laws – reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert.

“The government’s interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents,” the justices said.

The Trump administration plans to construct more than 300 miles of six-foot-tall vehicle barriers and supporting roads, relying on a 1996 law that authorizes the homeland security secretary to “waive all legal requirements”, including environmental and conservation protections, in areas designated as having high levels of illegal border crossings.

The plaintiffs argue that the project threatens wildlife and public lands, could destroy “iconic sections” of the Rio Grande’s protected river corridor, and would undermine the “carefully wrought web of laws meant to protect a vast universe of biological, historic, cultural, and other interests”.

The border wall plans have also faced bipartisan opposition from local residents, many of whom warn that construction could threaten their livelihoods and disrupt their communities.

A Customs and Border Protections map shows plans for barriers and patrol roads across Big Bend national park, including remote areas that would require extensive dynamite blasting. Construction is also planned in isolated canyons where there have been no documented unauthorized vehicle crossings and where vehicles cannot reach the US-Mexico border, the Center for Biological Diversity noted.

According to Rodney Scott, the CBP commissioner, the wall, which is being built out at about 12 miles a week, is expected to be completed by the end of Trump’s second term.

The Center for Biological Diversity condemned the supreme court’s decision, saying: “This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal. They’re signing off on the permanent destruction of the wildest place in Texas, and the theft of a great American river from all of us.

“The destruction we’ve already seen in Big Bend unleashed a firestorm of outrage so severe that the administration was forced to pause its plans. If the bulldozers return now, public opposition will only grow … The damage done to Big Bend will be felt for future generations of Texans and Americans, and this administration will bear responsibility for the natural heritage we lose,” the center added.

CBP has awarded five contracts worth more than $6bn for border security upgrades in Big Bend, including 30-ft steel fencing, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology, which the agency calls its “smart wall”.

Following a federal judge’s ruling that temporarily halted the construction in October, CBP said at the time: “We stand by our assessment and remain confident in our legal authorities to secure the border while preserving the unique landscape of the Big Bend region.”

The Guardian has reached out to CBP for comment on the supreme court’s latest ruling.

name: Human Rights
title: Chicago-area father dies shortly after ICE's deportation process to Pakistan
authors: Mark Rivera, Tom Jones, Barb Markoff, and Christine Tressel
description:
Ahmed's children shared with the I-Team emails sent to officials at ICE, Clay County, and the Pakistan Consulate in Chicago.
Finally, in late July, his children said Ahmed called to say he was on his way to Pakistan.
For eight days, Ahmed's children had no contact from their father.
Then, on Aug 3, Ahmed's family in Pakistan called his children to share the worst news possible: Their father was dead.
Ahmed's children are searching for answers, and neither the Pakistan Embassy nor the U.S. government have provided them any.
text:
CHICAGO (WLS) -- When a suburban family's 61-year-old father was arrested by federal immigration agents this past summer in Morton Grove, the patriarch and his children accepted his fate and tried everything they could to expedite his deportation.

But after a 38-hour flight on an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)-chartered plane, Ayaz Ahmed was dead.

ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch

And his family says months later, they are still searching for answers as to what happened, who was responsible, and what could have been done differently to keep their mentor and father alive after he voluntarily agreed to be removed from the U.S.

A former head of ICE, along with international human rights law experts, told the ABC7 I-Team the case raises serious questions over the government's current detention standards and deportation practices.

A spokesperson for ICE tells the I-Team, "Any claims of neglect or mistreatment," while Ahmed was in its care "are categorically FALSE."

Witnesses who were shackled beside Ahmed, both on the flight and after, say there were signs Ahmed needed help, but no medical aid was rendered.

The Trump administration's Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has consistently said its immigration enforcement efforts are targeting the "worst of the worst."

But for their father Ahmed, his children say that rang hollow as he had no criminal history and was a productive member of the many Chicago communities he lived and worked in since the late nineties.

"I lost somebody that was most precious to me in the world," said Ahmed's son, Jawwad Mehmood.

"He was like our warrior, you know?" said Ahmed's daughter, Saleha Sahar. "He lived and breathed for his kids."

For siblings Mehmood and Sahar, images of their father have now become invaluable; birthday parties, trips to downtown Chicago and the Adler Planetarium; memories of their mentor and dad, Ayaz.

Ahmed and his children moved from Pakistan to the Chicago suburbs in 1997. For nearly three decades, his children say he owned several local businesses and had never encountered law enforcement until this past summer.

On June 3, Ahmed was detained by federal immigration agents in the Morton Grove area for overstaying a visitor's visa. He was booked into ICE detention at the Clay County Justice Center in Indiana.

Rather than fight his arrest, Ahmed and his family decided to accept his fate, and focus on expediting his removal from the U.S. as quickly as possible.

His children say Ahmed had several underlying health conditions that made his ICE detention risky.

"We were in contact with ICE every second, even the consulate made them aware of his medical condition," Sahar said.

Ahmed's children shared with the I-Team emails sent to officials at ICE, Clay County, and the Pakistan Consulate in Chicago. Among those emails was a letter from Ahmed's doctor, explaining his "multiple chronic medical conditions" including type 2 diabetes, and the medications he needed daily.

But Ahmed's family said his health behind bars was deteriorating fast.

"In his two months of detention, all we witnessed our father do is suffer," said his son Mehmood. "They put him in isolation because he requested medical attention."

Clay County officials confirmed Ahmed was held in "medical isolation," and they couldn't comment further or share jail records due to health privacy laws.

Ahmed's daughter said she knew her father's health was at risk.

"All he would say is, 'I can't breathe. I can't sleep,'" Sahar said, adding her father told her, "'The circumstances here are very tough. Just send me home.'"

Sahar and Mehmood contacted lawmakers and the Pakistan Consulate, trying to expedite his deportation. They even offered to buy the plane ticket themselves.

Finally, in late July, his children said Ahmed called to say he was on his way to Pakistan.

"He said, 'Son, I think they're going to put me on a plane. So, I just want to say I love you all very much'" Mehmood recounted. "'May God protect you.' Those were his last words."

For eight days, Ahmed's children had no contact from their father. He disappeared from ICE's detainee locator website. And the family said the Pakistan Chicago embassy had no information on Ahmed's whereabouts.

"Everybody was questioning, 'Where is our father?'" Mehmood said.

Then, on Aug 3, Ahmed's family in Pakistan called his children to share the worst news possible: Their father was dead.

"This is not a convict," Sahar told the I-Team, fighting back tears. "The man worked, poured his sweat into this country. And to be deported the way he was."

What happened to Ayaz Ahmed? His children and the ABC7 I-Team have been trying to answer that question for months.

FlightRadar24 data analyzed by the I-Team shows it was July 29 at 7:25 a.m. when a GlobalX flight chartered by ICE took off from Fort Worth, Texas.

The 38-hour flight stopped in Maine, then Iceland, Bulgaria, and Georgia, before landing at a Pakistani Air Force Base on July 30 at 9:41pm.

People who were deported and on the same flight as Ahmed said they could see his health deteriorating over the course of the flight, and upon landing in Pakistan, according to recorded interviews with Ahmed's family.

"He was in such a bad condition, he just couldn't talk," said one person who was deported from the U.S., who agreed to share what they saw if the I-Team did not share their name, as they fear retaliation from federal authorities, including the Federal Investigations Agency (FIA) in Pakistan.

"The moment we got off the plane, they made us stand in a straight line. In that straight line, alone, he [ Ahmed ] fell," said one witness. "He fainted right then and there; I was standing next to him."

"The moment he fell, he should have been looked upon. All they did was take him, took him, and put him in the FIA offices, where they interrogated us," the witness said.

"Uncle was a good man," the witness recounted. "Even at the last minute, he gave me a hug."

Another witness, speaking in Hindi and who also asked not to be identified, said Ahmed urinated himself on the flight by the time it landed in Iceland, one of the first stops of the trip.

"The witness said that my father, you know, his health was deteriorating even inside the plane," Mehmood said. "And no medical attention was given."

A spokesperson for ICE declined our requests for an interview, but in a written statement said, "No medical emergencies occurred during the flight, no signs of medical distress were observed, and no individuals required hospitalization."

The family obtained a copy of a postmortem report prepared by the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) Islamabad and shared with the I-Team.

According to the report, Ahmed was "brought dead" to the facility by FIA officials on July 31 at 11:43am; 14 hours after the flight from the U.S. landed in Pakistan.

PIMS doctors wrote there was, "no sign of torture / assault noted on body. No sign of strangulation or hanging noted on body."

All final reports into Ahmed's cause-of-death were "handed over to FIA officials."

In a peculiar twist, Ahmed's family says FIA officials paid all expenses for their father's burial in Karachi, where he was born, but wouldn't provide any more information about what happened.

Neither the FIA nor PIMS responded to the I-Team's questions or repeated requests for comment.

A spokesperson for ICE said, " [ Ahmed ] received all his scheduled medications during the flight. ICE has no insight into the circumstances of Mr. Ahmed's death after his arrival in Pakistan."

ICE told the I-Team once a person is "repatriated and transferred to the custody of their home government," they are no longer in ICE custody, and "ICE does not have authority over their care or access to their medical or official records."

Former DHS officials point to the recent ramp up of immigration enforcement efforts as likely playing a role in Ahmed's death.

"When you're under this pressure to continue these removals, it forces you to make decisions I don't think you otherwise would have," said John Sandweg, who previously served as general counsel and acting director for ICE.

Sandweg served as acting director during a previous record-setting peak of deportations during the Obama administration.

"I genuinely believe ICE agents and ICE personnel try to provide the best care possible. However, that is very... it is very difficult," Sandweg said. "If ICE wasn't under this political pressure, and someone was having a medical crisis on a flight like this, the flight would have turned back to make sure the individual got the medical care he needed."

Hashim Siddique was the family's attorney and helped communicate with ICE, Clay County and the Pakistan Consulate prior to Ahmed's deportation and death.

Siddique believes there are many unanswered questions surrounding what happened to Ahmed.

"The exact passing of Mr. Ahmed, and his lack of identification or other belongings, draws into question whether ICE actually had his medication en route from ICE facility, to the airport, on the plane, or whether any medical aid was administered during the medical emergency," Siddique said by email.

As the I-Team previously reported, Ahmed isn't the only Chicagoan to die during the enhanced immigration enforcement operations of the second Trump administration.

Nenko Gantchev died while held in ICE detention from complications stemming from his type two diabetes. DHS attributed the death to natural causes.

Health experts have warned ICE detention death rates are nearing record highs, raising concerns over health standards.

Sitting in the family's Schaumburg smoke shop that father and son used to run, Mehmood said his days are now weighed down by the stress of mortgages, monthly rent, and car payments his father used to be responsible for, now on his children's shoulders.

The absence of his father is always present, Mehmood told the I-Team.

"My father gave a sacrifice for an American dream," Mehmood said. "He did not deserve to die just because he didn't have a green card."

Ahmed's children are searching for answers, and neither the Pakistan Embassy nor the U.S. government have provided them any.

"It's barbaric," his daughter Sahar said. "He worked so hard. For him to have gone through what he did... He did not deserve this. We didn't deserve this."

text:
The White House on Monday morning wouldn't rule out the administration working with Democrats on a "deal" for illegal immigrants who have been living in the U.S. for more than a decade as Republicans prepare to lose control of Congress in January.

President Donald Trump, in his first sit-down interview since sweeping GOP midterm losses, opened the door to the possibility of considering amnesty.

"The President never said the word amnesty," a White House official insisted to Fox News Digital.

"We want Democrats to show their cards," the official revealed.

TRUMP ADMITS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT MAY HAVE BEEN TOO 'TOUGH' IN FIRST INTERVIEW SINCE MIDTERMS

They said, "There has never been a President stronger on immigration enforcement than President Trump."

"Thanks to his efforts more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the U.S. and we have the most secure border in American history. Like the President has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to improve the lives of Americans and Make America Safe Again."

In a "60 Minutes" interview that aired on Sunday, host Ross Douthat asked Trump how he is open to working with Democrats on immigration as he enters a lame-duck final stretch of his presidency.

"I'd love to do something on immigration," the president replied. "I think [immigration] both helped and hurt. I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out, but I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation or breaking of the law — that was that they came into the country illegally."

Trump, however, maintained that there are people in the United States who want to see all illegal aliens deported.

FOX NEWS POLL: MAJORITY SAYS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT HAS CROSSED THE LINE

But, Trump said, "if they're good people working in a landscaping company or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases paying taxes, and there's a large group of people that think they should be allowed to stay."

"When you go into a hotel and you have a woman that's working there as a maid, as a cleaner as a this as a that, as a waitress, a lot of good things, great jobs, and all of a sudden they're being taken out of the country, it's tough. It's a tough thing," he said, adding that people who he called "far-right" want deportations regardless of whether the illegal alien is working.

FIRST ON FOX: DEMS' AFFORDABILITY CRUSADE COLLIDES WITH EYE-POPPING PRICE TAG FOR SOCIALIST IMMIGRATION PLANS

While Trump didn't say "amnesty," as the White House noted, he signaled in the interview his willingness to "work a deal" for people who have been in the United States illegally for "10 and 15 years" who haven't committed other crimes.

Rep. Maria Salazar, R-Fla., a longtime proponent of giving legal status to illegal aliens, celebrated Trump's comments on X.

"Well done, Mr. President! What you described on 60 Minutes is what the Dignity Act is all about," she said in the post.

Salazar's Dignity Act would offer legal status to people who have been in the United States continuously since 2020, provided they haven't committed other crimes and pay a restitution fee and back taxes.

The White House wouldn't clarify what such a deal could entail when asked Monday.

Notably, the interview was taped before Stephen Miller, a notorious immigration hawk, was selected to be Trump's new chief of staff.

Immigration restrictionism has been Trump's calling card since he first ran for president beginning in 2015. His comments in the interview that aired Sunday drew a sharp reaction from those favor immigration restriction.

TED CRUZ SAYS 'BLUE TSUNAMI' TOOK OVER TEXAS AFTER DEMOCRATS SWEPT STATEWIDE RACES

"To be clear, if President Trump struck an amnesty deal with the Democrat-controlled Congress, it would be a bigger betrayal than starting the foolish war in Iran," commentator Steve Cortes said on X, adding a clip of Trump promising "the largest deportation operation in the history of our country" during a campaign rally in 2024.

"This plan absolutely guarantees that Texas never again votes Republican," said radio show host Anthony Cumia. "More states will turn permanently blue if illegals are given amnesty. Regan did the same this and California became a forever democrat state. Trump can do the same to Texas. Disgusting."

text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB) - At least 10 law enforcement agencies in the area recently signed up for a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement program called 287(g), which targets undocumented residents, the WAFB I-TEAM found.

One police chief said the sign-ups come with $3,500 for each officer’s name submitted to the federal government. The Louisiana ACLU is calling for an end to the program and says local police should not be doing federal immigration enforcement.

The I-TEAM found Gonzales police, Grosse Tete police, Denham Springs police, the Livingston Parish Sheriff’s Office, the Pointe Coupee Parish Sheriff’s Office, Port Vincent police, Rosedale police and Springfield police departments signed up for one of the program’s three components over the past few months. Some agencies signed up as recently as two months ago.

Sarah Whittington, advocacy director for the Louisiana ACLU, described the three components. She said one is a task force model that deputizes officers to act on ICE task forces and as agents. Another is a warrant service office model in which officers serve warrants. The third is a jail enforcement model.

Gonzales police signed up for the task force model, which allows local officers to go on immigration roundups.

Gonzales Police Chief Sherman Jackson said his department receives $3,500 for each officer who participates. He declined an on-camera interview but said he submitted the names of 22 officers to participate.

“Here in Gonzales we respect the Hispanic community, and when they have issues they contact me directly,” Jackson said. “We can control the narrative when we participate with ICE versus when we don’t.”

Federal agents carried out immigration raids in Gonzales one year ago as part of a larger roundup operation. Surveillance video obtained by WAFB showed the agents targeting individuals in Baton Rouge as well.

The recent sign-ups come a day after President Donald Trump appeared on “60 Minutes.” Asked whether his deportation policy went too far, Trump said, “It was too tough, too tough.”

Whittington said she was happy to hear the statement.

“I would need to see some actions to back that up,” Whittington said.

The White House said it will not slow efforts to arrest and deport people in the country illegally who break the law or terrorize communities.

Whittington questioned the benefit of the program for local law enforcement.

“What is the law enforcement benefit here?” Whittington said. “And that if we truly want to talk about public safety, I think we can leave to the federal government the federal government’s responsibilities for immigration enforcement. And we should keep for the state and local law enforcement agencies all of the necessary public safety actions that we would want them to be engaging in.”

The I-TEAM found that, in addition to the new sign-ups, Louisiana State Police, the Attorney General’s Office, Alcohol and Tobacco Control, the State Fire Marshal’s Office and the Department of Wildlife and Fisheries have been part of the program for a year. The agencies have statewide jurisdiction, allowing ICE to enforce anywhere in the state, even if a local police department is not on the participant list.

Whittington said no city or town is required to enter a 287(g) agreement to support a federal immigration enforcement mission.

“But when the state is doing it, yes, at this point, the entire state of Louisiana effectively is under a 287G agreement because of that state-level participation,” Whittington said. “Don’t need to be invited in.”

To participate, law enforcement officers must have two years of experience and pass a background check.

The I-TEAM contacted ICE for comment on this story but did not receive a response.

The Los Angeles Times spoke with Ahilan Arulanantham, faculty co-director of UCLA’s Miñana Family Center for Immigration Law and Policy, about President Donald Trump’s appointment of Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff. Arulanantham said the promotion is unlikely to change the administration’s approach to immigration enforcement, but a Democratic-controlled Congress could have greater leverage to challenge its policies. Read more about UCLA in today’s New York Times, CNN and other outlets.

See our UCLA in the News daily archive.

More highlights from UCLA in the News: November 9, 2026

UCLA graduates lead veterans’ health research at LA VA | Santa Monica Daily Press

Graduates of UCLA’s [Fielding School of Public Health] have taken a leading role in research into veterans’ health, from lung disease and cancer to homelessness and mental health, through a partnership with the Department of Veterans Affairs in Los Angeles that dates back more than six decades. (UCLA’s Dr. Russell Buhr, Dr. Fola May, and Dr. Carlos Oronce were quoted.)

Outrage over data centers helped drive blue wave in midterms | CNN

“Data centers weren’t the biggest issue driving midterm election results. But exit polls show us that they were definitely on the minds of many voters. The issue just reinforced this perception, this narrative that President Trump is out of touch with the concerns of regular Americans,” said UCLA’s Megan Mullin.

Public transit issues expected to be high priority under Raman | Los Angeles Times

“I do think we’ll see a considerable amount of action on transit and multimodal transportation in the short run on a timeline that puts this work in the context of preparation for the summer of 2028,” said Juan Matute, deputy director of UCLA’s Institute of Transportation Studies.

Nithya Raman leads way as city’s progressives make their mark | The Guardian

“If there hadn’t been the Palisades fire in January of last year, I don’t think Nithya would have run. And I don’t think Karen Bass would have been defeated,” said Zev Yaroslavsky, the director of the Los Angeles initiative at the UCLA Luskin School of Public Affairs. “The majority of the people of the city, a significant majority, think that the city is on the wrong track. And the Palisades fire was really the poster child for all that people are unhappy about.”

What will policing in LA look like under Nithya Raman? | LAist’s “AirTalk”

As Nithya Raman officially becomes Los Angeles’ next mayor, a lot of folks will be looking at what’s next for the Los Angeles Police Department. She’s said she would like to maintain the size of the workforce and it’s unclear where she stands on firing LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell. Today on AirTalk, we dig into what Mayor-elect Raman has proposed and what might come to fruition with Jim Newton, lecturer of public policy at UCLA.

UN climate summit opens in Turkey with modest goals | Christian Science Monitor

“It’s not a coincidence that at the moment climate harms are affecting communities in really real ways, and affecting governments’ budgets in really real ways, it becomes harder to make progress on climate mitigation,” says Cara Horowitz, executive director of the Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at the UCLA School of Law, who will be in Turkey for her 10th COP.

Trump taps Stephen Miller as chief of staff | Los Angeles Times

Chris Zepeda-Millán, an associate professor of public policy, Chicana/o studies and political science at UCLA, said Miller always has been at the center of Trump’s anti-immigrant actions and policies, and his elevation should be understood as a threat to immigrant communities.

Is there a progressive tide playing out in LA? | Southern California News Group

Progressives are indeed having a moment in politics, said Chris Zepeda-Millán, a public policy professor at UCLA with expertise in racial and ethnic politics, political activism and social movements. But today’s progressive candidates are focused on issues different than those of the past, he said.

Even the right is debating whether MAGA face has gone too far | Washington Post

Trump’s second administration has brought even more scrutiny to the appearance of the women with which he surrounds himself, said Juliet Williams, a professor of gender studies at UCLA. “He has conspicuously made it a practice to elevate and appreciate women who have a very particular look and style, and the messaging there has been very clear that, from the standpoint of his administration, a woman’s value is very closely indexed to her appearance,” Williams said. “If you don’t look the part, you’re not going to get the part.”

Long wait for state high-speed rail | Los Angeles Business Journal

“Right now, it’s hard to see this train carving out a space in our infrastructure firmament,” said Michael Manville, professor of urban planning at the UCLA Luskin School of Public Affairs.

A promising new heart medicine fails unexpectedly | NPR’s “Weekend Edition Sunday”

“The take-home message is the story’s not over,” says Karol Watson, a cardiologist at the University of California, Los Angeles. “It’s kind of just starting.” (Watson was also quoted by CNN, NBC News, and The New York Times.)

Are women more sensitive to the effects of cannabis than men? | Medical Xpress

Men who use cannabis occasionally reacted more strongly to smoked cannabis than women with similar use habits, even though the amount of THC in their blood was about the same, according to a new study from UCLA Health. The findings run counter to earlier research suggesting that women are more sensitive to cannabis. (UCLA’s Ziva Cooper and Stephanie Lake were quoted.)

A simple supplement may help clear brain fog after cancer | ScienceDaily

For some breast cancer survivors, the effects of treatment can linger long after their cancer care ends. Memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, and persistent exhaustion can interfere with everyday life, sometimes for years. Now, researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center have found promising early evidence that a supplement containing a naturally occurring molecule could help relieve these symptoms. (UCLA’s Dr. Patricia Ganz was quoted.)
