description:
Last year, Attorney General Bonta and the coalition secured a permanent injunction blocking the imposition of these conditions, an injunction which remains in effect and which the Trump Administration’s most recent grant award notices violated.
“Court after court has rejected the Trump Administration’s unlawful attempts to condition unrelated grant funding on supporting the President’s hateful immigration agenda,” said Attorney General Bonta.
This includes counterterrorism grants, grants that allow states to prepare for terrorism in high-concentration urban areas, emergency preparedness grants, cybersecurity grants, and many others that are similarly not connected to civil immigration enforcement.
As such, the court declared that DHS’s decision to implement the FY 2026 Immigration Conditions violated the 2025 injunction, enjoined DHS from enforcing the FY 2026 Immigration Conditions against the plaintiff states, and ordered DHS to reissue award letters without the challenged conditions.
Attorney General Bonta is joined by the attorneys general of Illinois, New Jersey, Rhode Island, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Vermont, Washington, and Wisconsin in this lawsuit.
text:
OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today secured an order from the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island enforcing its prior judgment that blocked the Trump Administration’s effort to unlawfully impose immigration conditions on hundreds of millions of dollars in annual U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) grants. Attorney General Bonta co-led a multistate coalition in filing a motion to enforce the judgment after DHS attempted to impose a new, nearly identical set of immigration conditions on the grants they administer for the 2026 fiscal year. Last year, Attorney General Bonta and the coalition secured a permanent injunction blocking the imposition of these conditions, an injunction which remains in effect and which the Trump Administration’s most recent grant award notices violated.

“Court after court has rejected the Trump Administration’s unlawful attempts to condition unrelated grant funding on supporting the President’s hateful immigration agenda,” said Attorney General Bonta. “The safety of our communities is not a political bargaining chip. I applaud the court for swiftly reining in this latest attempt by the Trump Administration to circumvent court orders and Congress’ power of the purse.”

California receives funding from DHS every year to prepare for, protect against, respond to, and recover from terrorist attacks and other catastrophes. This includes counterterrorism grants, grants that allow states to prepare for terrorism in high-concentration urban areas, emergency preparedness grants, cybersecurity grants, and many others that are similarly not connected to civil immigration enforcement. State and local law enforcement already work closely with federal agencies on the counterterrorism measures that these grants fund.

In today’s decision, the court determined that the immigration conditions imposed by DHS on fiscal year 2026 funding fall within the scope of the prior judgment, which applied to cover future fiscal years and “materially similar” conditions. As such, the court declared that DHS’s decision to implement the FY 2026 Immigration Conditions violated the 2025 injunction, enjoined DHS from enforcing the FY 2026 Immigration Conditions against the plaintiff states, and ordered DHS to reissue award letters without the challenged conditions.

Attorney General Bonta is joined by the attorneys general of Illinois, New Jersey, Rhode Island, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Vermont, Washington, and Wisconsin in this lawsuit.

title: Arizona freshmen Shah, Mendoza and Lamb prepare for a House transformed - Cronkite News
authors: Sophia Braccio, Ellis Preston, Eileen Mamaghani
description:
Democrats JoAnna Mendoza and Amish Shah, who flipped GOP-held seats, and Republican Mark Lamb, who’ll replace gubernatorial runner-up Rep. Andy Biggs, are part of the largest House freshman class in decades.
JoAnna Mendoza Mendoza is the first female Marine elected to the House.
She’s also interested in the Homeland Security Committee.
“But I think we can do both because people really need us to.” Amish Shah Shah, an emergency room physician and former state House member, defeated Trump-backed Jay Feely by just under 25,000 votes.
“ It’s our constitutional duty.” Mark Lamb Lamb, the former Pinal County sheriff, put border security at the top of his list and said the fact he’ll be in the minority won’t change his priorities.
text:
WASHINGTON – Arizona’s three newest members of Congress arrived at the Capitol for freshman orientation Monday eager to deliver on their promises to voters.

Democrats JoAnna Mendoza and Amish Shah, who flipped GOP-held seats, and Republican Mark Lamb, who’ll replace gubernatorial runner-up Rep. Andy Biggs, are part of the largest House freshman class in decades.

Between closed-door orientation sessions on such topics as how to set up a congressional office, the three spoke with Cronkite News about their approaches to affordability and oversight of the executive branch, and their hopes for committee assignments.

When the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, at least 109 House members will be newcomers. That’s more than a quarter of the 435-member House.

Democrats will vastly outnumber Republicans after voters handed President Donald Trump and his party a stinging rebuke. Democrats attributed the result to high gas prices, corruption, executive overreach and Trump’s immigration and tariff policies.

As Arizona’s members get acquainted with Washington, they are each preparing for the opportunities of the 120th Congress with their own policy goals.

JoAnna Mendoza

Mendoza is the first female Marine elected to the House. She said she hopes to land a seat on the House Armed Services Committee, calling the Iran war a “huge concern.”

She ousted two-term Rep. Juan Ciscomani, R-Tucson, by about 28,500 votes in a district that includes Tucson and the southeast section of the Arizona-Mexico border.

She’s also interested in the Homeland Security Committee.

“In the military, you don’t ask people if they’re Republicans, independents or Democrats,” she said. “What you do is you build relationships, you earn trust, and then you accomplish the mission, and that’s exactly what I plan to do here.”

Like other Democrats, she said she intends to focus on affordability through reversing Medicaid cuts, a problem she heard about from many of her soon-to-be constituents.

The cuts under Trump, she said, are “going to be so devastating.”

Democrats also promised accountability and oversight in the midterms. Mendoza emphasized issues with tangible impact on her district, including healthcare, job security and cost of living.

“There’s going to be plenty of time for oversight and accountability,” she said. “But I think we can do both because people really need us to.”

Amish Shah

Shah, an emergency room physician and former state House member, defeated Trump-backed Jay Feely by just under 25,000 votes.

“Core function in medicine is to care for people,” he said. “We have to care for those people back at home in our district. Make sure we deliver.”

He’ll replace Rep. David Schweikert, R-Fountain Hills, who gave up his seat to run for governor. Biggs defeated him in the GOP primary.

The district includes northeast Phoenix, Scottsdale and Paradise Valley and had been trending more purple. Schweikert carried it by less than 4 percentage points two years ago.

Shah said he met with Schweikert after winning the seat.

“He was gracious, he was kind,” Shah said. “We’ve got to do the best we can for the constituents.”

Apart from the usual Democratic emphasis on affordability and healthcare, Shah also cited water policy. He campaigned in part on working across party lines but said that doesn’t mean shying from tough oversight of the Trump administration.

“Corruption is directly tied to cost-of-living increases and all the other issues that we’re facing back at home,” he said, referring to the Iran war, Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill tax overhaul, and the tariffs the president has slapped on major trading partners.

“Those things are going to be a focus for us to try to move costs in the right direction for the people,” he said.

As for a third impeachment of Trump, as some in the party’s progressive wing are demanding, Shah said: “We’ll see.”

“Impeachment is in the Constitution as a remedy, put in there by the founding fathers for high crimes, misdemeanors and egregious actions, and that is the law, and we will follow the law,” Shah said. “ It’s our constitutional duty.”

Mark Lamb

Lamb, the former Pinal County sheriff, put border security at the top of his list and said the fact he’ll be in the minority won’t change his priorities.

He narrowly won the 5th District with 51.7% of votes – a big drop from Biggs’ 60% tally in 2024.

“The border still needs to be fixed long term. That’s not an issue that has solidified,” he said before Monday morning’s orientation outside the Capitol Visitor Center auditorium. “While we’re doing great with it, I think a lot of Americans forgot how bad it could be – and it was – and we need to get back to fixing it again.”

A longtime Trump supporter, Lamb campaigned on closer cooperation between local law enforcement and federal immigration authorities, though he also offered an implicit critique of Trump administration policy, calling for prioritizing people who have committed crimes while in the country illegally.

He said he wants to “pare down big-government,” make life more affordable by cutting taxes – unlikely with Democrats in control – finding ways to lower energy costs and “getting inflation under control.”

The $40.5 trillion national debt puts the U.S. economy on a “collision course,” he said.

GOP leaders haven’t yet made committee assignments.

Lamb said he believes his background would serve him well on Homeland Security or Judiciary.

title: 14 Charged in Deadly Human Smuggling Scheme That Killed 7 Aliens Earlier This Year
description:
“There have been multiple rail car alien smuggling interdictions over the last many months.
Should you survive the journey, when we find you in the United States, you will be removed.
Once smuggled into the United States, aliens were often housed at stash houses or hidden in the brush along the Rio Grande River near Del Rio, Texas.
The organization then loaded aliens into shipping containers to transport the aliens further into the interior of the United States.
The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.
text:
A federal grand jury in the Western District of Texas returned a superseding indictment charging a total of 14 individuals, including seven illegal aliens, three non-citizens, and four U.S. citizens, for their roles in a conspiracy to smuggle aliens into the United States for profit. This included a failed human smuggling event that resulted in the deaths of seven people, including one child, who died after being loaded into a poorly ventilated shipping container.

“By allegedly orchestrating this deadly human smuggling scheme, these defendants showed no regard for the value of human life and put people in harm’s way to pad their own pockets,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Those who show a reckless disregard for the rule of law and treat human beings like cargo for their own financial gain will be held accountable under this administration. Cases like these are exactly why President Trump established the Homeland Security Task Force to strengthen our efforts to keep Americans safe from transnational crime.”

“Seven people are dead as the result of another callous alien smuggling scheme,” said U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas. “There have been multiple rail car alien smuggling interdictions over the last many months. Aliens found alive in those schemes will probably never realize how fortunate they are to have survived. To those who are placing their lives in the hands of dangerous alien smugglers, you must understand that there is no good outcome awaiting on this side of the border. Should you survive the journey, when we find you in the United States, you will be removed. To those alien smuggling organizations like the one responsible for these seven deaths, your date with American justice will come, and when it does, we will hold you accountable to the fullest extent of the law.”

“This indictment reflects Homeland Security Investigation’s (HSI) commitment to pursuing the criminal networks that profit by treating human lives as cargo,” said Special Agent in Charge John A. Pasciucco of HSI San Antonio. “As alleged, this smuggling network used cargo trains and sealed shipping containers to move people into the country’s interior, placing them in conditions that were inhumane and deadly. HSI and our law enforcement partners will continue to identify, investigate, and hold accountable those who exploit vulnerable individuals for profit and endanger lives in the process.”

Defendants include Karina Garcia, 37, of Del Rio, Texas; Edson Alejandro Perez, 18, of Del Rio; Seferino Huerta-Casillas, 35, an illegal alien from Mexico; Jonas Ulloa-Aguilera, 25, an illegal alien from Honduras; Mayra Alejandra Huerta, 32, of Del Rio; Maria Norma Neri de Moran, 56, of Mexico; Damian Huerta Analucas, 55, of Mexico; Rosario Cristal Lopez-Saldana, 26, an illegal alien from Mexico; Eric Hernandez, 40, of Eagle Pass, Texas; Franklin Williams Ayala Aguilera, 30, an illegal alien from Honduras; Pascual Raymundo Loarca, 34, an illegal alien from Guatemala; Juan Alvaro Membreno-Contreras, 40, an illegal alien from Honduras; Yuri Julissa Cuaresma Paredes, 34, of Honduras; and Mavis Aleyda Escalante Peraza, 38, an illegal alien from Honduras.

According to court documents, from at least April 2023 through May 12, 2026, the defendants and others operated a human smuggling organization that illegally used cargo trains to smuggle aliens further into the United States after smuggling them across the southern border from Mexico. Each smuggled alien, or their families and friends, paid smugglers in Honduras, Mexico, the United States, and elsewhere between $1,500 and $10,000. The organization was comprised of multiple smugglers who worked in concert with other groups of smugglers to accomplish their goals. This included coordinating and utilizing each other’s routes, guides, stash houses, and drivers. Once smuggled into the United States, aliens were often housed at stash houses or hidden in the brush along the Rio Grande River near Del Rio, Texas. The organization then loaded aliens into shipping containers to transport the aliens further into the interior of the United States. In February 2026, the organization began facilitating the smuggling of at least seven aliens, including one 14-year-old child from Honduras, into Del Rio. On or about May 9, after the smugglers illegally crossed the seven aliens from Mexico into the Del Rio area, the organization transported the aliens to an area near the Union Pacific train tracks in Del Rio. From approximately 1:18 p.m. to 1:25 p.m., while a Union Pacific train was stationary, smugglers, using red bolt cutters, allegedly cut the lock off a Conex shipping container’s door, loaded the aliens into the container, and then shut the door.

Red bolt cutters used to open the Conex shipping container’s door

The shipping container was stacked on top of another and had no ventilation or cooling system. Based on the investigation, the recorded outside temperatures for that day ranged from 88 to 92 degrees Fahrenheit. It was secured from the outside and could not be opened from the inside. The train then departed Del Rio and traveled east along U.S. highway 90 to San Antonio. Once the train arrived in San Antonio, smugglers opened the door to the Conex container and discovered the aliens in peril. The smugglers then fled the scene, allegedly leaving one of the deceased near the railroad tracks. Smugglers left the remaining victims in the shipping container. The next day, the train departed south along its route to Laredo.

On May 10, a worker at the Union Pacific Rail Yard in Laredo saw a leg sticking out from a Conex shipping container. Upon inspection, six people were discovered deceased in the shipping container. Laredo law enforcement contacted San Antonio agents for assistance. Later, San Antonio law enforcement discovered the seventh victim deceased and abandoned by the railroad tracks in San Antonio. Four of the deceased were Mexican nationals and three were Honduran nationals, including a 14-year-old child. The investigation revealed that at least one victim messaged a loved one, pleading for help.

Map depicting US-90 and the Union Pacific Railroad system from Del Rio to San Antonio Photo depicting broken seal from the Conex shipping container’s door Shipping container opened with deceased smuggled aliens inside

A total of 14 defendants are charged with offenses relating to their involvement with this human smuggling organization. 11 of the defendants were indicted in July. The superseding indictment charges 12 defendants with conspiracy to transport aliens resulting in death and aiding and abetting the transportation of aliens resulting in death. If convicted, the defendants face a maximum penalty of life in prison. 11 defendants are charged with seven counts of aiding and abetting illegally bringing aliens to the United States. If convicted of at least three counts, they face a minimum penalty of five years in prison and a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison. 12 defendants are charged with one count of conspiracy to bring aliens to the United States causing serious bodily injury and placing lives in jeopardy. If convicted, they face a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison. Additionally, 11 defendants are charged with conspiracy to commit money laundering. If convicted, they face a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison.

The case is being investigated by HSI Del Rio, U.S. Border Patrol, HSI Laredo, HSI San Antonio, HSI Monterrey Mexico, HSI Honduras, HSI Houston, HSI Dallas, HSI El Paso, and HSI’s Human Smuggling Unit in Washington, D.C. HSI received substantial assistance from U.S. Customs and Border Protection’s National Targeting Center’s International Interdiction Task Force, Texas Department of Public Safety, Bexar County Sheriff’s Office, Kendall County Sheriff’s Office, Seguin Police Department, San Antonio Police Department, U.S. Marshals, ATF, Union Pacific Railroad Police Department, and the Laredo Police Department.

Trial Attorney Paige Petersen of the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section (HRSP) and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Sarah Spears, Todd Keagle, and Ashley Ellis-Dotson for the Western District of Texas are prosecuting the case.

This case is supported by JTFA, the U.S. Department of Justice’s lead effort in combating human smuggling and trafficking committed by cartels and Transnational Criminal Organizations throughout the Americas. In partnership with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), JTFA investigates and prosecutes the most prolific and dangerous human smuggling and trafficking networks that impact public safety and border security. Led by HRSP and supported by other Criminal Division components, JTFA has dedicated prosecutors from U.S. Attorneys’ Offices along the Southwest border, Southern Florida, Northern New York, and Vermont. JTFA partners with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices throughout the country and supports high-priority cases in any district. All JTFA cases rely on substantial law enforcement resources from DHS components, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, HSI, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection, U.S. Border Patrol, and the Office of Field Operations. JTFA also partners with FBI and other law enforcement agencies. To date, JTFA’s work has resulted in more than 486 domestic and international arrests of leaders, organizers, and significant facilitators of alien smuggling and trafficking; more than 447 U.S. convictions; and more than 374 significant jail sentences imposed and forfeitures of substantial assets.

This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF comprises agents and officers from FBI; ICE HSI; DEA; ATF; U.S. Border Patrol; USMS; U.S. Postal Inspection Service; Department of Transportation; IRS Criminal Investigation; Texas Department of Public Safety; as well as local police departments and sheriff’s offices, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas.

An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

text:
Texas Border Business

WASHINGTON DC – President Donald Trump acknowledged that his administration’s immigration enforcement policies may have been too tough, particularly toward undocumented immigrants working in hotels, landscaping businesses and other industries, during an interview with CBS News’ 60 Minutes that aired Sunday, November 8, 2026.

Speaking with CBS News correspondent Ross Douthat at the White House on November 6, Trump said his immigration policies had produced mixed political results and said he was interested in negotiating an immigration agreement with Democrats after the midterm elections.

“I’d love to do something on immigration,” Trump said when asked what issue he would consider addressing with the incoming Democratic congressional majority.

Trump defended his administration’s border enforcement efforts but acknowledged that deporting undocumented immigrants who have established working lives in the United States had generated opposition.

“I think it both helped and hurt,” Trump said about immigration’s effect on the midterm elections.

He argued that closing the southern border had strengthened his political standing while removing undocumented immigrants employed in American businesses had created difficulties.

“For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out, but I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs,” Trump said.

He described workers whose primary immigration violation was entering the country illegally, including those employed by landscaping companies and hotels.

When Douthat asked whether his deportation policies had gone too far, Trump responded, “I think it might be too tough.”

Trump specifically discussed immigration enforcement involving hotel employees who had worked in the United States for years.

“When you go into a hotel, and you say, let me see your pass, and you have a woman that’s worked there as a, you know, as a maid, as a cleaner,” Trump said, describing workers who could face deportation.

“All of a sudden, they’re being taken out of the country. It’s tough. It’s a tough thing.”

Trump said Americans hold differing views about whether undocumented immigrants should be deported regardless of their employment history or allowed to remain under certain conditions.

He described one group favoring widespread deportations and another supporting the removal of people convicted of serious crimes while considering arrangements for longtime workers.

“Let the people that are here and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years work a deal for them,” Trump said, describing the latter position.

Asked whether an agreement could provide some form of legal status, Trump expressed optimism about reaching a compromise.

“We would work something out, and I think it’s something, I think that’s something that’s actually doable,” he said.

Trump also said Democratic lawmakers had already contacted him about immigration, although he did not identify them or provide details of any negotiations.

text:
After Democrats’ blowout win in the midterms, Congress will have a lot of formal power to check the administration, particularly through appropriations and oversight. The effectiveness of those checks, however, may depend importantly on something less tangible: Congress’s functional power to shape public opinion and delegitimate actions it considers unlawful or ill-advised. And that power, unfortunately, seems to have undergone a long-term decline.

At any rate, I speculate about this possibility in a forthcoming essay in the Notre Dame Law Review. (The essay is part of an excellent Gray Center symposium on “What Happened to Congress?”.)

My essay posits that a key feature of separation of powers in the United States has been a process of interbranch legitimation of government action. These days, people often imagine that effective government requires letting majorities get things done. That is true enough but if taken too far it misses that checks and balances may empower government even as they also restrain it. They do so in part by helping ensure the popularity of actions that run the gauntlet of interbranch checks. But checks and balances may also help generate that popularity in the first place by enhancing the legitimacy of actions that the branches jointly approve.

If that idea sounds fanciful, consider the historical role of the Supreme Court. Political scientists have long puzzled over why the political branches tolerate judicial review, given its potential to obstruct their goals. The answer, according to Keith Whittington and others, is that judicial review actually serves the political branches’ long-run interests. In some instances, the Court saves politicians from themselves by taking divisive options off the table. But more generally the Court has helped legitimate contested policies by validating them.

In other words, by blocking some actions, courts gain the credibility to settle legal and constitutional doubts about others. Politicians take the bitter with the sweet. Gaining validation from judicial approval requires accepting judicial defeats—a dynamic very much in evidence in the second Trump administration (and for that matter in the Biden administration, too).

My essay speculates that similar dynamics might be generalized across the three branches. In particular, Congress these days often finds itself in a position analogous to courts exercising judicial review.

Due to broad statutory delegations and accumulated executive practice, presidents can often pursue significant initiatives unilaterally. Congress is then in a reactive posture: it must decide whether to support or stymie executive initiatives. And while that process is partly a matter of exercising its formal power over continued funding, it is also, perhaps more fundamentally, a matter of functionally shaping public perceptions of such actions.

In any event, there is substantial evidence that Congress has historically played the leading role in sustaining broad public acceptance of federal governance. With its distributed representation and capacity for logrolling and compromise, Congress is best positioned among the branches to channel public opinion and promote acceptance of disputed policies. And on matters ranging from war mobilization and industrial policy to welfare and civil rights, Congress has done just that. It has been the central engine of legitimacy for federal governance.

Lately, however, this engine has seemed to splutter. Mired in partisan division, Congress has struggled to legislate on key questions like immigration and the environment; it has instead let the executive branch set policy on its own. Even worse, Congress has largely failed to defend its institutional prerogatives against repeated presidential usurpations. In the second Trump administration, executive officials have defied limits and mandates regarding spending and other matters in ways that even quite popular presidents in the past did not dare.

Now, with the return of divided government, congressional capacity faces an important test. It is possible that Congress will recover some of its ability to negotiate broadly supported compromises and enforce its institutional interests in bipartisan fashion; having larger and more ideologically mixed Democratic majorities in the House and Senate may help.

But Congress is likely to remain highly polarized and President Trump will surely seek to write off congressional checks as partisan posturing; he is reportedly planning to use executive power aggressively. A key question will then be whether congressional opposition stiffens resistance inside the executive branch to unlawful or unwise actions. Can Congress still strip force from actions of which it disapproves, or can presidents ride roughshod over congressional opposition unless and until courts step in to stop them?

Though Congress will hopefully succeed in restoring some of its former strength, I fear that, whatever happens over the next two years, Congress’s decline reflects deep-seated changes in media and society rather than more contingent factors. As Rick Pildes has pointed out, other western democracies with very different systems are facing similar governance challenges and problems of legislative incapacity. Just look at France.

While I don’t have great answers to this problem, the essay suggests two institutional adaptations. First, courts (and Congress itself) should buttress Congress’s ability to support or stymie executive initiatives through the “reactive” powers I mentioned earlier—Congress’s powers of oversight and funding. And second, courts themselves should take care to avoid the sort of excessive politicization that could undermine their own authority, much as fragmentation has done for Congress.

More generally, all sides of current debates should remember that American government has historically been effective because of checks and balances and not despite them. To that extent, removing restraints on majority will could prove self-defeating.

text:
Wearing a pressed button-down white shirt and slacks, a Haitian boy showed up at a routine immigration appointment in downtown San Diego. Moments later, the neatly dressed 8-year-old was being led away by three immigration officers.

As of Monday, his loved ones do not know exactly where he is being held, a California lawmaker said.

The scene was captured on a video NBC San Diego obtained Friday. The video was recorded Wednesday by a volunteer observer of immigration proceedings at ICE’s field office.

The San Diego Unified School District and members of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, an immigrants rights advocacy group, said the boy was separated from his cousins and uncle, who has been taking care of him after his father was deported last year.

Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said in a statement Monday that even though the uncle followed all the rules, “the child was taken into custody and subsequently transferred to the Office of Refugee Resettlement,” which takes custody of children deemed to be unaccompanied minors.

The boy, who has not been identified by name publicly, is a third grader at Fay Elementary School. He was stripped of his immigration protections this summer after a Supreme Court decision allowed President Donald Trump to end Temporary Protected Status for Haitians, according to a letter school district officials sent Friday to the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the Office of Refugee Resettlement.

Temporary Protected Status, better known as TPS, is a humanitarian designation that shielded hundreds of thousands of Haitians from deportation following Haiti’s 2010 devastating earthquake. The protections were renewed multiple times over the years as the Caribbean country sank deeper into crisis. Currently, a majority of the country’s capital is controlled by gangs after the president was assassinated in 2021.

After TPS was terminated, the child in San Diego received a letter summoning him to meet with ICE officers last week, school district officials said in their letter. His uncle complied and took him to the appointment “because he did not want to break the law,” added the letter, which NBC News obtained Monday.

A DHS spokesperson told NBC San Diego that “a man claiming to be the child’s uncle took him to an ICE check-in.” ICE officers said that they could not confirm the man was related to the boy and that “the alleged uncle could not establish legal guardianship of the minor.”

As a result, they determined the boy to be an unaccompanied minor, the DHS spokesperson said. “Out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety, ICE determined it was best to remove the child from the household,” the spokesperson said.

The Office of Refugee Resettlement told NBC News on Monday that it “does not comment on specific cases” in accordance with its own privacy policies to protect the children in its custody.

The third grader is among the 1,640 children considered unaccompanied minors who are under HHS care, according to the agency’s data. Immigration authorities have taken more than 8,000 children into custody over the past year, according to data from the Deportation Data Project.

The office of Rep. Juan Vargas, D-Calif., said that the boy’s family does not know where he is being held and that he is helping them obtain the information they need to find him.

“Targeting a child, taking them away from their community and classmates, and forcing them into detention is despicable. It is inhumane,” Vargas told NBC San Diego in a statement Friday. “Additionally, TPS protections must be restored for all who’ve had them unfairly ripped away.”

DHS has deemed allegations claiming the boy was “placed in detention” as “false.”

DHS also said the child was “illegally brought into the United States” at an unspecified time by “a man who alleged to be his father,” who was removed to Mexico by Customs and Border Patrol, not ICE.

Jozef said, “His father has already been taken from him and deported, now this administration has stripped him of the stability, family, and community every child deserves.”

James Canning, a spokesperson for the school district, told NBC News in a statement on Monday that educators at the boy’s school have pointed to “a general sense of concern for the student’s safety and wellbeing.”

School district officials said they are sending additional crisis counselors to Fay Elementary School this week “because the child’s fellow third grade students have expressed concern and fear for their friend.”

Canning said no one at DHS or HHS has yet responded to the school district’s letter asking them to reconsider how immigration enforcement policies are affecting students.

text:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume border barrier construction in the Big Bend region of West Texas, including the national park.

The decision paused a federal judge’s order last month that halted work because of her concern that the federal government exceeded its authority to waive environmental laws.

In an unsigned 8–1 ruling, the justices put U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone’s order on hold, allowing construction to resume while the Trump administration asks the Supreme Court to review the case. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented but didn’t provide a reason.

“The Government’s interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents,” the ruling says.

Monday’s ruling is temporary until the Supreme Court decides to hear the case or until it’s settled in the lower court in El Paso.

The ruling was a blow to environmentalists and residents who have said that Big Bend, which includes the counties of Brewster, Presidio and Jeff Davis, does not need a border wall because the rough and desolate terrain already makes it dangerous to illegally cross the border or smuggle drugs.

The Center for Biological Diversity, Friends of the Ruidosa Church, and Danny William Miller Jr., a local river guide, filed the lawsuit in April. It is among six lawsuits against the Trump administration seeking to halt border wall construction in Big Bend.

The U.S. Border Patrol’s Big Bend sector includes 517 miles of the U.S.-Mexico border, which accounts for about 1.6% of migrant apprehensions of the entire border. Still, the Trump administration has awarded $7.5 billion worth of contracts to firms to pave roads, erect barriers and install technology in the area.

“This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal,” said Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity. “They’re signing off on the permanent destruction of the wildest place in Texas, and the theft of a great American river from all of us.”

On Oct. 2, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone, who was appointed to the bench by President George W. Bush, halted construction after finding that the challengers were likely to prove the administration exceeded its authority to waive environmental regulations in a region with historically low levels of illegal border crossings. On Oct. 14, she released her written opinion.

The Trump administration appealed her decision to the U.S. Supreme Court because the waiver laws being challenged are written so that they bypass federal appeals courts.

The Trump administration argued that Cardone’s temporary ruling was baseless because Congress approved the federal government’s authority to waive environmental laws. Trump officials also argued that the delay was costing the federal government $500,000 a day.

text:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday allowed President Donald Trump to move forward with construction of his border wall in the remote Big Bend region of southwest Texas.

Construction there had been challenged by an environmental group and locals who say it would damage the environment and historic sites.

The justices blocked an injunction imposed by a federal judge in Texas that had blocked construction while litigation continues.

In a five-page unsigned decision, the court said that the federal judge who ruled on the issue had no authority to do so, adding that the Trump administration was “extremely likely to prevail” on that point.

The government, the court added, has “compelling interests” when a challenged policy involves border security.

Of the nine justices, only liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.

The segment of the border adjacent to the Rio Grande is sparsely populated, with the Trump administration saying 89,000 people have been detained trying to enter the United States there in recent years.

The move was challenged by the Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental organization; Friends of the Ruidosa Church, a nonprofit group dedicated to restoring a historic church in the area; and Danny Miller, a river guide who owns property in the area.

“This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal,” Laiken Jordahl, one of the environmental group’s lawyers, said in a statement.

James Percival, the Department of Homeland Security’s general counsel, welcomed the decision on X, saying the lopsided nature of the vote count shows how wrong the lower court judge had been.

“When we filed in the Supreme Court, I called the district court’s order halting wall construction ‘as unprecedented as it is flawed.’ We just won 8-1,” he said.

The section in question, which the government says would involve 341 miles of construction, includes Big Bend National Park. The legal dispute focuses on three waivers issued by then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in February and her successor, Markwayne Mullin, in May and July that allowed the government to evade environmental and conservation laws.

In a court filing, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said Congress in 1996 gave the government “broad authority” to build border infrastructure without getting tied up in red tape.

Lawyers for the challengers said that if construction goes ahead, it would “result in the permanent alteration of an irreplaceable landscape” and “threaten unique historic and cultural resources.”

Contrary to the government’s assertions, the Big Bend area has “the lowest apprehension rates” for migrants anywhere along the border, they added.

Government data shows that Big Bend has the section of the southern border with the lowest number of encounters between federal agents and migrants.

The plaintiffs say that the 1996 law only allows for limited waivers for border construction projects in areas where illegal crossings are pervasive.

U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone on Oct. 2 invalidated Noem’s waivers, saying the secretary lacked such sweeping powers.

Cardone declined to put her ruling on hold, prompting the administration to turn to the Supreme Court.

Trump’s pledge to build a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border has been one of his signature policies ever since his first presidential campaign in 2016. It is part of his hard-line immigration policy that focuses on border security and mass deportations.

Officials have warned that if other parts of the wall are built but the Big Bend area remains open, it would be exploited by those seeking to enter the country illegally.

Boosted by construction funding from the Republican-controlled Congress, the administration seeks to fulfill Trump’s plan by completing a 2,000-mile installation including steel panels, vehicle barriers and new surveillance technology.

WASHINGTON -- The Supreme Court cleared the way Monday for the Trump administration to resume border wall construction in the Big Bend region of Texas, a blow to bipartisan opponents who had argued the project is a waste of money that threatens the unique landscape.

The border wall is a signature project of President Donald Trump, who has long vowed to build a wall from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico.

Republicans in Congress last summer funded the project with $46 billion, and Customs and Border Protection has been rapidly erecting 12 miles of border barriers a week across the entire border.

The government has pushed forward by issuing sweeping waivers to bypass regulations. Those rules are aimed at protecting the environment, but have historically slowed down major construction projects.

In Texas’s Big Bend region, bipartisan opposition has rallied to fight back against the project, which would include 30-foot-tall steel walls in some areas as well as vehicle barriers and new roads.

They’ve argued that the barriers are a waste of money that threaten the local economy and lifestyle in an area of historically low illegal immigration. They say the job could be better done using only surveillance technology like drones.

A judge in Texas sided with opponents, finding that Congress likely had not clearly authorized such broad waivers for an area with the southern border’s lowest rate of migrant apprehensions. She ordered an immediate stop to all construction-related activity in the area, which includes Big Bend National Park as well as land up and down river in state and private hands.

The Trump administration filed an emergency appeal, saying there are illegal border crossings and drug seizures in Big Bend. More traffic could also be funneled there if there’s a gap in the wall, federal attorneys argued.

But the push to expand the border barrier through the popular national park has met pushback from conservationists, local officials and some members of Trump’s own Republican Party.

The lawsuit challenged waivers used by the agency to fast-track border construction and sidestep environmental and conservation laws.

(OSV News) — Days after midterm elections that saw Democrats win landslide victories in Congress and flip a number of statehouses across the U.S., President Donald Trump admitted his administration’s immigration crackdown “is too tough” and suggested that he could “work something out” with Democrats on immigration.

“I’d love to do something on immigration,” the president said on the CBS News program “60 Minutes” in a nearly half-hour interview in Washington with correspondent Ross Douthat, a Catholic and well-known political analyst. The wide-ranging interview, which aired Nov. 8, started with a look at the main issues that voters went to the polls about including the war with Iran and immigration.

“I think ultimately that hurt me,” Trump said, regarding his mass deportation push. He said the policy was “too tough,” in response to Douthat’s questions about the impact of his immigration policies on the election and whether he would pursue a deal with Democrats.

“I think it (immigration) both helped and hurt. I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out,” he said. “But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that — that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.”

Voters on Nov. 3 delivered historic losses to Trump, GOP

The Nov. 3 election saw voters deliver historic losses to Trump and the Republicans with the GOP suffering staggering losses not seen since the 1948 elections. As of Nov. 9, the U.S. Senate is now at 54 Democrats and 44 Republicans, with two races too close to call; and the U.S. House has 254 Democrats and 164 Republicans with 17 races yet to be called.

Trump told Douthat, “When you go into a hotel and you have a woman that’s worked there as– you know, as a maid, as a cleaner, as a this, as a that, as a waitress — a lotta good things, great jobs — and all of a sudden, they’re being taken outta the country, it’s tough,” he said. “It’s a tough thing. But there’s a group of people that I would say, on the sort of pretty far right, that would like everybody taken out.”

He added, “There’s also people that are more modified on that. In other words, get the killers out. Get all the– the rough ones out. Get the drug dealers out. But let the people that are here — and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years — work a deal for them.”

Trump said he believed Democrats in Congress would be interested in achieving an immigration deal and that “people have already called me.”

According to the Migration Policy Institute’s latest “Fact Sheet” report, 35% of the 980,000 people deported under the Trump administration — from January 2025 through July 2026 — involved people intercepted and turned around at the border. Another 34% were initially arrested at the border and then deported by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement after ICE processed them for removal within the U.S. The remaining 31% were people arrested in the U.S. and most likely to have had years of residing in U.S. communities.

Domestic arrests increased from 8,000 to 19,000 in Trump’s first 3 months

The October 2026 report also noted an increase in domestic arrests from 8,000 per month in the first three months of Trump’s term to 19,000 per month from May through July 2026.

It added that of those deported by ICE, 61% had been in the U.S. at least two years and 15% had lived in the U.S. 10 years or more. Of these immigrants, 71% had never been convicted of a crime, and 61% of those in the U.S. 10 years or more had no criminal convictions.

Catholics who work with migrants have expressed surprise and caution over the president’s words.

Dominican Father Brendan Curran, the Chicago-based promoter of justice and peace for the Dominicans of Canada and the United States, said he was “delightfully surprised by the tone and content” of what he called the president’s rhetoric on “60 Minutes.”

“Let us be clear,” Father Curran told OSV News Nov. 9. “No matter who is the leadership, no matter what party or their track record, it always has to deal with detail and actual real negotiation. What we’re delighted by is that the rhetoric is speaking of something more healthy, more productive and more reflective of what we see.”

People are asking for ‘an absolute sign of respect’

“The vast majority of folks in our communities, especially and particularly Catholics, want decency, dignity, held above all as a highlight and priority value,” he said. “And moving in this direction as the president indicated, in part, on recognizing decency and dignity needs to be adjusted, is an absolute sign of respect for what people are asking for.”

The head of the Catholic-run Coalition for Public and Spiritual Leadership, Michael Okinczyc-Cruz, expressed reservations, and pointed out the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown continues.

The coalition sued the Department of Homeland Security a year ago and was eventually granted daily entry into the ICE facility in the Chicago suburb of Broadview to give detainees holy Communion and spiritual care.

The Archdiocese of St. Louis filed a lawsuit Oct. 5 on similar grounds, saying ICE “prohibits Catholic priests from offering, and Catholic detainees from receiving, the sacraments of confession and communion.”

“The people who are being detained are most often mothers and fathers, siblings, grandparents, people who’ve been ripped and torn away from their loved ones in their parishes, in their communities,” Okinczyc-Cruz said, calling the experience “shattering” to witness.

Over 10 million Christians in U.S. vulnerable to deportation

A joint report issued last year by the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops’ Migration and Refugee Services, the Center for the Study of Global Christianity at Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary, and World Relief, found that more than 10 million Christians living in the U.S. would be vulnerable to deportation under Trump administration policies implemented in 2025. A majority of them were Catholic followed by a sizable number of evangelicals.

It also found more than 1 in 6 Catholics are either vulnerable to deportation themselves or could see a family member deported, barring law or policy changes.

“To recognize how many families have been devastated by a federal government’s actions is heartbreaking. And so we need comprehensive immigration reform in our country that is fair and just, and that offers people a pathway to citizenship,” he added.

Okinczyc-Cruz said he felt “neither hopeful nor pessimistic” about Trump’s remarks, because “the reality on the ground” is the same as before the midterm elections and after the “60 Minutes” interview aired.

Douthat noted in his narrative during the “60 Minutes” segment that an hour after the interview, Trump selected Stephen Miller, whom he called “the architect” of the administration’s mass deportation operations, to replace his White House chief of staff.

Immigration expert says reform is not an easy task

Kevin Appleby, senior policy and communications fellow with the New York-based Center for Migration Studies, pointed out immigration reform is not an easy task.

Catholic social teaching on immigration balances three interrelated principles — the right of persons to migrate in order to sustain their lives and those of their families, the right of a country to regulate its borders and control immigration, and a nation’s duty to regulate its borders with justice and mercy.

“Certainly the Church wouldn’t be opposed to a measure that moves the ball forward and we certainly wouldn’t say no to legalizing agricultural workers, for example,” Appleby told OSV News. “But in terms of an immigration reform bill, it has to include immigrants who have families, who have been here for a while, who have contributed over the years.”

Appleby expressed “healthy skepticism” regarding Trump’s remarks on making an immigration deal with Democrats.

“I would just be shocked if there was a bill that got to his desk, that would meet those criteria and that his base would allow him to sign,” he said.

text:
By: Jagan Tamirisa | November 09, 2026

Recent decisions by the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) have addressed several important issues affecting individuals facing removal proceedings in the United States. This court roundup highlights five significant decisions, their outcomes, and what they may mean for individuals navigating the U.S. immigration system.

Matter of Ontiveros-Diaz, 30 I&N Dec. 222 (BIA 2026) (November 5, 2026) - Missed Voluntary Departure Deadline? A Ten-Year Bar May Follow

The respondent was granted voluntary departure until June 3, 2025. However, he failed to leave the United States by that deadline. Two weeks after the deadline, respondent filed a motion to reopen his removal proceedings. His previous appeal was dismissed on April 4, 2025, as he failed to establish eligibility for cancellation of removal. In his motion to reopen, the respondent submitted evidence concerning his children's medical and educational needs, as new evidence that changes the situation concerning his reopening of the proceedings. However, the BIA determined that this evidence was unlikely to change the outcome of his case. The motion was denied. The BIA held that the filing of such motions after the date of voluntary departure doesn’t eliminate the consequences of failing to depart — and he was therefore barred from eligibility of immigration relief forms. As a result, the respondent remained subject to a ten-year bar on certain immigration benefits, including cancellation of removal.

The decision highlights the importance of complying with voluntary departure deadlines, as filing a motion to reopen after the deadline does not eliminate the consequences of failing to depart, including a ten-year bar on certain immigration benefits.

Matter of Jonathan Cruz Aijiaco, 30 I&N Dec. 218 (BIA 2026) (November 2, 2026) - BIA Examines Flight Risk, Residential Stability, and Eligibility for Relief in Bond Determinations

In this case, the DHS filed an appeal to vacate an earlier order from an Immigration Judge to grant the respondent a bond of $8,000. The BIA reversed the decision and ordered the respondent detained without bond. The reasons were that the BIA found the respondent to be a flight risk, showing evidence of disregard of legal obligation and laws through repeated motor vehicle violation arrests mostly revolving around license. Additionally, the respondent didn’t provide a clear fixed address, providing conflicting information about his residence and he did not fulfill the requirements for eligibility of relief, primarily the required 10 years of physical presence shown in the gap between his arrival in the U.S. and the date he was placed in removal proceedings.

The decision highlights that even without finding that an individual poses a danger to the community, repeated legal violations, an uncertain residential address, and limited eligibility for immigration relief may result in denial of bond.

Matter of Yang, 30 I&N Dec. 199 (BIA 2026) - Criminal History and Discretionary Eligibility for Cancellation of Removal

In this case, the DHS has appealed from an Immigration Judge order granting cancellation of removal to the respondent. DHS argued that the Immigration Judge failed to consider properly the seriousness of the criminal history of the respondent. Despite the equities (such as paying taxes, employment history, family ties, taking accountability, and expressing remorse) the BIS determined that the serious criminal history outweighed them, resulting in the ultimate reversal and ordered the respondent removed from the United States.

The decision highlights that even when an individual meets the basic eligibility requirements for cancellation of removal, approval is not guaranteed. Immigration Judges must consider both positive and negative factors, and serious criminal conduct may outweigh otherwise favorable circumstances.

Matter of Mata Rodriguez, 30 I&N Dec. 191 (BIA 2026) - Criminal History and Insufficient Rehabilitation Evidence May Defeat Cancellation of Removal

In this case, the respondent filed for cancellation of removal, and the Immigration judge granted it on August 11, 2025. However, DHS appealed the decision, arguing that the respondent’s criminal history was serious and long, including burglary, assault, drug-related, and combined with the lack of evidence of his tax returns, and steady employment. These adverse points significantly outweighed the positive aspects of his stay, such as family ties and community involvement. Additionally, the respondent did not provide sufficient evidence for rehabilitation. Therefore, the BIA ruled in favor of the DHS and the Immigration Judge’s earlier decision was vacated, and the respondent was ordered to be removed to Mexico.

The decision highlights that family ties and long residence in the United States may not overcome a serious criminal history, particularly when the individual fails to provide evidence of rehabilitation.

Matter of Pierre-Louis, 30 I&N Dec. 212 (BIA 2026) (October 30, 2026) - Can a Pending Green Card Application Reopen a Closed Immigration Case?

In this matter, the respondent filed a third motion to reopen his removal proceedings so that he could pursue adjustment of status (green card) with USCIS. The respondent was classified as an “arriving alien,” meaning USCIS, rather than the Immigration Judge, generally had jurisdiction over his adjustment of status application. His prior motions to reopen were denied. The respondent’s third motion asked the BIA to exercise sua sponte (meaning court exercises its discretionary power to reopen a case on its own initiative, even when the usual filing requirements have not been met) authority. However, the BIA declined to reopen the proceedings because the circumstances did not justify an exceptional reopening. The motion was also filed beyond the usual 90-day deadline, more than four years after the final decision, and exceeded the general limit of one motion to reopen.

The decision highlights that having a pending green card application with USCIS does not automatically justify reopening completed removal proceedings, particularly when the request is filed beyond the applicable deadlines or exceeds the permitted number of motions.

Conclusion

text:
Welcome to Court Crawl, Colorado Politics’ roundup of news from the third branch of government.

Multiple federal judges are investigating whether and how the U.S. Attorney’s Office and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement violated their orders, and voters decided against giving another term to three state trial judges.

Recommended Stories

▶

Retention results

• Three judges will not be returning to the bench in January after losing their retention elections: District Court Judges William Alexander of Pueblo County, JenniLynn E. Lawrence of Mesa County, and Dina M. Christiansen of northeastern Colorado.

• Each of them received critical evaluations from their citizen-led performance commissions. However, special circumstances were also at play. Lawrence’s commission deadlocked 4-4 about whether she met performance standards; under the law, the tie went to Lawrence. Christiansen’s performance commission also violated the law by failing to give her an initial evaluation and chance to improve, but voters apparently honored the recommendation anyway.

• A fourth judge, Crowley County Court Judge Jeremy P. Boyce, received a rare, unanimous finding from his performance commission that he did not meet the standards for a judge. While he chose to stand for retention, he evidently changed his mind and resigned right as voting started.

• And yet, the Colorado Secretary of State’s Office told Colorado Politics that it had not received withdrawal paperwork from Boyce. Therefore, his results will be certified and voters will have officially rejected four judges this year — the highest number in decades.

Heard on appeal

• The Colorado Supreme Court has directed Adams County Court Judge Marques A. Ivey to explain why he shouldn’t recuse himself from overseeing a contempt investigation into investigators who served him with a subpoena in his courtroom after he insisted he wouldn’t accept the document. The justices also ordered a Huerfano County judge to justify her repeated rejection of a plea deal in a traffic case.

• The Supreme Court will also decide whether two trial judges responded appropriately to evidence withheld in criminal cases, and whether two plaintiffs should be allowed to dismiss their tax protest in Fremont County and avoid a home inspection by the government.

• By 2-1, the Court of Appeals decided a defendant’s constitutional right to confront the witnesses against him wasn’t violated when a trial judge blocked the jury from hearing about how the victim owed the defendant a lot of money.

In federal news

• A federal judge dismissed University of Colorado Regent Wanda James’ lawsuit against seven of her fellow board members for censuring her and removing her committee assignments last summer.

• A judge rejected the government’s plea deal with a defendant for being “too lenient,” considering the defendant’s actions allegedly caused a man’s death.

• Based on the difficulty of documenting losses, the government asked for restitution on only 5% of an estimated million-dollar student loan forgiveness scam.

• The First Amendment doesn’t protect a defendant’s right to allegedly possess AI-generated child porn in interstate commerce, a judge ruled.

• A judge declined to block Colorado’s new requirements for training, an exam, and sheriffs’ authorization to purchase certain semiautomatic guns.

In immigration news

• Readers are likely aware that Colorado’s U.S. District Court has been facing a flood of “habeas corpus” petitions from those in immigration detention. Right now, the number is around 100 new petitions per week. If that holds, it more than doubles the court’s normal workload.

• Last week, Judge Charlotte N. Sweeney started an investigation into ICE’s practice of releasing petitioners according to judges’ orders, then re-arresting them on the spot.

• “We are now in a situation where this court’s order, and the orders of other judges of this court, are frankly being made a mockery of,” she told the U.S. Attorney’s Office and an ICE representative.

• Simultaneously, Judge Nina Y. Wang called out the U.S. Attorney’s Office’s failure to respond to her orders for more information, and questioned ICE about its unilateral imposition of release conditions that no judge authorized.

• Both judges spoke of a “memorandum of agreement,” dated Oct. 8, between the court and the U.S. Attorney’s Office. The agreement sets out a standardized procedure for processing habeas petitions. Importantly, it authorizes the government to refrain from responding to a habeas petition. If that happens, though, the consequence is release of the petitioner within 24 hours.

• This morning, the court, which previously declined to share the memorandum with Colorado Politics, posted it to its website. Attached is a new order from Chief Judge Regina M. Rodriguez, clarifying that all petitions will be assigned directly to a district judge.

• Previously, petitions from self-represented people were routed through Magistrate Judge Richard T. Gurley in Grand Junction for screening, as is the normal process for civil cases featuring a plaintiff who lacks representation.

Vacancies and appointments

• The governor has appointed civil litigator Victoria M. Cisneros to succeed retiring Jefferson County Court Judge Mark M. Randall.

• Applications are due by Nov. 20 for an attorney seeking to fill a vacancy on the Colorado Public Defender Commission, which reviews the appointment of the state’s public defender at regular intervals. Resumes and letters of interest should be sent to SCGeneral@judicial.state.co.us.

Miscellaneous proceedings

authors: Shireen Akram-Boshar, Mike Ludwig, Chris Walker, Alexis Goldstein, Colleen DeGuzman, Alex Nguyen, Jake Johnson, Joshua Davis, Whitney K. Taylor, Sharon Zhang
