text:
In a “60 Minutes” interview that aired on Sunday evening, President Donald Trump admitted that Republicans’ massive defeats in the midterm elections resulted from widespread frustration with the war on Iran, as well as his immigration policies.

Reiterating that he “was not on the ballot” — as if to suggest that support would have been higher for him personally — Trump said that Americans “didn’t like the war” and “the fact that gasoline went up,” claiming he “had it down at a low” prior to launching the war. In Trump’s assessment, public opposition to his war on Iran is reducible to gasoline prices.

Trump also stated that Republicans’ massive losses during the midterm elections were due to “a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel” — characterizing growing opposition to the U.S.’s relationship with the genocidal state as mere “dislike.”

Trump then said that his immigration policies may have also affected the midterms, and that he may have been “too tough.”

“I think I got an A+ for closing up the border,” he said. “I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out. But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally. And there’s a large group of people [that] think they should be allowed to stay.”

“So you think your deportation policy went too far?” asked CBS News’s Ross Douthat.

“I think it might be too tough,” Trump replied.

In the interview, Trump acknowledged a central contradiction in his administration: that he is caught between the priorities of his far right base, who “would like everybody taken out” [of the country], and the general population, which rejects his brutal policies.

Shortly after his “60 Minutes” interview on Friday, Trump announced that he was promoting political advisor Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff — suggesting that he does not, in fact, plan to soften his approach to immigration enforcement. Miller is known as the hardline, white nationalist architect of Trump’s mass deportation policies, including his policy of family separation.

Over the past year of his administration, Trump has been forced to temper the most overt aspects of his immigration crackdown, after Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) brutal “Operation Metro Surge” in the Twin Cities brought about widespread resistance, particularly after immigration agents killed Minneapolis residents Renee Good and Alex Pretti. As a result of widespread opposition, mass protests, and even a general strike in the Twin Cities, Trump replaced Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem with Markwayne Mullin, who promised that DHS operations would be less visible and stay out of the headlines.

While subsequent ICE operations have not been as brazen as that of Operation Metro Surge, the agency’s strategy has not fundamentally changed. In New York City in July and August, ICE’s “Operation Rotten Apple” resulted in the arrests of some 2,200 people — more than the amount detained by ICE during Operation Metro Surge earlier in the year. The New York City operation, however, managed to evade the same level of pushback, as ICE agents remained less visible, arriving in unmarked cars and detaining and disappearing people quickly, before resistance could emerge.

Trump also stated in the “60 Minutes” interview that he would work with Democrats on immigration. Indeed, his categorization of immigrants as either hard workers or “rough,” “drug dealers” and “killers” echoes rhetoric that has been key to both Republicans’ and Democrats’ approach to immigration since the 1980s — and to bipartisan “comprehensive immigration reform” policies that have increasingly ceded ground to the right.

While voters rejected Trump’s policies in the midterm elections, it is little surprise that Trump has offered to work with Democrats on immigration, as they do not represent an actual alternative to the criminalization, deportation, and precarity offered to undocumented immigrants and asylum seekers.

Meanwhile, the president’s promotion of Miller suggests that even as Trump’s own popularity falls, his aggressive deportation tactics are likely to continue.

name: Human Rights
title: The Voters Have Spoken. Who Speaks for Everyone Else? Human Rights After the Midterms
description:
The views expressed below are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of the Carr-Ryan Center for Human Rights or Harvard Kennedy School.
This commentary looks at the midterms from a human rights standpoint.
Most of what concerns human rights does not appear in any post-election analysis I have read.
America should again put its support behind human rights, democracy, and rule of law everywhere.
A human rights perspective cannot dictate a party platform, but it can ask whether any vision includes people who cannot vote.
text:
The views expressed below are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of the Carr-Ryan Center for Human Rights or Harvard Kennedy School. These perspectives have been presented to encourage debate on important public policy challenges.

Voters have told this administration that it must answer to them. The task now is to make power answer to everyone else too, and to hold ourselves to the same standard.

On November 3, American voters delivered the sharpest rebukes of a sitting president in half a century. The list of grievances is long: a war most Americans did not want, one that also raised prices at home; tariffs that unsettled farms, factories, and family budgets; immigration enforcement that left many Latinos, immigrant communities, and many others feeling that this country was not for them; a turn toward Moscow at Ukraine's expense; sustained pressure on universities, civil service, and public health agencies; threats and insults toward neighbors and allies, from Canada to EU countries to Greenland; and indifference to climate change and to the governance of AI. One could go on — and it is striking how long the list grows after only a minute's reflection.

On Tuesday, the electorate said that enough was enough.

Part of me wants to think the American electorate just did to Trump what Joseph Welch did to McCarthy in 1954: the electorate asked the president whether he had any sense of decency. From what I can tell, there is no serious doubt that this election was about America repudiating its president. But things are more complicated, and we should read this election in two registers. Voters held their government to account for what it did to them, and several of the issues I just listed mattered deeply for that. Whether the country will hold its government to account for what it does to everyone else is a separate question. Tuesday's returns do not settle it. This commentary looks at the midterms from a human rights standpoint.

Human rights rest on the idea that people have claims on those who hold power over them simply because they are people. Their lives are not bargaining chips, and their protection does not depend on citizenship, usefulness, loyalty, or membership in a favored civilization. The Universal Declaration opens with equal dignity, not with a ranking of peoples. So consider the election from the standpoint of those who cannot vote for or against the powerful: children who will inherit a hotter planet, foreigners at a border, civilians in a country under threat, people on the wrong side of a larger state's ambitions. For them, institutions are the means by which claims get pressed. When institutions are dismantled or captured, obligations become optional.

What happened

A few races remain uncalled at this writing, including Senate contests in Mississippi and Alaska, and House totals are still moving. The outline is not in doubt. Democrats won the House by a wider margin than most forecasts anticipated, and they won the Senate, a prospect widely considered out of reach a few months ago. Trump has often compared his election results to landslides. In this instance, that finally is true. He is now the president who lost the Republican Party Kansas, Texas, and South Carolina. Governor Ron DeSantis called the outcome "close to an extinction-level event" for Republicans.

Reuters found that Republicans lost ground, relative to Trump's 2024 showing, in 99% of the roughly 2,200 counties where most votes had been counted by Wednesday morning. Majority-Hispanic counties moved furthest. The New York Times estimates that Republicans lost the national House vote by about thirteen points, the worst result for a president's party since the aftermath of Watergate.

The clarity of these outcomes matters greatly, for the United States and for the world. It was widely expected that the Trump administration would move heaven and hell to contest election results. These margins make such contestation now immensely implausible. The American electorate has spoken too loudly and too clearly for that. Not even all the redistricting has done any good to the Republican prospects. It seems the Democrats won this particular fight. Without losing sight of all the damage Trump and his cronies have done to democracy, human rights, rule of law and plainly to the future of humanity — and they will take decades to repair — for now we can utter a sigh of relief. American democracy is resilient. The country, it seems, has started to free itself from Trumpism.

Why Republicans lost

The explanations that appeared within hours converge to an unusual degree, and they come from every direction.

Prices. Voters blamed the administration for the cost of living and linked it to tariffs and to the war with Iran, which closed the Strait of Hormuz and pushed fuel prices sharply up. About two-thirds of respondents in the AP Voter Poll said Trump's policies had made the economy worse. The facts created by this war are so stubborn that all of Trump’s gaslighting could not outmaneuver them.

The war. Roughly six in ten voters called the decision to attack Iran wrong, and large majorities said it figured in their vote. It also felt like a broken promise: Trump campaigned on no new wars. There used to be a perception of Trump that violence was repulsive to him. That perception has faded away during this second round in the White House.

Corruption. More than half of voters in the AP poll called government corruption crucial to their vote, and about two-thirds said Trump had the wrong priorities. The reporting about a ballroom financed with corporate donations, a family enriched by cryptocurrency, and a closing campaign speech devoted to a reflecting pool evidently landed. Resistance to corruption has deep roots in American conservatism. While conservatives were willing to give Trump credit for achieving many of their goals, his corruption finally might have proved too much for many of them.

Candidates. Trump pushed aside Senator John Cornyn for Paxton, whom two-thirds of Texas voters said lacked the character for the job, and installed Darline Graham, whom six in ten South Carolinians said lacked the experience. Voters in both states signaled that they expected more of Republican candidates than the president's favor. One gets the eerie feeling that with Paxton and Graham, Trump tried to assess how much he would get away with. The voters showed him his limits.

Congress. About seven in ten voters said Congress was not doing enough to check the president, including roughly four in ten Republicans. Separation of powers is a commitment that runs deeply in the American political psyche. The Republican Party of the current Congress, under Mike Johnson nominal leadership, has done little else but cozy up to the president. It is a fair guess that the 119th United States Congress – seated between January 2025 and January 3, 2027 — marks a true low point in the history of modern parliaments, with most of the blame going to the Republicans.

Two cautions are in order. The Democratic Party won no ringing endorsement: fewer than half of voters in the AP poll viewed it favorably, though more did so than viewed the Republican Party favorably. Many people voted Democratic as a rebuke. And the president's party usually loses seats in midterms, which explains part of the result but not its breadth.

What the vote tells us about answerability

Voters punished the administration chiefly for what it cost them: what they paid at the pump, what they feared about their prospects, who was getting rich. Most of what concerns human rights does not appear in any post-election analysis I have read. A country can reject a war because it is expensive. That is better than not rejecting it, but it is a rather thin foundation. If gasoline prices fall, the pressure to end the war might just fall with them, while the people in its path remain where they are. A rights-protecting politics cannot depend on the price of diesel. Americans can expunge Trumpism, and they can even investigate him and his cronies for their corruption — but Iranians and Ukrainians do not get a voice.

Still, the election did more than register pocketbook anger.

Checks and balances are popular. For two years the debate over executive power has been conducted largely in law reviews and among advocates. But what we see now is that voters hold the underlying view in plain form: the person at the top should have to answer to someone. That includes a large minority of Republicans.

Evidence still matters. The Times reports that after federal agents killed two people in Minneapolis in January, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both on video, Trump told advisers he did not like how the videos looked, and Democratic internal polling showed the party leading on immigration for the first time. A majority of Americans now hold an unfavorable view of ICE, according to Pew. Officials had characterized both victims as terrorists or assassins before any investigation. That effort to set the narrative met recorded evidence and public witnesses, and it did not hold. Video, a free press, and citizens who watch and compare are genuine rights infrastructure. Here it did indeed work.

Those closest to enforcement voted. Hispanic voters moved sharply away from Republicans. In Hidalgo County, on the Texas border, the Republican share fell by about twenty-five points compared with 2024. Black voters, especially Black men, also moved, according to the AP. Immigration enforcement was one factor among several, but people who live nearest the coercive power of the state — in this case, people who have experienced the new formations of what I have called the intimidating state — tend to know what it looks like, and they become a political force when given the chance.

Corruption is a rights issue voters recognized. When a president's family and associates profit from his office, and access to government appears to depend on tribute, public power is exercised for private ends and equality before the law is compromised. Voters did not need the vocabulary to feel the wrong.

What was not on the ballot

The election decided little about the matters below. Each tests whether power answers to people who cannot answer back at the polls.

Climate. In February the Environmental Protection Agency rescinded the 2009 finding that greenhouse gases endanger public health, which underpinned much federal regulation of them. In July 2025 the International Court of Justice advised that states have binding obligations to protect the climate system. Reasonable people disagree about carbon pricing, nuclear power, and who pays for a transition. A human rights approach does not settle those disputes, but it refuses to treat foreseeable threats to life, health, food, and water as negligible because responding would burden powerful constituencies. Those who bear the consequences, such as a child in a lethal heatwave, a farmer in a flooded delta, or a generation not yet born, are largely absent from American decisions. The irony is that high fuel prices helped sink a government that had just removed the legal basis for regulating the pollutant behind them. A reaction to prices is not a mandate on obligations to people who cannot vote here. Trump’s war on the future affects many who can do nothing about it whatsoever.

Iran. On April 7 the president wrote that "a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again," and ended the post with a blessing for the Iranian people. Whether it meets the elements of any offense is a question for lawyers. The UN Charter forbids threats of force, and the law of armed conflict forbids threats meant to terrorize civilians. What matters is what was said: a civilization is made of people, most of whom have no say in their government's decisions. Iran's government is repressive, but that does not make its population available for collective punishment. Voters objected to the cost of the war. They were not asked about its menace to those on whom it falls.

Ukraine. Russia's invasion violates the prohibition on aggression, and the International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin over the deportation of Ukrainian children. In February 2025 the United States voted with Russia against a General Assembly resolution condemning the invasion. Negotiation by itself is not betrayal, but the test is what diplomacy secures and whom it respects. Does Ukraine decide its own future? It is hard to tell a story about America's current relationship with Ukraine that does not involve treating Ukraine's security as a chip in a larger bargain with Putin, and abandoning values America once championed: human rights, democracy, the rule of law, and loyalty to those who share them. Congressional and Republican criticism of Trump's October agreement to buy Russian diesel, which blindsided Congress, was an institutional check operating belatedly.

Universalism. Human rights are not prizes for civilizational membership, and protection should follow need, not identity. That is why it matters that the refugee system has been sharply narrowed, with places going overwhelmingly to white South Africans. Their claims count as much as anyone's, and that is the point. People have also been removed to a notorious Salvadoran prison without hearings. In Noem v. Abrego Garcia the Supreme Court ordered the government to facilitate the return of a man wrongly sent there, so the state acted first and corrected itself only when forced. Due process matters because it comes before the government is proved right. The same troubling attitude shows toward friends: Canada was told it might become a "51st state," and Greenland's future was treated as open to American pressure. Peoples have a right to determine their own political status, not merely to state preferences before a stronger country decides. The Trump government has done great damage to a kind of universalism that the United States had done a lot to build in the first place.

Artificial intelligence. The administration's AI Action Plan makes American dominance its central aim, and it came some months after Trump rescinded Biden’s modest requirement that developers of the most powerful models share safety-test results with the government. Capability is not leadership. Leadership asks whether people subject to powerful systems can learn how decisions were made about them, challenge errors, and obtain a remedy. The alternative to public-interest regulation is not the absence of political choices; it can be political direction exercised through government contracts. Elon Musk, who spent more than $450 million to aid Republicans, lost in Texas. Great wealth cannot buy every outcome, but unaccountable private power has not gone away. Under Trump the American government has largely withdrawn from regulating AI, and American recalcitrance in this domain is the single biggest obstacle to global regulation around AI. As far as AI is concerned, to my mind the United States under Trump currently poses the biggest existential threat to humanity that might come from this technology because of its unwillingness to engage in serious oversight. In this regard too, the Trump administration wages war on the future.

Rights at home. The Justice Department has moved to dismiss police-reform agreements in Minneapolis and Louisville, and a 2025 order told agencies to abandon disparate-impact liability wherever possible. Particular applications of that doctrine can fairly be criticized, but abandoning it wholesale makes some discrimination hard to challenge at all. Students and scholars have been detained or had visas revoked over speech the government disliked. After Harvard declined demands about its internal governance, roughly $2.2 billion in research funding was frozen, and in September 2025 a federal judge found the terminations violated the First Amendment and federal procedural requirements. Universities have failed in real ways, but the remedy is open argument, lawful investigation, and a chance to answer, not a funding freeze outside any such process. That Harvard won in court shows that safeguards still work, and also what they exist to prevent.

Military restraint. A professional military is defined by restraint as much as by force, and military lawyers are the institutional form of the trust that soldiers will refuse unlawful orders. In February 2025 the Defense Secretary dismissed the top uniformed lawyers of at least some of the services. Since September 2025 the military has destroyed boats it says carry drugs, killing those aboard without trial. Human Rights Watch and many legal experts call this extrajudicial killing and have not accepted the claim that an armed conflict with trafficking organizations makes it lawful. Replacing officials does not by itself prove unlawful intent, and many service members uphold their values in hard conditions. My charge is against leadership that celebrates force while eroding the restraints that make its use legitimate. The attitudes toward military ethics articulated by Pete Hegseth are dramatic outliers in the historical canon of the Christian just war doctrine as well as in the American tradition of military ethics.

I certainly do not write from an imagined innocent America. Slavery, the dispossession of Indigenous nations, imperial wars, and torture are part of this country's record, and the standards I use judge every administration. This administration also deploys the language of freedom and peace. What sets it apart is the sustained effort to weaken the means by which that language could be held against it. A government that violates a principle can still be called to account. A government that dismantles the means of calling it to account has turned obligation into a matter of convenience. That is unfortunately the government that we currently have — and that is the government that got rebuked on November 3.

What power remains

I do not want to overstate the effect of the result. Four limits matter.

First, the president retains his constitutional authority over foreign policy, the military, and much of trade. The tariffs, the war, and the Caribbean strikes did not need Congress to begin, and ending them will require either a veto-proof majority, which Democrats lack, or a presidential change of mind. Trump has said he will become "Mr. Veto." The new Congress also does not take office until January. A weakened president might escalate, especially the conflict with Iran. Nothing in the returns retracts the threats of April.

Second, in June the Supreme Court held in Trump v. Slaughter that the president may remove members of independent regulatory agencies at will, overturning a ninety-one-year-old precedent. That weakens institutions on which enforcement of disclosure, competition, and consumer protection depends. The election does not reverse it. Moreover, Trump v. United States greatly limits possibilities of criminal prosecution against Trump for official acts.

Third, the harms already done are in important respects permanent. An election cures none of the following: those killed in Minneapolis or at sea or abroad, the trust spent with allies, the scientists who have left, the people removed without hearings. The world will not easily forget the ugly face that America shows under Trump.

Fourth, a majority built on dissatisfaction can dissolve if it is not used well. Clearly, America’s politics is a highly volatile affair.

The president said that he accepts the results and is willing to work with Democrats — and that does matter. He also wrote that "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE," and blamed "lazy" candidates. That is not a refusal to accept the outcome, but it reflects a habit of treating defeat as someone else's failure. It would be naïve to believe the president’s acquiescence in his resounding defeat will remain his prevailing attitude in the next two years. That he appointed MAGA hardliner Stephen Miller as his chief of staff as the first major response to his resound defeat speaks for itself.

And, yes, it is worth saying this one more time: Trump, just now, did indeed finally get his landslide.

Tests for the new majority

Rights standards are not partisan. They bind those who gain power as well as those who lose it. I would propose five tests for the incoming Congress.

Oversight must meet the standards it demands of the executive. Legitimate enforcement differs from its inversion in three ways: it applies the same standards to allies and opponents, it is proportionate, and the person investigated has a real chance to answer. House Democrats have promised aggressive investigations, and one prospective chair has summed up his plans in two words to the administration: "lawyer up." The discipline I ask is that investigations follow evidence, treat Republicans and Democrats alike, and respect targets' rights to counsel and response. If oversight becomes retribution, it will teach what the last two years taught: that accountability is for the other side.

Fair maps matter regardless of who benefits. Reporting indicates that Trump's mid-decade redistricting largely backfired. But Democrats in California and Virginia also redrew maps in response, and the Supreme Court's weakening of the Voting Rights Act allowed several Southern states to redraw districts that had been majority- or near-majority-Black. One party's gerrymander is not justified by the other's. Citizens are entitled to maps drawn by a process they can regard as fair, and Democrats now have both leverage and reason to want rules that bind everyone.

Lethal force and war powers deserve hearings. A Congress that wants to repair answerability should investigate the Minneapolis killings, the boat strikes, and the conduct of the Iran war, including civilian casualties such as the reported killing of children at a school in Minab, with subpoenas and public testimony. It should force the war powers vote the Constitution contemplates, and it should ask what legal advice the Defense Department received and why its senior lawyers were dismissed. These are not partisan questions. They are what any republic asks about the use of force.

Independence needs statutory protection. Statistical agencies, inspectors general, civil rights enforcers, and military legal officers can be insulated through legislation and appropriations, but only if the bills survive a veto, which will require Republican votes. The four in ten Republican voters who said Congress was not checking the president adequately are the constituency for this work.

Transparency about AI should not wait. Requiring developers of the most capable systems to disclose test results, permit independent examination, and preserve records of consequential changes is among the few measures with potential cross-party support. Whether the new majority pursues it will show whether it treats technology policy as more than a fundraising question. In recent times Republican lawmakers too have been increasingly worried about AI. We must hope they are now willing to act on these worries even if this might mean overruling Mr. Veto.

Apart from the operations of Congress, we must hope the Democratic Party will offer a vision for the future now that the country has asked precisely that of them. To my mind, economic justice should be central to this vision, including economic policies that integrate adaptation to and mitigation of climate change and policies that focus on AI in the spirit of augmentation rather than automation. America should again put its support behind human rights, democracy, and rule of law everywhere. America still needs its reckoning with the past, but such reckoning should be done in a way that does not make another culture war the dominant feature of political discourse. A human rights perspective cannot dictate a party platform, but it can ask whether any vision includes people who cannot vote.

Whom does power answer to?

The election shows that a president with low approval, unpopular policies, and flagrant self-dealing remains answerable to voters in the way the constitutional design intends. The same country that gave this administration two years of largely unchecked power has taken a large part of it back, in a single night. That is worth defending and building on. When courts rule, journalists report, videos circulate, and citizens vote, power can be made to answer.

But answerability to voters is not answerability to everyone the exercise of power affects. For those dependent on a government whose next move is anyone's guess, unpredictability is itself a harm. A child in a heatwave, a farmer in a flooded delta, a Ukrainian family sheltering from drones, an Iranian family hearing that their civilization might die tonight, a person at sea in a small boat, a man sent to a foreign prison without a hearing: none of them voted on November 3. No one on the ballot answered to them. Human rights exist for this gap. Some claims do not depend on whether the claimant can punish the powerful at the polls.

Closing that gap requires something no election supplies: a political culture in which Americans recognize that people on the receiving end of their government's decisions have claims whether or not they can reward or punish it, and institutions strong enough to act on that recognition. Voters have told this administration that it must answer to them. The task now is to make power answer to everyone else too, and to hold ourselves to the same standard.

title: Trump Opens the Door to Immigration Reform. Can Democrats Trust Him? - TIME
description:
President Trump signaled last week that he is open to working with Democrats on immigration, after two years of carrying out aggressive immigration enforcement across the country.
The prospects of Trump agreeing to an immigration deal drew wariness from both parties.
The crop of newly elected Democrats to Congress include many who campaigned against Trump’s immigration policies, specifically raids conducted by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
It’s unclear how many Republicans would work on any immigration deal in the new Congress.
The legislation ultimately failed to pass the House, with 112 Republican members joining all House Democrats in opposing the bill.
text:
President Trump signaled last week that he is open to working with Democrats on immigration, after two years of carrying out aggressive immigration enforcement across the country.

Days after the midterm election losses, Trump acknowledged during an interview on 60 Minutes filmed on Friday that his Administration’s mass deportation policies might be “too tough.” “Let the people that are here, and in some cases, here for 10 and 15 years—work a deal for them,” Trump said.

The offer by Trump follows a midterm election in which his Administration policies prompted a national backlash that strategists say played a role in delivering to Democrats one of their best election showings in decades. On Monday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin echoed Trump’s conciliatory remarks, telling reporters at a conference in Maryland that Trump has encouraged him to work with Democrats who have reached out about collaborating on immigration reform in the new Congress.

The prospects of Trump agreeing to an immigration deal drew wariness from both parties. Democrats were especially circumspect at Trump’s gentler tone days after tapping Stephen Miller, the architect of the Administration's immigration agenda, as his new White House Chief of Staff.

“Miller…is probably extremely unlikely to advise the president to sign a bad immigration bill or a sweeping amnesty,” says Andrew Arthur, a former immigration judge and a resident fellow at the conservative Center for Immigration Studies.

The crop of newly elected Democrats to Congress include many who campaigned against Trump’s immigration policies, specifically raids conducted by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Democratic Socialist Claire Valdez, who just won a House seat in New York which includes part of Brooklyn and Queens, said at a press conference on Sunday that congressional Democrats “have a mandate” to abolish ICE.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic Leader who is on track to be the next Speaker of the House, said in a CBS interview on Monday that any potential deal with Trump should start with restoring protections for recipients for programs like the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA), which covers undocumented immigrants who arrived in the U.S. as children, and Temporary Protective Status (TPS), which allowed immigrants who sought refuge from natural disasters or armed conflicts to stay and work in the U.S.

“We can begin by moving in the House, and ultimately in the Senate, the Dream and Promise Act in order to restore protection for DACA recipients and TPS recipients. And that should be a foundation for more broader work that can be done together,” Jeffries explained, adding that reforming ICE and ending mass deportation would also be a part of the discussion.

It’s unclear how many Republicans would work on any immigration deal in the new Congress. The House Freedom Caucus, which represents a bloc of ultra conservative lawmakers in Congress, posted on Monday that it rejected any potential efforts to offer amnesty to undocumented immigrants.

Mullin stressed that the administration would not support a blanket amnesty program, but was open to movement on programs that cover hundreds of thousands of immigrants in the country such as DACA. “If we want to have an immigration reform where we can look at DACA, and figure out a way that these individuals can become, maybe, legal permanent citizens…that’ll be up to Congress to do that. I’ll be open to talk to anything,” Mullin said, according to multiple outlets.

Yet, as one source in Congress familiar with the immigration policy discussions tells TIME, if Trump is serious about working with Democrats on immigration, he could prove it by slowing down or even pausing deportations across the country. In the meantime, his comments may be seen by many as little more than an empty gesture.

“It doesn’t seem like there is anything to work with him on at the moment but that may change next year,” the source adds.

Trump’s history with immigration reform

This isn’t the first time Trump expressed openness to some immigration reforms.

During his State of the Union address in 2018, Trump proposed a framework to congressional Republicans to pass legislation that would provide a pathway to citizenship for an estimated 1.8 million people eligible for recipients of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals. But the measure was viewed as a half-hearted measure by Trump, who acknowledged it lacked the votes in the Senate. The legislation ultimately failed to pass the House, with 112 Republican members joining all House Democrats in opposing the bill.

The last time that a comprehensive immigration reform bill was taken seriously by both chambers of Congress was in 2013, during Obama’s second term, according to Arthur. That measure would have allowed undocumented immigrants already in the U.S. to stay in the country while waiting to apply for a green card. The bill was ultimately killed in the House by far-right Republicans led by then-Rep. Jeff Sessions and his chief of staff, who was the same Stephen Miller Trump just promoted to the same role in his White House.

name: Litigation
title: Supreme Court says border wall construction can continue in West Texas - NPR
description:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday allowed the Trump administration to continue with its plans to construct hundreds of miles of border barrier and security infrastructure in west Texas, while a court hearing over the effort moves forward.
"The injunction thus impedes the Government from advancing its 'compelling interests' in border security and integrity," reads the unsigned decision.
The lawsuit argued that the Department of Homeland Security's plans are unconstitutional and that Big Bend residents would be "irreparably harmed" if the construction continues.
The Trump administration's plans for the beloved Big Bend region of Texas have provoked an unusual bipartisan backlash.
People across the political spectrum say a wall isn't needed in the Big Bend––a region known for its sweeping canyons, tough terrain and unforgiving desert heat.
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday allowed the Trump administration to continue with its plans to construct hundreds of miles of border barrier and security infrastructure in west Texas, while a court hearing over the effort moves forward.

The federal government's plans have stirred bipartisan backlash for its inclusion of Big Bend National Park, a beloved stretch of public land known for its sweeping canyons and unspoiled desert landscape.

In a five-page decision issued Monday, the high court wrote that the federal judge who ruled on the order didn't have the authority to weigh in.

"The injunction thus impedes the Government from advancing its 'compelling interests' in border security and integrity," reads the unsigned decision. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the lone dissenter in the decision.

The court wrote that federal law allows the Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to waive environmental protections and conservation laws, which they called a "clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert."

In an emergency application to the high court in late October, the federal government urged the justices to intervene and allow the work to begin again, saying that a gap in "border defenses" in the Big Bend region "would act as "a dangerous magnet for cartels and other bad actors."

A federal judge in El Paso issued the temporary injunction that halted the construction of 30-foot-tall steel barriers, patrol roads, surveillance systems and other border infrastructure.

The Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental advocacy group, brought forward the lawsuit, along with an area nonprofit working to preserve a historic church near the U.S.-Mexico border and a landowner who stands to lose his border property.

"This decision greenlights the contractors and allows the bulldozers to come roaring back into the region," said Laiken Jordahl with the Center for Biological Diversity. "It allows the dynamiting of national park canyon walls, the bulldozing of pristine desert."

The lawsuit argued that the Department of Homeland Security's plans are unconstitutional and that Big Bend residents would be "irreparably harmed" if the construction continues.

The Trump administration's plans for the beloved Big Bend region of Texas have provoked an unusual bipartisan backlash. People across the political spectrum say a wall isn't needed in the Big Bend––a region known for its sweeping canyons, tough terrain and unforgiving desert heat. They worry about the threats a wall or any other kind of infrastructure poses to the region, from the impact on the environment and Indigenous sites to the effect on the region's tourism-based economy and on wild animals.

In the Trump administration's emergency relief request to the Supreme Court, Solicitor General John Sauer called the injunction "baseless" and "unprecedented" and said any pocket of the Big Bend without a barrier would "become a funnel point for illegal alien crossings that are thwarted by barriers elsewhere."

text:
Attorneys representing the federal government argued to a federal judge on Monday that immediately re-arresting a Guatemalan man after the judge had ordered his release twice was not a violation of the judge’s orders.

U.S. District Judge John Tunheim told attorneys for both parties they had until 9 a.m. Saturday to file arguments in the man’s second release and re-arrest.

MPR News has confirmed at least eight cases of ICE instantly re-arresting immigrants at the Whipple building after federal judges ordered their release. Judges ruled the men’s original arrests were unlawful.

ICE has interpreted that to mean it gets an instant do-over.

Two federal judges, Eric Tostrud and Jerry Blackwell, have denied requests to order re-arrested men released again. Two others, Jeffrey Bryan and Tunheim, have ruled the re-arrests violated their release orders.

Monday’s hearing focused on Ivan, who has asked to be referred to by his first name out of fear of retaliation. He was one of two men who first alerted MPR News to ICE’s strategy in October.

Ivan is the first case MPR News has confirmed of ICE instantly re-arresting someone twice.

At the Monday hearing, the government’s lawyers told Tunheim the latest re-arrest did not violate his release orders. Tunheim had ordered the government to show why it shouldn’t be held in civil contempt for failing to release Ivan.

Ivan, 27, came to the United States from Guatemala in 2019 without presenting himself to immigration authorities. He works in construction in Minnesota to support his family. He was arrested by immigration agents on Sept. 11 on his way to work. Tunheim ruled ICE had unlawfully arrested him without a warrant and ordered him released. ICE released and instantly re-arrested him Oct. 1.

Since September, he’s been held in three Minnesota jails paid by ICE to hold immigrants as well as facilities in Louisiana and Texas. His lawyers, John Barham and Steven Appelget, said the constant moving around has made it difficult to speak with and represent him.

On Oct. 30, Tunheim ordered ICE to release Ivan again.

“Allowing an individual to step one foot outside a cell is not release in any sense of the term,” Tunheim wrote.

Tunheim also condemned the federal government’s position that it is entitled to arrest do-overs.

“A court-ordered release for a habeas petitioner is not an opportunity to cure prior wrongs and certainly cannot be an opportunity to further flout legal and constitutional requirements,” Tunheim wrote.

On Friday, Barham was escorting Ivan out of the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building to freedom.

“A guy wearing body armor and a face mask jumped from behind a barrier or from the bushes,” Barham said. Agents grabbed Ivan and bundled him into a vehicle.

“They just said they were re-arresting him. I said this is bullshit,” Barham said. “There was a judge's order specifically prohibiting you from doing this, and that's when [the agent] waved the administrative warrant in my face.”

In Monday’s hearing, the federal government’s lawyers, including Derek Ganzhorn, said the government was acting lawfully.

“I prefer to think of it as a new arrest,” said Ganzhorn, an ICE attorney acting as a special assistant U.S. attorney, who is part of a small team of lawyers regularly defending ICE in Minnesota’s federal court.

Ganzhorn had filed a letter with the court on Friday notifying the judge of Ivan’s release, but it left out his instant re-arrest. Ganzhorn told the judge he wasn’t aware of the re-arrest until later.

However, he’d already told the judge in writing that if Ivan didn’t leave the country by Nov. 4, his detention would be mandatory. Court documents and statements from ICE officials show a clear pattern of ICE pre-planning re-arrests.

The federal government’s argument for keeping Ivan in detention and trying to deport him hinges on the fact Ivan told an immigration judge he was agreeing to voluntary departure. Ivan’s lawyers said he was desperate to leave detention and felt pressured to choose voluntary departure before Tunheim had ordered his re-release.

When Tunheim’s order came through, Ivan asked to withdraw his request for voluntary departure.

Trump administration attorneys argued the departure order became a final removal order when Ivan didn’t leave by Nov. 4, though Ivan was in ICE custody at the time and on the way back from Louisiana because Tunheim had ordered his release in Minnesota.

ICE moved Ivan to Louisiana while his case was still playing out in court without notifying his lawyers. Now he’s in Sherburne County Jail, where Tunheim has ordered he must remain until he decides the case.

Ganzhorn told the judge the case was “tricky” and there was “confusion on our part” after Ivan’s first re-arrest.

“We believed we released him,” Ganzhorn said, adding it was a “mistaken belief.”

Ganzhorn has represented the government in at least two other re-arrest cases.

ICE’s tactics have frustrated Steven Appelget, one of Ivan’s attorneys. He filed a habeas corpus petition to challenge Ivan’s detention. A writ of habeas corpus roughly translates to “produce the body” in Latin and it requires the government to justify where and why it is holding someone.

“They have to dance around, have 20 gazillion forms of procedures to avoid producing the body,” Appelget said after the hearing Monday. “We have the great writ, they got shit.”

"We’re never going to allow amnesty to happen," Mullin added.

title: US citizen shot by ICE officer near children's bus stop sues government for $25m
description:
A US citizen who was shot by an immigration officer in southern California has filed a $25m lawsuit against the federal government, alleging he was wrongfully shot and arrested, then subjected to a “malicious prosecution”.
There was no officer in Jimenez’s path when he was shot, and there was no reasonable suspicion or probable cause to stop, threaten or shoot him, the complaint says.
The Department of Justice (DoJ) charged Jimenez with assault on a federal officer using a deadly or dangerous weapon, with a federal complaint saying he had “rapidly accelerated in reverse” toward an officer.
The lawsuit seeks damages for lost wages and medical expenses, saying Jimenez still has bullet fragments lodged near his lung.
The suit alleges excessive force, assault, false arrest and other violations and seeks more than $25m in damages.
text:
A US citizen who was shot by an immigration officer in southern California has filed a $25m lawsuit against the federal government, alleging he was wrongfully shot and arrested, then subjected to a “malicious prosecution”.

Carlos Jimenez, a father of three from Ontario, a city east of Los Angeles, was on his way to work at a food pantry on 30 October 2025 when he drove by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents carrying out an operation. It was around 7am, and Jimenez approached officers “calmly and slowly” to inform them that children in the neighborhood would soon be arriving at an adjacent bus stop, according to his complaint filed in federal court on Friday.

An ICE officer, later identified as Eusebio Ortiz, then pointed his firearm at Jimenez’s face, cursed at him and threatened to shoot if he did not leave, the complaint says, citing audio recorded by the officer’s radio. Jimenez complied and attempted a three-point turn because he was blocked by officers’ vehicles, but in the process, Ortiz, without warning, fired multiple gunshots into the car, hitting Jimenez in the back and right shoulder, according to the lawsuit.

There was no officer in Jimenez’s path when he was shot, and there was no reasonable suspicion or probable cause to stop, threaten or shoot him, the complaint says.

Afterward, FBI agents followed Jimenez to a hospital and “interfered with his medical care”, including by pulling a nurse away and preventing him from talking to medical staff, the suit alleges. FBI agents removed Jimenez from his hospital bed, locked him in a waist restraint and drove him back to the scene of the shooting for an “interrogation” while a bullet remained lodged in him, the complaint continues. While Jimenez was bleeding and vomiting in the agent’s van, officers told him not to “ruin their vehicle”, according to the complaint.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said at the time Jimenez had “attempted to run officers over by reversing directly at them without stopping” and that the officer had fired “defensive” shots. DHS has repeatedly accused people of “weaponizing” their vehicles against officers, but a Guardian review in July found that most of the vehicle “assault” cases touted by DHS have fallen apart under scrutiny in court.

The Department of Justice (DoJ) charged Jimenez with assault on a federal officer using a deadly or dangerous weapon, with a federal complaint saying he had “rapidly accelerated in reverse” toward an officer.

The lawsuit says the criminal charges were “fabricated”. Even though DHS publicly called the shots “defensive”, the criminal complaint did not include any statement from the officer claiming he felt in danger, the lawsuit notes.

The suit further alleges that the FBI falsely claimed that two neighbors witnessed the incident and told an agent that Jimenez’s vehicle had enough room to pull forward without reversing. When Jimenez’s legal team interviewed those witnesses, both denied making those statements and said they were unaware there had been a shooting until they saw news reports, the suit says.

As the case proceeded, Jimenez’s defense lawyers sought access to officers’ text messages, and in May, a judge ordered the government to produce records of agents’ communications. Prosecutors then agreed to resolve the case through “diversion”, which would allow the charges to be dropped at the end of October if Jimenez abided by certain conditions.

The suit alleges that prosecutors were trying to avoid the potential disclosure of communications and prevent the deposition of the FBI agent who allegedly fabricated witness statements.

The charges were formally dismissed last week.

The lawsuit seeks damages for lost wages and medical expenses, saying Jimenez still has bullet fragments lodged near his lung. The suit alleges excessive force, assault, false arrest and other violations and seeks more than $25m in damages.

DHS declined to comment, referring questions to the justice department. The FBI declined to comment. Ciaran McEvoy, a spokesperson for the justice department in Los Angeles, did not comment on the lawsuit, but said in an email that Jimenez “could have exercised his right to take the case to trial, but he instead requested that our office agree to resolve the case through a diversion agreement”.

text:
In Rosettenville, Gauteng, foreign shopkeepers and hairdressers said that police make routine stops at their businesses, threatening to arrest and deport those who do not pay sometimes substantial bribes. In Knysna, Western Cape, foreign workers in low-paying jobs say their transport runs to and from work are beset by police officers who demand payment – also under threat of arrest and deportation. Both groups said that the extent to which they are targeted by police has increased substantially in 2026.

Since at least 2015, civil society organisations such as Corruption Watch and Lawyers for Human Rights have routinely raised the alarm over police and Home Affairs officials abusing their power over migrants to solicit bribes large and small.

Lawyers for Human Rights has published similar reports in recent years, which highlighted the role of police and Home Affairs officials abusing their powers over immigrants to extort bribes. All 41 people it interviewed for a 2023 LHR report attested to the “pervasive solicitation of bribes… as a condition for their release”.

“Foreign nationals have become a lucrative business for all law enforcement,” added Sharon Ekambaram, the head of LHR’s Refugee and Migrant Rights programme, during a recent interview.

A cycle of catch-and-release in Rosettenville

Last month, officers at Booysens police station allegedly netted more than R10,000 in bribes from eight immigrant hairdressers after arresting and threatening them with deportation.

Viewfinder visited the area a few days after the eight were released and interviewed three of them, including the barbershop’s 38-year-old Congolese owner. They all asked not to be named for fear of further reprisal from the police.

They said that police officers, some of whom initially posed as plainclothes customers, raided their barbershop on the afternoon of 20 October.

The officers started demanding passports and unspecified “documents”. One of the barbers interviewed, a Burundian, said he produced his formal Recognition of Refugee Status document. But, it had expired. He explained to the police that the Department of Home Affairs had responded to his renewal application.

He was arrested along with seven colleagues – two men and five women – and driven to Booysens police station.

At the station, the group were not brought through the front for normal processing, they said. Instead, they were taken into an office in the back of the building and addressed collectively.

“They said, ‘talk to us. If you don’t wanna talk to us, were are gonna take you to jail,’” said one of the barbers who was interviewed.

Understanding this to be a solicitation for a bribe, the barber says he asked the police how much they wanted. He was told that the cost would be R2,000 per head. A negotiation ensued, in which a price was settled upon: the barbers were to pay R1,000 each, and the hairdressers were told to pay R1,500 each. The police believed this latter group made more money than their colleagues, the barber explained. The money was called for from friends and colleagues. Several hours and about R10,000 in cash later, all eight were released and driven back to the salon, they said.

The next day, one of the Burundian barbers spotted one of these same police officers parked outside the shop. He proceeded to ask for “lunch money”.

Viewfinder interviewed five other immigrant business owners near the salon. All said that the cycle of raids, arrests, extortion and release had become commonplace in the area. It is a new phenomenon, they said, which they understood to be connected to broader anti-immigrant mobilisation. Officers from the Booysens and Moffatview police stations were the worst offenders, they added.

While the amounts solicited were sometimes R1,000 or more, some of those interviewed described extreme pettiness on the part of the police.

One owner of a food stall described police visiting his stall and filling plates of food before walking off without paying. At other times, police were described as asking for “lunch money” and accepting as little as R100 to let targeted immigrants off the hook.

Foreign workers in Knysna describe predatory pattern

In Knysna, a group of foreign workers described the emergence of another routine pattern of police extortion. They said officers lay in wait for them on their routes to and from work. The police approach and demand money, under threat of arrest, they said. The people interviewed asked to be referred to by pseudonyms, fearing further reprisal from the police.

Marguerite, a Zimbabwean receptionist at a local hotel, said that she now routinely carries petty cash to pay bribes.

“I can’t walk for maybe 20 minutes without someone asking me for my documents,” she said.

“Even if you have everything, all your documents, they still want money.”

The demands reportedly happen on foot, at roadblocks and aboard taxis and buses carrying foreign nationals. Sometimes, Marguerite said, bus drivers negotiate directly with officers, telling passengers how much they must contribute to be allowed through.

“The driver will just say we must give R100 to pass.”

A gardener, Errol, described officers arresting migrants who could not produce identification. Then, he said, the police drive their victims a short distance and demand money for their release.

“They just move like 100 or 200 metres and say guys pay us R100 and then they release you,” he said.

But, as in Rosettenville, the amounts can sometimes be much higher, said Precious, a domestic worker. Officers would start by asking for R1,500 and negotiate down to R1,000 or less depending on what they felt their victim could afford.

“If I said yes I’m working then they will tell me: ‘Call your boss (and tell him) that we arrested you so we need the money.’”

Precious went on to describe an incident in which officers took household belongings, including a television, refrigerator and bicycle, from a foreign national they had threatened with arrest.

The workers interviewed said anti-immigrant mobilisation in 2026 had made their circumstances worse.

Errol described officers exploiting the fear generated by anti-immigrant groups, sometimes presenting themselves as protecting migrants before demanding money.

Marguerite said the atmosphere had become so frightening that she had sent her children back to Zimbabwe after her daughter was bullied at school for being foreign.

“When you live in South Africa as a foreigner, you live in fear,” she said.

Police queried

Viewfinder emailed queries directly to the station commanders of the Moffatview, Booysens and Knysna police stations, asking them to respond to allegations that officers under their command had routinely extorted foreign nationals, demanding bribes under threat of arrest or deportation, and, in some cases, unlawfully detaining and transporting them in police vehicles.

Only Colonel Nicholas Warnick, Knysna’s station commander, responded. He acknowledged the “serious allegations”, but requested that clear details of the officers allegedly involved in the extortion be furnished.

“This office cannot respond to vague assumptions,” he said.

Viewfinder is not in possession of details identifying the officers. DM

text:
NOVEMBER 8, 2026

Contact: info@haitianbridge.org, media@haitianbridge.org

SAN DIEGO, CA — Haitian Bridge Alliance (HBA) strongly condemns the Trump administration’s decision to take an eight-year-old Haitian boy into federal custody during a routine immigration check-in, separating him from his loved ones, school, and community. The third-grade student at Fay Elementary School had been living with his loved ones following his father’s deportation by the U.S government back in 2025 forcing him to live with loved ones in the absence of his father. Despite the fact that he followed all the rules and took the 8-year-old uncle to appear for a scheduled immigration appointment that was sent to him, the child was taken into custody and subsequently transferred to the Office of Refugee Resettlement leaving his cousins in tears.

It is important to note that when parents are taken into custody by ICE, they are not provided an opportunity to return home to see their children or to be able to transfer guardianship, ICE just incarcerated then deported without taking into account the wellbeing of the children left behind.

This is what we call “Orphans by deportation”

San Diego Unified School District officials have raised serious concerns about the devastating impact of immigration enforcement on children, including psychological trauma, educational disruption, and fear within school communities. Crisis counselors have been deployed to support students affected by their classmate’s disappearance.

Guerline Jozef, Executive Director of Haitian Bridge Alliance, issued the following statement:

“This is not child protection. This is state-inflicted trauma disguised as immigration enforcement. An eight-year-old child should be sitting in a classroom, learning, playing, and dreaming about his future, not being taken away and retraumatized by armed federal agents. His father has already been taken from him and deported, now this administration has stripped him of the stability, family, and community every child deserves.

“When a government’s immigration policies leave children traumatized and classmates afraid, we have crossed an extremely dangerous moral line. Black immigrant children are not invisible or disposable . We refuse to normalize this cruelty. No child should become a casualty of an immigration system that has abandoned compassion and humanity.”

The Haitian Bridge Alliance has been sounding the alarm on the terror that children and parents have been going through and will continue to stand alongside them, providing support and advocating tirelessly until the 8-year old child is safely reunited with his loved ones here in San Diego. HBA calls on federal authorities to facilitate his immediate reunification with his loved ones, ensure his safety and well-being, and provide full transparency regarding his circumstances. HBA further urges Congress to investigate this incident and calls on the Trump administration to restore Temporary Protected Status protections for Haitian families as Haiti continues to grapple with extreme conditions.

ABOUT HAITIAN BRIDGE ALLIANCE

Haitian Bridge Alliance (HBA), also known as “The Bridge”, is a grassroots community organization that advocates for fair and humane immigration policies, foreign policy, and provides migrants and immigrants with humanitarian, legal, and social services, with a particular focus on Black migrants, the Haitian community, women and girls, LGBTQIA+ individuals, and survivors of torture and other human rights abuses. HBA also seeks to elevate the issues unique to Black migrants and builds solidarity and collective movement toward policy change. Anpil men chay pa lou (“Many hands make the load light”). description:

text:
President Donald Trump has acknowledged that his administration may have been "too tough" in its immigration crackdown, days after elevating one of the policy's most prominent architects, Stephen Miller, to the role of White House chief of staff.

In an interview with 60 Minutes following heavy Republican losses in the midterm elections, Trump defended his record on the border and the removal of immigrants he described as dangerous. "I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out," he said.

The president added that his administration had also removed people with "good jobs" whose violation was entering the United States illegally. He cited people working in landscaping and hotels and who, in some cases, were paying taxes.

Read More on News

"I think it was too tough," Trump said. "I think it might be too tough. And a lot of people would say that it's great, but a lot of people think it's too tough. I think, ultimately, that hurt me."

Trump also said he would "love to do something on immigration" with congressional Democrats, who are set to control the House and Senate next year after a bruising midterm victory over the GOP.

Newsweek has contacted the White House for comment via email outside standard working hours.

More than half of voters said the administration's immigration enforcement had gone too far, while six in 10 disapproved of Immigration and Customs Enforcement's performance. But immigration ranked well behind the economy and concerns about democracy, with 14 percent calling it the country's most important issue, according to exit polls.

While Trump has acknowledged that elements of his immigration crackdown may have hurt him politically, it remains unclear whether there will be any change in enforcement policy.

Immigration Policies Miller Has Championed

The president's remarks stand in contrast to much of the rhetoric used by Miller, a longtime Trump adviser who was the chief architect behind the administration's hard-line immigration policy.

On Friday, Trump tapped Miller—who has served in the second Trump administration as the deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser—to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.

During Trump's first term, Miller advocated for the travel restrictions affecting several Muslim-majority countries, the administration's zero-tolerance policy that resulted in thousands of family separations, reductions in refugee admissions and tighter rules for legal immigrants who received public benefits.

Since Trump returned to office, Miller has pushed for at least 3,000 immigration arrests a day and backed a broader expansion of enforcement, including the use of the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 to deport alleged Venezuelan gang members, third-country deportations and proposals to use the National Guard to support mass removals.

He also championed the immigration provisions of Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which provided roughly $170 billion for immigration enforcement and border security. His elevation comes as the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress prepares to investigate the administration's immigration enforcement policies.

Democrats have signaled that Miller will face congressional scrutiny when they take control of Congress in January, with Representative Robert Garcia of California, who is set to lead the House Oversight Committee, saying Miller's role in the administration's immigration crackdown warrants investigation.

What Miller Has Said About Immigration

Miller has repeatedly supported expanding arrests and deportations since before Trump returned to the White House on January 20, 2025.

Miller told Jake Tapper on CNN on January 28, 2025, that ICE would prioritize terrorists, public safety threats and national security threats, but he made it clear that the agency's efforts would not be restricted to those groups.

When asked whether immigration officials would prioritize people convicted of violent crimes or pursue anyone living in the country illegally, Miller said, "Yes, but we're not going to immunize everybody that Joe Biden let in."

Miller also described an early target of 75 arrests per day for each ICE field office as a "floor, not a ceiling."

"The goal is to arrest at least that many but hopefully many more," Miller said. He also said the administration intended to enlist state and local law enforcement in federal immigration enforcement to "significantly increase the arrest number."

By May 2025, the administration was seeking at least 3,000 immigration arrests a day. Miller publicly discussed that target, while he and then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem pressed ICE officials to reach it.

Miller also strongly backed Trump's flagship domestic policy and tax-cut legislation, the One Big Beautiful Bill, which provided a major infusion of funding for ICE and the administration's immigration crackdown.

"The BBB will increase by orders of magnitude the scope, scale and speed of removing illegal and criminal aliens from the United States," Miller wrote on X. "For that reason alone, it's the most essential piece of legislation currently under consideration in the entire Western World, in generations."

He separately described the measure as containing "the most significant border security and deportation effort in history."

Miller also defended the administration's approach amid protests against immigration enforcement operations in Los Angeles in June 2025. He called the demonstrations an "organized insurrection" and accused California's government of having "aided and abetted" mass illegal immigration.

Miller faced backlash after calling Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old nurse whom immigration agents fatally shot in Minneapolis earlier this year, a "domestic terrorist" and an "assassin" who had "tried to murder federal agents."

In July, Miller said restricting migrants' access to financial services could encourage people to leave voluntarily.

"Illegal aliens have credit cards, they have bank accounts and they're paid with direct deposit," Miller told The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show. "So illegal aliens fully participate in the commercial systems, the financial systems of America. Shutting that down is a massive engine for deportation."

What Miller Said After His Promotion

There was little indication of a rhetorical shift when Miller spoke after his promotion to chief of staff.

Appearing alongside Trump on Friday, Miller praised the president for having "saved our border from annihilation." The new chief of staff added, "I pledge to you, Mr. President, my absolute loyalty, my unwavering commitment, and my total devotion to your success and the success of this country."

Adam Klein, a co-founder of Globali.ai and a former senior Department of Homeland Security official, said Miller's appointment raises concerns about the direction of immigration policy and the influence he could exert across government agencies.

"Given the influence he has already had over immigration policy, I find this development concerning, particularly because of what the position allows him to do across the government," Klein told Newsweek.

"Immigration law doesn't have to change for the experience of immigrants and employers to change dramatically," he continued, warning that agencies such as U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services could make immigration benefits harder to obtain through narrower eligibility interpretations, additional evidence requirements and increased scrutiny. "The benefit remains available under the law, but obtaining it becomes another matter."

A spokesperson for United We Dream Action, an immigrant advocacy group, said in a statement: "Stephen Miller's appointment is both a reminder and a warning to Democrats that the stakes working people are up against have not disappeared simply because of their recent victories. What's ahead will be a deliberate effort from the Trump Administration to double down on their brutal agenda and test the Democratic Party's resolve to deliver real results for working families."

text:
On November 6, 2026, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) issued an interim final rule (IFR) imposing substantially heightened requirements on foreign importers of record (IORs) and corresponding verification obligations on customs brokers. The rule implements portions of Executive Order 14411, “Strengthening Customs Enforcement,” and is primarily intended to address CBP’s difficulty identifying, monitoring, and collecting duties and penalties from foreign IORs.

The IFR is effective on, and public comments are due by, January 5, 2027.

New Distinction Between U.S. and Foreign IORs

The IFR creates a new 19 C.F.R. Part 110, which establishes regulatory definitions of U.S. and foreign IORs. It contains three principal provisions:

Section 110.1: Definitions

Section 110.2: U.S. importer of record

Section 110.3: Foreign importer of record

The new regulations provide a detailed substantive test for distinguishing a U.S. IOR from a foreign IOR.

An individual qualifies as a U.S. IOR if the person is a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident. An entity qualifies as a U.S. IOR if it:

Is organized under U.S. law;

Is located in the United States; and

Satisfies one of the following two additional tests:

At least 51% of its beneficial owners must at all times be U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents and have control of the entity; or

The entity must directly own a “significant amount” of unencumbered U.S. real property at all times.

An IOR that does not satisfy these requirements is deemed a foreign IOR. Critically, simply incorporating a subsidiary in the United States will not qualify that company as a U.S. IOR under the new definitions.

In the new Section 110.2(b), CBP reserves the right to verify whether specific individuals or entities qualify as U.S. IORs. CBP stresses that the facts supporting an entity’s qualification as a U.S. IOR vary depending on the circumstances in each instance. Relevant factors include (1) where an entity has its principal place of business; (2) the location and intensity of its physical operations, employees, and revenue-generation activities; and (3) the amount of its physical domestic assets, real estate, profitability, and capitalization. CBP’s Center of Excellence and Expertise Directors will have authority over verifications. Records related to verification must be retained for five years from the date verification is conducted.

New Beneficial-Ownership Rules Are Significant

The new U.S.-IOR test places significant focus on determining who ultimately owns and controls an importing entity, rather than simply looking to where that entity is incorporated. Under Section 110.1, CBP defines a “beneficial owner” as a natural person who directly or indirectly either:

Exercises substantial control over the importing entity; or

Owns or controls at least 25% of the ownership interests.

Every entity must have at least one beneficial owner for purposes of the rule. The “beneficial owner” definition includes circumstances where multiple layers of entity ownership exist between the natural person and the entity, such as a corporation that is owned by another corporation that is owned by a natural person, in which case the natural person is the beneficial owner despite the layers of entity ownership. An entity may have multiple beneficial owners, and there is no maximum number of beneficial owners.

Accordingly, a U.S.-incorporated subsidiary ultimately controlled by foreign natural persons could fail CBP’s new U.S.-IOR test unless it satisfies the alternative U.S.-real-property requirement.

The new regulations also provide for categories of persons who cannot be considered beneficial owners but might appear in an ownership or control chain, including, but not limited to, certain children of owners, agents, ordinary employees, creditors, and others deemed to not have sufficient beneficial ownership interests.

Foreign IORs and Customs Trade Partnership Against Terrorism (CTPAT) Involvement

CBP is adding two new sections to Subpart B of Part 141 (Section 141.21 and Section 141.22), pertaining to the right to make entry and declarations on entry. Pursuant to Section 141.21(a), a foreign IOR may no longer freely make consumption entries unless specific requirements are met. Rather, a foreign IOR must either use a CTPAT-validated customs broker or be CTPAT validated itself. CTPAT is a CBP voluntary trade program that focuses on security implementation throughout supply chains. CTPAT member companies and partners that undertake these supply chain protections receive facilitated processing by CBP.

Beginning January 5, 2027:

A CTPAT-validated foreign IOR may continue entering merchandise itself. If it uses a broker, that broker does not have to be CTPAT validated.

A foreign IOR that is not CTPAT validated must use a licensed, CTPAT-validated customs broker to make entry.

If the foreign party is not the owner or purchaser of the merchandise, the designated CTPAT-validated broker must act as the IOR for the entry.

These requirements apply to both formal consumption entries and informal consumption entries. CBP is not presently adopting the stricter option of categorically prohibiting foreign IORs from making informal entries, but expressly states that it will monitor those entries and could adopt such a prohibition later.

Under CTPAT’s current rules and structure, the only foreign IORs eligible for CTPAT validation are Canadian IORs. Thus, the new rules will require many foreign IORs to use a CTPAT-validated broker.

New Major Obligations for Customs Brokers

The rule does not merely regulate foreign IORs. It places significant new compliance obligations on brokers serving companies that claim to be U.S. IORs.

Before declaring a client to be a U.S. IOR, a broker must request and review records establishing that the client satisfies the criteria in Section 110.2. Relevant documentation can include:

Proof of citizenship or permanent residency;

Corporate charters;

Financial statements and financial records;

Purchase receipts; and

Documents of title.

Records associated with this verification generally must be retained for five years from the verification date.

CBP’s updated Forms 3461 and 7501 will also include new identification requirements, including a declaration as to whether the IOR qualifies as a U.S. IOR. These updated forms and their electronic equivalents become mandatory on January 5, 2027.

Rule Will Affect a Substantial Portion of Foreign Importers

Based on a review of entries made between October 1, 2020 and February 6, 2026, CBP estimates that foreign IORs represent approximately 16% of IORs making entry summaries. Only 0.4% of foreign IORs are CTPAT validated, although 68% already use CTPAT-validated brokers.

Approximately 32% of foreign IORs will have to change brokers or become CTPAT validated to continue importing under the new regime. Those companies account for approximately 2.6% of all entry summaries.

The broker market will also shift significantly. CBP’s review of past entries indicates that only 21% of active brokers are currently CTPAT validated. CBP estimates that CTPAT-validated brokers could experience approximately a 9.3% increase in clients and a 3.1% increase in entries as a result of the new requirements, while non-CTPAT brokers will lose foreign-IOR business unless they obtain validation.
