text:
Paula Albornoz Hernandez, a 23-year-old UC Berkeley student whose arrest by federal immigration agents at San Francisco International Airport caused an outcry on campus and from lawmakers, will be released Monday after more than a week in custody, according to court records.

Her attorney, Nikolas De Bremaeker, confirmed to KQED that Albornoz Hernandez will be released from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s California City Detention Facility in the Mojave Desert later Monday.

De Bremaeker said her boyfriend is already on the way to pick her up.

“She was incredibly happy to see the news and to hear about the news that the federal judge had ordered her released. … Her family is incredibly happy that she’ll be home,” the attorney said.

Albornoz Hernandez had escaped gender-based violence in Colombia, where she was born, and applied for asylum after entering the U.S. in 2022, De Bremaeker said.

She had been complying with all of her paperwork and hearings when she was detained at SFO while trying to travel to Portland with her boyfriend, her attorney said.

She was then transported to the remote ICE facility, where recent investigations have uncovered “inhumane” conditions and “crisis-level” medical staffing shortages.

“That detention center needs to be closed,” De Bremaeker said.

Her legal team argued that the sudden arrest violated her rights to due process guaranteed in the Constitution, and challenged the legality of her detention.

In a statement to KQED last week, the Department of Homeland Security said work authorization or a pending asylum application — both of which Albornoz Hernandez has — does “NOT confer legal status in the United States.”

The agency added that detention is “a choice,” since immigrants have the ability to “self-deport.”

U.S. District Judge Dena Coggins ultimately sided with Albornoz Hernandez, noting that ICE also failed to provide a “constitutionally compliant pre-deprivation bond hearing,” according to the court filing.

Coggins ordered Albornoz Hernandez released immediately, without additional restrictions like ankle monitors, and all of her possessions, including her passport, returned.

“Judges have been overwhelmingly finding these arrests by ICE to be unlawful and in violation of the Constitution,” De Bremaeker said.

In the days after her detention, Albornoz Hernandez’s friends, family and school community rallied around her. The Daily Californian reported that nearly 300 students flooded into the campus’s Sproul Plaza last Wednesday to call for her release.

In a campuswide email shared on Friday, the university said that it had “mounted a significant advocacy effort for Paula” and that approximately 30 letters of support were submitted by community leaders — including U.S. Reps. Lateefah Simon and Sam Liccardo, state Sen. Jesse Arreguín, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks and Berkeley Mayor Adena Ishii.

“All the support definitely had an impact,” De Bremaeker said. It “really showed that Paula had very strong ties to the community.”

In a statement on Monday, UC Berkeley Chancellor Rich Lyons said the school was relieved and overjoyed to have learned of Albornoz Hernandez’s release.

“This is a moment to remember what’s possible when our community comes together to support one of our own,” Lyons said.

Three Houston City Council members are pushing a plan that would codify Mayor John Whitmire’s decision Friday to limit how local police interact with federal immigration authorities.

The goal, according to Council Members Alejandra Salinas, Edward Pollard and Tiffany Thomas, is to prevent Whitmire or any future mayors from unilaterally changing the city’s policies on how Houston police interact with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.

The decision to try to codify Whitmire’s executive order on immigration enforcement in Houston comes days after the mayor abruptly changed his position on the issue after Democrats swept into office statewide in last week’s midterm election. The city’s policies on immigration have become a central conflict at City Hall ever since President Donald Trump’s administration added 700,000 civil “administrative” ICE warrants to a national police database as part of a wider immigration crackdown last year.

TIMELINE: How Houston police's ICE policy fight unfolded, from Whitmire's promises to Abbott's threats

“For more than a year, Houston families, workers and advocates have demanded that City Hall limit HPD’s cooperation with ICE,” the council members wrote in a joint statement. The new proposal, they said, “would codify the protections in the mayor’s executive order into city law to ensure they endure far beyond any one administration, uphold constitutional rights and keep HPD focused on solving serious crimes.”

The council members are filing the measure through Proposition A, a 2023 charter amendment that lets three council members add items to the council agenda, a power otherwise reserved for the mayor. The proposal also would force leadership at the Houston Police Department to include more details about each incident in which officers interact with ICE in quarterly reports the council directed HPD to start producing earlier this year.

The mayor, in a written statement, said he worried amending the ordinance would put the city at risk of violating state law, such as Senate Bill 4, which prohibits "sanctuary" cities.

"Mayor Whitmire stands by his executive order as the city's approach to addressing these challenges," according to the statement. "We must have confidence in the new leadership in Austin to revisit SB4 and in Congress to pursue meaningful immigration reform."

READ MORE: Inside the collapse of Houston’s ICE policy

Before changing his position Friday, Whitmire repeatedly had turned back calls to restrict HPD’s interactions with ICE, citing the risk of angering Gov. Greg Abbott and other state leaders. The midterm election made a change in policy possible, Whitmire said.

The mayor’s executive order says HPD will contact ICE “only if that person is already going to jail on new charges or other warrants.” Previously, officers were instructed to call ICE anytime they came across someone with an administrative warrant and wait “a reasonable amount of time” for an ICE agent to reach the scene – a directive that sometimes led officers to wait more than an hour.

Immigration advocates had questioned whether that policy violated the U.S. Constitution by directing officers to detain people based solely upon civil warrants and not criminal charges.

HPD’s prior policy had been negotiated with Abbott’s office, after the council in April passed an ordinance limiting police cooperation with ICE, only to quickly rescind it after Abbott threatened to pull $114 million in public safety grants from the city.

Under the prior policy, Houston police handed 17 people to immigration authorities from July through September, according to city data.

Another 13 people were charged with crimes and transferred to the Harris County jail, where they are likely to be released to ICE. That group would not be affected by Whitmire’s executive order or the council members’ proposal.

READ MORE: HPD quietly ended automatic probes of federal police shootings before ICE shooting of Lorenzo Salgado

After the council members file the proposed ordinance under Prop A, the city legal department will have a week to review it and determine whether it is lawful.

The soonest the measure could appear before the council would be in December, authors of the proposal said.

In addition to codifying the mayor’s executive order, the ordinance would require all HPD quarterly ICE reports to include information about the basis for a jail booking, whether an individual with a civil immigration warrant was a witness, victim or suspect in the incident and a brief summary of each incident.

text:
Whether a bipartisan immigration deal materializes remains an open and pressing question for the numerous builders facing ongoing job site disruptions.

Speaking to CBS News’ 60 Minutes on Sunday, President Trump suggested his administration’s immigration policies “might be too tough” and may have contributed to last week’s election outcome.

“When you go into a hotel…and you have a woman that’s worked there as a maid, as a cleaner, as a this, as a that, as a waitress – a lot of good things, great jobs – and all of a sudden, they’re being taken out of the country. It’s tough. It’s a tough thing,” Trump said.

Trump added that it may be “doable” to reach an agreement allowing undocumented workers who have lived in the U.S. for many years, construction workers among them, to legally remain in the country.

“Get the killers out. Get the rapists out. Get all the rough ones out. Get the drug dealers out, but let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them,” Trump suggested.

The administration’s mixed messaging

It’s unclear whether Trump’s softer rhetoric will translate into a bipartisan immigration deal. However, his administration’s decision to promote Stephen Miller, a longtime immigration hardliner, to White House Chief of Staff suggests an agreement may be less likely than Trump implied in his CBS News interview.

And in a post on Sunday, the Official White House Rapid Response account, in a post on X, denied that Trump will push for an amnesty deal with Democrats.

However, Trump has at times shown a willingness to soften his stance on immigration, at least briefly. In June 2025, the Trump administration momentarily directed ICE to pause job site raids in sectors like agriculture, hospitality and restaurants after facing blowback from business leaders worried about staffing shortages.

Within days, however, the administration reversed course. It later set a target of 3,000 ICE arrests per day, leading to a record number of immigration arrests in recent months.

Trump has also helped kill a bipartisan deal before. In early 2024, ahead of the presidential election, he urged Republicans to vote against a Senate border package introduced by Sen. James Lankford (R-OK) that would have tightened asylum requirements, ended releases of migrants into U.S. communities while they await hearings, and let the president close the border when asylum claims surged. The bill ultimately failed.

Some homebuilding organizations, like the National Association of Home Builders, now have their eyes on a different bipartisan measure, the Dignity Act, which would allow certain undocumented workers to remain in the U.S. without citizenship. Trump’s words signaled openness to such a proposal, but the administration’s actions since the election suggest otherwise.

Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, laid out in a post-midterms election post on X that the administration may be open to changing its approach to immigration, with less room for negotiation.

“Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement – by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you,” Vance wrote.

For homebuilders, immigration policy and its impact on the construction labor pool remains among the biggest policy questions heading into 2027. However, history suggests that a bipartisan deal may be a heavy lift, as Washington hasn’t passed comprehensive immigration reform since 1986, under President Reagan.

Whether Washington breaks its four-decade drought on immigration reform, and whether enforcement eases on job sites, remains a key policy wild card to watch in 2027.

text:
Former Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino’s aggressive tactics helped him become the face of immigration operations in L.A., Chicago and Minneapolis but also led to his downfall after numerous shootings.

The new documentary series "Thin I.C.E." explains why Bovino’s credibility was already in question before Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota.

Bovino's rise and fall

The backstory:

Gregory Bovino knew how to go viral.

The former Border Patrol Commander dominated social media feeds as he led immigration operations in Los Angeles and Chicago last year.

Videos, many produced by the federal government, showed Bovino questioning U.S. citizens, detaining immigrants and deploying tear gas on ICE observers.

By the time Bovino was leading Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota, he was a fan favorite for supporters of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

Bovino was "outright lying"

What they're saying:

"Bovino was a breath of fresh air," said Rep. Walter Hudson (R-Albertville). "He brought what was kind of like a folksy, old-timey, common sense approach to the enforcement of law."

What Hudson calls common sense, a federal judge called "outright lying."

Alex Pretti's family responds

The other side:

"He is a brazen liar," said civil rights attorney Theresa Kleinhaus.

Bovino was forced out last winter shortly after falsely accusing Alex Pretti of attempting to "massacre" federal law enforcement.

"The federal government went on TV and lied about Alex. They tried to slander his memory," Susan Pretti, Alex’s mother, said at a press conference in October.

Alex Pretti was repeatedly and fatally shot while he was pinned to the ground by numerous federal agents.

"What they said was cruel. It was a lie," said Steve Schleicher, the Pretti family attorney. "They stood up in front of the country and told lies."

Trump administration playbook

What we know:

Bovino and other Trump administration officials appeared to follow the same playbook after other shootings.

Alex Pretti, Renee Good and Marimar Martinez were all accused of interference and domestic terrorism after being shot by federal agents during operations led by Bovino.

"They said the same thing against Ms. Good, the same against Mr. Pretti, and they did it with Marimar," said Chris Parente, Martinez’s attorney.

Charges against Martinez, who survived five shots to her chest and lower body, were eventually dismissed after evidence undercut the border patrol agent’s claims.

As those claims fell apart, so did Bovino’s credibility.

A federal judge in Chicago found Bovino was "outright lying" under oath when asked about his use of force.

At one point during a seven-hour deposition, Bovino repeatedly denied tackling a protester even as he was shown a video of him taking the man to the ground.

"What are you talking about…we all just saw it," Kleinhaus said. "And we played that clip in our hearing and everyone could see it."

ICE assault claims fall apart

Why you should care:

Lying under oath didn’t stop Bovino from leading immigration agents to Minneapolis.

"It did not bode well for us," said Luis Argueta Jr. with Unidos MN.

During Operation Metro Surge, Bovino and former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem consistently accused ICE observers and protesters of attacking federal agents.

Dig deeper:

Most of those cases have since been dismissed due to insufficient evidence and allegations of government misconduct.

Bovino and Noem were also forced out, but the Trump administration has not backed off their initial claims.

"No one has recanted those lies, nor has anyone reached out to Susan, Michaela, our daughter, and myself to apologize," said Michael Pretti, Alex’s father.

Watch "Thin I.C.E." documentary series

What's next:

Thin I.C.E. is a three-part series by FOX 9 Documentaries detailing the Trump administration's immigration operations in Chicago and Minneapolis that resulted in constitutional challenges, violent tactics and deadly shootings.

Thin I.C.E. Part I: "Worst of the Worst" is streaming now on FOX LOCAL and the FOX 9 YouTube channel.

description:
The Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume construction of a border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas.
The dispute began earlier this year, when then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her successor, Markwayne Mullin, issued three waivers of various environmental and conservation laws to authorize construction of the wall in the Big Bend region, which includes parts of Big Bend National Park.
When they announced the waivers, Noem and Mullin indicated that the Big Bend area “is an area of high illegal entry” requiring additional walls and barriers.

text:
The Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume construction of a border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. In a four-page, unsigned opinion, the justices granted the government’s request to pause an order by a federal district judge that had temporarily halted the project. Only Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated, without explanation, that she would have denied the government’s request.

The dispute began earlier this year, when then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her successor, Markwayne Mullin, issued three waivers of various environmental and conservation laws to authorize construction of the wall in the Big Bend region, which includes parts of Big Bend National Park. Noem and Mullin relied on a provision of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 that gives the DHS secretary the power to “waive all legal requirements” necessary “to ensure expeditious construction” of border walls and roads. When they announced the waivers, Noem and Mullin indicated that the Big Bend area “is an area of high illegal entry” requiring additional walls and barriers.

A group of plaintiffs opposed to the construction – an environmental group, a local landowner who works as a river guide, and a group formed to preserve a church – went to federal court to challenge the waivers’ legality. On Oct. 2, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone temporarily barred the Department of Homeland Security from continuing construction on the border wall in the Big Bend region “until and unless” the government complies with environmental and other applicable laws.

In a written opinion that she released on Oct. 14, Cardone reasoned that the challengers were likely to prevail on their claim that the DHS secretary did not have the authority to issue the waivers. She relied on the major questions doctrine – the idea that if Congress intends to give a federal agency the power to make decisions of vast economic or political significance, it must say so very clearly. In particular, she emphasized, the Big Bend region is not an area with a high number of illegal entries. To the contrary, she stated, although it “comprises over 25% of the U.S.-Mexico border,” it makes up only a tiny percentage (“between 0.3% and 2.2%”) of the migrants apprehended while crossing the border. Therefore, she wrote, “if the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector, and the waiver authority would apply to the entire U.S.-Mexico border. If that were the case, Congress could have simply authorized construction ‘to deter illegal crossings.’” The major questions doctrine instructs courts to avoid “interpretations that would render limiting language meaningless,” Cardone concluded.

After Cardone declined to pause her ruling to give the government time to seek Supreme Court review, the Trump administration came to the Supreme Court, where it asked the justices not only to temporarily freeze Cardone’s order but also to grant review and summarily (that is, without additional briefing or oral argument) reverse it. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued that Cardone lacked the power to consider the challengers’ claim based on the major questions doctrine because their complaint specifically alleged that the DHS secretary “lacked ‘clear congressional authorization’ … to issue the waivers” under the IIRIRA – which, he said, was a statutory claim that “Congress denied district courts” the authority “to entertain.” But in any event, Sauer continued, even if the DHS secretary’s power to issue waivers under IIRIRA “implicates a question of ‘vast economic and political significance,’ Congress did clearly authorize the Secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction.”

The challengers urged the justices to leave Cardone’s order in place. Eric Glitzenstein, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs, told the justices in a 40-page filing that if her order were paused or lifted, it would permit the Trump administration to “immediately resume blasting, bulldozing, road construction, and other border barrier-related construction across one of the most remote and ecologically and culturally significant landscapes in the United States.”

The challengers argued that the major questions doctrine applied to their claim. They emphasized that the DHS secretary’s “decision to waive myriad federal, state, local, and tribal laws across vast geography for the purpose of building border infrastructure, even through national and state parks where border crossings are miniscule, is a truly ‘extraordinary’ assertion of power.” Because Congress “did not clearly authorize the sweeping exercise of power asserted here,” they wrote, the government’s “actions therefore amount to a constitutional violation of the major questions doctrine.”

In Monday’s opinion, the justices denied the government’s request to summarily reverse Cardone’s ruling but granted its request to put it on hold. “The Government,” the court explained, “is exceedingly likely to prevail on its argument” that Cardone did not have the power to consider the challengers’ “so-called major-questions-doctrine claim.” That claim, the court emphasized, contends only “that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority,” which is not a constitutional claim. This is true, the court continued, even if the challengers rely on the major-questions doctrine, because that doctrine is a rule used to interpret laws. “There is no such thing as a ‘constitutional’ major-questions claim.”

The other factors that courts normally consider in deciding whether to pause a lower court’s decision also point in the government’s favor, the justices said. For example, Cardone’s order “delays the Government’s construction of border barriers and roads in the Big Bend Sector” and, as a result, “impedes the Government from advancing its ‘compelling interests’ in border security and integrity.” Moreover, the government is suffering permanent harm from the costs – “nearly half a million dollars … per day” – that it is incurring while the construction is on hold, but which cannot be recovered. Finally, the court wrote, “[t]he Government’s interest … outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by” the challengers.

text:
[Episcopal News Service] The Episcopal Diocese of San Joaquin has filed a “friend of the court” brief in a federal appeals court in support of seven immigrants who sued the Trump administration over the conditions of their confinement in the biggest immigrant detention facility in California.

In the legal brief, dated Nov. 6, the diocese said its own volunteers regularly visit detainees at the California City Detention Facility in Kern County and affirm that conditions there are in some ways even worse than those described in the lawsuit. Food and water are often unfit for consumption. Medical care is lacking. The living spaces are often cold. And detainees are kept isolated from the outside world.

“For some of these people, a diocese volunteer is the first visitor they have had in over a year of detention,” the Diocese of San Joaquin said. “They are held in conditions we would not inflict on the worst felons.”

Yet these detainees typically have not been accused or convicted of any crime. “The men and women held inside were, until recently, our neighbors, co-workers, friends, and family members,” the diocese said. “They are guilty of nothing more than doing what liberty-loving immigrants have done since this country’s founding.”

The detainees are represented by a legal team that includes the American Civil Liberties Union. They filed their lawsuit in the U.S. District Court of Northern California in November 2025, and in February 2026, that court partially granted the plaintiffs’ request for a preliminary injunction against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and the private company, CoreCivic, that manages the detention facility. The defendants have appealed the lower court’s ruling to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.

Although the Diocese of San Joaquin is not a party to the lawsuit, its legal brief is considered by the court while weighing both sides. The diocese chose to go on record in support of the plaintiffs “not out of politics, but out of deeply held, core theology,” Bishop Greg Kimura said in a written statement, a version of which he incorporated into his Nov. 6 address to the Central Valley diocese’s convention.

The diocese “has the infamy” of having four immigrant detention facilities within its boundaries, Kimura said. The standing committee and diocesan council voted unanimously to file the “friend of the court” brief citing the diocese’s volunteers’ experiences ministering to detainees at those facilities.

“No other diocese has this experience and the on-the-ground witness to these inhumane conditions, specifically at Cal City. Therefore, no other diocese has the same moral authority to call for equal justice under law,” Kimura said. “God has called our diocese to be prophetic. … It is our baptismal covenant to respect the dignity of every human being. This is our moment to act with boldness on those things we say we believe.”

The diocese’s legal brief cites the work since 2019 of the diocesan San Joaquin Refugee and Immigration Support and Empowerment commission. Shortly after the California City Detention Facility opened in August 2025, volunteers from congregations across the diocese began visiting detainees, typically four to six men and women a week.

“They do not choose the people they see, and they do not excite hope where there is none. They listen,” the diocesan brief said. “In all, they have sat with close to one hundred people.”

Those volunteers can attest to inhumane conditions at the facility, the diocese said.

“The district court’s findings [in favor of the plaintiffs] are not only amply supported by the record but, if anything, understate the gravity of the situation,” the diocese said.

The volunteers have continued to visit the facility throughout the court proceedings, including now, as the government’s appeal is pending. “The pods are still cold. The food still goes uneaten. People still ask the volunteers for help reaching a nurse, and people are still agreeing to removal because they cannot bear to stay.”

The legal brief underscores that the diocese’s advocacy for the rights of immigrant detainees is rooted in Christian teachings.

“They proclaim that God creates every person as a beloved child of God, of immeasurable worth, whatever that person’s immigration status. For Christians, living out these commandments is not optional; they believe they will one day be judged before the throne of God on how faithfully they have done so.”

Episcopalians across the country have joined similar calls for an end to the Trump administration’s expansion of the federal detention system to accommodate Homeland Security’s push for mass deportations, a central campaign promise in the president’s second term.

authors: Diego Medel, Brian Kirkpatrick, Ken Rodriguez
description:

text:
The Department of Homeland Security has agreed to conduct an environmental review of a planned immigration detention facility on San Antonio’s East Side, according to Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones, potentially resolving the central dispute in a federal lawsuit filed by the city last month.

Speaking on Texas Public Radio’s The Source on Monday, Jones said federal officials agreed to comply with environmental review requirements after San Antonio sued DHS and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Oct. 13.

“DHS has said that they will comply and do an environmental review, and so that was the whole crux of the case,” Jones said.

The city filed its lawsuit seeking to halt the conversion of a nearly 640,000-square-foot warehouse on Southeast Loop 410 into an immigration detention and processing facility capable of holding up to 1,500 people.

The lawsuit alleged that federal officials failed to conduct a required environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA, before purchasing the warehouse and moving forward with plans to renovate it.

City officials argued the review was necessary to evaluate the facility’s potential effects on the surrounding community, including its infrastructure, economy and environment.

Court records show that the city and federal officials began negotiating a potential agreement shortly after the lawsuit was filed, prompting San Antonio to request that a federal judge remove an Oct. 26, deadline to seek a stop to the conversion.

“The parties are now negotiating a stipulation that would obviate the need for immediate emergency relief,” a motion filed on Oct. 22 stated.

U.S. District Judge Jason K. Pulliam granted the request that same day, placing the pending request for injunctive relief on hold and ordering both sides to provide the court with a status update by noon on Nov. 30.

Jones’ comments Monday provide the first public confirmation from city leadership that DHS has agreed to conduct the environmental review sought in the lawsuit.

However, the court filings do not specify the terms of any agreement, and it remains unclear whether federal officials have agreed to suspend renovations or other development activities while the review is conducted.

Jones acknowledged that the scope of the review remains an important question, saying the city wants to ensure it meets the requirements officials originally sought to enforce.

“We want to make sure that that [the review] is in line with what we expect,” Jones said.

DHS did not respond to a request for comment last week over the agreement. DHS did not respond to requests Monday for comment about the mayor’s statements or the status of the environmental review.

Jones said the city would continue monitoring the project and could take additional legal action if federal officials fail to follow through on the review or proceed with development activities before it is completed.

“We continue to monitor, and we continue to make sure that we understand what is and is not happening,” she said.

The mayor characterized the federal government’s agreement as an early success for the city’s legal challenge, comparing it to similar disputes in other communities where local governments have sought environmental reviews of proposed detention facilities.

The development comes after months of unsuccessful attempts by San Antonio officials to obtain information about the proposed facility. Before filing the lawsuit, the city sent five letters to DHS and ICE requesting details about the warehouse’s conversion, environmental impacts and opportunities for public input.

Although the agreement could address the immediate legal dispute, it does not mean the city has abandoned its opposition to the detention facility.

City Council previously approved a resolution directing city officials to explore additional legal and administrative measures to prevent or delay the facility, while also expanding those efforts to include two federal office leases at Brooks.

Jones said the city is still awaiting updates on those leases, which would establish a longer-term federal immigration-related presence on the Southeast Side.

For now, the mayor said the city’s legal efforts have produced the results officials were seeking, even as their broader objective remains unchanged.

“Look, pushing back has had the effect that we want up until now,” Jones said. “Obviously, the ultimate effect is no ICE detention facility in San Antonio.”

text:
Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume building a border wall and other infrastructure through a remote area of West Texas while litigation over the project moves forward.

In an unsigned decision, the high court agreed to lift a district court's injunction that temporarily stopped construction of the wall and related infrastructure in the Big Bend sector, which covers more than 500 miles of the southern border and includes Big Bend National Park.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson said she would have denied the Justice Department's request for emergency relief.

In its five-page decision, the Supreme Court said in part that the lower court's order delays construction of the border barrier and roads in the Big Bend region and "impedes the Government from advancing its 'compelling interests' in border security and integrity."

The challengers to the wall project "claim that construction in the Big Bend Sector will diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area," the court said. "But Congress's enactment of [immigration law] — which permits the Secretary to waive the requirements of environmental-protection and other conservation laws — reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert."

The Center for Biological Diversity, one of the plaintiffs that sued to stop wall construction, lambasted the Supreme Court's decision.

"The Trump administration and its contractors are hellbent on destroying one of America's greatest national parks, and the Supreme Court just gave them the green light," Laiken Jordahl, the group's national public lands advocate, said in a statement. "This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal. They're signing off on the permanent destruction of the wildest place in Texas, and the theft of a great American river from all of us."

The Trump administration had asked the Supreme Court last month to step into the legal fight over the border wall in the Big Bend region and argued that the halt ordered by U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone frustrated its ability to combat illegal border crossings in the area.

Stopping construction of the wall and roads along that portion of the U.S.-Mexico border would have serious consequences, Solicitor General D. John Sauer warned, including "disruption of the government's ability to secure a quarter of the southern border against cartel incursions, drug trafficking, and illegal entry; creation of a massive vulnerability in border protection that risks funneling illegal entry and trafficking into the unsecured Big Bend Sector; and irreversible delays, costs, and operational harms from halting already-begun construction."

But an environmental nonprofit, a professional riverboat guide and a religious organization, which filed a lawsuit challenging the project, argued that allowing the Trump administration to resume construction of roads and the wall would permanently alter an "irreplaceable landscape" that includes Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, and nearly 200 miles of the Rio Grande Wild and Scenic River corridor.

"Once habitat is destroyed, vegetation cleared, historic resources damaged, livelihoods and private property destroyed, and wilderness landscapes fragmented by roads, barriers, and associated infrastructure, no final judgment can restore the status quo," lawyers for the plaintiffs wrote in a Supreme Court filing.

President Trump has promised to build a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border for more than a decade and has made the 30-foot barrier a cornerstone of his plan to tackle illegal immigration.

To speed up construction of the wall and other barriers along the southern border in Texas, the secretary of Homeland Security — first Kristi Noem and then Markwayne Mullin — issued a total of three waivers for project areas in the Big Bend region beginning in February.

The federal government would typically have to ensure compliance with federal environmental protection and historical preservation laws before moving forward with construction. But the Department of Homeland Security invoked a 1996 federal immigration law that gives the secretary the authority to waive all legal requirements deemed necessary to ensure "expeditious" construction of barriers and roads near the southern border.

In response to the move, the plaintiffs filed their lawsuit to stop the Trump administration from building new 30-foot bollard walls and other infrastructure in the Big Bend region. The waivers issued by DHS, they said, would "authorize massive projects that would cleave through the Chihuahuan Desert, sever public and wildlife access to iconic sections of the Rio Grande, and mark one of the final—and most consequential — steps towards completing 'the Wall.'"

Separate from the litigation, the president's planned wall garnered pushback from Republican and Democratic lawmakers, cattle ranchers and local law enforcement in Texas when photos and videos shared to social media in August showed bulldozers arriving at Big Bend National Park.

In response to the backlash, Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott announced that construction inside the park would be paused until the end of September. Scott has said that the proposed 30-foot border wall will not cut through Big Bend National Park, but other infrastructure would, including more than 200 miles of patrol roads and roughly 17 miles of a vehicle-barrier system, according to CBP.

Construction of a 47-mile-long stretch of wall in Hudspeth County, which is part of the Big Bend region, began in September, according to immigration agencies.

But last month, Cardone, the district judge, granted a preliminary injunction that barred the Trump administration from building border barriers or related infrastructure, or engaging in "any construction or ground disturbing activities" in the Big Bend sector.

Cardone found that the secretary of Homeland Security exceeded his authority when issuing the waivers that allowed construction of the wall to proceed.

The Trump administration and the challengers to the project were at odds over whether the Big Bend sector is an area of "high illegal entry" requiring additional border barriers.

The government has argued that immigration officers apprehended more than 89,000 people trying to cross into the U.S. illegally in that area between 2021 and 2025.

But the plaintiffs said that Big Bend ranks last for apprehensions compared to the other six sectors along the southern border. While the area covers more than 25% of the U.S.-Mexico border, annual apprehensions in the Big Bend Sector ranged between 0.3% and 2.2% of total border-wide apprehensions, according to court filings.

text:
LONDON (AP) — For Joe Reeve, the midterm afterglow faded fast.

The London startup founder was among the wave around the Trump-weary world awakening to the stunning news that Americans had sharply rejected President Donald Trump's fist-in-the-eye stewardship of the United States that had started a war with Iran, forged no peace in Ukraine or the Mideast and made gas and food so expensive.

Voters, Reeve saw online, had flipped control of both houses of Congress, handing the power to check the president to his rival Democrats. American democracy, 250 years on, had survived the Trump era.

But a deep and profound distrust of the United States had survived the vote, too. And from national leaders to aspiring American immigrants, no one seemed confident that change was afoot.

"What everybody's learned," Reeve, 29, the husband of a Ukrainian, said a day later in an interview, "is that America's system does allow for these wild swings. We all know, now, that America has an ability to rotate on a dime and spit in our faces."

Interviews by The Associated Press around the world since the vote revealed a sense that "one election alone does not restore anything," as Kim So-jung, 49, an office worker in Yongin, South Korea, put it. "We have to see what they actually do, and see that they are doing something different to gain at least a little trust back."

And now? 'What happens next matters a lot more'

That 77 million Americans voted to elect Trump to a second term, along with the administration's combative conduct on his tariff war, Israel's conduct in Gaza, immigration and Iran, had already shaken trust in America around the world.

By the time Americans awakened Wednesday, global leaders and regular people from Europe to Australia had moved beyond the "wow" to a reckoning with the reality that Trump still retains enormous powers.

"Quite frankly, Trump has largely governed without Congress for the past two years. Why should that change now?" German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said a few hours after voters flipped control of the House and Senate.

Trump's apparent detachment from the results and his focus on building projects in the days before and after the drubbing did little to calm speculation about how he governs. He could dissociate completely, some observers said. Or he could lean into foreign policy and become even less predictable.

READ MORE: Trump says his deportation policy 'might have been too tough' for midterm voters

"For the country's allies, the question isn't whether America is back," Ian Bremmer, president and founder of Eurasia Group, wrote in Think China. "It's back to what — and for how long?"

The stunning midterm elections were not enough to reverse policies that have strained economies and finances and put dreams of making it in America on hold for many across the globe.

Trump's tariff war has roiled markets and economies. He canceled humanitarian aid for millions and upended the world's postwar order. Under Trump, American immigration policy turned violent and deadly — and makes the U.S. look to many like a place better avoided.

There was no sign of Trump letting up. On Friday, he promoted longtime aide Stephen Miller, a key architect of his hard-line immigration policy, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.

"I don't think all is forgiven," ReadtheLine.ca Editor Jen Gerson said during an online discussion Thursday. "The President's hold on power over two terms is — and ought to remain — a warning sign to Canada and to all of America's allies."

America's political and economic uncertainty can affect businesses like Synetica, an Indonesian tech company, one of its business development managers said.

"For me, regaining trust means seeing America consistently respect democratic institutions, the rule of law and its international partners," Aditya Surya, 40, of Yogyakarta, Indonesia, told the AP. "The election is a good start, but what happens next matters a lot more."

For many, reversing tariffs is a key test of restoring trust in America

Many eyes are trained on whether the Democrats can reverse Trump's costly tariff regime as the incoming majority has promised in its 100 days agenda — and whether Trump accepts or vetoes any such changes.

Hamish McIntyre, an Australian beef producer, suspects not. With a Southern Hemisphere spring harvest underway in parts of Australia, farmers are grappling with diesel prices inflated by the Iran war, contributing to what the government forecasts will be a 39% drop in large farm profits.

"The midterm result is unlikely, in itself, to fundamentally change the direction of U.S. tariff policy," said McIntyre, president of the National Farmers' Federation agricultural advocacy group. The election, he added, does not "prevent the administration from continuing to pursue its broader trade agenda."

Ivan Slatkine, president of the Federation of Romandie Enterprises in French-speaking Switzerland, said he's heartened that the election showed America's institutions remain robust. That's worth some confidence, he added.

But.

"Let us not be naive," Slatkine said. "The 'America First' concept is not going to be abandoned anytime soon, and I doubt the new majority will reverse all the decisions made by the president."

Hong Kong businessman Danny Lau gained some hope from the elections. More than 30% of the orders received by his aluminum-coating factory in the southern Chinese city of Dongguan come from American clients. But his business was paying a tariff of nearly 81%.

"Trump started the tariff war," Lau said. "If he loses his influence, would that help at all on the tariff front? At the very least, hopefully he won't raise them any further."

Michael Lu, CEO of gift-box producer Brothersbox in southern China, said he believed political tensions remain elevated, particularly after Washington's earlier trade war against China. But no matter who won the midterms, he didn't expect drastic changes in Washington's overall stance against China. The U.S. accounts for roughly 20% of Lu's company's business.

The political shift in the U.S. doesn't change the fact that "continuing to strengthen the alliance and economic relations with the U.S. is essential for Japan," said Yoshinobu Tsutsui, chairman of Keidanren, the Japan Business Federation, a lobby group that represents 1,500 companies. He said he expects Trump to come out even stronger, not weaker, with the Democrats in control of Congress.

For some, the American dream is still on hold

Ambika, an Indian citizen who asked to be identified only by her last name, works in IT in America and has long yearned to make America her permanent home. But Trump's immigration crackdown and latest green card restrictions have given her pause.

"Recent visa policy changes have left me worried," she said this week while visiting family in India. "I don't know if ... the midterm results would lead to any policy change that could benefit those of us who want to move to the U.S."

There's no more accurate look at how America is changing than U.S. elections. And these midterms produced the biggest shift in political power since the post-Watergate election of 1974.

But what now?

"Time and again, we are presented with these chances for change, only for greed to snatch defeat from the jaws of victory," U.K.-based commentator Martin McSweeney wrote on his "Truth Matters" Substack at 5 a.m. the day after the election. "Will this time be different? That's up to the American people, and that makes me very nervous given past experience."

Associated Press writers across the globe contributed to this report. They include: Kanis Leung and Thomas Chan in Hong Kong, Rod McGuirk in Melbourne, Sheikh Saaliq in New Delhi, Kim Tong-hyung in Seoul, South Korea, Yuri Kageyama in Tokyo, Edna Tarigan in Jakarta, and Jamey Keaten in Geneva.

text:
Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, putting pressure on his fellow Republicans to decide whether to remove one of the Trump administration’s most prominent figures after the GOP’s sweeping midterm election losses.

The impeachment resolution from Massie, a renegade Republican from Kentucky, focuses largely on the war in Iran. It also includes references to Hegseth’s role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela. A vote in the House could come by mid-week.

Hegseth said he would hold a press conference on Tuesday — his first in over 180 days — on the looming impeachment threat, adding that the war was necessary, even if unpopular.

The House and Senate were back in session as of Monday for just six short weeks — a lame-duck sprint to finish the Republican agenda before the GOP majorities end with the change of power on Jan. 3, 2027. Congress is returning to a changed Washington as the Capitol halls swell this week with the collision of incoming and outgoing lawmakers.

Here's the Latest:

Jeffries says Trump's new chief of staff is not a viable working partner for Democrats

The House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries was asked during a news conference at the Capitol if the new White House chief of staff could be a viable partner as Democrats take charge of Congress.

Jeffries responded flatly: No.

“Stephen Miller is a stone-cold racist,” Jeffries said. “His track record speaks for itself.”

Jeffries, who is in line to become the House speaker in the new Congress, said: “I’ve gotten zero interest in working with that kind of individual.”

The key architect of President Trump’s hardline immigration agenda, Miller was elevated Friday to become Trump’s chief of staff.

Trump names David MacNeil, auto accessories CEO, as special envoy for manufacturing

President Trump has long sought to add David MacNeil, the founder of the auto accessories and floor mats company WeatherTech, to his administration.

Trump said in a social media post that he would be the “Special Envoy for Manufacturing,” saying that the Republican donor “knows how to create jobs, bring Manufacturing back home, and put America First.”

The president has previously nominated MacNeil for other posts. In 2025, he selected him to be the “Ambassador at Large for Industrial and Manufacturing Competitiveness,” but the nomination was returned to him on procedural grounds.

In January, Trump nominated MacNeil to the Federal Trade Commission. But there has been no progress since on the nomination.

Democrats have a mandate to ‘get things done,’ Jeffries says

Following the Democratic sweep of the midterm elections, the party's House leader Hakeem Jeffries said House Democrats will have the largest majority of any party in this century.

“It is a clear mandate for House Democrats to get things done,” Jeffries said at a Capitol news conference.

He said Monday that the party’s priorities will be “to make life more affordable for the American people, to hold the president accountable and to make sure that this country can return to be the best version of herself.”

Massie says lawmakers will have to answer for their vote amid push to impeach defense secretary

Whether they are leaving office in January or were reelected, Massie says his colleagues will “have to live with that vote.”

If they’re leaving Congress, “what do they have to lose?” the GOP congressman from Kentucky said. And if they plan to run for reelection in two years, they’ll have to answer to voters.

“This is the best vote you can take right now to put some daylight between yourself and the failed policy of this war in Iran and the way that it’s been handled,” Massie said.

Earlier Monday, Massie moved to force a vote to impeach Pete Hegseth, setting the stage for a dramatic vote on whether to remove the defense secretary and one of the most prominent Trump administration figures.

Schumer says Democrats want to ‘prove ourselves worthy’ of Americans’ trust

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer says Democrats “are going to deliver” on affordability issues that helped them win new majorities in Congress.

He said that includes stopping President Donald Trump’s tariffs, lowering health care costs and banning public officials from stock trading.

In his opening remarks as the Senate went back into session Monday, Schumer said the party will make “government more competent and their capital less corrupt.”

“We’re going to spend every second of every day striving to prove ourselves worthy of Americans’ trust,” Schumer said.

House Democratic leader Jeffries demands full congressional briefing on Nvidia

Hakeem Jeffries, leader of House Democrats, said Monday that the Nvidia issue did come up during a closed-door session with the CIA director and the Director of National Intelligence that was primarily about Iran.

“We’re going to need a full briefing, specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue, so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened,” he said, “and what the implications are in terms of America’s national security.”

Shares of Nvidia tumbled more than 5% Monday after the computer chip maker, central to the artificial intelligence race, opened an investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

Nvidia’s announcement of the investigation Sunday followed Huang’s acknowledgment he had been intimate with a business executive who, according to The New York Times, U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for China

US stocks rally, recouping more recent losses as oil prices drop

The U.S. stock market rallied to its best day since April and clawed back more of its big loss from last week as oil prices swing lower.

The S&P 500 jumped 2.3% Monday, its second straight gain following a wipeout on worries that Democratic victories in the midterm elections could mean a slowdown in the construction of AI data centers.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 2.2%, and the Nasdaq composite rallied 2.7%. Brent crude’s price dropped 5.8%, which helped lift the market. The strength came even though Nvidia, one of Wall Street’s most influential stocks, sank.

House Democratic leader says Hegseth has ‘got to go’

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries said he’s a hard yes on impeaching Hegseth and called the Defense secretary the architect of the “reckless and costly failed war of choice” in Iran.

“The fact that Pete Hegseth is still around makes zero sense,” Jeffries said at the Capitol.

“The national nightmare that has been Pete Hegseth can end this week,” he said, referring to the House impeachment vote, “if the president doesn’t make the decision on his own to terminate him.”

Thune warns Democrats against ‘liberal fantasies’

Senate Majority Leader John Thune says Republicans are willing to work with Democrats when they take the Senate majority next year. But he said the election was not a mandate for “radical policy and socialist fantasies.”

Opening the Senate on Monday, Thune, R-S.D., said Republicans’ defeat at the polls last week was a sign of frustration with the high cost of living, and that growing the government is not the answer to those problems.

“I hope my Democrat colleagues realize what this election was and what it was not,” Thune said.

Massie urges House leaders to allow a prompt vote on Hegseth impeachment

He warned that Speaker Mike Johnson could try to delay a vote on his impeachment measure by moving to table it or refer it to a committee.

That would effectively kill the impeachment push, he said.

“They may try to get out of an actual vote on the substance of this,” Massie said. “We should have a vote and a rigorous debate on these eight articles of impeachment.”

Massie says Hegseth should be impeached because he broke the law

Massie says his push to impeach the defense secretary is not about how well he’s done his job. Rather, he’s looking to remove Hegseth because “he’s broken the law and he’s violated the Constitution.”

“We’re not indicting him for being bad at his job,” Massie said in a news conference moments after reading his articles of impeachment on the House floor.

Supreme Court clears the way for border wall construction in Texas’s Big Bend to resume

The Supreme Court is allowing the Trump administration to resume border wall construction in the Big Bend region of Texas for now.

The border wall is a key project for President Donald Trump, who has promised to build it from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico. Republicans in Congress funded the project with $46 billion last summer.

Customs and Border Protection have been building 12 miles of border barriers a week. In the Big Bend region, bipartisan opposition argues the project wastes money in an area with historically low illegal immigration. They suggest using surveillance technology instead.

Johnson says voters made ‘wrong choice’

House Speaker Mike Johnson is lamenting the outcome of the midterm elections.

“I’m sorry that the voters made the wrong choice,” Johnson said. “I really do believe that this next two years is going to be a bit of a circus. It’s going to be chaos, and I hate to say that.”

He also called the results a “great tragedy” because if Republicans had kept the majority, they would have stayed on “course to continue delivering for the people.”

Johnson’s remarks came as he briefly took questions from reporters as lawmakers returned to Washington for the first time following election results that gave Democrats control of the House and Senate in the next Congress.

Talarico meets with GOP’s Cornyn on Capitol Hill

Democratic Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas says he met with outgoing Sen. John Cornyn at the Republican’s office in Washington.

Talarico said in a statement that Cornyn “has served our state honorably, and I’m grateful for his advice and guidance.”

Trump backed Cornyn’s primary rival Ken Paxton, who went on to lose to Talarico as Democrats swept Texas. Democrats plan to use new power to rein in Trump’s education agenda.

Democrats in Congress are preparing to flex their soon-to-be majorities in opposition to some of President Donald Trump’s marquee education policies, starting with the dismantling of the U.S. Education Department. But with Trump threatening to use his veto power, they may be limited to opening investigations and using federal funding as leverage.

The White House has given no sign of backing away from its campaigns to close the department and to end diversity, equity and inclusion policies. But Democrats are preparing to use their oversight and appropriations powers to push back against Trump administration decisions that have reverberated through schools and universities.

Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia, the top Democrat on the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, said he plans to “leave no rock unturned” as he takes the helm of the panel’s investigative powers.

Rubio gives more sober assessment of Russia-Ukraine peace efforts a day before US officials mediate talks

Hours after U.S. officials described Russia indicating a new openness to ending the war, Rubio said that the process still has “ways to go,” and that getting Europeans to the table with the Russians has still not happened.

His comments come as U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are set to mediate talks with Moscow and Kyiv in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, with Germany, the U.K. and France there on the sidelines.

“It’s been difficult to get anything productive out of that,” Rubio told reporters. “But we’ll keep trying. And that’s what we’ve been trying to do the whole time, is try to be creative and find ways that we can help bring that conflict in that war to an end.”

Melania Trump gets kudos at the UN for her work in arranging a ceasefire in Ukrainian town

Diplomats from Europe, Pakistan, Colombia and Bahrain, among others, praised the U.S. first lady at a U.N. Security Council meeting Monday called by Ukraine after recent deadly Russian attacks on a school, a hospital, a train platform and other civilian sites.

U.N. political director for Europe Kayoko Gotoh commended Melania Trump as well as Pope Leo XIV and Ukrainian and Russian officials for the recent six-day ceasefire in the town of Oleshky.

It was “an encouraging example of what can be achieved with the necessary political will to save lives and provide humanitarian respite,” she said. “It also gave us some hope that it could be replicated in other areas where civilians are suffering, contributing to broader de-escalation.”

But Latvia’s foreign minister, Baiba Braze, who presided over the meeting as this month’s council president, said regrettably the “glimmer of hope” from the U.S.-brokered ceasefire was short-lived.

“Russia has resumed its brutal attacks, killing and injuring civilians – and that’s the reality we are facing,” Braze said.

Rubio defends Hegseth as doing a ‘great job,’ calling Massie impeachment effort ‘unfair’

As Rep. Thomas Massie introduced the resolution, Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended his fellow Cabinet secretary, saying that he believes he has been doing “a great job” and that it’s unfair that a Republican is pushing the effort.

“I think Pete’s done a good job, I really do. Again, I work with him. And so I see perhaps a side of him that the media doesn’t see and members of Congress may not see,” Rubio said, speaking to reporters at the Group of Seven industrialized democracies gathering in Paris. “But I think Pete works really hard. He’s incredibly smart.”

Massie launches articles of impeachment against Hegseth

The renegade Republican congressman took swift action as soon as the House chamber opened, a move that is expected to force an impeachment vote in the days ahead.

Thomas Massie is reading the resolution into the record from the floor of a nearly empty House. Few lawmakers are on hand, but the visitors’ gallery has dozens of people watching the proceedings unfold.

He said Hegseth “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders” and “remains a threat to the Constitution.”

Massie said Hegseth “thus warrants impeachment.”

Johnson blasts Hegseth impeachment effort

Speaker Mike Johnson is criticizing an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, calling it a “terrible look” in the middle of hostilities abroad.

“We don’t impeach Cabinet secretaries for political gain or for cheap tricks, and I think that’s what this is, and I think everybody knows it,” Johnson told reporters.

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie is pushing the impeachment resolution forward over the objections of House GOP leadership.

US aiming to widen Russia-Ukraine talks to include European partners, officials say

Ahead of Tuesday’s trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi, the Trump administration said one of its main objectives is to get Moscow to agree to a multilateral format for negotiations that includes Western countries critical to establishing long-term European security.

That is according to two U.S. officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity to disclose sensitive diplomatic efforts. The scheduled talks in the Emirati capital come after a nine-month lull in negotiations mediated by Washington.

The U.S. officials added that if this week’s meetings go well, Trump’s special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff could be headed for another face-to-face with Ukraine and Russia’s leaders.

Senate to consider sweeping energy legislation in first major action since Democrats swept midterms

Lawmakers will take a procedural vote Monday on bipartisan legislation to speed up permitting for data centers and other infrastructure projects.

The move comes after Democrats swept last week’s election in a setback for Trump and congressional Republicans.

The bill aims to shorten the timeline for starting energy projects, including clean energy and fossil fuels.

Trump supports the measure, calling it a win for U.S. energy independence. Many environmental groups oppose it, citing concerns about fossil fuel development and weakened safeguards.

Sponsors have added amendments to address concerns about tribal consultation and strengthened opportunities for states to weigh in.

Supporters say the bill will save households billions on electricity costs, create jobs, cut emissions and force big corporations to pay their full share for data centers.

▶ Read more

Hegseth says Iran war necessary even if not popular

Asked about Vice President JD Vance blaming the Iran war for the massive GOP losses in the election, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth noted that Trump said he would do it again, and “I agree.”

He repeated a line that Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters a day earlier, “It doesn’t have to be necessarily popular, but it can be necessary.”

He reiterated that “Iran is devastated” though the Islamic Republic has been able to keep striking military bases in the Middle East used by the United States, causing billions of dollars in damage, as well as commercial ships in the disputed Strait of Hormuz.

Hegseth said the war was necessary because “someone had to confront the Iranian regime’s pursuit of a nuclear weapon.”

Hegseth will defend his policy choices at press conference Tuesday

Facing an expected impeachment resolution in Congress, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said he’s eager to litigate the policy choices that he and President Donald Trump have made in Iran and Venezuela.

“If you want to take issue with what we did in Epic Fury or Rough Rider or nabbing Nicolás Maduro, you’re taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished, which is historic,” Hegseth told reporters Monday.

He also announced that he would hold a press conference — his first in over 180 days — on the looming impeachment threat on Tuesday.

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie has pushed the impeachment resolution forward over the objections of House GOP leadership as momentum grows to hold Hegseth accountable for the Iran war, which many Republicans blame for the party’s midterm election wipeout.

Democrats prepare to investigate alleged corruption and ICE policies

Democrats appear ready to use the power of congressional oversight in response to voter anger.

Nationally, about 6 in 10 voters said the Trump administration had “gone too far” on immigration enforcement, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters. A similar share disapproved of how ICE was doing its job. And about 6 in 10 voters said immigrants to the U.S. today do more to “help the country,” while less than half, about 4 in 10, said they do more to “hurt the country.”

Rep. Robert Garcia, a Los Angeles-area Democrat who will take over the House Oversight Committee, warned the administration to “lawyer up.”

The next Congress will “address the Trump administration’s assault on the rule of law and hold those responsible accountable,” said Mississippi Rep. Bennie Thompson, the ranking Democrat on the House Homeland Security committee.

Democrats want to rein in Trump’s immigration agenda, but the president has a veto pen

After Democrats’ overwhelming midterm victories this week, winning candidates spoke of the need, once they are sworn in, to rein in Trump’s mass deportation machine. Some suggested putting forward a new vision for immigration reform while both houses of Congress are in Democratic control.

But there are clear limits to what Democrats can achieve, even after their epic win, with Trump wielding veto power for another two years. Republicans have frontloaded billions of dollars for immigration enforcement, and the key architect of the president’s hard-line immigration agenda, Stephen Miller, is now his chief of staff.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin vowed on social media after the GOP wipeout that “Deportations will continue.”

Secret Service investigating after 2 people arrested outside White House

At around the same time a driver crashed into a sign just north of the White House on Monday morning, the Secret Service says another person jumped over a barricade.

A police bomb squad was called in to sweep the car as a precaution, and roads around Lafayette Square were closed. A spokesperson for the Secret Service says that both the driver and the person who breached the barricade have been arrested.

Temporary fencing has been up around Lafayette Square for months, and the Trump administration has been pushing for more permanent gates cordoning off the area historically a gathering spot for everyone from tourists to protesters.

The National Capital Planning Commission has also been considering a proposal for a White House visitors security screening center south of the Treasury Department.

G7 ministers to press Rubio on Ukraine and Iran

Foreign ministers from the Group of Seven industrialized democracies began two days of talks in Paris on Monday as they grapple with multiple unresolved global crises amid questions about how Trump will approach foreign policy after his Republican Party’s heavy losses in the midterm elections.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is likely to face questions about whether the administration will shift its positions on the Russia-Ukraine war, the Iran conflict, energy security and artificial intelligence at the meetings between top diplomats from the U.S., Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and Japan on Monday and Tuesday.

It is Rubio’s first overseas trip since Republicans lost control of Congress, partly because of the Iran war and other deeply unpopular policies. The talks also come amid major protests across Europe.

▶ Read more

US missing in action at UN climate summit after another disastrous year

The United States — the world’s second-largest polluter after China — is again absent as world leaders, delegates and climate activists opened annual talks on curbing the global warming causing deadly heat waves in Europe and disasters such as the devastating floods in Nepal.

This U.N. Conference of the Parties, or COP31, comes as the war in Iran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, hiking global prices of gasoline, oil and products made with them, such as fertilizers and pesticides. The disruption has pushed governments to rethink energy policies and increase investment in renewable energy sources like wind and solar.

“The climate crisis is now a global health crisis of pandemic proportions,” U.N. climate chief Simon Stiell said on Monday. “At this COP, nations face a choice: electric or shock. Rewire the global economy for the electric age. Or accept ongoing fossil fuel cost pain for families, firms and governments.”

Voters demanded economic relief. Will Trump and Democrats deliver?

Voters want Trump and the new Democratic congressional majority to repair the damage inflation has done to the economy.

Trump was defiant after Friday’s strong jobs report showed the unemployment rate dipping to 4.1%. “Democrats may control Congress, but I will NEVER stop fighting for you, and I will VETO anything that hurts America,” he texted supporters.

Democrats are seeking to check Trump’s power and are preparing for early fights on government spending. Other challenges include chronic budget deficits, tariffs, artificial intelligence and difficult choices about a Social Security system that could run short of money in as little as six years.

But as long as rising prices keep making middle-class lives less affordable, Democrats and Republicans risk angering and alienating voters in the next elections.

▶ Read more

Iranians were put on a US deportation flight before it was canceled, attorney says

A U.S. deportation flight of at least eight Iranian nationals who were eventually bound for Iran has been abruptly canceled. That’s according to a legal group involved in a pending lawsuit that’s shed some light on the planned deportations.

Ali Rahnama is an attorney with the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund. He says at least eight Iranians were loaded onto a plane Sunday in Arizona bound for Pakistan.

The Iranians were told they would then be transported to Iran. But Rahnama says the flight was then canceled without explanation.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security refused to comment on the details of removal operations.

▶ Read more:

Republicans hold House and Senate leadership votes this week

The closed-door meetings could end up being blame-casting sessions about what went wrong in the elections.

House Republicans are bracing for a contentious leadership battle after Mike Johnson decided to step aside, setting up a showdown between the No. 2 Republican, Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana, and Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, the brawling former wrestling coach allied with the hard-right conservatives.

The two men had confronted one another when trying to become House speaker three years ago, but neither was able to win enough support from the Republican rank and file, leading to Johnson’s rise. With the House Republican numbers now shrunken, lawmakers could seek wholesale change in leadership.

In the Senate, Majority Leader John Thune is expected to retain his job as Republican leader, though in the minority after Democrats flipped Republican-held seats, including milestone wins in Texas and Kansas.

Congressional Democrats are expected to elect leaders this month

At least two newcomers to the Senate — Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Adam Hamilton of Kansas — have declined to publicly support Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer’s majority leader bid, but no challenger has emerged.

“I think we need somebody who’s going to bring us together ... somebody who’s going to come with fresh ideas,” Hamilton said Sunday on CNN.

Hakeem Jeffries, on track to make history as the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, also faces skepticism.

“Every single member here is going to have their individual vote,” said Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, chairman of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, at a Capitol press conference Sunday, flanked by newly elected lawmakers, including a handful from the Democratic Socialists of America.

“What we talked about at orientation today was not about any individual person, but about policy,” Casar said. “How we set a progressive path forward.”

Kushner says US working hard for ‘lasting peace’ in Ukraine

Trump is determined to bring an end to the “horrible” war between Russia and Ukraine.

That’s according to Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, who’s scheduled to begin talks on Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates with Russian and Ukrainian negotiators. Kushner wrote on social media Monday that he and special envoy Steve Witkoff would meet first with leaders from Ukraine and other European nations.

Kushner says the U.S. is “working hard to find a negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine within a more stable European security environment.”

While Trump vowed to end the war within 24 hours of starting his second term, the war is nearing its five-year mark.

Trump defends Hegseth as Democrats say it’s time for him to go

Trump defended Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to reporters on Sunday night before he flew back to Washington after spending the weekend at his Florida home.

“He’s guilty of two things, basically winning two wars,” Trump said. “I believe we saved the Middle East and Israel combined. And it’s awfully hard to say let’s impeach somebody who did that.”

Democrats are expected to widely support impeaching him and a number of Republicans have signaled they could join them.

“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Sunday on ABC.

Jeffries said it’s time for Hegseth to go, and that the secretary “has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran.”

Congress returns to changed Washington after GOP’s election wipeout

Congress is reconvening in a changed Washington, with Trump doubling down on his political threats despite the landmark GOP losses.

The halls of the Capitol will swell this week with the collision of incoming and outgoing lawmakers, as the newcomers attend orientation sessions while the retiring lawmakers start to clear out. It’s creating a jumble of split-screen moments reflective of the new political landscape.

Dozens of jubilant Democrats, families and suitcases in tow for freshman orientation appeared emboldened by the party’s sweep of power. The trickle of Republicans coming in spoke soberly of the GOP’s vast challenges ahead.

Trump’s war against Iran not ‘necessarily popular’ but needed to stop a nuclear threat, Rubio says

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday that Trump launched the war against Iran even if it was not “necessarily popular” to safeguard the world from the country’s nuclear ambitions.

He would not comment directly about the Republican wipeout in Tuesday’s elections, which delivered a resounding rebuke to Trump. The unpopularity of the Iran war and its impact on gasoline prices and other parts of the economy helped Democrats seize control of Congress.

Asked about Vice President JD Vance’s social media post last week that largely blamed the war for the Republican losses, Rubio told reporters that Trump “identified a very real threat” in Iran and worked to stop the Islamic Republic from pursuing a nuclear weapon.

“He addressed it even though oftentimes the right thing to do for the country — confronting difficult challenges for the security of our country — doing it isn’t necessarily popular, but necessary,” Rubio said in Florida before heading to a Group of 7 foreign ministers meeting in Paris.

▶ Read more

Trump says he was just kidding about making UFC’s Dana White his press secretary

Trump said Sunday he was only kidding about making UFC boss Dana White his next White House press secretary after announcing on social media he had offered his close friend the job.

After his party’s deep losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections, Trump shook up his administration on Friday by replacing his chief of staff and followed up on Saturday with a post that said he had offered the press secretary job to White. On Sunday, Trump said it was “just a little fun.”

“I was kidding, but I think Dana likes the idea, and he is a very capable guy,” Trump said, speaking to reporters in Florida before departing for the White House. White is set to visit him at the White House on Monday.

Trump does not currently have a press secretary after briefly giving the job to Katie Zacharia, who faltered behind the lectern and in interviews, and left the post after five days.

▶ Read more

Trump and Justice Department stand defiant as Democrats prepare investigative blitz

Trump and his Department of Justice are taking a combative stance toward Democrats after their election victories in the midterms, signaling intense conflict to come as lawmakers prepare aggressive investigations into the executive branch next year.

Trump set the tone, declaring on social media that investigative requests already made by Democrats are “extortion at the highest level, and they should be held accountable.” Attorney General Todd Blanche echoed the Republican president and said criminal investigations of Democrats are possible.

“They are not allowed to just go around threatening existing members of the administration, to go around threatening companies, and that’s what President Trump is extremely worried about and he should be,” Blanche said as he and congressional Democrats appeared on the Sunday news shows to discuss the repercussions from last week’s elections.

Rep. Robert Garcia, who is poised to chair the powerful House Oversight Committee in the next Congress, is preparing investigations into what he calls the “Trump crime family.” He said Democrats are not going to be intimidated.

Democrats have made clear that impeachment is an option.

▶ Read more

Trump says his deportation policy ‘might have been too tough’ for voters in the election

President Donald Trump, in his first major interview since his party lost control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, said he thinks his administration was too aggressive on deportations and that he thinks he can work with Democrats in the new Congress on some kind of immigration deal.

Trump said his deportation policy was part of the reason Republicans lost, telling CBS’s “60 Minutes” in an interview that aired on Sunday: “I think it might be too tough, yeah.”

He added that he thinks he could reach an agreement with the new Democratic majority. “The deal would be we would work something out. And I think it’s something -- I think that’s something that’s actually doable,” he said in the interview.

Trump did not give specifics about what that deal would look like — and shortly after taping the interview on Friday, Trump named the key architect of his hard-line immigration agenda, Stephen Miller, as his new chief of staff.
