text:
New interactive tool examines the role of states in shaping immigration policy

WASHINGTON, D.C., Nov. 9, 2026 — As state leaders look ahead to next year’s legislative session following the midterm elections, a new analytical tool by the American Immigration Council examines how states across the political spectrum have adopted policies that support immigrants’ well-being and inclusion into their communities. While comprehensive immigration reform continues to elude Congress, states are passing policies focused on immigrant communities — from limiting coordination with federal immigration enforcement to strengthening local economies and creating greater prosperity for all residents.

The States Index is a comprehensive assessment of state policies across four key areas: workforce, education and occupational licensure; access to services and basic needs; government infrastructure; and immigration enforcement and federal cooperation. States received a score for each policy category and subcategories capturing the extent to which their policies support or hinder an inclusive environment where immigrants can thrive and fully participate in their communities.

One policy area with support across the political spectrum is workforce, education and occupational licensure, with red, purple and blue states focused on immigrant workforce integration.

FIND THE STATES INDEX HERE

One example highlighted in the Index is North Dakota, which directed its Global Talent Office to develop strategies that help businesses recruit and retain immigrant workers. The initiative reflects how states that have not traditionally been major immigrant destinations are recognizing the economic opportunities that immigration brings, particularly in areas facing workforce shortages.

“Policymakers in state houses around the country are recognizing that the economy continues to be the primary concern for most Americans. By embracing policies focused on economic opportunities and the well-being of all community members, including immigrants, states can create safe, connected communities and promote the small businesses that truly power the country,” Jeremy Robbins, executive director of the American Immigration Council, said in a statement.

The Index also finds that many states experiencing the fastest growth in their immigrant populations have been slower to adopt policies that help newcomers fully utilize their skills, education, and professional experience.

States with the fastest-growing immigrant populations scored an average of 1.05 out of 5 on the States Index, compared to the overall state average of 1.65. This points to a disconnect between where immigrant populations are growing and where states have adopted policies that allow communities to maximize immigrants’ contributions. As a result, employers and communities may be missing valuable opportunities to address workforce shortages and support economic growth.

The Index is designed to help policymakers identify practical approaches that support, protect, and uplift all community members, including through policies that promote economic growth and foster inclusive environments for all residents. In Oregon, for example, policymakers created a statewide right-to-counsel program to connect immigrants to legal services, while New Jersey has worked to expand language access across state government services.

While the federal government sets the rules for who can enter and stay in the U.S., states are playing a major role in how immigrants experience daily life. By examining policies already adopted across the country, the States Index presents a clearer picture of where states currently stand and what they can learn from one another.

“By using the States Index, local communities can learn from the experiences of other states to better understand the implications of immigration-related policies. It’s a tool that can inform state advocates and policymakers as they develop a roadmap in response to the needs of their constituents,” Nan Wu, director of research at the American Immigration Council, said in a statement.

“The States Index captures the pivotal role that states play in the protections and well-being of all residents, including immigrant communities. It also gives policymakers and advocates a tool to better understand the range of state policies available to them, allowing them to learn from other states, iterate and improve policy ideas, and advance solutions informed by local needs, political context, and best practices,” Rich André, director of state and local initiatives at the American Immigration Council, said in a statement.

title: Ex-acting ICE chief says Democrats have few levers to curb Trump deportations
description:

"Typically they would have sort of the power of the purse to fund the agencies that are doing the enforcement," Fahey said.
He argued that the president's existing executive authority, combined with previously approved funding, will allow immigration enforcement to continue despite political opposition.
The House also has the constitutional power to impeach federal officials, while the Senate has authority to conduct impeachment trials.

text:
President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement agenda could face new scrutiny as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress, raising questions about whether lawmakers can use investigations, subpoenas and federal funding restrictions to challenge the administration's deportation policies.

With Democrats set to control both the House and Senate in January, congressional leaders could pursue investigations into Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations, summon Department of Homeland Security officials to testify and introduce legislation aimed at limiting certain enforcement activities.

But former federal prosecutor and former acting ICE Director Jonathan Fahey argues that the administration will retain significant authority to enforce existing immigration laws, even as congressional opposition intensifies.

Fahey joined The National News Desk to discuss the legal limits of congressional oversight, President Trump's reported calls for investigations into Democratic lawmakers and renewed scrutiny surrounding the 2022 leak of the Supreme Court's draft decision overturning Roe v. Wade.

"Congress really doesn't have that much power anymore," Fahey said when asked whether Democrats could stop the president's immigration enforcement efforts.

He explained that Congress traditionally has significant influence over federal agencies through its authority to approve funding, but argued that previous legislation has already limited some of those options.

"Typically they would have sort of the power of the purse to fund the agencies that are doing the enforcement," Fahey said.

"But as you remember, just last year and the year before, ICE and DHS was funded through 2029."

Fahey argued that the multiyear funding already approved for immigration enforcement could make it more difficult for Democrats to use annual appropriations negotiations to restrict ICE operations.

"That's one of their biggest weapons that's already been taken off the table," Fahey said.

Congress retains constitutional authority over federal spending and can pass legislation changing agency funding or enforcement requirements. However, any new legislation would generally require the president's signature or enough congressional support to override a veto.

Fahey said he expects Democrats to make immigration enforcement a major issue during the next congressional session, but questioned how much they can accomplish without cooperation from the White House.

"They're going to make a lot of noise, complain about it and make it a big issue and maybe try to pass legislation," Fahey said.

"But President Trump doesn't have to sign any."

He argued that the president's existing executive authority, combined with previously approved funding, will allow immigration enforcement to continue despite political opposition.

"They're going to make a big push, but they don't have a lot of power or a lot of levers to pull here," Fahey said.

The discussion comes after an election in which immigration enforcement emerged as a major political issue, with Democrats criticizing some of the administration's deportation tactics and Republicans defending the president's efforts to enforce federal immigration laws.

Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns about the treatment of migrants, detention conditions, enforcement operations in communities and the legal protections afforded to people facing deportation.

The Trump administration has maintained that its immigration policies are necessary to uphold federal law, strengthen border security and remove individuals who are in the country unlawfully.

With Democrats gaining control of congressional committees, lawmakers will have greater opportunities to examine those policies through hearings, document requests and subpoenas.

Fahey acknowledged that congressional investigations could increase significantly.

"I do agree that they are going to use their investigative power to look at things that ICE has done," Fahey said.

He said Democrats could examine specific enforcement incidents and require senior officials to explain their decisions before congressional committees.

"Look at certain incidents on the ground and try to bring officials up to Capitol Hill to testify and to account," Fahey said.

Congressional oversight can include investigations into agency spending, compliance with federal law and the conduct of government officials.

Lawmakers may also seek testimony and records concerning controversial immigration operations.

However, Fahey questioned whether those activities would substantially interfere with ICE agents carrying out enforcement responsibilities.

"Ultimately, does that really trickle down to the ground as a disruption? I don't think it really is," Fahey said.

He pointed to Trump's recent decision to appoint Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff as an indication that the administration intends to maintain its immigration enforcement priorities.

Miller has been a central figure in developing Trump's immigration policies, including expanded deportation efforts and stricter enforcement measures.

"If you see what President Trump just did by appointing Stephen Miller chief of staff, I think they are going full steam ahead on the immigration agenda," Fahey said.

He acknowledged that congressional investigations could create administrative and political challenges but said he does not expect them to stop the broader enforcement effort.

"They may have some disruptions along the way by Congress," Fahey said.

"But will it be effective? I don't think so."

The interview then turned to a separate dispute involving President Trump and Democratic lawmakers who have threatened investigations or impeachment proceedings against senior administration officials.

Trump has reportedly called for an investigation into Democratic lawmakers over threats to impeach Attorney General Todd Blanche and other officials.

The controversy raises questions about the constitutional authority of Congress to conduct oversight and impeachment proceedings, as well as the limits of political pressure directed at executive branch officials.

Fahey said the disagreement centers on whether lawmakers are exercising legitimate oversight responsibilities or attempting to interfere with the administration's lawful activities.

He referenced comments from some Democrats warning administration officials to prepare for investigations once the new Congress takes office.

"A lot of this was President Trump's response to some of these Democrats immediately got in office and say things like 'lawyer up' and other things," Fahey said.

He argued that Trump views those statements as threats intended to obstruct his administration's agenda.

"President Trump is essentially saying, you're not going to use your threat of investigative power to stall the agenda or to prevent people from doing their legitimate jobs," Fahey said.

At the same time, Fahey acknowledged that Congress has a constitutional responsibility to oversee federal agencies and investigate potential wrongdoing.

"Certainly they have an oversight power that they can legitimately look into things that the government's doing to make sure money is being spent well and things are being done lawfully," Fahey said.

Congress has broad investigative authority when inquiries serve a legitimate legislative purpose. The House also has the constitutional power to impeach federal officials, while the Senate has authority to conduct impeachment trials.

The exercise of those powers does not, by itself, constitute criminal wrongdoing.

Fahey argued that the legal and political concerns arise when investigations are used primarily to interfere with lawful government operations rather than examine potential misconduct.

"I think the line where the Democrats crossed is just basically, we're going to use investigations to stop your lawful agenda," Fahey said.

He characterized Trump's reported response as a warning that congressional investigators could face scrutiny themselves.

"President Trump is basically saying, oh, well, we'll investigate you too," Fahey said.

The comments reflect Fahey's interpretation of the dispute. Whether any lawmaker has engaged in unlawful conduct would require evidence of a specific criminal offense, rather than political disagreement or the use of constitutionally authorized oversight powers.

The discussion then shifted to the Justice Department's reported decision to revisit the investigation into the leak of the Supreme Court's draft opinion in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, the landmark case that ultimately overturned Roe v. Wade.

The draft majority opinion was published in May 2022, weeks before the Supreme Court formally issued its decision in June of that year.

The unprecedented disclosure prompted an internal investigation into how the confidential document became public.

In January 2023, the Supreme Court released a report explaining that investigators had been unable to determine who was responsible for the leak.

The possibility of renewed federal scrutiny has raised questions about whether disclosing a draft Supreme Court opinion constitutes a federal crime and what evidence prosecutors would need to bring charges.

Fahey said investigators may focus on whether individuals provided false information during the original inquiry.

"Here's what they're probably looking into," Fahey said.

"This was investigated. This occurred back in 2022, investigated into 2023. They may be looking at, did people tell the truth to the investigators then?"

He explained that prosecutors could examine whether the leak involved other potentially criminal conduct, such as theft of government property or unauthorized access to computer systems.

"The things that they were probably investigating were things like theft of government property, unlawful access to information systems and things like that," Fahey said.

The unauthorized disclosure of a draft judicial opinion is a serious breach of the Supreme Court's confidentiality procedures, but leaking the document is not automatically a federal crime.

Prosecutors would need to establish that the conduct violated a specific criminal statute.

Fahey noted that the passage of time could also complicate any potential prosecution.

"Those types of things would have a statute of limitations that would be five years," Fahey said.

He suggested that investigators could face challenges proving offenses connected directly to the original disclosure, depending on the evidence and applicable deadlines.

However, Fahey argued that false statements made during the initial investigation could provide a separate avenue for prosecutors to examine.

"I think if some of these people lied during the investigations, that might be one of the major problems," Fahey said.

Federal law generally prohibits knowingly and willfully making materially false statements in matters within the jurisdiction of the federal government, although the application of that law depends on the circumstances and the investigating authority.

Fahey said proving that an individual intentionally misled investigators could potentially be more straightforward than establishing a criminal offense based solely on the disclosure of the draft opinion.

"That might be easier to prove than sort of some of these other things that are a little bit ambiguous whether or not they could really prove a crime for actually leaking the opinion," Fahey said.

The interview highlighted several legal disputes likely to draw attention as Washington prepares for a change in congressional control.

Democrats will soon have greater authority to investigate the Trump administration, particularly its immigration enforcement policies, while the White House retains significant executive powers and the ability to veto legislation.

Fahey argued that congressional investigations may create political challenges for the administration but are unlikely, on their own, to halt immigration enforcement.

He also emphasized the distinction between legitimate congressional oversight and allegations of unlawful interference with government operations.

Meanwhile, the Justice Department's reported renewed interest in the Supreme Court leak could bring additional scrutiny to one of the most significant breaches of confidentiality in the court's history.

For Fahey, the central questions involve what investigators can prove, which legal authorities apply and whether the evidence supports potential criminal charges.

"They may have some disruptions along the way by Congress," Fahey said of the administration's immigration agenda.

"But will it be effective? I don't think so."

text:
Republican and Democratic students at Santa Fe College and UF might disagree on how the country should be governed, but they agree on one thing: The midterm elections were a chance to reflect on where the government has fallen short.

UF College Republicans held a press conference Nov. 5 outside Turlington Hall, where the organization addressed the results of the midterm elections. Democrats won control of the House and Senate and flipped six governor’s offices.

A Nov. 5 Instagram post announcing the event asserted, “The GOP failed.”

Michael Andre, a 21-year-old UF finance senior and UFCR president, spoke at the 6 p.m. press conference.

“Republicans just suffered from a defeat that has not been witnessed since the midterm elections of 2006,” Andre said.

In 2006, Republicans lost 30 seats in the House of Representatives and six seats in the Senate. At this time under the Bush administration, the war in Iraq was unpopular among voters where they also felt frustrations with the government.

This year's midterm elections saw seven Republican seats lost in the Senate and 40 Republican seats lost in the House.

Andre called this midterm election a loss for Republicans. Now, the Trump administration could find it hard to pass legislation with Democrats holding the majority in Congress, he said. He pointed to President Donald Trump’s first term, when Democratic control of the House led to increased congressional opposition, including two impeachment proceedings against the president.

The midterm election results reflected a loss for the Republican Party, Andre said. But UFCR maintained its satisfaction with Florida remaining red, with the wins of Sen. Ashley Moody and Rep. Kat Cammack, he added.

As a group of young Republicans, Andre said, UFCR wants nothing more than to stand side by side with party members who stick to their principles and keep their promises.

One of Trump’s reelection promises was not to enter in any new wars, but a year into his presidential term, the U.S. entered a war with Iran. Andre said the involvement in the conflict has caused more harm than good.

“The youth is not pro-war,” he said. “They hate it. I hate it.”

Amid the war, energy prices, inflation and unaffordability have skyrocketed, Andre said. Republicans were also promised an economic turnaround to relieve the “broken economy,” but that promise was also broken, he said.

“The members of the UF College Republicans love our country, and we love our party,” Andre said, “but we also acknowledge that some element of change must occur to serve in our best and most faithful capacity.”

Andre encouraged Republicans to listen to younger voters and recognize where the party has fallen short. He said Republicans should learn from Democrats’ ability to engage younger voters and need to do more to bring young people into political conversations.

“No one is going to fight for us but us,” Andre said.

For some young conservatives, the election raised questions about whether the Republican Party still represents the next generation.

Landon Roughton, a 20-year-old UF history junior and outreach coordinator of UF Turning Point USA, attended UFCR’s Nov. 5 press conference.

Roughton agreed with Andre when he said the war with Iran hasn’t been popular with the youth or, as the midterms reflected, many Republicans.

Trump also ran on strict immigration enforcement, he said, but Roughton said Trump backed off when it faced controversy in some Democratic states. Still, the administration's immigration efforts have remained strong and have reduced the undocumented immigrant population by almost 3 million.

“He had the opportunity while everything was red to get everything done, and then he kind of didn’t,” Roughton said.

Immigration was a significant issue for Trump voters in the 2024 election. About 9 in 10 Trump voters said his pledge to secure the border and combat illegal immigration was a major reason they supported him.

Seeing Republicans share their disappointment with the Trump administration, Roughton said the MAGA movement was “decapitated” by the midterm election results.

“In my opinion, I think MAGA is dead,” he said.

Despite the loss Republicans faced in the midterms, Roughton thinks many young conservatives in Florida will continue to vote red. Because about 3 in 5 Floridians are Christian, he said, their values align with conservatives, so they’ll continue to vote Republican.

The Trump administration’s broken promises have also been felt on the opposite side of the political spectrum, said Jacob Kaluski, a 19-year-old Santa Fe College student enrolled in a welding and GED program.

Kaluski serves as the harassment grievance officer for UF’s Young Democratic Socialists of America. Following the midterm elections, Kaluski said he and other young left-leaning voters remain frustrated with the Trump administration, particularly with immigration enforcement and involvement in the war in Iran. He also said the Democratic Party needs to improve its campaign efforts and make changes the youth wants to see.

He doesn’t think Trump will withdraw troops from Iran until he gets a win, he added, suggesting he might want to add to his presidential accomplishments.

“I just don’t think our soldiers should be there in the first place,” he said. “I think they should withdraw.”

Immigration enforcement is another source of frustration among young people, said Kaluski, who believes many are upset by Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids and the fear they create in communities.

Candidates like Democrat Angie Nixon rallied support among younger voters, which he said is because voters gravitate toward candidates who offer a different political direction, such as focusing on economic inequality, healthcare and corporate influence. He suspects that’s why left-leaning candidates like Zohran Mamdani, Abdul El-Sayed and James Talarico won their elections, he said.

Candidates like Nixon ran on platforms like “Fight the oligarchy,” which rallied the support of young voters desperate for a change.

“They are fed up with data centers, fed up with billionaires that have infinite wealth, with the U.S. sending our tax dollars to Israel … murdering Palestinians and stealing their land, ICE raids, and the Iran war,” Kaluski said.

description:

Crow and Liccardo would need all current House Democrats and a handful of Republicans to sign on to their discharge petition to reach the necessary 218 signatures.

text:
A pair of House Democrats will try to bypass Republican leaders and force a vote to restore Temporary Protected Status to Afghan nationals in the United States by introducing a discharge petition when Congress returns Monday night.

Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., and Rep. Sam Liccardo, D-Calif., will file the petition, which would require signatures from 218 members to bring forth legislation to grant Afghans protection from deportation until mid-2029.

TPS, created by Congress in 1990, is a Department of Homeland Security program that allows migrants to live and work in the U.S. for up to 18 months if their home countries have been designated as unsafe. The time period can be extended.

President Donald Trump’s administration terminated the status for Afghanistan in May 2025, a designation that former President Joe Biden’s administration had granted in 2022.

“This administration is returning TPS to its original temporary intent,” then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said at the time. She added that “Afghanistan has had an improved security situation, and its stabilizing economy no longer prevent them from returning to their home country.”

While the Trump administration recently planned to deport dozens of Afghan immigrants and asylum-seekers to Pakistan, a federal judge last week temporarily blocked that move.

Crow and Liccardo would need all current House Democrats and a handful of Republicans to sign on to their discharge petition to reach the necessary 218 signatures. The pair already introduced a special rule on Oct. 1, allowing them to start collecting signatures as soon as they submit the petition on Monday.

“Our Afghan partners put their lives on the line to help protect American servicemembers like me,” Crow, who served as a paratrooper and an Army Ranger in Iraq and Afghanistan, said in a statement. “I’m working to force a vote that will protect Afghans already in the United States because I won’t let our nation leave these brave Afghans behind.”

If Crow and Liccardo are successful in reaching the 218-signature threshold, GOP leaders would be forced to bring forward the Afghanistan TPS Act for a floor vote. That bill, which the pair introduced in July, would grant TPS to Afghans until July 2029. The legislation would need a majority vote on the House floor to pass.

The bill already has four Republican co-sponsors: Reps. Don Bacon of Nebraska, Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, Joe Wilson of South Carolina, and Morgan Luttrell of Texas. It also has the backing of Rep. Kevin Kiley, a Republican-turned-independent from California.

“Thousands of Afghans risked their lives alongside American troops because our country made them a promise: We would not abandon them,” Liccardo said. “Now, we risk sending them back into the hands of the very Taliban forces they helped us fight. This cannot wait until the Democratic majority takes over.”

The bill has the backing of more than 50 organizations, including Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America, Veterans of Foreign Wars and Amnesty International USA.

Once rare, discharge petitions have been successful several times in the 119th Congress as a small number of Republicans have bucked party leadership to join Democrats in getting measures to the floor.

In April, the House voted to reinstate temporary protection for Haitian immigrants after a few Republicans joined with Democrats on that discharge petition. The legislation passed 224-204, with 10 Republicans joining all Democrats in support. While the White House had vowed that Trump would veto the bill, Senate Republicans blocked the legislation from going to his desk.

Other successful discharge petitions have included votes on aid to Ukraine, extending Affordable Care Act subsidies and the Epstein Files Transparency Act put forth by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif.

The House is scheduled to be in town this week and next before a Thanksgiving recess.

title: UK's ICE: Immigration raids without warrants reach record high - TBIJ

text:
Customers were sitting down for dinner at Sultanz, an Indian restaurant in a quiet town by the Cornish coast, one Friday last month when two unmarked vans pulled up outside and around 20 immigration officers emerged.

The town has seen barely any raids but Samsu Ali, the restaurant’s owner, says it felt like his business was being “invaded” that evening. He says: “As soon as they park … everyone runs to the kitchen, front door, back door, everywhere.”

The officers, from the Home Office’s ICE (immigration, compliance and enforcement) team, had no warrant and entered the premises without explaining the terms of access, says Samsu. Once they were in, they asked every worker for their details, to be checked against a government database. Everyone’s records checked out apart from one: 40-year-old Nanu Mia, who had been packing meals for collection.

Remembering the incident, Nanu says he asked, in broken English, for a translator. Instead, he was offered Google Translate. He gestured with his hands, offering to write down his name, but was ignored.

Suddenly, he was grabbed, cuffed and marched into a waiting van. Nanu suffers from asthma and when the panic set in, he struggled to breathe. He was in shock, unsure what was happening.

Samsu knew there had been a mistake: Nanu is allowed to work in the UK as a dependant of his wife, a care worker. So he called Nanu’s sister, who rushed to the restaurant with his ID card.

This time, when the officers ran his name through the system, his details came up. Nanu was released. But without Samsu’s last-minute intervention, things could have gone differently. In the weeks since, Nanu has developed a habit of looking out the window, worried the officers might return.

Raids like this are increasingly common in our high streets. The Home Office has said they are necessary to “restore order” to the immigration system. It posts videos showing migrants being detained, invites journalists on ride-alongs and boasts of arresting people in record numbers.

At the start of the year, home secretary Shabana Mahmood said the government had “surged enforcement activity to the highest level in British history” ensuring “illegal migrants … have nowhere to hide”.

However, we can reveal that the majority of people bearing the brunt of this crackdown have not breached any immigration laws – in fact, two-thirds of so-called “enforcement visits” resulted in no arrests last year. What’s more, they are increasingly being carried out without warrants, which are now used in just a quarter of raids compared to more than 40% a decade ago.

Experts say this points to the Home Office carrying out “fishing expeditions” based on weak intelligence and hearsay. The upshot is wasted resources, disrupted businesses and traumatised individuals.

“Thousands upon thousands of lives are impacted,” says Concepta Cassar, head of policy at Migrant Rights Network. She said she knows of businesses that have been targeted every few months even though nobody has been found to be doing anything wrong.

The government’s objective isn’t simply to detain people, says Cassar, but to show it has control over an “invented political problem” that scapegoats migrants for societal issues it has failed to address.

Mothin Ali, deputy leader of the Green party, said our findings were “alarming” and called for the government to “end these unjustified raids and protect people’s rights.”

“People are being humiliated and whole communities terrorised …This is racist harassment dressed up as immigration enforcement,” he says.

“The falling use of warrants is deeply concerning and raises serious questions about the legality of these operations. Businesses may be intimidated into letting officers in without realising they can refuse. Britain must not import Trump’s ICE playbook.”

60 raids every day

Between 2023 and 2025 the number of immigration “enforcement visits” rose by about 40%, to more than 23,500. That’s in excess of 60 per day. The figures include raids on workplaces and homes, as well spot checks in public places: streets, train stations, ports.

Of the 23,500 carried out last year, more than 15,500 (66%) resulted in no arrests.

The Home Office did not respond to our requests for comment.

While immigration raids are expected to continue to increase, operations by the UK’s ICE teams have received much less scrutiny than their US counterparts.

To better understand how these operations are conducted and the impact they have on communities, we spoke to workers and businesses, filed freedom of information requests to the Home Office, and presented our findings to experts including a former immigration officer.

Kevin Barker left the Home Office in 2015 after telling senior staff that the department’s officers were often entering people’s premises illegally. He now helps businesses overturn fines for allegedly employing people who do not have the right to work in the UK. He doesn’t condone people breaching this immigration law but he says the fines are often issued unfairly.

Officers don’t have formal targets, he explains, but they are encouraged to clock up as many raids as possible and the evidence to justify them doesn’t need to be strong. As a result, many are based on tenuous tip-offs – a fact Barker says is reflected in the declining use of warrants.

“You’re not allowed to apply for a search warrant if the intelligence you’ve got is old or an anonymous allegation that can’t be corroborated … but it doesn't stop them from doing the visit,” he said.

By the government’s own admission, this is a bad use of resources. A 2016 report from the independent chief inspector of borders and immigration (ICIBI) highlighted that about two-thirds of allegations in the Home Office’s management system had come from members of the public. It cited an earlier review stating that this was “not the most efficient way for [immigration enforcement] to direct its activity”.

It’s not hard to see why. As Barker explains, anyone can send an anonymous tip-off – a disgruntled worker or a business competitor. Or just a member of the public who assumes a worker is illegal because of their poor English: “They think they’re doing the right thing, but actually they’re being a bit prejudicial.”

Recent data we obtained, though, suggests this has only worsened. Last year, 89% of leads on “immigration crime” came from the public or from the Crimestoppers, a charity that collects anonymous tip-offs. Around 2% came from the police.

The consequences for businesses can be devastating, as Sultanz’s owners have discovered.

The restaurant was lauded in the local press during the pandemic for giving free food to hospitals and homeless shelters. But since the raid last month, it has seen a stark drop-off in customers, Samsu said.

In a local Facebook group, a question about the incident at the restaurant prompted a number of racist and threatening comments. One person wrote: “People with somewhat darker skin are literally taking over our community and causing a lot of unrest.”

“Fucking migrants and illegals...All over Camborne and Redruth,” posted another person.

Someone even wrote: “Attack before we’re attacked” followed by “make them unwelcome”.

Nobody clarified that all of Sultanz’s staff had the legal right to work in the UK.

The comments left Samsu struggling to sleep for days. “They don’t understand how much money I spent on this business,” he says. “How much time I have spent in the last six years. How much hard work I did.”

‘An element of coercion’

If officers don’t have enough to secure a warrant, they can rely on other powers to enter the premises. If it’s a licensed shop or restaurant, they can use licensing powers. Or, in most cases – more than 12,000 last year – they can ask for the consent of the tenant, manager or owner.

When using this power, officers are meant to inform the person of their rights, including the fact that they are free to revoke their consent at any time. But this doesn’t always happen. It didn’t at Sultanz. And as recently as 2024, government inspectors criticised immigration officers for entering premises without consent.

“There’s an element of coercion here,” says Cassar of the Migrant Rights Network. She says people allow officers to enter their homes or businesses because they do not fully know their rights, that they can ask further questions or that they can question the power under which these raids are being done. In other cases, they might worry that their business could face even greater disruption if they resist.

“So they’re left in that situation of powerlessness and of fear. And who protects you? Where do you report to? Because these people are the law.”

In one instance after a business refused to consent to a search, officers found another way to get in. On 5 August this year officers arrived with no warrant to South Motorcycles, a garage in London. Staff refused to let them in, but officers went away, made a phone call and came back with an “assistant director” letter that granted them the power to enter.

These letters are meant to be reserved for urgent cases where officers do not have time to apply for a warrant. They need to have a strong reason to believe that a specific person who is in breach of certain immigration laws is inside.

But paperwork we’ve seen suggests the South Motorcycles operation was another fishing expedition. A section of a form handed to the business, which was then crossed out, said they were looking for “no named offenders”.

Officers did detain two customers who were at the garage and then released them on bail, but did not find anyone working there in breach of immigration law.

Barker told us that, in the case of South Motorcycles, officers had likely entered unlawfully.

There is a long history of officers misusing this power. In 2014, the ICIBI found officers had used these letters unlawfully to bypass the need for a warrant. Their use was justified in less than a third of cases examined.

“You’re used to walking into premises and saying… ‘Let us in’. And then all of a sudden somebody challenges you,” Barker said. “Then you're like, ‘Right, I'll show you. Let me get my [assistant director] on the phone.’”

‘ICE is here’

While most people might not know what their rights are when ICE officers turn up at their door, anti-raids groups in many cities across the UK are trying to change that, said Griff Ferris, a spokesperson for the Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants.

These groups will often hold workshops or provide information to residents about their rights. They can also go further by filming raids, questioning officers or trying to stop arrests.

“Every day people are resisting raids in their communities,” Ferris said.

In recent years residents in London and Glasgow have stopped immigration raids by blocking vans in which people had been detained for several hours. On one occasion protesters blocked a coach that was intended to carry asylum seekers to the controversial Bibby Stockholm barge, where conditions were so poor one resident died by suicide.

Several councils have said they will refuse to hand over data to the Home Office if it will be used for immigration enforcement, and pledged to support residents or businesses affected by raids.

Meanwhile, both the Conservatives and Reform have floated policies that they say will increase the number of arrests and deportations.

Reform’s include paying people who make anonymous tips-offs that result in companies getting fined. The Conservatives want to adopt some of the methods used by ICE in the US, where agents have been accused of warrantless arrests, kidnapping and unlawful killings.

In a debate earlier this year, the Liberal Democrat home affairs spokesperson Max Wilkinson asked Labour’s Mahmood to condemn ICE and to rule out “ICE squads in the streets of Britain”.

Mahmood dodged the question, saying the UK government had managed to deport record numbers of people without arming officers, as is the case in the US.

But Cassar said there are already stark parallels: much like its counterpart, the UK’s ICE targets minority and migrant communities with little accountability.

“They’re not a militarised force yet but we have the same need for community defence and the need to look out for each other,” she said .“People don’t realise that we have ICE. They’re like ‘ICE is coming to the UK’. No, it’s here.”

If you have faced or witnessed an immigration enforcement operation you think was handled unfairly or unlawfully, please get in touch with our reporter emilianomellino@tbij.com

text:
Shabana Mahmood’s ICE-style raid agency has been accused of engaging in “fishing expeditions” after figures disclosed that almost two-thirds of enforcement visits result in no arrests and nearly three-quarters are conducted without a warrant.

The home secretary has hailed the expanded use of immigration enforcement teams, and claimed they will help to secure the UK’s borders by removing a key incentive for irregular migration.

Under her leadership, raids have targeted establishments associated with informal “black market” work such as nail bars, car washes, barbers, takeaways, construction sites and warehouses, as well as people’s homes.

They have been accompanied by videos posted on TikTok showing arrests of people working without authorisation being tackled to the ground by enforcement officers and locked in the back of vans.

Freedom of information requests, however, show that:

There were 23,538 immigration enforcement engagements such as workplace raids, home raids and spot checks in 2025 – or 60 a day. Of these, 15,578, or 66.1%, resulted in no arrests.

Only 25.81% of visits where a premises was accessed used a warrant. Critics say this suggests the Home Office is launching “fishing expeditions” based on weak intelligence.

Nearly nine out of 10 (89%) of leads alleging “immigration crime” in 2025 came from the public or from Crimestoppers, a charity that collects anonymous tip-offs. Around 2% came from the police.

The Home Office vigorously disputed claims that the agency launches “fishing expeditions”, claiming that intelligence is thoroughly examined before launching an immigration raid.

The findings have emerged after inquiries by the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the Guardian amid growing concerns about the effect on innocent workers and businesses.

Officers from immigration enforcement swooped from unmarked vans last month on Sultanz, an Indian restaurant in Camborne, Cornwall, as customers sat down to eat.

The restaurant’s owner, Samsu Ali, said it felt as if his six-year-old business was being invaded. “As soon as they parked … everyone runs to the kitchen, front door, back door, everywhere,” he said.

The officers had no warrant, he said. Once in, they asked every worker for their details.

Nanu Mia, a Bangladeshi employee who had been packing meals for collection, gave his details to the officers, but they struggled to understand him.

Mia was handcuffed, arrested and marched to a van. He was de-arrested and released after his sister rushed to the restaurant with his ID card, which helped to prove that he was allowed to work.

The restaurant’s customer numbers have fallen steeply since the raid despite being cleared of any immigration breaches, Ali said.

In a local Facebook group, a question about the incident resulted in racist and threatening comments. One person wrote: “People with somewhat darker skin are literally taking over our community and causing a lot of unrest.”

The comments left Ali struggling to sleep. “They don’t understand how much money and time I have spent in the last six years,” he said.

If immigration enforcement officers do not have a warrant, they can rely on other powers to enter the premises.

They can enter licensed premises – a restaurant, pub, hotel, cafe or any business that sells alcohol or provides late-night hot food – without a warrant under section 179 of the Licensing Act 2003. Or, in most cases – more than 12,000 last year – they can ask for the consent of the tenant, manager or owner.

When using this power, officers are meant to inform the person of their rights, including the fact that they are free to revoke their consent at any time.

Once inside, officers have the power to question individuals about their immigration status. They can ask to see identity documents. They are not supposed to detain someone without reasonable suspicion that the person is an immigration offender.

Kevin Barker, a former immigration officer who now works with businesses wrongly accused of employing people who do not have the right to work in the UK, said raids are often “fishing expeditions” based on tenuous tipoffs.

“You’re not allowed to apply for a search warrant if the intelligence you’ve got is old or an anonymous allegation that can’t be corroborated … but it doesn’t stop them,” he said.

Mothin Ali, the deputy leader of the Green party, said the findings were alarming and called on the government to “end these unjustified raids and protect people’s rights”.

“This is racist harassment dressed up as immigration enforcement,” he said.

“The falling use of warrants is deeply concerning and raises serious questions about the legality of these operations. Britain must not import Trump’s ICE playbook.”

Arrests of people from abroad working illegally in the UK have doubled since Labour has been in government. The Home Office said in August that more than 17,000 had been made since July 2024, a 122% increase on the previous two years, with a record number of immigration raids and arrests in 2026.

Opposition parties have claimed that opportunities to work illegally in the UK act as a pull factor for migrants, encouraging people to cross the Channel in small boats.

text:
A federal judge in Colorado interrogated the leader of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Denver office on Monday about his directive to immediately re-arrest people who were freed on judges’ orders from immigration detention.

U.S. District Court Judge Charlotte Sweeney said she has received filings across multiple cases from people who said that “everyone is terrified” in the privately run Aurora detention center that their releases from custody will be illusory.

Recommended Stories

▶

“It has instilled a new level of fear in that facility that I find completely inappropriate and needs to be addressed,” she said.

Sweeney, a Joe Biden appointee, scheduled the Nov. 9 hearing last week after she first summoned the U.S. Attorney’s Office and an ICE representative to her courtroom to address the immediate re-arrest of a man she had ordered released.

After that initial hearing, an unnamed government spokesperson suggested to news outlets that prohibiting immediate rearrests amounted to “sabotage.” The U.S. Attorney’s Office quickly distanced itself from that characterization.

“My office did not know this statement was going to be submitted. We were not provided with the statement that was going to be submitted,” Kevin Traskos, the chief of the civil division, told Sweeney.

For more than a year, Colorado’s federal trial court has faced a flood of “habeas corpus” petitions from those in immigration detention, pushing court filings to unprecedented levels. Over several months, petitioners have challenged their denial of bond, the constitutional adequacy of bond hearings, conditions ICE has unilaterally imposed on their release, and other practices.

In the case directly before Sweeney, Ramon Quintero Alvarez of Wyoming filed a habeas petition seeking release from Aurora. The U.S. Attorney’s Office did not file a response challenging his petition, triggering his automatic release.

However, Sweeney heard testimony last week that ICE agents transported Alvarez and other detainees to the Centennial office, then back to the Aurora facility, and re-arrested them.

“I received a direct order,” testified assistant field office director Nichole Black, “to re-detain habeas releases that had some kind of criminality.”

She said the order came from deputy director George Valdez, who in turn received the directive from acting director Nathan Rasper. Black later testified she was “told that charges were not filed” against Alvarez.

“Frankly, I am unclear how anyone can argue with a straight face that what you believed was appropriate and could lawfully occur,” Sweeney responded. “Releasing somebody momentarily is not releasing somebody at all.”

She then ordered Rasper into her courtroom to learn more about the directive he gave. She also asked for a list of everyone who was released pursuant to habeas orders and re-arrested. Although the government submitted its list, the ACLU of Colorado intervened, saying it was incomplete and concerned there were even more instances of re-arrests.

Rasper, a 20-year ICE employee who has served as acting director since mid-October, said he came to Denver and heard that “there were a lot of arrests being found unlawful, and those arrested were being released.”

“Is it your understanding that ICE has an obligation to make lawful arrests?” asked Traskos in a packed courtroom where U.S. Attorney Peter McNeilly was also present.

Yes, said Rasper. He added that he heard from “colleagues” in Minnesota that “the courts had allowed the immediate rearrest of an alien released.”

He said he spoke with ICE’s principal legal advisors and his deputy director and ultimately gave a verbal instruction to re-arrest people released on judges’ orders. Rasper believed ICE had the legal authority to do so after fixing “paperwork errors” with arrest forms. He did not personally review Alvarez’s case before the re-arrest.

Rasper confirmed he had since stopped the re-arrests based on Sweeney’s hearing last week.

While questioning Rasper, Sweeney referred to an Oct. 8 memorandum of agreement between the federal trial court and the U.S. Attorney’s Office that provides a standardized method for handling habeas cases. Part of the agreement provides for the automatic release of petitioners if the government opts not to file a defense of their continued detention.

“Were you aware of that agreement when you started the practice?” she asked.

No, responded Rasper. He confirmed his employees would no longer immediately re-arrest someone who was released on a judge’s order. Rasper also said Black’s testimony to Sweeney was an “overly compressed” version of his original instruction.

Since Sweeney’s original hearing, other federal judges in Colorado have responded quickly to the release-and-re-arrest practice.

On Nov. 5, in response to a petitioner’s warning about Rasper’s directive, U.S. District Court Judge Gordon P. Gallagher amended his release order to clarify that ICE could re-arrest the man only on a final order of removal. The next day, U.S. District Court Judge Philip A. Brimmer told ICE it “may not re-detain petitioner without advance notice to this Court” that cites ICE’s legal authority to detain the man.

“The notion that ICE could self-review to find technical violations is not something the court will tolerate. What happened to Mr. Alvarez is not a technical violation. It’s a due process violation,” Sweeney said. “I think the only bright spot in all this is that the process was brought to our attention fairly quickly and looks to have been in place for about a week and was then stopped.”

She noted that she had invited Alvarez to attend the hearing, but he was not present.

“Who can blame him?” she said, adding that Alvarez likely “has no faith that he will not be picked up again, even despite two court orders trying to guarantee that for him.”

Sweeney will issue a written order deciding whether she will initiate contempt proceedings.

Daniel Suitor, an attorney in Minnesota who has litigated around 70 habeas cases, said there is not a “blanket” allowance there for re-arrests, but recent decisions have largely decried the release-and-re-arrest practice, with one judge writing that a habeas petitioner was “never released from custody” when ICE re-arrested him one minute after release.

“These re-arrest decisions did not start coming down until September,” Suitor said. “The District of Minnesota has a has a lot of infra-district splits about lots of different issues. But when it comes to re-arrest, there are two judges who have said ‘no way.’”

title: Trump Admits His Signature Immigration Policy Was 'Too Tough' After Midterm Catastrophe
description:
Donald Trump is on a collision course with Stephen Miller after admitting his new top aide's hardline immigration policy was "too tough."
He admitted that the immigration policy, which was designed and overseen by Miller, had targeted people with established jobs whose only offense was entering the country illegally.
Asked whether his deportation agenda had gone too far, Trump conceded that removing such law-abiding workers from the country had been unpopular.
Trump's comments sparked anger among MAGA supporters who interpreted his suggestion of an immigration compromise as a potential amnesty.
The political damage became clear on Election Day, with 58 percent of voters surveyed believing Trump's immigration enforcement had gone too far, according to CBS News.
text:
Donald Trump is on a collision course with Stephen Miller after admitting his new top aide's hardline immigration policy was "too tough."

The president made the extraordinary concession that he'd like to soften his position on mass deportation, which he admitted had hurt him at the ballot box, in a CBS 60 Minutes interview. His sit-down with CBS's Ross Douthat was recorded on Friday, three days after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress in a devastating midterm defeat.

However, Trump's remarks aired Sunday, the day after he appointed Miller, 41, the architect of the deportation campaign, to take over on Monday as his White House chief of staff—raising accusations that the two positions were incompatible.

Prompted by a question from Douthat about what one thing he wanted to work on with the incoming Democratic majority, Trump appeared to shock the CBS correspondent when he replied: "I'd love to do something on immigration."

He admitted that the immigration policy, which was designed and overseen by Miller, had targeted people with established jobs whose only offense was entering the country illegally. He pointed to landscaping businesses and hotel workers, as well as immigrants who paid taxes.

Asked whether his deportation agenda had gone too far, Trump conceded that removing such law-abiding workers from the country had been unpopular. "I think it might be too tough, yeah," he said, adding, "I think ultimately—that hurt me."

In the interview, which has horrified Trump's MAGA base over fears of an amnesty, the president suggested that undocumented immigrants who had spent years working and paying taxes should potentially be allowed to remain in the country.

He suggested an agreement could be struck for such people who had lived in the country for 10 or 15 years, potentially allowing them to remain while continuing to deport serious criminals.

Saying he wanted to negotiate with Democrats, who will take control of Congress in January, Trump claimed they had "already called me" about a potential immigration compromise. He added that he was confident he could reach an agreement with the party that had just delivered him a humiliating electoral defeat, but provided no further detail on what that might look like.

Trump accepted that even by suggesting a softening of immigration policy, he was opening up a bitter ideological divide within his own administration, describing a faction on the "pretty far right" that wanted everybody deported, regardless of circumstance. "Do any of those people work in your administration?" Douthat asked. "Yes," Trump replied.

He did not name Miller, but his replacement for Susie Wiles as chief of staff has been the administration's most prominent advocate of mass deportations and aggressive immigration enforcement.

Trump's comments sparked anger among MAGA supporters who interpreted his suggestion of an immigration compromise as a potential amnesty.

Right-wing commentator Nick Sortor wrote: "NO AMNESTY. Not now, not EVER. EVERY SINGLE ONE must GO." MAGA former West Virginia lawmaker Derrick Evans joined the backlash, posting, "He might as well have said the word amnesty. I have no words for this."

Their fury pushed the White House's official Rapid Response account into a damage-limitation exercise, in which it insisted "the word 'amnesty' was never even said in this entire exchange."

Trump's admission is a remarkable reversal for a president whose second term has been dominated by a brutal immigration crackdown that has brought death, bloodshed and widespread public anger to American streets.

Federal agents swept through American cities, arresting thousands of immigrants, including those with no convictions, while splitting up families and provoking furious demonstrations.

Miller has been instrumental in directing that campaign, including pushing ICE to pursue 3,000 arrests a day, joining daily calls about deportation numbers, and berating staff for not deporting enough people.

But the visible street enforcement reached boiling point in Minneapolis in January, when federal immigration officers shot dead two American citizens.

Renee Good, a 37-year-old mother, was killed by ICE agent Jonathan Ross on Jan. 7, and three weeks later Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old VA ICU nurse, was fatally shot by Border Patrol officers during another protest.

The killings led to protests and a backlash inside the agencies responsible for the crackdown, with some agents privately expressing anger over Pretti's killing and wanting the operation abandoned.

Miller personally inflamed the controversy after Pretti's killing, describing the nurse as a "domestic terrorist" and "would-be assassin" on social media, despite Reuters-verified footage showing Pretti holding a cellphone rather than a gun immediately before federal agents tackled him. Miller subsequently acknowledged that the agents might not have followed official procedures.

The human misery has extended into American prisons, with Human Rights Watch documenting 52 deaths in ICE detention during the first 500 days of Trump's second presidency, a horrifying statistic that the Daily Beast has chronicled.

The political damage became clear on Election Day, with 58 percent of voters surveyed believing Trump's immigration enforcement had gone too far, according to CBS News. Republicans also suffered significant losses in heavily Latino areas that had supported Trump in 2024.

Despite this, former Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem was mocked last Wednesday after claiming the first year had been "too successful."

There is also little indication that the administration is preparing to change course. Officials inside ICE and DHS have received no orders to reduce enforcement following the midterms, according to CBS News. The network reported that ICE had been instructed before the election to target approximately 19,000 arrests a week.

DHS said Sunday that its agents would not be "backing away or slowing down," while White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis insisted the administration remained committed to deporting immigrants it considered threats to public safety.

Trump's apparent change of heart has drawn immediate criticism from Democrats, who said it was not compatible with Miller's elevation. "That's not a course correction. That's a promotion," Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer wrote on X, condemning Trump's decision to put Miller in charge despite his admission.

The Daily Beast has contacted the White House and DHS for comment.

title: Texas' Flip to Blue Is Major Blow to Red States' Legal Fights - Bloomberg Law
authors: Jacqueline Thomsen, Alex Ebert, Jordan Fischer
description:
The Texas attorney general’s office — known for taking innovative stances in litigation, leading multistate actions, and incubating conservative talent — will be getting a Democratic makeover.
At the US Supreme Court, Texas led the red states’ amicus filing in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Org.
But that too comes with downsides: State litigation is funded publicly, while private groups would have to fundraise.
The Texas Attorney General’s office alone employs more than 4,000 people.

text:
The midterms punched a Texas-sized hole in the GOP attorneys general coalition, creating leadership questions for red states and handing Democrats new players to challenge the Trump administration.

The Texas attorney general’s office — known for taking innovative stances in litigation, leading multistate actions, and incubating conservative talent — will be getting a Democratic makeover.

Add Ohio, Georgia, Iowa and Kansas to the mix, and the blue wave is placing thousands of government lawyers under Democratic control.

“The red-state coalition has effectively been beheaded,” Michelle Kallen, a former Virginia solicitor general, said of Texas’ loss.

At the US Supreme Court, Texas led the red states’ amicus filing in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Org. opposing the constitutional right to abortion. And the Lone Star State’s top attorney has been one of the biggest thorns in the side of Meta and other tech giants.

“This completely shakes up the traditional multistate dynamics, and the state that has served a leading role, if not the leading role, is now going to be part of a different coalition,” added Kallen, a partner with Steptoe.

The upheaval has major implications for where high-impact litigation gets filed, which red states emerge as leaders, what matters reach the Supreme Court, and how much pressure corporate America feels to make deals before power shifts in January.

“If you see an AG that’s coming in and focusing on something that you have pending, you might want to resolve that ahead of time,” Foley & Lardner partner Siran S. Faulders said in a post-election training call for lawyers representing businesses facing state regulation.

Texas Turnaround

The blue wave in Texas will upend outgoing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton’s playbook for scoring victories defending Texas laws or dealing blows to Democratic presidents by bringing suit in the state’s federal courts.

Paxton could rely on the state’s federal courts stacked with President Donald Trump‘s judicial appointees, and appeals bound for the Fifth Circuit controlled by a Republican-appointed super majority.

That roadmap is expected to be tossed out by Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson (D).

Johnson may try to file more actions in state courts, as Democrats were largely successful in the state’s judicial elections, said Judd Stone, a former Texas solicitor general.

“You would have a much more favorable audience and a much more favorable record going up through the state courts than through the federal courts,” said Stone, a partner with Stone Hilton.

The new Democratic attorney general could pursue cases against the Trump administration in federal court that had never been brought by the state before, as the Texas attorney general and Trump are typically aligned, said Paul Singer, who worked in the Texas attorney general’s office for over two decades.

“So it is going to certainly create a whole new level of scrutiny and question about some of these actions from the court,” Singer, now an attorney with Kelley Drye & Warren, said of the Fifth Circuit.

No Republican attorney general will serve in a southern border state starting next year.

That tees up Johnson and his Democratic colleagues to take a leading role in combating the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. Still, as long as they’re in federal court, they’ll run into conservative judges on the Fifth Circuit, and potentially the US Supreme Court.

“The most important thing about the election results is they don’t change anything about the federal judiciary,” Stone said.

Private Challengers

Stone said he’d expect some outside conservative groups would “privatize some of the functions” that a Republican-controlled state would typically take on.

But that too comes with downsides: State litigation is funded publicly, while private groups would have to fundraise. And states have doctrines that make it easier to prove they’re injured by the action they’re going to court over, whereas private parties face a higher burden in establishing standing.

Private groups are going to keep picking favorable turf for their litigation, and the federal judiciary may see few changes over the next two years due to Democrats taking control of the Senate.

“Our public policy strategy regarding legislation will be affected and will require some adjustments. But the litigation strategy is not affected by this election,” said Mat Staver, founder and chairman of Liberty Counsel, a group that brings religious liberty cases.

States’ litigation strategy is another matter, said Jesse Panuccio, a partner at Boies Schiller Flexner and former acting associate attorney general in the first Trump administration.

“Texas was at the forefront of litigation you’d consider conservative. With that office and its significant resources gone, I think Florida will naturally emerge in that space, along with others like West Virginia, Alabama and Tennessee,” he said.

Supreme Court

The shift could also resonate at the US Supreme Court, where Texas and Iowa have taken leading roles in pushing red-state interests.

The Texas Attorney General’s office alone employs more than 4,000 people. Its 750 plus attorneys include 17 dedicated full-time to the solicitor general’s office.

“One of the things that Texas brings to the table in more complex areas like antitrust or DEI stuff is the sheer number of hours” they can muster, according to former Indiana solicitor general Thomas M. Fisher, now litigation director at the nonprofit EdChoice.

It will be difficult for any individual state to fill Texas’ manpower gap, Fisher said.

“Attorney general budgets don’t expand just because you want them to,” he said.

It was Texas that helmed Republican states’ amicus brief in the case that overturned Roe v. Wade, a generational fight for conservatives. And Iowa, alongside Tennessee, led the red states siding with the Trump administration over birthright citizenship.

Talent Pipelines

The Texas solicitor general’s office has also served as a key conservative legal talent pipeline. Former heads include Judge James Ho, who now sits on the Fifth Circuit, and Jonathan F. Mitchell, who argued successfully at the Supreme Court in 2024 against Colorado’s attempts to disqualify Trump from the ballot.

West Virginia, which is already an active player in energy litigation, is ready to step up and may seek to entice conservative attorneys who may soon be leaving other offices, Solicitor General Michael R. Williams said. He expects other Republican states to do the same.

Williams said the losses create opportunities for states like Montana or Kentucky in major Second Amendment, religious liberty, or immigration litigation. But Texas’ expansive portfolio alone may take several other states to cover.

Florida Focus

As the third-most populous — and largest GOP-controlled — state, Florida could become the leader of Republican coalitions, practitioners told Bloomberg Law.

Without Texas, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier emerges as an even more powerful player, said Ashley Taylor, Troutman Pepper Locke partner and co-leader of its state attorneys general practice.

“When there’s a political blowout, you are part of the team that got blown out, and you survive — that creates opportunities,” Taylor said. “He was well-positioned before this — now he’s one I’d expect to be very prominent.”

Uthmeier has been the second-most active Republican top cop, after Texas, in pursuing Big Tech. He’s also taken on culture war issues like abortion and parental rights, and leveraged state antidiscrimination and antitrust law to drag huge corporations — from Starbucks to pharmacy benefit managers — into state court.

The 450-attorney office has often relied on private firms for reinforcements in big cases.

It’s also the lone holdout seeking a big payday against Meta after 48 states signed an $18 billion settlement, and New Mexico won billions taking its social media cases to verdict.

“This office has been leading these fights since the day I took office, and we’re going to keep leading them,” Uthmeier said in a statement.

text:
Stephen Miller, the architect of Donald Trump’s mass deportation policy and hardline crackdown on immigration, took up his new role as White House chief of staff on Monday.

Miller, 41, began his new role serving as Trump’s right-hand man after Republicans suffered massive losses nationwide in the midterm elections. He was previously serving as a deputy chief of staff.

On Friday, Trump announced on Truth Social that Miller – his most controversial aide – would replace Susie Wiles, his former chief of staff.

The announcement came as a surprise, because members of the Trump administration had denied reports that Wiles was on her way out. In recent weeks, several top women in the administration have stepped down, including Harmeet Dhillon, a top justice department official, and Katie Zacharia, who spent just five days as press secretary after replacing Karoline Leavitt.

Miller’s promotion came just days after voters rebuked the US president’s agenda just two years into his administration in the midterm elections.

Democrats accused Trump of not listening to voters by elevating Miller to a top role – especially because Trump’s harsh anti-immigration crackdowns rocked the nation over the last year.

Trump said himself that his mass deportation policy was “too tough” in an interview with CBS’s 60 Minutes which aired over the weekend.

“I think it was too tough,” Trump said. “I think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough.”

Despite that, Trump chose after the interview to elevate the man behind one of his most controversial policies to a larger role in the White House.

More administration staffing changes could be coming soon, in the wake of the midterm results and Miller’s appointment. Richard Walters, a White House deputy chief of staff who was one of Wiles’s closest allies, announced he would also be leaving the administration.

text:
In the days leading up to the midterm elections, hundreds of people left their "I voted" stickers on a memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Houston man killed by federal immigration agents earlier this year.

"The fact that people were thinking of my dad and thinking of other immigrants — that just means the world to me," said Ronaldo Salgado, Salgado Araujo's son, told NPR.

Those votes resulted in a seismic political shift in Texas: for the first time, a Latina, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, will be governor. Texans also elected the state's first Democratic U.S. senator in nearly 40 years, and the Texas House of Representatives flipped.

"Unfortunately, Texas has become like the epicenter of ICE enforcement and like gross violence against immigrants," Ronaldo Salgado said. "Well, the voters have spoken — incoming lawmakers now have a duty to listen to us."

The political fallout

Immigration policy was one of the top issues on voters' minds this election, according to exit polling. Artemio Muñiz of the Texas Federation of Hispanic Republicans, told NPR "with these anti-immigrant-type policies, I think the Hispanic community got fed up."

That seems more true than ever in the counties along the U.S.-Mexico border, which flipped Democratic after supporting Trump in 2024.

"I think the message is clear from the Texas Hispanic community that the only acceptable or effective Hispanic outreach from the Republican Party in Texas is one that includes a reasonable solution for immigration," Muñiz said, suggesting the solution should include secured borders and a legal pathway for undocumented immigrants who have been in the U.S. for decades.

In Texas, Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa is facing calls to end the state's partnership with ICE.

"That's something that can happen on day one," said César Espinosa, the executive director of the Houston-based advocacy organization FIEL. He said his group would also like to see Hinojosa and the Texas legislature to push for driver licenses for undocumented immigrants. Already, Houston's mayor is reducing his police department's cooperation with ICE.

Nationwide, immigration advocates say they want to see ICE defunded, or severely restricted.

"We demand that the incoming Congress hold ICE accountable", says Murad Awawdeh of the New York Immigrant Coalition.

What could the new Congress actually do?

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to become the next chair of the House oversight committee, had two words of advice for Republicans on Election Day: "Lawyer up."

Garcia has promised to look into several issues, including ICE accountability.

ICE is the highest funded federal law enforcement agency in the U.S. Congress essentially gave immigration enforcement a blank check in 2025 and in 2026 they awarded ICE and Customs and Border Patrol around $240 billion.

It's enough funds to run the mass deportation operation for the remainder of Trump's term.

Congress could claw back that money. And lawmakers are already eyeing more stringent oversight.

"We have to rein ICE in because its illegal, out-of-control activities (have) killed individuals … assaulted individuals … have incarcerated individuals," said Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., who is likely to chair the House Homeland Security Committee. "That system has to have accountability for the men and women who work in it."

He said he'd like to legally require policies, like requiring the use of body-worn cameras for federal immigration agents and banning them from wearing face coverings.

The major hurdle is President Trump: following the midterm election results the President said he would welcome the nickname "Mr. Veto."

Another possible indication of how the administration will be seeing immigration enforcement moving forward came Friday, a few days after the midterm elections. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller was promoted to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Miller's central project in government has been immigration control and mass deportations. Miller is considered the architect of the first Trump administration's child separation policy, and as NPR reported, was deeply involved in the project of turning large warehouses into immigration detention centers.

Naureen Shah at the ACLU says she thinks one of the most powerful things that could happen to change ICE behavior is Congressional oversight via subpoenas.

"ICE has to be afraid," she said. "They have to be afraid of losing their funding, they have to be afraid of being subpoenaed and asked extremely hard questions before a live audience of the American people."

The Trump Administration vows that "Deportations will continue".

The day after the Midterm elections, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin posted a three-word tweet : "Deportations will continue."

Vice President JD Vance took to X to share his thoughts on the Republican Party's big loss. He said he believes it is due to voter's concerns over the economy, inflation and the war with Iran. He left immigration enforcement off that list.

He did, however, say he is open to changing enforcement tactics by focusing more on businesses that hire undocumented workers. But he said immigration amnesty is not the solution.

Shah of the ACLU says she believes ICE enforcement and the current state of the economy are inextricably linked. "What's really clear is that the stories of life becoming harder for everyday Americans are actually also stories about ICE's impact. People are afraid to take their kids to school, afraid to go to work. It impacts our schools, our teachers. It impacts the labor force when people aren't showing up for their jobs. So Democrats have an opportunity through their oversight device to tell a story about how to make everyday life more affordable for all Americans."

Could we see more oversight on ICE detention facilities?

The Trump administration has spent billions of dollars to expand ICE detention facilities — many of which have faced criticism and protest over dire conditions. There have been a record number of deaths in detention since the start of Trump's second term.

The day after mid-term election results the two major private detention center companies that contract for ICE, CoreCivic and the GEO Group , had their quarterly investor calls.

The main question asked by investors at the CoreCivic call was: how will the result of the midterms affect ICE operations?

CoreCivic President Lucibeth Mayberry optimistically, pointing out that "[ICE] have again began increasing enforcement activity. They have the secure funding to do so." But then she offered a word of advice to ICE about purchasing new detention centers: "we would urge the ICE administration to move quickly."
